itineraries.title: Aude Road Trip: Carcassonne, Cathar Country & the Mediterranean
itineraries.subtitle: 7 days among medieval fortresses, charming villages and wild coastline. From Carcassonne to the beaches of Leucate, via the mysteries of Rennes-le-Château.
itineraries.notes: Loop circuit starting from Carcassonne (TGV station and airport). Plan to visit the Lastours castles early in the morning to avoid summer heat. Rennes-le-Château is a detour from Quillan — narrow road for the last few kilometers.
itineraries.climate: Best time: April-June and September-October, temperatures 15-25°C. Avoid July-August (intense heat up to 35-40°C, strong tramontane winds on the coast). Mild winters in lowlands but cold in Montagne Noire.
specialties: Blanquette de Limoux 1531 world's first sparkling wine

visits.text: Enter through the Porte Narbonnaise — built in the late 13th century under Philippe III le Hardi — and let the 3 km of ramparts wrap around you. The Cité of Carcassonne, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997, boasts 52 towers and a double ring of fortifications whose Gallo-Roman foundations are still visible on the inner face. It draws between 4 and 5 million visitors annually and remains home to about fifty permanent residents. Start by wandering through the lices, the space between the two walls: this is where you'll instantly grasp the defensive logic of the place, impossible to breach without taking fire from both sides at once.

The Château Comtal is the fortress within the fortress. Built in the 12th century by the Trencavel viscounts — those lords who patronized troubadours and sheltered Cathars — it became in 1209 the prison of Raymond-Roger Trencavel, defeated by Simon de Montfort after a fifteen-day siege. Dead in his own dungeons a few months later, Trencavel remains the tragic figure of the Albigensian Crusade. The rampart walk (1.3 km, 35 towers) from the castle offers the finest view of the Pyrenees and the Montagne Noire. Book your ticket online: queues can be long in July-August.

Before leaving the Cité, step inside the Basilica of Saint-Nazaire — free admission. Begun in 1096 at the initiative of the Trencavels, it blends a sober Romanesque nave with a 14th-century Gothic choir whose flying buttresses soar skyward. Its 13th-century stained glass windows rank among the oldest and best-preserved in southern France. Try to visit late in the day: the light filtering through the stained glass creates an atmosphere you won't find anywhere else in the region.

activities.text: Walk around the lices in late afternoon, when the low light gilds the stonework and the tour buses have left. It's also the perfect time for dinner inside the Cité itself — cassoulet on the menu, of course, the emblematic dish of the Aude.

visits.text: Cross the Pont Vieux — built between 1315 and 1320, twelve semicircular arches spanning the Aude — and descend into the Bastide Saint-Louis. Founded in 1260 by Saint Louis to resettle inhabitants expelled from the Cité after their 1240 rebellion, it preserves its medieval grid layout. Place Carnot, the heart of the lower town, is paved with red marble from Caunes-Minervois (quarried some twenty kilometers away) and animated by its Saturday morning market. Its fountain depicting Neptune was installed in 1771. If you're there on a Saturday, don't miss the bustling market stalls.

The Canal du Midi has skirted the Bastide since 1810 — it took over a century after the canal's 1681 inauguration for Carcassonne to finally be connected to the waterway. Designed by Pierre-Paul Riquet under Louis XIV to link the Atlantic to the Mediterranean over 241 km, it has been a UNESCO site since 1996. The walk along the banks between the station and Square André Chénier is particularly pleasant in the shade of the plane trees. Operators offer hour-long narrated cruises from the port, with lock passages.

Return to the Pont Vieux in the evening — it's probably the best vantage point in Carcassonne to see the illuminated Cité reflected in the Aude. This medieval bridge was for centuries the sole link between the upper and lower town. It's now pedestrian-only.

activities.text: Operators offer narrated cruises of 1 to 2.5 hours departing from the Canal du Midi port. You'll pass through at least one lock, and the guide recounts the epic of Riquet and the 12,000 workers who built the canal between 1666 and 1681. An original way to view the Cité from the water.

visits.text: The four castles of Lastours — Cabaret, Tour Régine, Surdespine and Quertinheux — are staggered between 260 and 285 meters altitude along a 600-meter rocky ridge, encircled by the Orbiel river and the Grésilhou torrent. Cabaret was already the largest Cathar stronghold in the Carcassès at the beginning of the 13th century, frequented by bishops and perfects. In 1209, Simon de Montfort besieged it unsuccessfully — it's one of the rare sites to have resisted the crusade. Allow 1.5 hours for the complete visitor trail. Then drive to the Montfermier belvedere, 2 km away, to see all four silhouettes lined up against the backdrop of the Montagne Noire: the panorama is worth the detour.

The Giant Chasm of Cabrespine, about twenty kilometers to the east, is one of Europe's largest open chasms: 250 meters deep, up to 80 meters wide. Balconies suspended 200 meters above the void, a glass walkway, red and white aragonite crystals in the galleries. The temperature is constant at 14°C — bring a jacket even in midsummer.

Montolieu is a hilltop village on the edge of the Montagne Noire that has reinvented itself as a book village: some fifteen bookshops and second-hand dealers occupy the stone houses of the old centre. The Musée des Arts et Métiers du Livre traces the history of printing from Gutenberg onwards. Allow time for a break, browsing the shelves on a terrace with the hills in view. About 15 km from the overnight town, 20 minutes by road.

activities.text: The complete castle circuit is actually a hike: you pass through all four fortresses and the castrum of Cabaret, with an elevation gain of about 250 meters. Good shoes essential — the terrain is rocky and exposed to the sun. Set off early in the morning in summer.

map_keywords: Village de Lagrasse Plus Beau Village

visits.text: The Abbey of Sainte-Marie de Lagrasse was founded in 779 at Charlemagne's behest — according to legend, a monk named Nimphridius multiplied bread for the Emperor's soldiers, who thanked him by establishing this monastery. For over a millennium, its 64 successive abbots played a major political role between Languedoc and Catalonia. Sold during the Revolution, it's now divided in two: a public section (courtyard of the abbatial palace, monks' dormitory, lapidary museum with sculptures by the Master of Cabestany) and a private section occupied since 2004 by a community of canons who are patiently restoring it. In 2014, the cloister restoration won the Grand Trophy for most beautiful restoration organized by Le Figaro Magazine.

Cross the Pont Vieux from 1308 — three unequal arches, once topped by two towers now gone — and climb into the village lanes. Lagrasse is classified as one of France's Most Beautiful Villages and holds the Villes et Métiers d'Art label. Its medieval half-timbered houses, 14th-century covered market and Maison du Patrimoine (15th-century painted ceilings, free admission) make it one of the best-preserved villages in the Corbières.

In summer, a swimming area is set up facing the abbey in the Orbieu river. If you arrive on a Saturday, the morning market under the plane trees is the perfect spot to gather farmstead cheeses, olives and local products from the Corbières.

activities.text: Lagrasse lies at the heart of the Corbières appellation. Estates in the surrounding area offer tastings of robust reds and crisp whites produced on these garrigue and schist lands. Several are housed in former abbey priories. Check with the tourist office for the day's visiting options.

practical_info.booking: Inquire at the village tourist office

map_keywords: Canal de la Robine Pont des Marchands Narbonne

visits.text: The Cathedral of Saint-Just-et-Saint-Pasteur is the city's most soaring monument. Begun in 1272 in the Rayonnant Gothic style, it was never completed — Narbonne's consuls refused to demolish the ramparts to allow the nave to extend. Result: only the choir exists, but what a choir — 41 meters under vault, making it France's fourth tallest cathedral, after Beauvais, Amiens and Metz. Climb the Gilles-Aycelin tower (1295-1306, 42 meters) for the best view over the city and the Canal de la Robine.

Descend beneath Place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville to the Roman Horreum. These underground galleries from the 1st century BC — probably a public market or warehouse — are the only ones of their kind still visible in France. Narbonne, the first Roman colony outside Italy founded in 118 BC, was then the capital of Gallia Narbonensis and the region's primary port. Allow 45 minutes for the circuit.

The Archbishops' Palace, built and expanded over eight centuries, occupies an entire side of Place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville. Its art and archaeology museums house Flemish paintings, Orientalist halls and the Via Domitia — the Roman road's paving stones are visible directly in the floor of the Passage de l'Ancre. Take time for the Passage de l'Ancre, a covered lane linking the palace to the cathedral.

The Canal de la Robine is a UNESCO-listed branch of the Canal du Midi. Its Pont des Marchands — one of France's rare inhabited bridges with its colorful houses perched on seven arches (only one is visible from the canal side) — links the Roman quarter on the right bank to the medieval quarter on the left. The Promenade des Barques, running along the quays, is Narbonne's loveliest stroll in fine weather.

The Narbonne Covered Market, built in the early 20th century in a Baltard-style of metal and glass, opens every morning. Fishmongers, butchers, cheese shops, olives, oysters from the lagoon — it's the liveliest spot in town to lunch standing at the counter or to pick up a picnic.

activities.text: In the evening the quays of the Robine come alive with terraces and street musicians in summer. Sunset over the canal is worth the detour.

visits.text: The old village of Gruissan is built in a "circulade" — its lanes spiral like a snail shell around a large limestone rock crowned by the Barberousse Tower, remnant of a 10th-century medieval castle. Climb up: the 360-degree view over the lagoons, pink salt marshes, sea and Massif de la Clape is spectacular, especially late afternoon.

The Plage des Chalets is Gruissan's most famous image. Its 1,330 colorful chalets arranged in 11 rows facing the sea are the invention of Narbonne families in the mid-19th century, who came seeking sea bathing and gradually raised their huts on stilts to protect them from storm surges. Destroyed in 1943 by Germans fearing a Mediterranean landing, they were rebuilt in the 1950s — this time in a staggered pattern so everyone would have a sea view. Jean-Jacques Beineix's 1986 film "Betty Blue" ("37°2 le matin") made it an iconic location: Betty and Zorg's chalet no longer exists, but cinephiles still make the pilgrimage.

The Salt Marshes of Île Saint-Martin cover 400 hectares exploited since Antiquity. In summer, the salt tables turn bright pink due to a micro-algae, dunaliella salina. Guided tours allow you to see salt workers at work and encounter pink flamingos, stilts and avocets. Bring good shoes — the path runs along the basin edges.

activities.text: The Plage des Chalets and the Massif de la Clape offer 15 km of sand. If you have energy after swimming, climb to Pech Redon (214 m) via the trail from the beach: plunging view over the lagoons and sea, with AOC Clape vineyards in between.
Oyster farms around the Gruissan lagoon offer tastings directly from the producer, waterside. A simple, flavorful moment, typical of the Aude coast.

map_keywords: Cap Leucate falaise sentier du Guetteur
Plage des Coussoules La Franqui Leucate

visits.text: The limestone cliffs of Cap Leucate plunge 40 to 51 meters straight into the Mediterranean — the town's name reportedly comes from the Greek leukos (white) for the rock's whiteness. The Sentier du Guetteur (4.3 km round trip) runs along the plateau edge between the lighthouse, semaphore and cliff to La Franqui. On clear days you'll glimpse the Canigou at 2,784 meters and the entire Pyrenees range. Morning light is best for photographs.

The Plage des Coussoules at La Franqui stretches 8 km, classified Natura 2000, wild and battered by the tramontane — a wind that blows here about 300 days a year. It's one reason Leucate has become Europe's kitesurfing and windsurfing mecca. Every spring, the Mondial du Vent has gathered the international elite here since 1996. Outside competitions, it's one of the most unspoiled and spacious beaches on the Aude coast.

The Leucate lagoon spans 5,400 hectares between sea and maritime Corbières. Its 280 bird species (89 protected) make it a major ornithological site — pink flamingos, egrets and terns appear seasonally. On the Grau, colorful oyster farmers' huts offer their oysters waterside.

The village of Leucate just above its cliff has all the hallmarks of an ideal Mediterranean village: shaded square, colorful lanes, castle ruins. Climb to the ruins for sunset over the lagoon — the golden light on the water and salt marshes is one of the coast's finest spectacles.

activities.text: Leucate is the best kitesurfing and windsurfing spot on the French Mediterranean coast. Local operators offer beginner courses on the lagoon (flat water, ideal for learning) and more committed sessions on the sea side. Book ahead in high season.

practical_info.difficulty: Beginner courses available on the lagoon

visits.text: Rennes-le-Château, population 89 on a rocky spur at 450 meters altitude, is France's most mysterious village. It all begins with Abbé Bérenger Saunière, appointed parish priest of this poor parish in 1885: from 1891 onward, he spent considerable sums renovating the church, building a luxurious villa (Villa Béthanie), a crenellated neo-Gothic tower (Tour Magdala), gardens and an orangery — all in the name of his housekeeper Marie Dénarnaud. Where did the money come from? Treasure of the Visigoths, of the Templars, of the Cathars, a secret of the Church? Nobody knows. Saunière died in 1917 without revealing anything. Enter the Church of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine: right at the porch, a Latin inscription warns — "This place is terrible" — and on the left a devil named Asmodeus, guardian of treasures, supports the holy water font. The church is free.

Then climb to Tour Magdala, built from 1900 at the hill's edge. Saunière used it as a library and meditation retreat. From the crenellated platform, you can see some twenty villages of the Corbières and Pyrenees. The estate (villa, gardens, presbytery converted to museum, rampart walk) charges admission — allow 1.5 hours to see everything.

On the return route toward Quillan, don't miss the Gorges de l'Aude — the canyon between Quillan and Axat, including the Gorges de Pierre-Lys (road carved into the cliff) and the Gorges de Saint-Georges, two spectacular passages that take you along the river between limestone walls rising tens of meters high.

activities.text: Operators in Axat and Quillan offer rafting descents on the Aude ranging from 7 to 17 km. Class III-IV rapids, passages named "triple chute" and "flipper". Accessible from age 6 or 12 depending on routes. Book the day before or morning — the activity depends on river flow.

visits.text: Place de la République in Limoux hosts the world's longest carnival: from January to March, every Saturday and Sunday, the costumed bands of "Fécos" parade three times daily (11am, 4:30pm, 10pm) under the medieval arcades. Each band represents a neighborhood of the town. The ritual concludes each year with the "Nuit de la Blanquette" and the burning of His Majesty Carnival on Place de la République. If you're not there in season, stroll under the arcades and seek out the medieval Pont Vieux over the Aude.

Blanquette de Limoux is the world's oldest sparkling wine: in 1531, a monk at the Benedictine abbey of Saint-Hilaire (7 km from Limoux) discovered by chance that wine bottled and sealed with a cork stopper formed bubbles — a century before champagne was invented. The Abbey of Saint-Hilaire, whose origins date to the 9th century, also preserves a marble sarcophagus-reliquary attributed to the mysterious Master of Cabestany — one of the great anonymous Romanesque sculptors of the 12th century, whose works dot Languedoc and Catalonia. Cellars in Limoux and estates throughout the area offer visits and tastings.

Make the 3 km detour to the sanctuary of Notre-Dame de Marceille. This 14th-century Gothic church houses a Black Virgin venerated since the Middle Ages and a spring pilgrims consider miraculous. From the esplanade, the view of the Pyrenees in clear weather ranks among the region's finest.

activities.text: At a cellar in the Limoux area, a guided tour takes you down into underground galleries to see manual riddling, disgorgement and corking — the traditional method inherited from the monks of Saint-Hilaire. The final tasting includes Blanquette méthode ancestrale (100% Mauzac, under 7° alcohol) and Crémant de Limoux. Allow 1 hour.

practical_info.booking: Check opening hours depending on cellar chosen

activities.text: If you're in Limoux between January and March, the carnival is free and open to all. Three daily outings on Saturdays and Sundays — the evening session (10pm) is the liveliest and most authentic. The masked "Goudils" dance from café to café offering wine to spectators.

seo.h1_title: Aude Road Trip: Carcassonne, Cathar Country & the Mediterranean
seo.intro_paragraph: Over 7 days, the Aude unfolds an itinerary that begins beneath the 52 towers of Carcassonne (4 to 5 million visitors annually, UNESCO 1997), crosses the Cathar ruins of Lastours and the millennial abbey of Lagrasse, descends toward Gallo-Roman Narbonne, the stilt chalets of Gruissan and the cliffs of Cap Leucate. The loop closes via Rennes-le-Château and its unsolved mysteries, before a Blanquette tasting in Limoux — the world's oldest sparkling wine, invented in 1531.
seo.seo_hook: UNESCO Carcassonne, Cathar castles, Leucate lagoon and 1531 Blanquette: the Aude in 7 days between medieval ramparts and the Mediterranean.
featured_list: Carcassonne: 52 towers, 3 km of ramparts and a double curtain wall, a medieval fortress listed by UNESCO in 1997
Lastours: four Cathar castles on a rocky ridge, resisted Simon de Montfort's siege in 1209
Narbonne: unfinished Gothic cathedral (41 m under vault, France's 4th tallest) and underground Roman galleries from the 1st century BC
Limoux: birthplace of sparkling wine since 1531 and the world's longest carnival (3 months, January to March)

places_taglines.FR::lastours: Four Cathar sentinels defying the heavens from their rocky throne
places_taglines.FR::lagrasse: A Benedictine jewel cradled between Charlemagne's walls and a rushing river
places_taglines.FR::narbonne: Where Roman emperors once walked beneath soaring Gothic vaults

places_taglines.FR::leucate: White cliffs where the tramontane wind meets Mediterranean blue

highlights: Carcassonne: 52 towers, 3 km double walls, UNESCO inscribed in 1997, between 4 and 5 million visitors annually
Castles of Lastours: four Cathar fortresses on a rocky ridge, site competing for UNESCO status with the Royal Fortresses of Languedoc
Blanquette de Limoux: world's first sparkling wine, invented in 1531 by monks of Saint-Hilaire abbey, a century before champagne
Cap Leucate: limestone cliffs 40 to 51 meters high, 300 days of wind annually, Plage des Coussoules classified Natura 2000 over 8 km

itineraries.title: Aveyron Road Trip: Causses, Tarn Gorges and Villages
itineraries.subtitle: From the Soulages Museum to the Roquefort caves, between Romanesque heritage and causse landscapes
itineraries.climate: Best time: May-June and September-October, temperatures 15-25°C, ideal light for causses and gorges. Avoid November-March (harsh cold on Aubrac plateau, snow risk at Laguiole, fog). July-August: hot but bearable due to altitude, tourist crowds.

visits.text: The Soulages Museum opened in 2014 with nearly 500 works by the Rodez-born painter. The architecture by Catalan firm RCR Arquitectes features Corten steel that develops a patina over time. The galleries alternate between varying heights and half-light to showcase Soulages' creative periods.

Notre-Dame Cathedral required 300 years of construction, from the 13th to the 16th century. Its bell tower reaches 87 metres and offers a 360° view after climbing 400 steps. The interior houses ancient and contemporary stained glass windows, a monumental organ, and richly decorated choir stalls.

The Fenaille Museum holds the largest collection of statue-menhirs in Europe. These sculptures from the 3rd millennium BC remain enigmatic. The building occupies the Hôtel de Jouéry, saved from demolition in the early 20th century by Maurice Fenaille.

activities.text: Follow the historic centre trail available from the tourist office on Place de la Cité. The numbered route takes you past the Maison d'Armagnac, the bishop's palace, and Renaissance façades.

The market takes place on Wednesday and Saturday mornings. You'll find Aveyron specialities there: farçous, aligot, and Aubrac beef. The brasseries in the centre serve these dishes throughout the week.

visits.text: Belcastel Castle dates from the 11th century with its square keep and corner towers. Fernand Pouillon restored it from 1975 to 1982, involving numerous local craftsmen. Visit the water-filled moat, medieval chapels, and art galleries exhibiting contemporary works.

Alzias de Saunhac had the bridge built in the 15th century. It connects the Sainte-Madeleine Church to the village on the other bank of the Aveyron river. Passers-by once paid for their crossing with prayers and offerings at the altar stone.

The 15th-century Sainte-Madeleine Church houses the tomb of Alzias de Saunhac with its recumbent effigy. You will also see the Saunhac family coat of arms and four statues listed as historic monuments. Casimir Ferrer created an extraordinary Stations of the Cross for the church.

activities.text: The Maison de la Forge is over 200 years old and displays the tools of the blacksmith, farrier, clog-maker, and fisherman. Guides explain the use of the twitch to restrain horses and the tail docker.
Climb to the Roc d'Anglars located 500 m upstream from the village. This 5th-century fort occupies the heights above the Lourdou cave. The 3 km hike offers views of the village and the Aveyron river.

visits.text: The Sainte-Foy Abbey Church was built from 1041 by Abbot Odolric. The Last Judgement tympanum features 124 sculpted figures on 24 blocks of yellow limestone. The interior contains 250 Romanesque capitals spread over two levels.

The Treasury houses the reliquary statue of Saint Foy, a unique piece of Carolingian goldsmith work set with gold and precious stones. This collection bears witness to nine centuries of pilgrimage on the Way of Saint James.

Pierre Soulages worked from 1987 to 1994 to create 104 stained glass windows for the abbey church. He carried out nearly 700 trials with master glassmaker Jean-Dominique Fleury to achieve a unique translucent glass. The light changes throughout the day thanks to variations in grain size.

activities.text: The Conques Nocturnes take place from May to October to illuminate the polychrome tympanum. The reimagined polychromy reveals the restored medieval colours.

Visit the abbey church galleries to get up close to the Soulages stained glass windows. The guided tour lasts 45 minutes and explores the painter's creative approach. Booking recommended, open to visitors aged 12 and above.

practical_info.booking: Booking recommended at the tourist office

visits.text: Estaing Castle dates back to the 13th century with its octagonal keep surrounded by turrets. The d'Estaing family owned it for eight centuries before it was acquired by Valéry Giscard d'Estaing in 2005. The exhibition retraces the presidential term and the advances of his mandate.

François d'Estaing had the Gothic bridge built in the early 16th century. This UNESCO-listed structure is crossed each year by pilgrims heading to Santiago de Compostela. The wrought-iron cross in the middle is a symbol of Aveyron craftsmanship.

The 15th-century Church of Saint-Fleuret holds the relics of the Bishop of Clermont who died here in the 5th century. The saint is known for his miraculous healings. Grey-blue schist houses with lauze stone roofs line the narrow streets.

activities.text: The Maison de la Vigne, du Vin et des Paysages tells the story of the vineyard. The Vignerons d'Olt cultivate 20 hectares that earned the AOC Estaing designation in 2011. The wine was once shipped throughout Europe via the Lot river.

The Saint-Fleuret procession takes place on the first Sunday of July. Locals wear costumes representing saints, angels, and members of the d'Estaing family. This historical and religious re-enactment brings the whole village to life.

visits.text: Entraygues comes from the Occitan entraigas meaning between the waters. The Lot and the Truyère rivers meet here at an altitude of 219 metres. Two 13th-century Gothic bridges link the banks from the medieval castle.

The historic centre retains half-timbered houses from the 15th and 16th centuries. The cantous are small covered passageways running beneath the houses. Some façades still shelter craftsmen's workshops.

The Entraygues-Le Fel vineyard covers 20 hectares of terraces between schist and granite. Five winemakers carry on a winemaking tradition dating back to the Roman occupation. The AOC was granted in 2011, following the VDQS classification of 1965.

activities.text: The Espace EDF Truyère occupies the former control room of the Couesques dam power station. This 600 m² educational trail explains how hydroelectricity works and the industrial adventure built around water.

The Calvaire viewpoint offers a panorama of the confluence of the Lot and the Truyère. Head towards Aurillac, cross the Cambeyrac dam and stop after a hairpin bend. A 5-minute path leads to the viewpoint marked by a large cross.

practical_info.access: By car then 5 min on foot

visits.text: Visit the cutlery workshops in the heart of Laguiole village. The cutlers handcraft each piece with the forged bee, chiselled spring, and guillochage patterns. Several manufacturers offer tours and assembly demonstrations.

The Forge de Laguiole lets you watch the complete making of a knife. The artisans hot-forge the blades, sculpt the bee with a file and punch, then assemble the different parts. Handles are made from precious wood, Aubrac horn, or stag antler.

Laguiole village is also the birthplace of the Aubrac cattle breed and the Laguiole AOC cheese. Burons dot the plateau where the cows graze. Aligot is the local speciality made from fresh tome cheese and potatoes.

activities.text: Explore the Aubrac plateau between 1,000 and 1,400 metres altitude. The landscapes alternate between summer pastures and peatlands. The traditional burons were used to make cheese during the transhumance.
Taste the aligot in the village restaurants. This mashed potato dish mixed with fresh tome cheese is beaten at length until it forms long ribbons. Each inn has its own recipe and technique.

visits.text: The Millau Viaduct reaches 343 metres in height, taller than the Eiffel Tower. Spanning 2,460 metres, it links the Causse Rouge to the Causse du Larzac. The visitor area features a 220 m² interactive exhibition and a viewing platform with free 24/7 access.

The glove-making workshops have been Millau's claim to fame since the 19th century. Maison Fabre has been making gloves in the same family since 1924. Visit the workshops to see the artisanal crafting of a pair of Made in Millau gloves.

The La Graufesenque site was one of the most important pottery centres of the Roman world. The Millau museum displays pieces that were exported across all Roman lands. The Belfry and the Baltard-style metal hall complete the town's heritage.

activities.text: The Explorers' Trail takes you under the viaduct deck with an Eiffage guide. The tour reveals the construction secrets of this steel giant. Booking required, the trail is suitable for all ages.

Millau is the capital of outdoor sports. Paragliding, rock climbing, via ferrata, canyoning, and mountain biking are all available on the surrounding causses and gorges. Certified instructors offer introductory sessions and courses.

practical_info.activities: Paragliding, rock climbing, via ferrata, canyoning

visits.text: The Roquefort Société caves welcome over 100,000 visitors a year. The one-hour guided tour takes you through natural caves carved beneath the Combalou rock. The fleurines naturally ventilate the caves at 10°C with 80% humidity.

Penicillium roqueforti develops spontaneously in the caves. This mould gives the cheese its characteristic blue-green marbling and flavours. The master refiners carefully select and cultivate their own strains.

Roquefort was the very first AOC in history, granted in 1925. It celebrates its centenary in 2025. The AOP requires raw Lacaune ewe's milk, daily pasturing within the Roquefort area, and ageing in natural caves.

activities.text: A tasting of the three Roquefort AOP cheeses concludes the visit. The caves also offer workshops pairing wine and cheese. The standard tour costs €7.50, or €15 for the tour with a guided tasting.
The village is home to seven Roquefort producers. Maison Gabriel Coulet offers a free self-guided tour with a presentation film. The Papillon caves also provide discovery tours.

map_keywords: Notre-Dame de la Miséricorde church Saint-Affrique

visits.text: Saint-Affrique stretches along the banks of the Sorgues in the heart of the Grands Causses Regional Natural Park. The Pont-Vieux, listed as a Historic Monument, connects the two banks. The centre retains stone houses, small squares, and vaulted passageways.

The Rocher de Caylus offers a panoramic view over the town and surrounding hills. A cross tops this landmark site. The Notre-Dame de la Miséricorde Church features a tall Gothic spire visible from afar.

The Maison de la Mémoire du Pays Saint-Affricain displays objects, stories, and photographs of daily life in times past. The Tribunal des Arts occupies the former courthouse and exhibits works by local artists.

activities.text: The Saturday morning market brings the town centre to life. Producers sell local cheeses (Pérail, Roquefort, Recuite), charcuterie, and regional specialities. The atmosphere is friendly and Aveyron delicacies are plentiful.

The landscapes around Saint-Affrique range from blazing red-soil rougiers to wild causses and green valleys. The Rougier de Camarès to the south offers spectacular red earth, about 20 km from the stopover town, a 20-minute drive. Hiking, mountain biking and climbing are all possible nearby.

seo.h1_title: Aveyron Road Trip: Causses, Tarn Gorges and Villages
seo.intro_paragraph: Visit the Rodez Cathedral and the Soulages Museum, the villages of Belcastel, Conques, and Estaing — all listed among France's Most Beautiful Villages — admire the Millau Viaduct, a world record holder, explore the Roquefort caves, France's very first AOC, and the Laguiole knives.
seo.seo_hook: From Soulages Museum to Roquefort caves, discover Conques, Millau Viaduct and France's Most Beautiful Villages between causses and Tarn gorges.
