itineraries.title: Auvergne Circuit: Perched Villages and Volcanoes
itineraries.subtitle: From the infant Loire to the Cantal highlands: 8 stages blending medieval basalt architecture with volcanic landscapes
itineraries.climate: Best time: May-June and September, temperatures 15-23°C, ideal for hilltop villages. Avoid November-March (harsh cold, frequent snow at altitude, roads sometimes tricky). July-August: decent weather but tourist crowds.

visits.text: As the road winds down into the valley, Arlempdes appears without warning: an 80-meter basalt dyke crowned by a medieval castle, encircled by the young Loire in a dramatic meander. The sight is breathtaking. This village, ranked among France's Most Beautiful Villages, sits barely thirty kilometers from the river's source — earning it the nickname 'first castle on the Loire,' built here from the 13th century onward by the Lords of Montlaur. The fortress has witnessed its share of drama: in 1429, Anna de Montlaur made it part of her dowry when she married Charles III de Poitiers, whose granddaughter Diane de Poitiers — King Henri II's mistress — served as Lady of Arlempdes from 1550 to 1566. In 1585, the Huguenots took the castle by surprise after bribing a guard to open a secret door on the riverside.

Push open the door of Saint-Jacques chapel (12th century) at the heart of the castle ruins, then walk down to the village's Saint-Pierre church — a 12th-century Romanesque building with a single nave and a bell-gable with four arches, elegant and unadorned like all Auvergnat Romanesque architecture. Inside, look for a 16th-century Pietà. Don't miss the 11th-century postern gate at the village entrance, with its soaring broken-barrel vault — it's been listed as a Historic Monument since 1971.

Walk the loop along the castle walls that follow the basalt columns — remarkably regular prisms that look almost machine-cut, though they're entirely natural volcanic formations. Descend to the banks of the Loire: from the pebble beach, the view of the castle clinging to its sheer rock face is dizzying. Bring good shoes for the climb back up.

activities.text: The Arlempdes gorge loop (3–4 km, with sections along balcony paths above the Loire) starts right from the village. It follows basalt flows that sometimes form volcanic organ pipes and offers perspectives on the meander the river has carved through the rock. Allow 1h30 at a gentle pace — the trail is waymarked and not technical.

Every July, the Théâtrales du Velay festival takes over the castle ruins for several weeks of performances. If you're visiting during this period, check the programme: watching a play inside a medieval fortress once owned by Diane de Poitiers beats any indoor theatre in the world.

visits.text: Pradelles perches at 1,150 meters on a volcanic spur above the upper Allier valley. Ranked among France's Most Beautiful Villages, this town is inseparable from the Via Régordane — that ancient route between the Massif Central and the Mediterranean that muleteers called the 'Régourdans road,' hauling wine, salt, and olive oil from Languedoc into Auvergne. King Saint Louis himself stopped here in 1254. Start at Place de la Halle: surrounded by arcades and Renaissance houses from the 15th–17th centuries, it forms the historic heart of Pradelles. The Maison Frévol (16th century) and the covered gallery deserve close attention.

Walk the circuit of the remaining ramparts: Porte de la Verdette is the only medieval gate still standing, and Tour Rochely recalls the town's defensive strength. Beneath the town, pass under the arch of the 17th-century former road hospice — one of only four such surviving structures left in Europe. This building once sheltered travellers and pilgrims heading down to Saint-Gilles-du-Gard. Pradelles also preserves the Notre-Dame chapel (built in 1613, literally straddling the road) with its miraculous statue of the Virgin discovered, according to legend, in a buried chest in 1512.

Before leaving Pradelles, walk up to the calvary hill: on clear days, you can see the statue of the Virgin on the keep of Luc castle from here, the next stop on the Via Régordane. The two fortresses once communicated by fire signals. The view of Lake Naussac spreading through the valley below makes a striking contrast with this high-altitude Auvergne landscape.

activities.text: In 1878, Scottish writer Robert Louis Stevenson passed through Pradelles with his donkey Modestine during the journey he recounted in 'Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes.' Both the GR 70 (Stevenson Trail) and the GR 700 (Via Régordane) start from the village. A 2–3 km loop on the heights around town offers fine views over the Devès plateau and Lake Naussac — allow 1h15 to reach both main viewpoints.

The former Le Puy-Langogne railway line has been converted to a vélo-rail (pedal-powered railcar) starting from Pradelles station: trips from 1h to 5h (return on 18 km) let you cross the gorse moorlands, lentil fields, and peat bogs of the plateau. It's an ideal family activity for exploring volcanic landscapes at a leisurely pace. Book ahead in high season.

visits.text: As you arrive in Murat, look up: three basalt rocks aligned along a single fault rise above the houses. These are three ancient Cantal volcanic plugs from eruptions 3.6 million years ago — the Bonnevie, Bredons, and Chastel rocks. Bonnevie towers 140 meters over the town with some of Europe's finest basalt organ pipes, now crowned by an 8-meter cast-iron Virgin erected in 1878. This is where the imposing fortress of the Viscounts of Murat once stood — in the 12th century, the viscounty included 25 fortified castles, 29 châteaux, 59 villages, and 110 fiefs. In 1633, Cardinal Richelieu spent six months razing it to the ground. Wander the medieval lanes between basalt and phonolite houses, following the circuit of 26 heritage interpretation panels.

Don't miss Saint-Pierre de Bredons church, perched on its rock 1.5 km from the town centre: a Benedictine priory founded around 1050 by monks from Moissac, a jewel of Cantal Romanesque architecture with its gilded wooden altarpieces and billet-moulding portal. The view over the Alagnon valley from the esplanade is spectacular. The climb from below takes 20 minutes on foot via a paved path.

The Collégiale Notre-Dame des Oliviers in the heart of Murat dates from 1380 — its construction was authorized by the Bishop of Saint-Flour after a lightning-caused fire in 1493 destroyed and rebuilt it. Its 19th-century bulb tower stands out in the Auvergnat landscape. Inside, look for the Virgin and Child that Saint Louis supposedly brought back from the Holy Land. The Maison de la Faune, a 16th-century townhouse, is also open for visits in season.

activities.text: Climb to the top of Rocher de Bonnevie via the trail from the tourist office: allow 30 minutes one way to reach the Virgin and the basalt organ pipes. From the summit, the view of Murat terraced in an amphitheatre and the Cantal valleys is one of the region's most spectacular. The path passes the site of the former razed castle — from up here, you understand better why it took Richelieu six months to demolish this fortress.

Murat is served by the Aurillac-Clermont-Ferrand railway line. In the evening, a walk through the old town's doorways, mascarons, and former shops reveals Renaissance architectural details often overlooked by hurried visitors. The Des Danses et Musiques du Monde festival, held every year in early August, transforms the town into an open-air stage for several days.

visits.text: Tournemire stretches along a volcanic ridge above the Doire valley, one of thirteen valleys radiating from Puy Mary. The village — one of France's Most Beautiful Villages — centres on its 12th-century Romanesque church, which preserves a relic of the Holy Thorn brought back from the Crusades by a local lord. At the far end of the village, Château d'Anjony rises from its basalt mound with four slender towers reaching 40 meters high. Built around 1430 by Louis d'Anjony, companion-in-arms of Joan of Arc and charged by Charles VII with restoring order in Haute-Auvergne, it has remained in the same family for six centuries. To reach the entrance, you walk through the village from the car park (15 minutes) — factor this into your timing.

The château's interior is worth the visit: the Hall of the Nine Worthies frescoes (around 1575) depict nine legendary knights — Charlemagne, King Arthur, Alexander the Great — life-size on their horses. They were rediscovered in the early 20th century behind 18th-century panelling. The chapel, meanwhile, is decorated with 16th-century Passion scenes. This castle also has a vendetta story worthy of a novel: the Anjony and Tournemire families, neighbours too close for comfort, feuded bitterly for two centuries. In 1523, Claude d'Anjony was assassinated by the Tournemires; in 1623, a duel in front of the church left three dead on each side. The visit is guided, approximately 60 minutes.

activities.text: The viewpoint loop above the Doire (3–4 km, ~1h30) offers sweeping views of the Cantal mountains and pastoral valleys. From the ridges, you can see the basalt organ pipes of neighbouring rocks and, on clear days, Puy Mary. Proper walking shoes essential — paths can be slippery after rain.

Study the houses of Tournemire in detail: lauze stone roofs, dark andesite window frames, carved lintels. This perfectly preserved traditional Cantal architecture represents an open-air manual of volcanic construction. The village is small, but every façade tells a story of craft, century, and family name.

visits.text: Salers sits at 951 meters altitude and welcomes 400,000 visitors a year — for a population of just 312 — and with good reason: this village has remained virtually intact since the Renaissance. Ranked among France's Most Beautiful Villages since 1982, its silhouette in black volcanic stone is the iconic image of Cantal. In the 15th century, the village became the seat of the Bailliage des Hautes Montagnes d'Auvergne: wealthy magistrate families built the turreted townhouses with mullioned windows and lauze stone roofs you admire today. Place Tyssandier d'Escous, at the heart of town, is lined with these mansions and dominated by a statue of the agronomist who improved the local cattle breed. In season, guided tours grant access to normally closed interior courtyards.

Saint-Mathieu church (13th century) houses five 17th-century Aubusson tapestries and a remarkable polychrome 15th-century Entombment — don't miss going inside. Afterwards, head to the Esplanade de Barrouze, a grassy terrace on the village heights: from here opens the finest plunging view over the Maronne valley and Cantal ridges. In autumn, the contrast between black stone and golden forests is striking.

Walk the circuit of the ramparts passing through Porte du Beffroi (15th-century clock tower with a bell dating from 1604) and Porte de la Martille with its two round towers. The so-called Maison des Templiers and Maison de Ronade with its vaulted gallery adorned with gargoyles are the two townhouses not to miss — ask at the tourist office about access.

activities.text: The Salers hill loop (3–5 km) lets you leave the fortified town and understand its position on the volcanic promontory above the Maronne valley. Allow 1h30–2h, easy level. Keen trail runners and hikers can head for Puy Violent, accessible from Col de Néronne a few km away (3h30 return, intermediate level, 360° views over the Cantal mountains).

Salers is also a gastronomic destination: the mahogany-coated, lyre-horned Salers cow produces one of the rare PDO cheeses made exclusively on farms, in summer pastures, from raw milk — Salers cheese. Local producers open their farms to visitors around the village. Don't leave Salers without trying truffade and, if you find it, Cantal gentian liqueur.

visits.text: Saint-Floret nestles against the rock at the entrance to a narrow gorge the Couze Pavin has carved through granite — Stendhal wrote there was 'nothing more picturesque.' The village developed around a seigneurial castle built from the 13th century by the Dauphins of Auvergne. Dare to push open the door of the castle's lower hall: you'll discover 13 exceptional frescoes painted around 1370 recounting the Romance of Tristan and Iseult — the only French depiction of this version of the medieval romance. The colours are vivid, the figures life-size. Visits are guided only, April to September (check times with the Issoire tourist office). In June 1944, the village was bombed by the Luftwaffe in reprisal — one section of town remains in ruins, deliberately preserved as a witness.

Cross the old Pont de la Pède from the 15th century: a single arch topped by an oratory housing a polychrome Romanesque Virgin in Majesty from the 13th century. This bridge is said to be miraculous since, during the 1944 bombing, the only bomb that failed to explode fell precisely here. Then climb to the Chastel site on the granite mound: a 12th-century Romanesque church surrounded by a necropolis with anthropomorphic tombs carved in rock, a pyramidal ossuary, and 14th-century frescoes inside — an archaeological site of rare density.

A few kilometres upstream from the village, don't miss the Tête de Lion spring: an impressive limestone concretion with a feline profile formed by deposits of calcium carbonate carried by the water (travertine). It's one of the most spectacular mineral springs among the 600 catalogued in Auvergne. The path follows the Couze Pavin — allow 20 minutes from the spring car park.

activities.text: The Couze Pavin gorge trail (3–5 km, moderate elevation gain, ~2h) follows the river upstream through its canyon between granite walls. Rock climbing sites line the river for enthusiasts — local operators offer introductions in the gorges. The Couze flow can be strong during rainy periods: check locally on conditions.

visits.text: Saint-Saturnin perches on a basalt flow overlooking the Monne gorges, 15 km south of Clermont-Ferrand. Its monumental duo seen from the road — Romanesque church and medieval castle in golden arkose and Volvic lava — is one of Auvergne's most photographed sights. Notre-Dame church is one of five so-called 'major' Romanesque churches in Auvergne, alongside those of Issoire, Orcival, Clermont, and Saint-Nectaire — listed as a Historic Monument in 1862. Built in the 12th century, its octagonal bell tower is one of the best preserved in Auvergne, and its capitals are carved from local volcanic lava. Allow 45 minutes for the interior visit in season (guided tours in July-August).

Right next to the church, the Royal Château de Saint-Saturnin was built in the 13th century by the La Tour d'Auvergne family, then embellished in the Renaissance by Catherine de' Medici — Countess of Auvergne — who added a formal French garden. In 1566, King Charles IX and his entire court stopped here. In 1586, Queen Margot passed through before her exile in Usson. The visit (about 50 minutes, guided) grants access to the keep, wall-walk, and furnished rooms.

Walk along Rue de la Boucherie with its medieval shop and houses from the 15th–17th centuries, then reach the Renaissance fountain from the 16th century between the church and castle — its decoration bears the La Tour d'Auvergne coat of arms. The 12th-century Romanesque Sainte-Madeleine chapel adjoins the former cemetery transformed into a garden. On the lintel of the door, read the 1668 inscription: 'We have been like you, one day you will be like us, Think well on it.' Rarely has an invitation to contemplation been so direct.

activities.text: The washhouses walk descends to the Monne from the Renaissance fountain, following the flank of the basalt flow. On the south-facing slopes (the Serre mountain), old vineyard terraces and dry-stone huts recall that Puy-de-Dôme was France's second-largest wine-producing department in the 19th century. If you search carefully in the walls, you'll find fossilized stromatolite impressions 25 million years old.

Saint-Saturnin is 15 km from Clermont-Ferrand and makes a fine last stop before the city. The Saint-Jacques de Compostela path Via Arvena meets the Via Podiensis here — several waymarked loops explore the Monne valley and its steep gorges, accessible on foot or mountain bike from the village.

visits.text: Clermont-Ferrand is the logical way out of this Auvergne circuit: rail link to Paris, airport, and a regional capital whose black lava-stone centre is remarkably well preserved. The Gothic cathedral of Notre-Dame de l'Assomption (13th-14th century) is one of the few cathedrals in France built entirely from local volcanic andesite, a deep black that gives it an almost threatening look. Its 13th-century stained glass is worth stepping inside for. The basilica of Notre-Dame-du-Port, right next door, is one of the five major churches of Auvergne Romanesque art that you have met along this circuit.

The Vieux-Clermont quarter, around Place de la Victoire and Rue des Gras, displays medieval houses, fountains, and townhouses in black stone. The Saturday morning market at Place Saint-Pierre is one of Auvergne's largest — cheeses, green lentils from Le Puy, Aubrac lamb, wines from Issoire. A must-stop before hitting the road or catching your train.

activities.text: If you have a free morning before your train or flight, climb Puy de Dôme (accessible from Clermont by shuttle to the base of the Panoramique des Dômes funicular railway): at 1,465 meters, the panorama over the Chaîne des Puys — a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2018 — sums up in one view the 300 million years of Auvergnat volcanism you've travelled through over this entire circuit.

practical_info.booking: Funicular recommended — no car access in season

seo.h1_title: Auvergne Circuit: Perched Villages and Volcanoes
seo.intro_paragraph: From the infant Loire to the Cantal highlands, this circuit links eight medieval villages all built on volcanic rock: Arlempdes with its castle perched on an 80-meter basalt dyke, Salers with its 15th-century black stone townhouses, Saint-Floret with its unique frescoes of the Romance of Tristan and Iseult, and Saint-Saturnin with its Romanesque church once in Catherine de' Medici's domain.
seo.seo_hook: Castles on basalt dykes, medieval frescoes unique in France, Romanesque Auvergnat heritage, and PDO cheeses — volcanic Auvergne in 8 stages.
featured_list: Arlempdes: first castle on the Loire, built in the 13th century on an 80-meter basalt dyke
Saint-Floret: 13 frescoes from 1370 illustrating the Romance of Tristan and Iseult, the only French representation
Salers: 400,000 visitors a year for 312 inhabitants, a 15th-century museum-town in black volcanic stone
Tournemire: Château d'Anjony built in 1430 by a companion of Joan of Arc, inhabited by the same family for six centuries

places_taglines.FR::arlempdes: Where medieval stones crown a volcanic spike above the infant Loire
places_taglines.FR::pradelles: A mountain stronghold at 1,150m where King Saint Louis once rested
places_taglines.FR::murat: Three volcanic plugs rising like sentinels over black basalt streets
places_taglines.FR::tournemire: Where Joan of Arc's companion built a fortress that never left his bloodline
places_taglines.FR::salers: Renaissance elegance frozen in black volcanic stone since the 15th century
places_taglines.FR::saint-floret: Home to France's only frescoes of Tristan and Iseult's forbidden love
places_taglines.FR::clermont-ferrand: Gateway to volcanic Auvergne, built from the dark heart of ancient eruptions
places_taglines.FR::saint-saturnin-63: Volcanic village with the royal castle of Catherine de' Medici and one of Auvergne's five major Romanesque churches

highlights: Arlempdes: the only Loire castle perched on an 80-meter volcanic dyke, inhabited since the 11th century and mentioned in a papal bull by Pope Clement IV in 1267
Saint-Floret: the 13 frescoes from 1370 depicting the Romance of Tristan and Iseult are the only French representation of this version of the medieval text
Tournemire: Château d'Anjony, built in 1430, has never changed families in six centuries and preserves Nine Worthies frescoes rediscovered in the 20th century
Salers: 400,000 visitors a year for 312 inhabitants — the 15th-century town, seat of the Bailliage des Hautes Montagnes, has remained virtually intact since the Renaissance

itineraries.title: Charente Circuit: Cognac and Romanesque Heritage in 4 Days
itineraries.subtitle: From centuries-old cellars to Romanesque churches, the Charente between vineyards and river
itineraries.climate: Best time: April-June and September-October, 15-25°C, ideal for castle tours and cognac tastings. Avoid November-March (grey, rainy, damp cold). July-August: hot (28-32°C) but manageable, perfect for riverside terraces.

visits.text: The Cité internationale de la BD occupies a former cognac cellar on the banks of the Charente. Over 20,000 original comic plates, cutting-edge temporary exhibitions, and Europe's largest comic book library. Allow 2 hours to make the most of it.

The Cathédrale Saint-Pierre is Romanesque, not Gothic — and that changes everything. The sculpted 12th-century façade tells the story of the Ascension and the Last Judgement across 70 stone figures. The contemporary Treasury by Jean-Michel Othoniel is worth a detour.

The ramparts walk offers a full panorama over the Charente below. Angoulême sits on a rocky spur — you can see why it served as a stronghold. It's also the best vantage point for spotting the comic book murals.
Over 30 monumental murals across the streets: Titeuf on a gable end, Lucky Luke at a crossroads, Blake and Mortimer round a corner. Free map at the tourist office. Kids love it — adults too.

Under the Halles centrales, producers sell pineau, rillettes and cagouilles (local snails). Around them, cobbled lanes climb towards the town hall housed in the former counts' castle. Good bistros in the area.

activities.text: Guided tour 'Comics in the City'. The guides know the stories behind every mural: who painted what, why there, the hidden details. Duration 1h30, departure from the tourist office.

practical_info.booking: Booking recommended in summer and during the Festival

activities.text: Walk along the Charente riverbanks. The towpath runs from the Cité BD along the river. Canoe hire available at the watersports centre in season. Quieter option: traditional gabare boat with commentary.
Musée d'Angoulême in the former bishop's palace, behind the cathedral. Varied collections: Charente archaeology (the famous gold Agris helmet), African arts, regional paintings. Small but well done.

visits.text: The Château de La Rochefoucauld has belonged to the same family since 1019 — a French record. The three-storey Renaissance galleries recall Italian palaces. Legend has it the spiral staircase was designed by Leonardo da Vinci.
The castle's four libraries hold 21,000 volumes. The guided tour (compulsory for this section) includes the Treasury room where the guide handles eight-century-old archives. Impressive.

The town at the foot of the castle is worth a stroll: half-timbered houses, cobbled lanes along the Tardoire. This is where the charentaise was born — the slipper, not the local woman. Specialist shop on Rue des Halles.

activities.text: Full castle visit. Self-guided section (salons, kitchens, galleries) + guided tour of the libraries and archives. Allow 2 hours total. Children can dress up as knights or princesses — costumes provided.

practical_info.tickets: At the wine merchant at the bottom of the drive
practical_info.tip: Children's costumes available free of charge

activities.text: Chocolaterie d'Antan at the foot of the castle. Watch artisans at work from the shop. Local speciality: the pichotte, a chocolate-almond-icing sugar sweet. Open even on Sundays.
Hike along the Tardoire. Waymarked trails from the castle into the rolling countryside. Landscapes that hint at the neighbouring Périgord. Several loops from 5 to 15 km.

visits.text: The Pont-Vieux in Confolens has spanned the Vienne since the 11th century (on ancient foundations). Postcard view of half-timbered houses reflected in the water. This is where the Goire meets the Vienne — hence the name 'confluent'.
The old town climbs the hill in winding lanes. Medieval half-timbered houses, craft shops, small shaded squares. The Saint-Barthélemy quarter keeps its old-world atmosphere.
The church of Saint-Maxime overlooks the upper town. Sculpted Romanesque doorway, square bell tower typical of Poitou. Inside, historiated capitals and contemporary stained glass. Free entry.

activities.text: Walk along the Vienne. The towpath leads from the Old Bridge towards the countryside. Anglers, grey herons, abandoned locks. Peaceful atmosphere guaranteed.
Canoeing on the Vienne. The watersports centre offers routes from 2 hours to a full day. Calm water, no technical difficulty. Hire includes life jackets and dry bags.

Confolens Festival (mid-August). Since 1958, France's biggest folklore festival. Troupes from around the world, costumed parades, free concerts. If you're passing through at this time, it's unmissable.

practical_info.tip: Book accommodation well in advance

visits.text: The Château de Verteuil dominates the village from its rocky spur. Owned by the La Rochefoucauld family for 1,000 years (sold in 2020), it welcomed Charles V, who planted a yew there that still stands.
The Moulin de Verteuil at the foot of the castle, with its waterwheel still turning. Now a restaurant with a terrace by the water. The castle + mill + Charente view = the perfect photo.

The church of Saint-Médard (12th century) hides a life-size Entombment in polychrome terracotta. Seven figures around Christ, attributed to the workshop of Germain Pilon. One of the Charente's hidden treasures.

The village lanes lead to the fairground shaded by lime trees, on the banks of the Charente. The Maison du Sénéchal (15th century) with its mullioned windows, remains of the old Protestant temple, wash houses. A Petite Cité de Caractère.

activities.text: A walk around the outside of the castle. The castle can no longer be visited, but the outline of its towers can be seen from the lanes of Verteuil-sur-Charente and from the banks of the Charente. The fairground and the surroundings of the mill offer the best viewpoints.

practical_info.tickets: At the Jeux de Pots wine shop
practical_info.open: Check opening hours, closed some days

activities.text: Lunch at the Moulin de Verteuil. Terrace facing the waterwheel, local cuisine. Booking advised at weekends. Alternative: Jeux de Pots overlooks the Charente.

practical_info.booking: Advised at weekends and in summer

activities.text: Hike around the castle. 6.6 km loop through the countryside and hamlets, returning along the Charente banks. Easy, 1h30–2h. Start from the castle car park.

visits.text: The Hennessy house offers the most spectacular tour: solar-powered boat crossing of the Charente, ageing cellars where the 'angel's share' floats in the air, guided tasting. Booking essential.

Martell, the oldest of the great houses (1715), has renovated its historic site with its Art Deco tower. Tour of the centuries-old cellars and the founder's house. A more intimate atmosphere than Hennessy.
The Château de Cognac, birthplace of Francis I, houses Baron Otard cognacs. Renaissance vaulted cellars, rooftop view over the Charente. French history entwined with the story of cognac.
Old Cognac is best explored on foot: medieval houses with walls blackened by the cognac fungus (the famous Torula), merchants' townhouses, quays where gabares loaded barrels.
The Musée des Arts du Cognac traces the history of this spirit: stills, cooperage, vintage labels, retro advertisements. A good complement to cellar tours. Housed in two townhouses.

activities.text: Tour of a major cognac house. Hennessy for the immersive experience, Martell for intimacy, Rémy Martin for connoisseurs (expert tours available). Allow 1h30 to 2h including tasting.

practical_info.tip: Book 2–3 weeks ahead in summer

activities.text: Cruise on the Charente. Traditional gabares with commentary (1h30) or licence-free electric boat hire. The river at the pace of the barrels of old.
Cycling along the Charente. The Flow Vélo (national route) passes through Cognac. Bike hire available in town. Flat route to Jarnac (15 km) or Saint-Brice (8 km).

visits.text: The Courvoisier house stands in its château on the banks of the Charente. Tour of the cellars including the famous 'Paradis' where the oldest eaux-de-vie age. Tasting overlooking the river.
The church of Saint-Pierre blends eras: 11th-century Romanesque foundations, a 12th-century crypt where the former Counts of Jarnac rest, later alterations. Tombs of the local lords in the crypt.

The Musée Donation François-Mitterrand occupies a former cognac cellar. State gifts received during his terms: paintings, sculptures, ceramics from around the world. The former president was born here and rests here.
The Jarnac quays line up trading houses and bourgeois residences. The Charente flows peacefully, white façades reflected in the water. Starting point for river cruises.

activities.text: Tour of the Courvoisier house. More low-key than the Cognac giants, with a family feel. The 'Paradis' cellar holds century-old eaux-de-vie. Tasting included.
River cruise Jarnac–Cognac. Licence-free barge for the day or guided gabare. The river winds between vineyards and villages. Manual locks, contemplative pace.
Visit to François Mitterrand's birthplace. The house where the former president was born in 1916. Guided tour by appointment, intimate atmosphere.

visits.text: The medieval castle of Châteauneuf has vanished. Only the name and presumed site near the current fairground remain. However, the Logis de Barqueville (15th century) facing the church forms a handsome ensemble with the square. Pleasant walk along the shaded riverbanks.

The church of Saint-Pierre (12th century) boasts one of the finest façades in the Charente: three sculpted tiers, a horseman representing Constantine crushing paganism. Inside, carved Romanesque capitals and a little snail hidden in high relief.
The river port brings the town to life. A stop on the Charente for pleasure boaters and canoeists. Café terraces, shaded picnic area. Watersports centre in summer.

activities.text: Canoeing on the Charente. The watersports centre hires kayaks and canoes with return shuttle. Routes from 2 hours to a full day. Calm water, swimming possible at designated stops.

practical_info.includes: Life jackets, dry bag, return shuttle

activities.text: Swimming at the Bain des Dames. The leisure area, labelled Station Sport Nature, has the only laid-out beach on the Charente in the Cognac destination. Lawn, toilets, snack bar. Free.
Fishing on the Charente. Quiet spots upstream and downstream of town. Zander, pike, carp. Daily fishing licence available at the tobacconist.

visits.text: The underground church of Saint-Jean is the largest in Europe: 27 m long, 16 m wide, nearly 20 m high, carved into the cliff in the 12th century. Monumental nave, reliquary hewn from the rock, some 170 tombs in the floor. Stunning.

The church of Saint-Jacques at the top of the village: Romanesque façade with Hispano-Moorish carvings, a reminder of the pilgrims passing through on the Way to Compostela. Finely chiselled archivolt portal.

The village tiers like an amphitheatre above the Dronne. Pebble-paved lanes, white houses with tiled roofs, Spanish-style flower-decked balconies. Classified as one of the Most Beautiful Villages of France since 1993.
The Place Ludovic Trarieux, heart of the village, honours the founder of the League of Human Rights, born here. Lime-tree-shaded terraces, shops, artisans. The spot for a coffee.

activities.text: Visit the monolithic church. Open year-round except 25 Dec and 1 Jan. Bring a layer — it's cool inside. The exceptional acoustics occasionally draw concerts.

practical_info.tip: Bring a layer (cool inside)

activities.text: Swimming in the Dronne. The managed beach below the village has sand, a shaded lawn, slides. Lifeguards in summer. Canoe hire on site.
Canoeing on the Dronne. Gentle routes from the village base. Clear water, wooded banks. Return by shuttle.
Artisan workshops. The village is home to potters, painters, sculptors. Open studio-shops in summer. One-off pieces, meet the creators.

visits.text: The Château de Villebois-Lavalette crowns its hilltop with seven round towers visible for miles. Medieval fortress reworked during the Renaissance, two-storey Romanesque chapel. Guided or self-guided tour with booklet.
The 17th-century covered market hall stands against the castle walls. Chestnut timber frame, stone pillars. On Saturday mornings, the market comes alive: cheeses, poultry, garden vegetables.
The village retains some fine old houses, a restored Romanesque church, and an end-of-the-world feel. At the far edge of the Charente, the Périgord is only a few kilometres away.

activities.text: Guided tour of the Château de Villebois-Lavalette. The association's guides bring history to life: two-storey Romanesque chapel (pilgrims below, lords above), medieval towers, 17th-century residence. Family escape games available.
Saturday morning market. Under the 17th-century hall, local producers and village atmosphere. Goat's cheese, free-range chickens, seasonal vegetables, honey. A real country market.

practical_info.tip: Arrive before 10 am for the best choice

activities.text: Hike around Villebois. Waymarked trails through wooded hills. Mixed-farming landscapes, isolated farms, views of the castle. Several loops from 5 to 12 km.
Drive to Angoulême on back roads. Through southern Charente: vineyards, honey-stone villages, rolling hills. 40 km in an hour at a gentle pace.

seo.h1_title: Charente Circuit: Cognac and Romanesque Heritage in 4 Days
seo.intro_paragraph: From the cognac cellars to Renaissance castles, from the comic book murals of Angoulême to the underground church of Aubeterre: the Charente marries the art of living with a thousand years of heritage. A leisurely circuit along the river, between tastings and character villages.
seo.seo_hook: Cognac ages in centuries-old cellars, Romanesque churches line the Charente: a journey at the rhythm of eau-de-vie.
featured_list: Cognac: tour of the great houses, boat crossing, tasting
Angoulême: comic book capital, Romanesque cathedral, painted walls
La Rochefoucauld: Renaissance castle inhabited for 1,000 years
Aubeterre-sur-Dronne: church carved into the rock, Most Beautiful Village of France

places_taglines.FR::angouleme: comic book capital perched on its rock
places_taglines.FR::la-rochefoucauld: a thousand years of history in a Renaissance castle
places_taglines.FR::confolens: old bridge and half-timbered houses on the Vienne
places_taglines.FR::cognac: birthplace of the world's most famous spirit
places_taglines.FR::villebois-lavalette: six-towered castle and local produce market

practical_context.group_type: Couple or family
highlights: Cité de la BD and Angoulême's painted walls
La Rochefoucauld Renaissance Castle (1,000 years of history)
Cellars of the great cognac houses: Hennessy, Martell, Rémy Martin
Aubeterre monolithic church, Europe's largest
Cruise or canoe on the Charente
Village of Verteuil and its mill at the foot of the castle

itineraries.title: Charente-Maritime Road Trip: La Rochelle, Île de Ré, Fort Boyard and Roman Saintonge
itineraries.subtitle: From La Rochelle's medieval towers to Vauban citadels, between luminous islands and wild estuary
itineraries.climate: Best period: May-June and September-early October, temperatures 18-24°C, optimal sunshine and fewer crowds. Avoid July-August if you want to skip the massive tourist influx on the islands (Ré, Oléron), though temperatures remain pleasant (22-28°C). Mild but rainy and windy winters, not recommended for coastal visits.

map_keywords: Tower of the Lantern La Rochelle
Museum of the New World La Rochelle

visits.text: The three towers of the Old Port are remnants of La Rochelle's medieval fortifications. The Saint-Nicolas Tower (14th century), slightly tilted like Pisa, rises to 37 meters. A chain once linked it to the Chain Tower to close the harbor each evening – the original chain is visible at the tower's base.

The Lantern Tower, with its 55-meter octagonal Gothic spire, served as both lighthouse and prison. Some 600 graffiti carved by English, Spanish and Dutch corsairs adorn its walls – ships, figures, and even a locomotive. Rabelais mentions it in his Fifth Book.

La Rochelle's Old Port was the largest port on the Atlantic coast in the 15th century. Stroll along Cours des Dames and Quai Duperré, lined with terraces. In the evening, the illuminated towers reflect in the basin – one of the most beautiful scenes on the French coast.

The arcades of the city center have sheltered passersby since the Middle Ages. Over 3 km of covered galleries line the shopping streets. Under stone and wooden vaults, half-timbered houses and Renaissance mansions tell of the prosperity of La Rochelle's shipowners.

activities.text: Visit of La Rochelle's three towers. A single ticket grants access to all three monuments. Climbing to the top of Saint-Nicolas Tower offers a complete panorama over the port and roadstead. Allow 2 hours for the full visit.

practical_info.note: Saint-Nicolas Tower closed for renovation (check before visiting)

activities.text: Walk along the rampart walkway between the Chain Tower and Lantern Tower. This section of rampart, called 'Rue sur les Murs', overlooks the Saint-Jean-d'Acre esplanade and offers stunning views of the port.

La Rochelle central market. Under the wrought iron and wooden halls, producers sell Marennes-Oléron oysters, Pineau des Charentes, mogettes (white beans) and tourteau fromager. Lively atmosphere every morning.

practical_info.when: Every morning until 1:30pm, best on Wednesday and Saturday

map_keywords: Tower of the Lantern La Rochelle
Museum of the New World La Rochelle

visits.text: La Rochelle Aquarium is one of the largest private aquariums in Europe. Over 12,000 marine animals in 3 million liters of water. The shark tank and jellyfish gallery are spectacular. Allow 2 to 3 hours for the visit.

The New World Museum occupies Hôtel Fleuriau, an 18th-century shipowner's mansion. Collections on the triangular trade, the French West Indies and the slave trade. An unflinching look at La Rochelle's wealth built on slavery.

The Gabut district, a former bastion converted into a colorful village. Brightly painted wooden houses, artists' studios, terraces facing the marina. An unexpected Scandinavian atmosphere on the Atlantic shore.

activities.text: The Sea Bus and the Ferry connect both sides of the port. A 5-minute crossing, a pleasant alternative to walking around. The electric ferry operates year-round.

Concurrence Beach, the closest to the city center. Fine sand, calm water, view of the towers. Lifeguarded in summer. The Mail promenade lined with tamarisk trees runs along the coast toward Les Minimes.
Yellow bike rental (Yélo) self-service. La Rochelle pioneered bike-sharing in France. Cycle paths lead to Les Minimes beaches and the marina.

visits.text: The Île de Ré bridge, 2.9 km long, has connected the mainland to the island since 1988. Toll on entry (free on exit). The crossing offers a first view of the salt marshes and the black and white bell tower of Ars-en-Ré.

The fortifications of Saint-Martin-de-Ré, built by Vauban between 1681 and 1691, form a 14 km star-shaped rampart. UNESCO World Heritage since 2008, they could shelter the entire island population in the event of an English invasion. Walking or cycling the ramparts is spectacular.

The port of Saint-Martin-de-Ré, nestled within the fortified walls, has quays lined with terraces. Convicts bound for Cayenne departed from here – the citadel served as a depot. Climb the church tower for a panoramic view of the island.

The Phare des Baleines, at the western tip of the island, rises to 60 meters. 257 steps lead to the top - a 360° view over the ocean and the island. The name comes from the whales that used to be stranded on this coast. The old Vauban tower (1682) and a lighthouse museum complete the site. Allow about 15 km from the stopover town, 15 minutes by road.

activities.text: Île de Ré by bike: 110 km of cycle paths connect the island's ten villages. Rentals available in every village. The Saint-Martin → Baleines Lighthouse route (15 km) crosses salt marshes and pine forests.

practical_info.rental: Many rental shops in each village

activities.text: Visit the salt marshes of Loix or Ars-en-Ré. Salt workers harvest fleur de sel by hand using age-old techniques. Guided walks in the marshes, explanations of the work and tastings.

practical_info.tip: Book guided tours in summer

activities.text: Île de Ré beaches: fine sand on the south coast (Bois-Plage, La Couarde), wilder to the north. Fish traps, semi-circular stone walls, catch fish at low tide – an ancestral technique still practiced.

visits.text: The Royal Ropeworks of Rochefort, built between 1666 and 1669, measures 374 meters long – more than the height of the Eiffel Tower. This manufactory supplied ropes to the Royal Navy for two centuries. The International Sea Center presents the arsenal's history and seamanship techniques.

The Louis XV dry dock saw the rebirth of the Hermione, a replica of the frigate that carried La Fayette to America in 1780, rebuilt over 17 years by naval carpenters. The ship has now left for restoration and can no longer be visited in Rochefort. The dock and the arsenal workshops can be seen from the quays, a step away from the Royal Ropeworks.

The National Naval Museum occupies Hôtel de Cheusses, Rochefort's oldest civilian building. Ship models built at the arsenal, navigation instruments, figureheads. The arsenal produced 550 ships between 1666 and 1927, including France's first submarine (Le Plongeur, 1863).

activities.text: Accro-mâts, in the Louis XV dry dock, recreates the Hermione's masts. A treetop adventure course at 30 meters height to experience the sensations of 18th-century topmen. Spectacular final zip line.

practical_info.age: From 7 years accompanied, from 12 years alone

activities.text: Stroll through the Arsenal gardens: the Garden of Returns, the Navy Garden and the King's vegetable garden. Palm trees, Virginia tulip trees, begonias – plants brought back from maritime expeditions. Peace and shade facing the Charente.

The Rochefort transporter bridge (1900), the last of its kind in France, connected both banks of the Charente by a suspended gondola. Listed as a Historic Monument in 1976, restored between 2016 and 2020. Gondola crossings available.

practical_info.note: Check schedules on the official website

visits.text: Brouage, a citadel asleep in the marshes. Founded in 1555, it was Europe's leading salt port before silting up. Richelieu made it an impregnable stronghold between 1628 and 1633 under Pierre d'Argencourt, then Vauban reinforced the fortifications in 1685. Samuel de Champlain, founder of Quebec, was born here around 1570. Today, 500 inhabitants and an uncanny silence.

The Brouage rampart walk (2 km) offers views over former salt marshes turned bird reserve. Black-winged stilts, egrets and spoonbills nest here. The powder magazines, forge and restored church can be visited.

Marennes, oyster capital. The Marennes-Oléron basin produces 45% of French oysters. The Saint-Pierre church bell tower (85 m) is the tallest in Charente-Maritime. The Oyster City explains aging in 'claires', those brackish water pools that green and refine the oysters.

activities.text: Visit an oyster shack. Producers open their establishments to explain farming and aging. Tasting on site with views of the claires – a glass of local white accompanies the oysters.

practical_info.tip: Prefer months with an 'R' for tasting

activities.text: Walk in the Brouage marshes. Marked trails through former salt marshes. Binoculars recommended for watching migratory birds. The sunset over the pools is memorable.

visits.text: Île d'Oléron, the largest French Atlantic island (30 km long). The free viaduct (1966, 3 km) links it to the mainland. Varied landscapes: pine forests in the south, salt marshes in the north, fine sand beaches on the west coast.

The Chassiron lighthouse, at the northern tip of the island, has worn its black and white bands since 1836. 224 steps up to the lantern - a view of Fort Boyard and the Île d'Aix in clear weather. The spiral garden at the foot of the lighthouse echoes the patterns of oyster shells. Allow about 27 km from the stopover town, 30 minutes by road.

Le Château d'Oléron, former stronghold at the island's entrance. The Vauban citadel guarded the estuary. Today, its ramparts house an artisan and local produce market (summer). The colorful port cabins have become artists' studios.

Fort Boyard, oval fortress built between 1801 and 1857 between Oléron and Île d'Aix. Never used militarily, it became famous through the TV game show. No visits inside, but cruises circle it – an iconic silhouette set on the ocean.

activities.text: Cruise around Fort Boyard. Departures from Boyardville or Saint-Denis-d'Oléron. A full circuit of the fort, passing close to the Île d'Aix. Commentary on the history of the construction and stories from the filming. Boyardville is about 15 km from the stopover town, 15 minutes by road.

Oyster tasting at the port of La Cotinière, the leading small-scale fishing port of Charente-Maritime and the sixth in France. Fish auction in the morning, tasting huts in the afternoon. The fines de claire and spéciales oysters from Oléron have an incomparable briny flavor. Allow about 12 km from the stopover town, 15 minutes by road.

Île d'Oléron beaches: Grande Plage at Saint-Trojan, Les Saumonards at Boyardville, Vert-Bois in the south. Maritime pine forests stretch to the sand. The little Saint-Trojan train crosses the forest to Gatseau beach.

visits.text: Royan, a seaside resort rebuilt after the 1945 bombings. The 1950s architecture, called 'Cinquante Glorieuses', now holds the Ville d'Art et d'Histoire label. Modernist villas, curved seafronts, luminous concrete.

Notre-Dame Church of Royan (1958), a raw concrete masterpiece by Guillaume Gillet. A 45-meter elliptical nave, inverted V-shaped vault, abstract stained glass. Controversial at its construction, it is now a listed Historic Monument.

Royan central market, a concrete and glass structure by Louis Simon and André Morisseau (1956). Undulating dome 52 meters in diameter, spectacular natural light. Seafood, orchard fruits, Charentes specialties. One of the finest covered markets in France.

Royan's seafront stretches across 5 beaches: Grande Conche, Foncillon, Chay, Pigeonnier, Pontaillac. Promenade along modernist villas, casino, congress center. Elegant seaside atmosphere facing the Gironde estuary.

activities.text: Guided tour 'Royan 1950s'. The tourist office offers architectural tours with commentary: the Parc district villas, congress center, Protestant temple, bus station. A fresh look at 20th-century heritage.

Grande Conche beach, 2 km of fine sand in an arc. Lifeguarded in summer, surf and sailing schools, terraces facing the ocean. The Cordouan lighthouse, 'Versailles of the sea', stands on the estuary horizon.
Royan-Le Verdon ferry. The 20-minute Gironde estuary crossing offers a unique view of both the Charente and Médoc coasts. Option to continue to Cordouan lighthouse at low tide (guided excursion).

visits.text: Talmont-sur-Gironde, a village of 100 inhabitants perched on a rocky promontory. Listed as one of France's Most Beautiful Villages, it overlooks the Gironde estuary. Lanes lined with hollyhocks, white houses with blue shutters, artisan shops.

Sainte-Radegonde Church of Talmont (12th century), Romanesque Saintonge style, stands at the cliff edge. Its apse overlooks the estuary – the sea has eaten away the cemetery. Sculpted facade, single nave, golden light. One of the most photographed churches in France.

The carrelets of Talmont, fishing huts on stilts equipped with square nets. A traditional estuary technique for catching shrimp, eels and mullet. Some can be rented overnight – a unique sunset experience.

activities.text: Talmont market (summer). In the village lanes, local producers and artisans. Pineau, cognac, jams, soaps. Festive atmosphere on summer evenings with concerts on the square.
Talmont cliff trail. 3 km walk along the estuary, between carrelets and vineyards. View of the Meschers cliffs and their troglodyte caves on the other side of the Gironde.

visits.text: The Arch of Germanicus (19 AD), a two-bay Roman arch that marked the entrance to the bridge over the Charente. Moved stone by stone in 1843 to escape demolition. Dedicatory inscriptions to Tiberius, Germanicus and Drusus Caesar are readable on the attic.

The Gallo-Roman amphitheater of Saintes (1st century) could hold 15,000 spectators. Carved into a valley in the hillside, it retains its tiers, vomitoria and elliptical arena. Summer concerts and shows in this ancient setting.

The Abbaye aux Dames (11th-12th century), the first women's monastery in Saintonge. Romanesque facade sculpted with grimacing heads and fantastic animals. Conical bell tower covered in stone scales. Now a cultural center and home to an early music festival.

Saintes old town stretches between the Charente and the hillsides. Saint-Pierre Cathedral (rebuilt after the Wars of Religion), 18th-century mansions, medieval lanes. Wrought iron halls for the market.

activities.text: Guided tour of Gallo-Roman Saintes. The tourist office offers a complete circuit: Arch of Germanicus, Saint-Saloine baths, amphitheater, archaeological museum. Mediolanum Santonum was capital of the Aquitaine province.

Cruise on the Charente departing from Saintes. Traditional gabares or electric boats head upriver toward Cognac. Meadow landscapes, weeping willows, grey herons. Commentary on the history of cognac river transport.
Pineau and cognac tasting. Regional producers open their cellars for guided visits. Pineau des Charentes, a blend of grape must and cognac, is enjoyed chilled as an aperitif.

seo.h1_title: Charente-Maritime Road Trip: La Rochelle, Île de Ré, Fort Boyard and Roman Saintonge
seo.intro_paragraph: From La Rochelle's medieval towers to Île de Ré's Vauban ramparts, from Rochefort's Royal Rope Factory to Oléron's oyster shacks. Charente-Maritime unfolds its coastline between sleeping citadels, iconic lighthouses and villages perched above the estuary. A journey between maritime heritage and Atlantic gentleness.
seo.seo_hook: Medieval towers, salt marshes, claires-aged oysters: Charente-Maritime lives to the rhythm of the tides, between heritage and the Atlantic.
featured_list: La Rochelle: the three towers of the Old Port
Île de Ré: UNESCO Vauban fortifications and Baleines lighthouse
Rochefort: Royal Ropeworks and naval arsenal
Oléron: oysters and Fort Boyard views
Talmont-sur-Gironde: Romanesque church on the cliff
Saintes: amphitheater and Arch of Germanicus

places_taglines.FR::ile-oleron: largest island on the French Atlantic

itineraries.title: Corrèze Road Trip: Villages and Dordogne Valley
itineraries.subtitle: From Tulle to Pompadour, a journey through the heart of Limousin
itineraries.climate: Best time: May-June and September-October, temperatures 15-25°C, lush greenery. Avoid November-March (cold, wet, often overcast) and late-summer afternoon storms. Hilly Massif Central region, bring layers for cool mornings.

visits.text: Notre-Dame Cathedral of Tulle. Built from 1103 on the site of a Merovingian abbey, it blends Romanesque and Gothic styles. Its octagonal spire bell tower rises between 73 and 75 meters depending on sources - it's the tallest in Limousin. Inside, the Great Organ from 1839 is listed as a Historic Monument, and the large blue stained glass window by Jean-Jacques Grüber (1979) tells the story of the Lunade, a procession that ended a plague epidemic in the 14th century.

13th-century Gothic cloister. The only remaining cloister in Bas-Limousin, it adjoined the former Saint-Martin Abbey. The "gallery of angels" features sculpted vaults. The chapter house preserves two 14th-century murals depicting the Last Supper and Christ's Entry into Jerusalem. Listed as a Historic Monument since 1840.

Cité de l'Accordéon et des Patrimoines. Opened in April 2024 in the former Bank of France, it presents three exhibition paths: the accordion (Tulle is the French capital of the instrument with the Maugein manufacture since 1919), lace in "poinct de Tulle" and the history of the Arms Manufacture. Interactive museum with audio guide available in Occitan.

Loyac House. Architectural masterpiece from the 16th century located in the Enclos quarter. The facade blends Renaissance and Flamboyant Gothic styles, adorned with pediments sculpted with plants and animals (lion, greyhound, wild boar, mermaid). Two watchtowers frame the columned doorway.

activities.text: Stroll through the Trech quarter and the Enclos. Tulle's medieval heart revolves around the cathedral. Sloping streets, staircases, tall 15th-16th century houses with corbelling and wooden balconies. Don't miss the Coin des Clampes fountain, "the meeting place of the gossipers" in Occitan, immortalized by a 1984 sculpture.

practical_info.tip: The town extends 4 km along the Corrèze river, nicknamed "La Coureuse" (The Runner)

activities.text: Tulle Market. The banks of the Corrèze come alive on Wednesday and Saturday mornings. Local products, friendly atmosphere along the river.

visits.text: Saint-Pierre Church and its sculpted tympanum. Romanesque building from the 11th century with a rare detail: the tympanum representing Christ's Ascension is made of white Turenne limestone, which contrasts with the surrounding red sandstone. The octagonal gabled bell tower exceeds 20 meters. The church was divided in two during the Wars of Religion to accommodate both religious services simultaneously.

Penitents' Chapel (Saint-Maximin). 14th-century Gothic chapel, it served as a burial place for noble families including the Maussacs (coat of arms visible on a vault keystone). From the mid-17th to the late 19th century, the Black Penitents brotherhood met here. Saved from ruin in 1927 by the Friends of Collonges, it houses a stained glass window by Francis Chigot (1937) depicting the Resurrection, and two contemporary stained glass windows by Didier Mencoboni and Olivier Juteau (2016).

Vassinhac Castle. Built in 1583, this manor belonged to the lords of Collonges who were also governors of the Viscounty of Turenne. The facade features typical Renaissance mullioned windows, and two round towers frame the structure. Not open for interior visits.

Mermaid House. 16th-century residence that owes its name to the mermaid sculpted to the right of the entrance door. It houses a small museum of folk arts and traditions with a reconstruction of a traditional Corrèze interior.

16th-century grain hall. Under this covered hall, the wine and walnut oil market was held. The floor is paved with red sandstone. It was here that Charles Ceyrac, former mayor, launched the association of Most Beautiful Villages of France in 1982. Collonges was the first village to receive the label.

activities.text: Walk through the streets with 25 towers. Allow 2 hours for the complete tour. The noble houses with blue schist or slate roofs were built by officers of the Viscounty of Turenne between the 15th and 16th centuries. Vines climb the red facades - the green/red contrast is striking. The red sandstone comes from a geological fault between Brive and Meyssac, rich in iron oxide.

practical_info.tip: Arrive early in the morning or late afternoon to avoid summer crowds
practical_info.parking: Two paid parking lots at the village entrances (mid-March to mid-November)

activities.text: Tasting of Corrèze straw wine. This sweet wine is produced from grapes dried on straw racks. A few local producers offer tastings in the village or around Meyssac.
Meyssac Market. 1.5 km from Collonges, the neighboring village holds a market on Tuesdays and Fridays year-round, and on Sundays in July-August.

practical_info.special: Local Producers Market Friday evening 5pm-8pm in Saillac (3 km) in summer

visits.text: Caesar's Tower (13th century). Circular keep 18 meters high. The 63 steps of the spiral staircase lead to the top offering a 360° panorama over the Corrèze causse. Turenne was the seat of a powerful viscounty for 10 centuries, virtually independent from the Kingdom of France: the viscounts minted coins and levied taxes. On May 8, 1738, Charles-Godefroy, the last viscount riddled with gambling debts, sold everything to Louis XV. End of the saying "Happy as a viscomtin".

Treasure Tower (13th century). Rectangular keep with buttresses measuring 9.50m by 12.50m where the viscounty's archives and treasure were kept. The Guards' Room, 10 meters high under vaulted ceiling, features a beautiful fireplace and a collection of Louis XIII salt chests.
Collegiate Church of Notre-Dame Saint-Pantaleon. 17th-century church built by the viscounts of Turenne. The interior contains a gilded altarpiece and period woodwork.

activities.text: Climb via Rue Droite. The main street climbs from the bottom of the village to the towers. Houses with turrets, watchtowers and Renaissance windows testify to past prosperity. Good shoes recommended, the slope is steep and the cobblestones sometimes slippery.

practical_info.tip: Parking at the bottom of the village, then walking uphill required

visits.text: Saint-Pierre Abbey Church and its Romanesque tympanum. Founded in the 9th century, the Benedictine abbey features a tympanum sculpted around 1125 representing the Parousia (Christ's return at the end of times). It's one of the masterpieces of Limousin Romanesque sculpture, comparable to Moissac or Conques. Christ in Majesty is surrounded by apostles, angels and monsters symbolizing evil.
Penitents' Chapel. On the banks of the Dordogne, this 12th-century chapel with its bell gable is reflected in the water. Iconic view of Beaulieu from the river.
Renaissance House. 16th-century turreted residence in the village center, witness to the prosperity of the era.

activities.text: Gabare boat ride on the Dordogne. The gabare "Adèle et Clarisse", built in 2002 using traditional methods, offers 45-minute narrated cruises about the history of the gabariers. These boatmen once transported wood, Auvergne cheeses and coal to Bordeaux.

practical_info.booking: Reservation required at Dordogne Valley Tourist Office
practical_info.summer: Festive or gourmet cruises on Fridays at 6pm in July-August

activities.text: Tasting of Beaulieu strawberries. The mild climate of the "Limousin Riviera" allows strawberry cultivation. Local producers at Wednesday market.

visits.text: Quai Lestourgie. Row of houses with wooden balconies and stone-slab roofs that testifies to Argentat's gabarier past. It was the main loading port and departure point to Aquitaine - gabares were also called "argentats" because many were built here. Three historic ports line the Dordogne.
Heritage House. Exhibition on the history of the gabariers and life in the Dordogne valley before the construction of the dams.

activities.text: Gabare cruise through the Dordogne gorges. Theatrical cruises with actor departing from Grafeuille (10 min drive from Argentat). Duration 1h15, minimum 8 people per departure. A storyteller brings to life the epic of the gabariers in the wild gorges upstream of the town.

practical_info.booking: Reservation required, tickets at Tourist Offices or online
practical_info.summer: Cruise in English on Monday 6:15pm, in Dutch on Wednesday 10:15am. Nature cruise on Monday 9am

activities.text: Canoe trip down the Dordogne. Several routes possible from Argentat: sporty 8 km route (1h30-2h) with class 2 rapids to Monceaux, or adventure route of 22-25 km (full day) to Beaulieu. Wild landscapes, Corrèze forests, possibility of picnic break on pebble beaches.

practical_info.providers: Escapade Nature, Saga Team Dordogne, Copeyre Canoë

activities.text: "Tous sur le pont" Festival. First weekend of July, Argentat celebrates its gabarier past with entertainment, reenactments and the legend of the Coulobre, a monstrous serpent that terrorized boatmen.

visits.text: Saint-Pierre Abbey Church. Former Benedictine abbey church built from 1030, consecrated in 1095. The gabled bell tower, typically Limousin, rises from a square base to an octagonal plan. The 11th-century crypt, unique in Bas-Limousin, housed the relics of Breton saints Léon and Coronat, transferred here for protection from Vikings. Listed as Historic Monument in 1840.
Bécharie Gate. 14th-century fortified gate, sole remnant of the medieval ramparts that protected the town.

activities.text: Walk on the rocky promontory. Uzerche is nicknamed the "Pearl of Limousin". The local saying goes "Who has a house in Uzerche has a castle in Limousin". The village perched on a spur overlooks a meander of the Vézère. The towers and turrets of noble houses testify to the town's past importance. Panoramic view from the Lunade esplanade.

practical_info.tip: Remarkable viewpoint from the bridge spanning the Vézère on the west side

visits.text: Saint-Pardoux Church. Church from the late 15th century housing an exceptional treasure: the reliquary shrine of Saint Stephen, a masterpiece of 12th-century Limoges enamel. Also several ancient statues and liturgical objects.
Notre-Dame du Rosaire Chapel. White Penitents' chapel located on the village's main street.
Ruins of Roche Haute Castle. Medieval ruins overlooking the village, visible from the main street.

activities.text: Gimel Waterfalls - Vuillier Park. The Montane river plunges in three spectacular falls totaling 143 meters: the Grand Saut (45 m), the Redole (38 m) and the Queue de Cheval (60 m) which dives into the "Inferno abyss". Painter Gaston Vuillier developed this park between 1893 and 1899 with staircases and observation points. Abel Hugo, Victor's brother, was the first to describe the site's beauty in "Picturesque France" (1883). Listed site since 1912.

practical_info.access: Entrance fee (around €6), steep path with stairs
practical_info.warning: Good shoes essential, not accessible for strollers
practical_info.tip: Café-terrace with view of the Grand Saut in the park

activities.text: Hike to the 4th waterfall and Pont du Péage. Free circuit of about 1h30 one way to discover an additional waterfall outside the paid park. The "cascadelles" are also accessible via the Short Circuit in the forest.

practical_info.tip: Map available at Tulle Tourist Office

visits.text: Labenche Museum. Located in a 16th-century Renaissance mansion listed as Historic Monument, this art and history museum presents 17 rooms. Unique collection in France of 10 tapestries from the English Royal Mortlake Manufactory (17th century). Also features Claude Debussy's piano, prehistoric and Gallo-Roman archaeological collections, and sections on local traditions.
Saint-Martin Collegiate Church. 12th-century Romanesque church in the heart of the old town. The 6th-century baptistery, discovered during excavations, testifies to the site's antiquity.
Saint-Libéral Chapel. 15th-century Gothic building converted into a contemporary art space, programmed by the Labenche Museum.

activities.text: Brive Market. On Saturday morning, it's one of the most renowned in the region. Under the Georges Brassens hall and on the surrounding squares, local producers and market gardeners offer regional specialties. Don't miss the violet mustard of Brive, a specialty made with grape must.

practical_info.days: Main market Saturday morning, smaller market Tuesday and Thursday
practical_info.specialties: Violet mustard, foie gras, Périgord walnuts

activities.text: Tasting of Corrèze specialties. The region offers generous gastronomy: farcidures (grated potato dumplings with bacon), mique (poached dough ball served with salted pork), millassou (potato pancake), tourtous (buckwheat crepes), potato pie, flognarde (apple flan).

practical_info.tip: Les Délices de Mathou for potato pie, Neige grocery store to buy traditional farcidures grater

visits.text: Pompadour Castle. Fortress rebuilt in the 15th century by the Hélie family. In 1745, Louis XV bought the estate and gave it with the title of Marquise to his favorite Jeanne-Antoinette Poisson - who never visited it, deeming the property too far from the Court! She resold it in 1761. The following year, Louis XV bought it back and transformed it into a Royal Stud Farm. Tour of 11 rooms including the library, with furniture, Aubusson tapestries and Limoges porcelain.
Marquise Stables and Orangery. House the National Stud horses. The Orangery hosts equestrian shows in summer.

Chignac Estate Broodmare Stud. France's only national broodmare stud, birthplace of the Anglo-Arab breed created in Pompadour in the 19th century. You can see foals being born and growing (present from March to October). Visit to discover breeding and selection methods.

activities.text: Horse racing at the racecourse. Classified 1st category for steeplechase and 2nd category A for flat racing, it's one of the most beautiful racecourses in France with its 2000-meter natural sand track facing the castle. 11 race days per year in summer.

Equestrian shows at the castle. In July-August, equestrian cabarets are organized in the evening on the castle terraces or in the Orangery riding hall. The company "Christophe et Max Hasta Luego" notably offers internationally renowned shows.
Horse Festival - August 15th. Major annual event: Saint Hubert mass at the racecourse, show jumping competition, horse races, demonstrations and equestrian shows.
Limousin Apple Route. Pompadour is also the starting point of this route that crosses the PDO Limousin Apple orchards. Farm visits possible in summer.

practical_info.tip: Inquire at Terres de Corrèze Tourist Office for visits

seo.h1_title: Corrèze Road Trip: Villages and Dordogne Valley
seo.intro_paragraph: Visit Collonges-la-Rouge and its sandstone buildings, the hilltop village of Turenne, Beaulieu-sur-Dordogne, the Gimel waterfalls, Uzerche on its peninsula, and the Pompadour stud farm. Corrèze, charming villages by the water.
seo.seo_hook: Collonges red stone, Gimel waterfalls, hilltop villages: discover Corrèze, between heritage and emerald rivers.
featured_list: Collonges: red stone beauty
Beaulieu: riverside charm radiates
Turenne: castle crowns cliff
Gimel: waterfall plunges spectacularly

highlights: Collonges-la-Rouge's unique red sandstone architecture
Spectacular Gimel waterfalls with 143-meter drop
Traditional gabare boat rides on the Dordogne
Historic Pompadour stud farm and equestrian shows
Medieval hilltop villages with panoramic views
Rich Corrèze gastronomy and local markets

itineraries.title: Burgundy's Grand Crus Route: Dijon to Santenay
itineraries.subtitle: 1 days along the Champs-Élysées of wine: from Côte de Nuits to Côte de Beaune, through Gevrey-Chambertin, Beaune, Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet.
itineraries.notes: The Hospices de Beaune auction takes place on the 3rd Sunday of November, an exceptional occasion to visit. Santenay has no direct TGV; Chagny station (5 km) connects to Dijon or Lyon.
itineraries.climate: Best time: May-June and September-October, temperatures 15-25°C, vines in bloom or harvest season. Avoid winter (frequent frost, dormant vineyards) and July-August (heat and heavy tourist crowds). Fall is ideal for colors and gastronomy.

map_keywords: Palais des Ducs de Bourgogne Dijon
Château du Clos de Vougeot Vougeot

visits.text: The day begins in Dijon, capital of the Dukes of Burgundy and natural starting point of the Route des Grands Crus. Place de la Libération forms a classical hemicycle designed by Jules Hardouin-Mansart in 1685, the same architect who worked for Louis XIV at Versailles. Behind the façade lies the medieval ducal palace with its Tour Philippe le Bon, standing 46 meters high—you can climb it for sweeping views over the city's rooftops. The palace-museum complex has been inscribed alongside the Climats of Burgundy on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 2015.

Gevrey-Chambertin, about ten kilometers south of Dijon, is the largest wine-producing commune in the Côte de Nuits with its 409 hectares and 9 grands crus. This village carries a notable anecdote: Napoleon Bonaparte made it his favorite wine—before each meal, his valet would serve him half a bottle of Chambertin, diluted with water according to the memoirs of chamberlain Constant Wairy. During the 1812 Russian campaign, his aide-de-camp kept the bottle against his chest to maintain the proper temperature. The first vines in Gevrey date back to the 1st century BC, as identified by archaeological excavations.

The Château du Clos de Vougeot stands as Burgundy's most emblematic wine monument: Cistercian monks from Cîteaux Abbey began planting here between 1109 and 1115, gradually assembling a 50-hectare estate in a single block—the largest grand cru in the Côte de Nuits. The current Renaissance château was added in 1551 by Dom Jean XI Loisier, Abbot of Cîteaux. In 1944, the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin made it their headquarters. Allow an hour to visit the four monumental oak capstan presses and the 12th-century Cistercian cellar—they remain in their original position.

Vosne-Romanée is the most celebrated village in the Côte de Nuits, though you'll see little more than rows of vines, a Romanesque bell tower and a few houses. Stop at the crossroads of the wine routes: signposts indicate the parcels of Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, Richebourg—names that drive auction prices skyward worldwide. Romanée-Conti covers barely 1.8 hectares and produces around 5,000 bottles per year. If you walk up into the vineyards, you'll gain a view of the slopes in their entirety: this is where you'll physically grasp what a Burgundian 'climat' truly means.

Nuits-Saint-Georges closes the day with its blue stone streets and 12th-century Romanesque church. The town is known for its full-bodied red wines—it has no grand cru but numerous renowned premiers crus such as Les Vaucrains, Les Saint-Georges or Les Cailles. Wander the wine-town streets before heading to Beaune for the night.

Cassissium, in Nuits-Saint-Georges, is the museum space dedicated to Burgundy's crème de cassis: the fruit, the liqueur, and the history of this emblematic product that goes into kir. The contemporary building offers a sensory journey with tastings.

activities.text: Guided tasting at a Côte de Nuits estate: a winegrower or wine merchant walks you through the hierarchy of Burgundy appellations—village, premier cru, grand cru—on the same grape variety, Pinot Noir. It's the best way to concretely understand what terroir changes in the glass. Book ahead, as time slots are limited.

visits.text: Beaune is the wine capital of Burgundy, and its landmark, the Hôtel-Dieu, ranks among the finest civil buildings of the Middle Ages in France. Founded in 1443 by Nicolas Rolin, Chancellor of the Duke of Burgundy, and his wife Guigone de Salins as a 'palace for the poor'—Rolin, immensely wealthy, sought in this way to buy his salvation. The flamboyant Gothic edifice served as an active hospital until 1971. Inside, the Salle des Pauvres measures 50 meters long and can accommodate 30 beds. The collection's masterpiece is Rogier van der Weyden's Last Judgment polyptych, commissioned by Rolin—allow at least 1h30 for the visit. Every third Sunday of November, 41 cuvées from the Hospices wine estate are auctioned under the Halles de Beaune, the world's most famous charity sale.

Beaune's ramparts form Burgundy's finest fortified enclosure: built in the 15th and 16th centuries, they remain virtually intact and enclose several kilometers of cellars carved into limestone rock. Walk the complete circuit on foot—35 towers and 12 bastions—to see the town from the outside before diving into its medieval lanes. The 12th-century Collégiale Notre-Dame also deserves a visit for its Flemish tapestries depicting the Life of the Virgin.

Savigny-lès-Beaune, 5 km north-west of Beaune, is worth a detour for its 14th-century château and its 'unusual collections': some fifty racing motorcycles and a collection of military aircraft. Savigny's vineyards produce fruity, approachable Pinot Noirs; the appellation is often the best value for money on the Côte de Beaune.

Aloxe-Corton marks the entrance to the Côte de Beaune with its emblematic hill. Corton and Corton-Charlemagne are the only red and white grands crus in the Côte de Beaune—Charlemagne is said to have owned vines here in the 8th century. Stop at the viewpoint to see the wooded crown of the Corton hill overlooking the vine rows: it's the most photographed image of the area.

Pommard, whose name alone sets the tone, is the Côte de Beaune's best-known Pinot Noir village with its 28 premiers crus. The village is classic: a Romanesque church, stone winegrowers' houses, a small square. But tasting cellars abound, and the Clos des Épeneaux vineyard, a monopole parcel at the heart of the appellation, is visible from the road.

activities.text: Commented tasting in the Côte de Beaune at a winery or négociant: Pinot Noir here tends to be suppler than in the Côte de Nuits, and Chardonnay begins to appear. It's an opportunity to compare the two côtes in a single glass. Ask to taste a village wine alongside a premier cru from the same estate—the price difference always makes more sense in the glass.

visits.text: Meursault is nicknamed the 'white wine capital of Burgundy'—and the title is well deserved. Its 400-hectare vineyard devotes 95% of its surface to Chardonnay, on clay and limestone soils ideal for this grape variety. Tour the village starting with the 14th-century Gothic church, then walk past centuries-old cellars: the winegrowers' 'little châteaux' testify to ancient opulence. Thomas Jefferson, future President of the United States, wrote to his supplier on January 22, 1789: 'I am in urgent need of Meursault... it is the one I prefer!'

Puligny-Montrachet is the commune of the world's most sought-after white wines: its 4 grands crus—Montrachet, Chevalier-Montrachet, Bâtard-Montrachet and Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet—are often designated as the planet's finest Chardonnays. The Montrachet grand cru itself covers only 7.99 hectares, straddling Puligny and Chassagne. Walking among the rows, look for the signs marking the parcels—sometimes just a few meters separate a village appellation from a premier cru, and a €50 bottle from a €500 one.

Chassagne-Montrachet, Puligny's neighbor, shares two of the same grands crus but is also known for its red wines—discreet but excellent. Stroll through the honey-stone village to feel the atmosphere of a place where every house conceals a cellar. The commune added Montrachet to its name in 1879, to capture the renown of the grand cru it shares.

Santenay closes the Côte de Beaune—and with it the UNESCO-inscribed Climats of Burgundy, which stretch from Dijon to here. The commune bears a dual vocation: viticultural, with 12 premiers crus in Pinot Noir, and thermal—its waters are Europe's richest in lithium and have been known since Roman antiquity. The Château de Santenay dominates the vines; Philippe le Hardi, Duke of Burgundy, was one of its owners. From atop Mont de Sène (521 m), called the 'Mountain of the Three Crosses,' the view extends on clear days to the Jura and Mont Blanc.

activities.text: The Voie des Vignes cycling route follows small roads between Beaune and Santenay over a 35 km section without excessive elevation: it passes through Pommard, Volnay, Meursault, Puligny and Chassagne. Rental shops offer bikes—traditional or electric—in Beaune and the villages. It's the slowest and most pleasant way to read the wine landscape: you'll see the changes in soil, exposure and stone colors from wall to wall.

practical_info.booking: Bike rental should be booked in advance during peak season

activities.text: Hot air ballooning over the Côte de Beaune, departing from the Beaune or Pommard area, is the experience that gives this entire vineyard its geographic meaning. Seen from above, the Côte resembles a mosaic of puzzle pieces—each parcel has its own soil color, slope, exposure. Flights take place early morning or late afternoon, depending on winds. Operators offer regular departures from May to October; book several weeks ahead in summer.

practical_info.booking: Booking essential, several weeks in advance in summer

seo.h1_title: Burgundy's Grand Crus Route: Dijon to Santenay
seo.intro_paragraph: The Route des Grands Crus follows 60 kilometers of vineyards between Dijon and Santenay, traversing the world's most renowned appellations: Gevrey-Chambertin where Napoleon had his Chambertin delivered even during military campaigns, Vougeot with its 50-hectare Cistercian estate in a single block, Beaune and its Hôtel-Dieu founded in 1443, Meursault with its Chardonnays favored by Thomas Jefferson, and Puligny-Montrachet with its 4 grands crus often designated as the planet's finest white wines.
seo.seo_hook: Gevrey-Chambertin, Clos de Vougeot, Hospices de Beaune, Meursault and Montrachet: 1 days along the Champs-Élysées of Burgundy wine.
featured_list: Hospices de Beaune: Gothic Hôtel-Dieu founded in 1443, Rogier van der Weyden's Last Judgment and November wine auction
Château du Clos de Vougeot: 50 hectares of Cistercian vineyard in a single block, 12th-century presses, home of the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin
Meursault: 400 hectares of Chardonnay, white wine capital of Burgundy, annual Paulée on the Monday of the Trois Glorieuses
Puligny-Montrachet: 4 grands crus including the 8-hectare Montrachet, often considered the world's finest white wine

The Château du Clos de Vougeot, 12th-century Cistercian foundation, 50 hectares in a single block with medieval presses still in place
