Yellow Train crossing the Pyrenees up to 1,600 meters altitude
Odeillo solar furnace concentrating solar energy to 3,500°C

itineraries.title: Alsace and the Wine Route: Strasbourg to the Vosges
itineraries.subtitle: 6 days between Strasbourg's Gothic cathedral, the wine villages of the Wine Route, and the pink sandstone forests of the Northern Vosges
itineraries.notes: Haut-Koenigsbourg castle is closed January 1st, May 1st, and December 25th. The Schoenenbourg fortification (Maginot Line) is open seasonally only. Saverne's rose garden is accessible from late May through late August.
itineraries.climate: Best time: May-June and September-October, temperatures 18-25°C, ideal for the Wine Route. Avoid July-August (intense heat up to 35°C, frequent storms) and January-February (grey, cold, possible snow in the Vosges). Semi-continental climate with harsh winters.

visits.text: Strasbourg Cathedral deserves at least an hour outside alone. Its 142-meter spire in pink Vosges sandstone, completed in 1439 by Jean Hültz of Cologne, made this the tallest building in Christendom for over two centuries—from 1647 to 1874. Victor Hugo called it a 'prodigy of the gigantic and the delicate'; Goethe fell in love here for the first time. Inside, don't miss the 1574 astronomical clock and the 14-meter rose window. If you want to climb to the 66-meter platform (330 steps), go in the morning—lines are short and the light on the rooftops is beautiful.

From Place de la Cathédrale, dive into La Petite France. This medieval tanners' quarter—one of the best-preserved in Europe—concentrates 16th-century half-timbered houses that reflect in the arms of the Ill River. The Grande Île as a whole has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1988: it was the first historic city center in France to earn this designation. Wander aimlessly toward the Ponts Couverts—three 13th-century towers that once guarded the entrance to the quarter.

The Palais Rohan, built between 1731 and 1742 for Cardinal Armand de Rohan-Soubise, houses three museums within its rococo salons: the Decorative Arts Museum (with royal apartments where Marie-Antoinette stayed), the Fine Arts Museum, and the Archaeological Museum. Budget at least 90 minutes if you visit all three, 45 if you only tour the apartments. The riverfront façade alone is worth the detour.

activities.text: In the evening, step into the Alsatian Museum, housed in three 17th-century houses connected by wooden galleries. The reconstructions of Alsatian interiors from the 18th to 20th centuries—kitchens, bedrooms, shops—are strikingly precise. The atmosphere feels like a giant family attic, warmly lit.

End the day at Place Kléber, Strasbourg's beating heart. General Kléber's statue stands at the center of this grand paved square. The brasserie terraces around the square are ideal for catching your breath and watching Strasbourg life unfold. If you come in December, the Christmas market held here since 1570 is one of Europe's oldest—the first records date precisely to that year.

visits.text: The Neustadt quarter holds a surprise: this extension of Strasbourg built between 1871 and 1918, when the city was German, has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2017. The Wilhelminian architecture—imposing, ornamental, designed to manifest the power of the Second Reich—contrasts radically with yesterday's medieval core. Place de la République with its Rhine Palace (1889) and the University (1884) are the centerpieces. Take time to walk along Boulevard de la Victoire.

Climb to the terrace of the Vauban Dam for one of Strasbourg's finest panoramas. This late-17th-century military work, designed by Vauban on Louis XIV's orders, could flood the entire lower town within hours to stop an invading army. From the terrace, you take in the Ponts Couverts, La Petite France, and the city's steeples—it's free and worth the climb.

Parc de l'Orangerie stretches across 26 hectares in the heart of the European quarter. Created in the 17th century then redesigned for Empress Joséphine in 1804 (a pavilion is dedicated to her), it's Strasbourg's oldest public park. Storks nest here every spring—the symbolic bird of Alsace. It's the perfect spot to unwind after two intensive days in the city.

activities.text: Board a boat for a cruise on the Ill. Several operators offer 70-minute circuits that follow the Grande Île then the Neustadt, with multilingual commentary on board. It's the best way to see the cathedral, La Petite France, and the Palais Rohan from the water—the angles are completely different. Book ahead in summer.

Take the detour to the European district, a 20-minute walk from the center. The European Parliament in glass and steel, inaugurated in 1999, symbolizes Strasbourg's role as a capital of Europe. The European Court of Human Rights is just opposite. The architectural ensemble is striking.

visits.text: Obernai concentrates the best of medieval Alsace on a single square. At Place du Marché—where the weekly market has been documented since 1301—the Renaissance Town Hall (1523, remodeled in 1610), the 1554 Corn Exchange (originally a butcher shop and salt store), the 1579 Six-Bucket Well, and the Kappellturm belfry form a remarkably cohesive ensemble. Arrive in the morning for the light and before the tour buses descend.

The Kappellturm belfry dominates the square at 60 meters tall. It's what remains of a chapel built in the late 13th century—the chapel was destroyed in 1873 but the bell tower survived, with its six bells, the two oldest dating from 1429 and 1474. The gallery with its watchtowers was added in 1596-97. On the northeast buttress, you'll find the official measurements of the ell and dagger carved into the stone—medieval measurement standards.

Obernai is the legendary birthplace of Saint Odile, patroness of Alsace, born blind in the 7th century and said to have regained her sight on the day of her baptism. The medieval ramparts that still encircle the center—1,400 meters of walls with towers and moats—testify to the town's strategic importance. In 1354, Obernai joined nine other cities to found the Decapolis, the league of free imperial cities of Alsace. A walk along the rampart path gives you a good sense of the scale of the work.

Saints Peter and Paul Church, built between 1867 and 1872 in monumental neo-Gothic style, preserves two classified treasures: the 1882 Merklin organ and the 1504 Holy Sepulchre altar, which depicts the risen Christ surrounded by the Holy Women with striking realism for its time.

activities.text: Climb to Mont Sainte-Odile, 15 km from Obernai, Alsace's foremost pilgrimage site since the 7th century. The Abbey of Hohenbourg perches at 764 meters and offers views on clear days as far as the Bernese Alps and the Black Forest. Around the abbey runs the Pagan Wall—a 10 km enceinte of cyclopean stones whose origin remains debated, probably Celtic. An 11 km hiking circuit allows you to walk its full perimeter.

In the evening, linger in Obernai's lanes to taste Alsatian specialties in a winstub: tarte flambée, baeckeoffe, choucroute garnie, and sweet kouglof for dessert. The town is the Bas-Rhin's second tourist destination after Strasbourg—restaurants are numerous and quality is generally good.

visits.text: The Humanist Library of Sélestat is one of the Bas-Rhin's finest surprises. Housed since 1889 in a former neo-Romanesque corn exchange built by Gustave Klotz (1843-1845), entirely restructured by Rudy Ricciotti and reopened in 2018, it preserves one of Europe's most precious collections. Its treasure: the 423 volumes of the personal library of Beatus Rhenanus (1485-1547), friend of Erasmus born in Sélestat, bequeathed to his native city at his death. The collection has been inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register since 2011. Notable items include a 7th-century Merovingian lectionary—the oldest book preserved in Alsace—and a copy of the 1507 Cosmographiae Introductio where the name 'America' appears for the first time.

Sélestat's Romanesque church of Sainte-Foy dates from 1094 and is part of the Alsatian Romanesque Route. Its three-aisle nave in pink Vosges sandstone and octagonal tower are perfect examples of Rhenish Romanesque art. Before it, visit the Gothic church of Saint-Georges—built between the 13th and 15th centuries—which once housed the parish library of Sélestat's Latin school, with some volumes chained to lecterns to protect them from theft.

Wander through Sélestat's historic center—its Renaissance houses, Vauban ramparts, and fountains tell of a time when it was one of the ten free cities of the Alsatian Decapolis. An amusing detail: the city archives preserve the world's first written mention of a Christmas tree, dated 1521, where the city notes the purchase of wood to 'make a Christmas tree'.

activities.text: From Sélestat, admire the silhouette of Haut-Koenigsbourg castle perched at 757 meters on its rocky outcrop—it dominates the entire Alsace plain and can be seen from many points in town. You'll visit it in detail tomorrow, but seeing it from the plain already gives you a good sense of its imposing character and the political dimension of its restoration.
In summer, Sélestat's Corso Fleuri transforms the town with its giant floral floats. Check the local program according to the period of your visit.

visits.text: Haut-Koenigsbourg castle is history within history. First mentioned in 1147, razed by Swedish troops after a 52-day siege in 1633, it lay in ruins for two and a half centuries before the city of Sélestat offered it in 1899 to Emperor Wilhelm II of Hohenzollern. He saw in it a symbol of Alsace's Germanic identity and entrusted the restoration to architect Bodo Ebhardt—a project from 1900 to 1908 that resurrected the castle as it was around 1500, in the Thierstein era. Pass through the high gate: two-thirds of the walls are medieval, the rest reconstructed using documented methods. Nearly 550,000 visitors per year.

The castle's lower court houses a forge, water mill, and reconstructed inn—a village within the village, which functioned self-sufficiently during sieges. The ramparts extend 270 meters. Two artillery towers flank the great bastion. Climb to the bastion terrace for the panorama: the Alsace plain, the Black Forest to the east, the Vosges to the west, and on exceptional days the Swiss Alps. Bring warm clothing—even in summer, it's often 5°C cooler than in the plain.

The banquet hall—called the 'Kaiser's Hall'—is the castle's most overtly political room. Wilhelm II had it enlarged beyond its original dimensions (a gallery indicates the initial height) and covered with heraldic frescoes by Léo Schnug illustrating Alsace's Germanic character. The imperial eagle dominates the coats of arms of Alsatian cities. Propaganda in stone worth seeing for what it reveals about the restoration's political ambition.

The medieval garden arranged in the lower enceinte cultivates aromatic and medicinal plants according to medieval methods—squares bordered by woven branches called 'plessis,' which protected against wild animals. Jean Renoir filmed a scene from 'La Grande Illusion' (1937) here, and illustrator John Howe, who worked on 'The Lord of the Rings,' says he was inspired by the castle.

activities.text: Theatrical tours animate the castle in season, with costumed actors reenacting scenes from medieval life. Check the castle's website program before your visit—time slots are often limited and animations vary by day and season.

visits.text: Riquewihr had the fortune to pass through both world wars without a single bombing—its relative geographic isolation earned it this miraculous preservation. The result: 300 half-timbered houses from the 13th to 18th centuries, intact, in a village of 1,200 inhabitants surrounded by 368 hectares of vineyards. Listed among France's Most Beautiful Villages since 1982, it attracts over 1.5 million visitors per year. Arrive at opening time or late afternoon—during the day, the main street is packed.

The Dolder, a 25-meter bell tower erected in 1291 along with the first fortified enceinte, is Riquewihr's symbol. Its Alsatian name means 'the highest point.' On the exterior side, it's austere and defensive; on the town side, it presents a half-timbered façade. Climb to the museum at the top for views over the rooftops and vineyard—from up there you understand better why the two grand crus Schoenenbourg and Sporen surround the village.

The 13th-century Thieves' Tower—former prison of the Wurtemberg seigneury—preserves its medieval torture instruments and the interior of a 16th-century winemaker's house. The atmosphere is dark and authentic, very different from the picturesque main street. Not to be confused with the castle of the counts of Wurtemberg-Montbéliard, a 16th-century Renaissance building that today houses a museum of communication in Alsace.

activities.text: Push through the doorways into interior courtyards—behind the main street façades lie winemakers' cellars that welcome visitors for tastings. About fifteen family estates still produce the village's two grand crus: Schoenenbourg, renowned since the 16th century for its rieslings of remarkable minerality and longevity, and Sporen, more clay-and-marl, the preferred terrain of gewürztraminer.

practical_info.tip: Direct sales from producers

activities.text: The vineyard trail of the Grands Crus starts from rue de la Piscine and winds through the vines of Schoenenbourg and Sporen. In summer, winemakers lead guided tours followed by free tastings. Allow 90 minutes for the complete circuit. It's the best way to understand the soils and topography that make Riquewihr wines distinctive.

Make the 5 km detour to Ribeauvillé, at the foot of the Vosges. A marked 7 km circuit (2h30) connects its three ruined medieval castles perched on the ridges: Saint-Ulrich castle, Girsberg, and Haut-Ribeaupierre. The panorama from each embraces the Alsace plain and the vineyards below.

visits.text: Cross the fortified bridge of 1514 in pink sandstone that spans the Weiss—unique in Alsace, it's equipped with arrow slits and a shrine housing an 18th-century statue of the Virgin. Formerly, it also served as a 'temporary prison' for petty offenders exposed to passersby's mockery. From there, the view of 15th and 16th-century half-timbered houses and the castle ruins on the hill is one of Alsace's most photographed. Kaysersberg, meaning 'Emperor's Mountain,' was elected France's Favorite Village in 2017.

Climb to the medieval castle ruins that dominate the town by 50 meters. The castle was built from the 13th century onward to control the passage between Alsace and Lorraine via the Col du Bonhomme. Its circular keep, with walls 4.42 meters thick, withstood the Thirty Years' War. From the summit, the panorama extends over the Weiss valley, terraced vineyards, the Alsace plain, and on clear days the Black Forest.

The Church of the Holy Cross preserves a late-15th-century carved altarpiece, considered one of the masterpieces of Alsatian wood sculpture. The scenes of Christ's Passion are treated with striking finesse and realism. The Romanesque bell tower dates from the 12th century.

The birthplace of Albert Schweitzer, 1952 Nobel Peace Prize laureate, has become the Schweitzer Center. Schweitzer was born here in 1875—physician, theologian, musician, and philosopher, he founded the Lambaréné hospital in Gabon and devoted most of his life to it. The museum traces his exceptional journey with personal documents and objects. An interactive exhibition has been presented since a new extension opened.

activities.text: Local operators offer tastings in the cellars of wine estates surrounding Kaysersberg. The Grand Cru Schlossberg (its name directly evokes the castle—'Schloss'—and the mountain—'Berg') is one of the most prestigious appellations. Independent winemakers receive visitors directly in their cellars.

practical_info.tip: Direct sales

activities.text: Kaysersberg's Christmas market, the four weekends of Advent, is considered among Alsace's most authentic. Wooden chalets settle in the central square and lanes, local artisans present their work, and the scents of bredele (small Alsatian cookies), mulled wine, and gingerbread fill the town.

visits.text: Saverne's Château des Rohan astonishes with its proportions. Nicknamed the 'Little Alsatian Versailles,' its neoclassical pink sandstone façade extends exactly 140 meters—no accident: it's the equivalent, horizontally, of the height of Strasbourg Cathedral. Built in the late 18th century by architect Nicolas Salins de Montfort for Cardinal Louis René de Rohan-Guéméné, it's the fourth building erected on this site since the Middle Ages. Its museums (Gallo-Roman collections, art and history, Louise Weiss archives) deserve 90 minutes.

A few kilometers from Saverne, Haut-Barr castle merits the detour. Nicknamed 'the Eye of Alsace,' this 12th-century medieval castle perched at 470 meters on three sandstone rocks offers a panorama over the entire Alsatian plain as far as Strasbourg Cathedral on clear days. The Devil's Bridge footbridge, suspended between two rocks, is a highlight of the visit.

Saverne's rose garden extends at the foot of the pass—France's second-oldest rose garden, it assembles nearly 5,000 rose bushes from 800 varieties. Open from late May through late August, it's particularly spectacular in June during the Rose Festival.

activities.text: The Saint-Louis-Arzviller inclined plane, about ten kilometers from Saverne, is a unique engineering feat in Europe. Opened in 1969 to replace 17 locks over 3.8 km, this transverse inclined plane allows barges to cross 44 meters of elevation on the Marne-Rhine Canal in a single 35-minute operation. Operators offer tourist boat rides on the inclined plane in season.

Stroll along the Marne-Rhine Canal facing the Château des Rohan. The 70-berth marina, installed in the large basin, gives the town particular animation. Operators offer bike rides along the canal toward Arzviller or eastward. The greenway is pleasant and easy.

map_keywords: Parc naturel régional Vosges du Nord

visits.text: La Petite-Pierre occupies a pink sandstone outcrop that overlooks in one sweep the Northern Vosges forests. Its castle—first traces dating to the 13th century—was considerably remodeled by Vauban in 1684 for Louis XIV, who made it a strategic control point between Alsace and Lorraine. Today headquarters of the Northern Vosges Regional Nature Park, it houses a permanent exhibition on the history of fortifications and the park. Entry to the courtyard is free.

The Staedtel—the old fortified town—rises in tiers on the sandstone outcrop with its ramparts, underground cisterns carved directly into the rock, and pink sandstone houses. The church preserves remarkably well-preserved 15th-century painted frescoes depicting biblical figures in ochre and blue tones. One of Alsace's least-known treasures.

The Alsatian Seal Museum and the Museum of Popular Arts and Traditions of La Petite-Pierre respectively exhibit the heraldic history of Alsatian families and local popular traditions, notably Springerle—these little white cookies molded in shapes of flowers and animals that are part of Alsatian Christmas bredele.

activities.text: The Northern Vosges Regional Nature Park has been a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 1989—one of northeastern France's most extensive protected natural areas with 135,000 hectares of pine and sandstone forests, streams, and ruined castles. Over 2,600 km of marked trails cross the park. From La Petite-Pierre, several hiking circuits reach directly to spectacular sandstone rocks and medieval castle ruins buried in the forest.

practical_info.tip: Maps available at the Park House in the castle

activities.text: The rampart path circles La Petite-Pierre's outcrop and follows the fortifications for about 250 meters long by 80 wide. The underground cisterns—carved into the sandstone to supply the garrison during sieges—open for guided visits at certain times. Inquire at the Park House.

visits.text: The Abbey Church of Saints Peter and Paul in Wissembourg is one of Alsace's great Gothic edifices—the second after Strasbourg Cathedral. Founded around 660, rebuilt in Gothic style from 1262 onward, it possesses a curiosity unique in France: a 14th-century mural painting depicting Saint Christopher carrying the Christ child, 11 meters tall—the largest preserved medieval full-length figure in both countries. The north transept stained glass windows, some dating to the 12th century, are among Alsace's oldest.

The Maison du Sel, an imposing 1448 edifice in the center of Wissembourg, was originally a bourgeois hospital then a salt warehouse—a lucrative monopoly in medieval times. Its monumental two-pitched roof and massive proportions make it one of the Bas-Rhin's most remarkable civic buildings. It can be visited from the outside.

The Bruch quarter runs along the Lauter, the river that today marks the Franco-German border. The 16th-century Maison de l'Ami Fritz reflects in the water—this picturesque image is worth the detour, especially in late afternoon when the light is warm. Heading back toward the ramparts, the medieval towers that still survive recall that Wissembourg was a Decapolis member since 1354.

activities.text: Walk Wissembourg's green belt along its ramparts. The promenade on the former moats, now public gardens, passes several medieval watchtowers still standing. It's a pleasant 45-minute walk that circles the old town.

About twenty kilometers from Wissembourg, the Schoenenbourg fortification is a Maginot Line work open to the public. This underground fort, built between 1931 and 1935, could shelter 630 men and protect 17 km of front. Its galleries extend 3 km underground, of which 1,500 meters are accessible to visitors. Absolutely bring warm clothing: the interior temperature is 12°C year-round. Open in season only.

practical_info.tip: Warm clothing required, 12°C year-round

activities.text: The German border and Palatinate vineyards are a few kilometers away. Local operators organize tastings of Alsatian crémants and wines from the Wissembourg vineyard, which has produced for decades as an extension of Alsatian vines.

practical_info.tip: Direct sales

seo.h1_title: Alsace and the Wine Route: Strasbourg to the Vosges
seo.intro_paragraph: Strasbourg and its 142-meter Gothic cathedral in pink sandstone, the tallest in Christendom for two centuries—then the Wine Route through Obernai, Sélestat, Riquewihr, and Kaysersberg. The Bas-Rhin combines in 6 days the ruined castles of the Vosges, half-timbered villages preserved from wars, and Alsatian grand crus between Riesling and Gewürztraminer.
seo.seo_hook: From Strasbourg Cathedral to the grands crus of Riquewihr: 6 days between half-timbered villages and Vosges castles.
featured_list: Strasbourg: 142 m Gothic cathedral, spire completed in 1439, Grande Île inscribed UNESCO in 1988
Riquewihr: wine-producing gem of 1,200 inhabitants surrounded by Schoenenbourg and Sporen grand crus, intact since the Middle Ages
Haut-Koenigsbourg: castle restored from 1900 to 1908 for Wilhelm II on rocky outcrop at 757 m altitude
Kaysersberg: fortified bridge from 1514, medieval castle and birthplace of Albert Schweitzer, 1952 Nobel Peace Prize

itineraries.title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace
itineraries.subtitle: From Wissembourg to the Swiss border, fifteen stops through half-timbered villages, terraced vineyards, and medieval fortresses — Alsace in all its diversity.
itineraries.notes: Road trip primarily by car. Riquewihr and Kaysersberg are very crowded in July-August — early morning arrival recommended. Neuf-Brisach is best seen from the air (microlight flights available) or through the relief model at the Vauban Museum.
itineraries.climate: Best time: May-June and September-October, temperatures 15-25°C, ideal for strolling through the villages. Avoid July-August (heat up to 30°C and heavy tourist crowds). December draws visitors for Christmas markets but expect temperatures near 0°C.

visits.text: Start with the Abbey Church of Saints Peter and Paul, founded around 660 by Austrasian nobles on an island in the Lauter River — an actual island, since the monastery sat between two river arms linked by a canal whose location corresponds to today's Rue Stanislas. Rebuilt in Gothic style between 1262 and 1293 under Abbot Edelin, it's the second-largest Gothic church in Alsace after Strasbourg Cathedral. Don't miss the Saint Christopher fresco covering an entire nave wall: 11 meters tall, it's the largest medieval full-figure painting in France and Germany. The Christ of Wissembourg stained glass has been moved to the Strasbourg museum, but the 12th-century Romanesque rose window depicting the Virgin and Child remains in place.

Wander through the historic center crossed by the Lauter and its canals. The 15th and 16th-century half-timbered houses line streets that quickly give the impression of straddling the Franco-German border — which isn't far from the truth, since Germany is two kilometers away. Spot the statue of King Dagobert along your way, legendary founder of the abbey according to an apocryphal 12th-century charter. Wissembourg is also the home of Hans Trapp, the Alsatian version of the Bogeyman, whose legend draws from a notorious local lord who once dammed the Lauter to drain the town.

Walk the circuit of medieval ramparts — they date from the 13th to 18th centuries and encircle the old town for several hundred meters. The tower known as Schartenturm (15th century) to the southwest and the Powder Tower (13th century) are the best preserved. From the walkway, the view over Alsatian rooftops and the Lauter winding below is worth the detour.

activities.text: Follow the pedestrian loop along ramparts and canals — about 3 to 4 kilometers of easy walking that covers the essentials of the old town. If you're there in the morning, local bakers offer Brezel and rye bread before 8 a.m. Plan an hour for a leisurely stroll.

Climb the wooded heights northwest of town for panoramic views of the Palatinate Forest on the German side and Alsatian vineyards on the French side. Marked trails from the Club Vosgien depart directly from the town center and lead to several viewpoints in under an hour.

map_keywords: Fort de Schoenenbourg Hunspach Ligne Maginot

visits.text: In Hunspach, Alsace changes its palette. Forget the multicolored facades of the south — here, everything is white. The half-timbered houses, built between the 18th and 19th centuries with local wood and lime, form a restrained and striking chromatic harmony. Voted France's Favorite Village in 2020, the village owes its fame to two architectural details: the curved window panes on the facades — baroque glazing that allowed residents to look out onto the street without being seen — and the swing-beam wells dotting the courtyards that open onto the street. Strict rules still require the white facades and the green or blue shutters today.

Push on to Fort Schoenenbourg, 5 kilometers north of Hunspach — it's one of the most important installations of the Maginot Line in Alsace, built between 1931 and 1935. Its underground galleries stretch for 3 kilometers, carved 30 meters beneath the earth, and the fort could house 600 men for three months in complete autonomy. It was the most heavily attacked installation of World War II and withstood nine days of intense bombardment in 1940. The guided tour lasts about 1h30 — bring a jacket, it's cool even in summer.

activities.text: Follow the village's marked historical walk — about 45 minutes to spot remarkable facades, swing-beam wells, and hidden symbols on lintels. The tourist office also offers guided tours with anecdotes about each house. If you want to learn more about old rural life, the Petite Ferme d'Antan (Small Farm of Yesteryear) in the heart of the village displays the tools and utensils.

Head to Seebach, 5 km northeast, another white half-timbered village of the Outre-Forêt, organized in a 'ladder' pattern with two parallel streets connected by three cross streets. Its Festival of Flowered Houses in July is a rare spectacle. Cycling enthusiasts can link both villages on the 49 km circuit that then follows the Rhine.

visits.text: Obernai's Market Square is one of the finest in Alsace — and one of the liveliest. It concentrates several centuries of architecture in a single space: the belfry known as Kappellturm, rising 60 meters and serving over time as watchtower, chapel steeple, and belfry, is unique in Alsace. Right beside it, the town hall blends 14th-century Gothic elements with a Renaissance facade built between 1462 and 1523. Stop before the Six-Bucket Well of 1579: its three columns support six wrought-iron buckets, one for each of the families who held usage rights at the time.

Obernai proudly claims to be the legendary birthplace of Saint Odile, patron saint of Alsace — born blind, she miraculously regained her sight during her baptism. The Fontaine Sainte-Odile that stands on the square has honored her since 1904. Mont Sainte-Odile, Alsace's spiritual high place with its 8th-century convent, is just 20 minutes by car and offers exceptional panoramas over the plain.

Obernai's medieval ramparts are a remarkable feature: the town had three distinct defensive systems. The inner ramparts from the 13th century, 1.4 km long, are the best preserved and can be walked from Rue du Maréchal Foch. From the walkway, you'll glimpse the still-intact towers and, looking up, the weathervanes and hearts adorning the Alsatian rooftops.

activities.text: Follow the intra-muros circuit by tracing the marble plaques on the ground — a route of about 3 km that passes all the squares and historic buildings. The half-timbered houses in vibrant colors — ochre, blue, green, red — rival the geraniums on the balconies. Obernai is the second most touristic town in Bas-Rhin after Strasbourg, so arrive early morning for the best photos.

Climb the Schenkenberg vineyard trail, perched above Obernai like a balcony. Information boards explain the various Alsatian grape varieties and the stages of the wine's development, and the panoramic view over the Alsace plain and the Vosges is one of the finest in the region. Local wine estates offer tastings of Riesling, Gewurztraminer and the rare red Pinot Noir of Ottrott.

visits.text: Mittelbergheim breaks sharply with its Alsatian neighbors: no colorful half-timbering here, but pink Vosges sandstone cut into regular blocks, Renaissance houses with carved gables and flowered courtyards. The village was founded by the Franks in the early 6th century under the name 'Berge,' and its wine prosperity in the 16th and 17th centuries allowed it to build this exceptional architectural ensemble. The town hall dates from 1620 and houses, in its vaulted cellar, a treasure unique in Alsace: the Weinschlag, a wine accounting register kept since 1456 that records wine prices, harvests, and landmark village events over more than five centuries.

Don't miss the Musée Mémoire de Vignerons (Winegrowers' Memory Museum), opened in 2008, which presents a collection of old tools related to viticulture in a preserved rural setting. In the town hall cellar, a wine library preserves bottles from village winemakers — the oldest, a Sylvaner Zotzenberg, dates to 1959. This is where you'll understand why Mittelbergheim is different: its medieval ramparts surround not houses but vineyards, a configuration unique in Alsace.

activities.text: Head out on the Grand Cru Zotzenberg trail — the vineyard that built the village's international reputation. This south-facing terroir, on Jurassic marls and limestone between 215 and 315 meters altitude, is the only Grand Cru in Alsace where Sylvaner is permitted, since the 2005 vintage. Tasting a Sylvaner from Zotzenberg at a local winemaker's means experiencing a wine found nowhere else. Plan 2 to 3 hours for the loop, with views of Mont Sainte-Odile and the plain.

Stroll the cobbled streets to spot dated lintels and cart entrances — gateways wide enough to let grape-laden wagons through. Every house hides a wine cellar in its limestone foundations. The wine festival takes place the last weekend of July: estates open their cellars and the atmosphere is especially convivial.

map_keywords: Remparts Bergheim XIVe siècle Porte Haute

visits.text: Bergheim is protected by a double medieval enclosure erected from 1311, among the best preserved in Alsace. Its walls extend over 2 kilometers and shelter nine still-visible towers. The Porte Haute or Obertor, erected in the 14th century and remodeled in the 16th, is the only one of the three old gates to survive. From the walkway on the north side — the most spectacular flank, with its five flanking towers and outer moat — the view plunges onto Gewurztraminer vineyards and Vosges peaks. Bergheim was voted France's Favorite Village in 2022, after Eguisheim (2013) and Kaysersberg (2017) — an Alsatian longevity in this ranking.

The House of Witches, housed in a building from 1550, traces with historical rigor the 40 witchcraft trials that took place in Bergheim between 1582 and 1683. Forty women were condemned to the stake, including 22 in the space of five months for the year 1630 alone. The last trial occurred in 1683, one year after Louis XIV issued an ordinance decriminalizing witchcraft. The museum relies exclusively on preserved historical archives and raises the question of intolerance without any folklore. Open late June to October.

Don't leave Bergheim without finding the Tanzlinde — a linden tree planted in 1313, classified as a Remarkable Tree since 2017, whose trunk exceeds 1.80 meters in diameter. Popular festivals took place beneath its branches as early as the 14th century. The neo-Romanesque synagogue from 1863, rebuilt at the exact location of a 14th-century medieval synagogue, is also worth visiting: it's the only synagogue in Alsace never to have left its original site.

activities.text: Walk the complete circuit of the ramparts from the walkway — about 2 to 3 km of pleasant promenade offering panoramas over the vineyard and the Vosges. The 4 km hike on the trail of the Grands Crus Altenberg and Kanzlerberg, just outside the town, is punctuated with explanatory panels on the terroir. A tasting at local winemakers is essential — Bergheim's Gewurztraminer is among the finest on the Wine Route.

map_keywords: Tour des Bouchers Ribeauvillé XIIIe siècle

visits.text: Ribeauvillé's Grand'rue unfolds a kilometer of 15th to 18th-century half-timbered houses, punctuated by Renaissance fountains, the oldest dating to 1576. Spot the Butchers' Tower from the 13th century, a remnant of the ramparts that owes its name to the guild charged with defending this sector in case of attack. The House of the Minstrels, with its 1683 facade carved with musical motifs, recalls Ribeauvillé's central role in the Alsatian guild of itinerant musicians — since 1481, minstrels gathered here every first Sunday of September to elect their king. This tradition still produces the Pfifferdaj today, a procession of 1,500 costumed participants in medieval dress.

Three castles dominate Ribeauvillé from the heights — Saint-Ulrich, Girsberg, and Haut-Ribeaupierre — and they were known three centuries ago in an old saying: 'Three castles on a mountain / Three churches in one enclosure / Three towns in one valley — that's all Alsace.' Saint-Ulrich, founded before 1038 and rebuilt around 1200, is the most imposing: its 32-meter square keep and knights' hall with aligned Gothic windows are accessible on foot in 40 minutes from the high school. A 1h30 hike allows you to visit all three castles in one go.

activities.text: Climb to Saint-Ulrich castle via the marked trail (red rectangle) that starts from the sports field behind the high school and climbs through the vineyard. Count 40 minutes of ascent to the Saint-Ulrich ruins. From there, you can continue to Girsberg and Haut-Ribeaupierre — 1h30 total for all three castles, with plunging views over Ribeauvillé and the Alsace plain.

Wander the alleys around the Grand'rue to discover fountains, oriels, and wrought-iron signs adorning the winegrowers' houses. The 1437 Wheat Hall, the 18th-century town hall with its silver goblets offered by the Counts of Ribeaupierre, and the Riesling and Gewurztraminer cellars deserve attention. If you pass through in early September, the Pfifferdaj transforms the town into a living medieval setting.

visits.text: The fortified Church of Saint James the Greater is one of the iconic images of Alsatian wine country. Perched on a knoll above the village and surrounded by a hexagonal enclosure with six bastions pierced by arrow slits, it served as a fortified refuge for residents in case of attack — a keep dressed as a church. Built in the 15th and 16th centuries on the remains of an 11th-century sanctuary, it's been classified as a Historical Monument since 1972. The interior reveals a curiosity unique in Alsace: the 16th-century pink sandstone pulpit is only accessible via a staircase passing through a church pillar. Since 1687, Catholics and Protestants have shared it in simultaneum — a cohabitation forced by Louis XIV that continues today.

Below the church sits the Fontaine Sainte-Hune, from which the village takes its name: according to legend, the 7th-century holy washerwoman transformed water into wine during a bad harvest. Beside the washhouse, the 1517 town hall still bears on its facade the coats of arms of Hunawihr's overlords: the antlers of Württemberg, the lozenges of the Duchy of Teck, the double-headed eagle of the Holy Roman Empire, and the two fish of the County of Montbéliard.

activities.text: Walk the circuit through the vines around the church to enjoy panoramas of Ribeauvillé, Zellenberg, and Riquewihr — a trio of villages you'll glimpse all three from the vineyard path. The Grand Cru Rosacker, whose name comes from the wild roses planted at the vineyard edges, produces high-class Rieslings and Gewurztraminers here. Easy loop of 3 to 4 km, 1 hour.

The NaturOparC in Hunawihr is the reintroduction center for white storks in Alsace — the regional symbol that nearly disappeared in the 1970s. Fishing shows feature otters and cormorants. The Exotic Butterfly Garden, located right next door, lets hundreds of tropical butterflies live freely in a greenhouse and botanical park. Both sites are worth the visit, especially for families.

visits.text: Zellenberg is the village you visit from below — perched at 285 meters altitude on a wine-covered hill, its huddled houses stand out from afar against sky and vines. Up close, the curved streets that hug the hill's contours form a compact labyrinth where the church and summit square offer unobstructed views of Riquewihr below and the Alsace plain to the Black Forest. The village retains traces of its old medieval enclosure wall visible at several points.

From the church square, the view embraces a wine panorama that few places in Alsace equal: Riquewihr at 2 km, Hunawihr at 3 km, the Schoenenbourg and Sporen hillsides opposite. Circle the town via the alleys that follow the remnants of old moats — 30 to 40 minutes suffice for the entire village.

activities.text: Take the contour trail around the hill for a complete circuit on foot — 2 to 3 km of easy walking between the vines, with successive viewpoints over the Ribeauvillé valley to the north and Riquewihr hillsides to the south. The village's wine estates offer tastings of wines from surrounding grands crus — notably Schoenenbourg and Sporen.

visits.text: Pass through the Dolder Tower, built in 1291 with the first fortified enclosure by Burkhardt II of Horbourg — and you're in one of the most photographed villages in Alsace. This 25-meter belfry is Riquewihr's emblem: on the street side, its 1565 corbelled floors are garnished with flower-filled windows; on the countryside side, it presented a severe face turned toward the enemy. Inside, the museum traces the history of a fortified wine town from the 13th to 17th century and presents the functions of watchman, night watchman, and gatekeeper. The small bell at its summit, recast in 1842, bears the inscription: 'It is joy, it is alarm that my sound produces.'

Riquewihr's main street is a parade of 15th and 16th-century houses whose colored facades — pale blue, yellow, mauve, lime green — constitute one of the most complete architectural panoramas in Alsace. Riquewihr has the good fortune of having miraculously escaped destruction in both world wars, including during the Colmar Pocket in December 1944. The village appears in sources as early as 1094 and obtained city status in 1320. Disney reportedly drew inspiration from these streets for the village in Beauty and the Beast — an image that fits the setting without being rigorously documented.

The Thieves' Tower, in the 1291 enclosure, houses a museum on the village's old prison — the oubliettes, torture instruments, and watchman's chamber are preserved. Leaving, explore the alleys to discover inner courtyards, old wells, and hidden fountains that tourist guides don't always mention.

activities.text: Walk the 1291 ramparts — they still form a continuous arc on the north and west flank. From the esplanade, the view of the 1621 southwest bastion and the 1539 Château des Wurtemberg, built in Rhine Renaissance style, opens an unexpected perspective on the town's political history. Then take the wine trails toward the Schoenenbourg and Sporen hillsides for a tasting directly at the winemakers.

visits.text: Kaysersberg's fortified bridge is unique in Alsace. Built in 1514 of pink sandstone, it spans the Weiss and is equipped with parapets and arrow slits to prevent any attack via the river. At the bridge's center, a shrine houses an 18th-century polychrome Virgin — residents once came to pray here before leaving the town. It also served as an 'open prison' for petty offenders exposed to public ridicule. Crossing this bridge means entering the oldest part of Kaysersberg, whose 15th and 16th-century half-timbered houses number among the finest examples of Rhine Renaissance in Alsace.

Climb to the imperial castle ruins, erected shortly before 1227 by a bailiff of Emperor Frederick II of Hohenstaufen to control the passage between Lorraine and Alsace. Its circular keep — walls 4.42 meters thick — dominates the town by 50 meters. The castle was ruined in 1632 by Swedish mercenaries during the Thirty Years' War. From the summit platform, the view embraces terraced vineyards, the Weiss valley, the Alsace plain, and on clear days, the Black Forest.

Kaysersberg was the birthplace of Albert Schweitzer, born here in 1875. Physician, theologian, philosopher, and musician — and Nobel Peace Prize laureate in 1952 — he founded the hospital of Lambaréné in Gabon and developed his philosophy of 'reverence for life.' The museum dedicated to him in his birth house traces his exceptional journey; his personal objects, organ scores, and correspondence are displayed in a contemplative atmosphere.

activities.text: Walk Rue du Général-de-Gaulle from the fortified bridge to the end of the historic center — 800 meters of Renaissance houses where every facade holds a detail to notice: carved oriels, wrought-iron signs, twisted posts. The 1521 town hall, the Renaissance well decorated with dolphins in the inner courtyard, and the 1594 Maison Brève Faller, which belonged to a cooper, are the masterpieces of this open-air museum.

Join the terraced vineyards above Kaysersberg via the ramparts trail for panoramas of the Vosges and Black Forest. Local cellars offer tastings of Grand Cru Schlossberg — the name evokes the castle and mountain, and the wines produced combine finesse and power. If you're there in December, Kaysersberg's Christmas market is renowned for its authenticity.

visits.text: Turckheim is one of the rare Alsatian towns to preserve all three fortified gates intact: the Porte de France (around 1315, the oldest), the Porte du Brand, and the Porte du Munster. Since Emperor Henry VII elevated the village to Imperial Free City in 1312 and granted the right to build an enclosure, the town has been part of the Alsatian Décapole. The Porte de France, where storks regularly settle on the summit nests, opens onto Place Turenne — named for the marshal who won the last decisive battle here in 1675 against the Imperials, rendering Alsace definitively French.

The Corps de Garde built around 1580 now houses the tourist office. It's from this sandstone building, with its double-headed imperial eagle on the facade recalling the Free Imperial City status, that the Night Watchman begins his rounds every evening at 10 p.m., May to October. In period costume — tricorn, halberd, horn, and lantern — he sings the hours through the alleys, calling on residents to extinguish fire and candle. A centuries-old tradition, interrupted from 1939 to Liberation, that makes Turckheim one of the only towns in France to perpetuate this profession.

activities.text: Join the Night Watchman's rounds in the evening — departure from the Corps de Garde at 10 p.m., May to October. He sings, comments, and reveals the town's secrets in Alsatian and French, followed by a procession of visitors that lengthens through the streets. If you want a front-row spot, arrive 15 minutes early.

Climb to the hillsides of Grand Cru Brand, one of Alsace's most renowned vineyards, whose granite soils warm the grapes all day and give the heat back at night — producing particularly concentrated wines. The wine trail from the north ramparts offers views of Colmar and the Rhine plain. The Cave de Turckheim, founded in 1955, brings together the village's winemakers and offers tastings open to all.

map_keywords: Maison du Fromage Gunsbach vallée Munster

visits.text: Munster owes its name to the Benedictine abbey founded around 660 at the confluence of the two Fechts — 'monastery' in Latin, Munster in Alsatian. It was Benedictine monks from Italy who developed the first techniques for preserving milk through aging, giving birth to the cheese that bears the town's name. Munster cheese has held AOC status since 1969 and European AOP since 1996. The Maison du Fromage (Cheese House), located in Gunsbach 3 km from Munster in old 2,000 m² farm buildings, offers a 1h30 semi-guided tour with films, stable, aging cellars, and tasting.

Munster's center preserves on the Market Square the vestiges of the old abbey around which the town developed. The two parks along the Fecht — Parc Frédéric Hartmann and Parc Albert Schweitzer — form a pleasant green corridor in all seasons. The town was an Imperial Free City from 1287 before losing its freedoms under Louis XIV in 1679.

activities.text: The Munster valley opens toward the Vosges high pastures as soon as you leave town. Mountain farm inns offer traditional meals — tourte (meat pie), roïgabrageldi (sautéed potatoes), and farmhouse Munster aged on-site — in high-mountain settings accessible by car or on foot. Some are open year-round, others only May to October: check before going.

Climb a valley side for an overview — several marked trails from Club Vosgien depart from Munster center and lead to ridges at 700-800 meters altitude in 1h30 to 2h. The Reichackerkopf (778 m) offers a panorama of both Vosges sides and the Alsace plain.

map_keywords: Sentier viticole Eguisheim Grand Cru Eichberg

visits.text: Eguisheim is built in concentric circles around its octagonal central square — a configuration unique in Alsace dating back to the village's creation around an 8th-century castle. This castle is the presumed birthplace of Pope Leo IX, born Bruno of Eguisheim in 1002, the only pope of Alsatian origin. The central square with its fountain and hollyhocks is the village's most iconic image, voted France's Favorite Village in 2013. The inner streets — sometimes so narrow they look like streets in a doll's house — unroll multicolored and flower-filled half-timbered houses that give the impression of turning endlessly around a central axis.

Outside the concentric streets, the vestiges of two elliptical medieval enclosures testify that Eguisheim's vocation was more economic than military — it was about protecting the rich tithe courtyards where tithes were stored. Climb to the Three Towers of Schlossberg, on the hill above the village at 591 meters altitude: these three ruined keeps silhouetted against the sky served as sundials for workers in the plain. The view from up there embraces Colmar, the Alsace plain, and the Black Forest.

activities.text: Walk the complete circular circuit of inner streets — 2 to 3 km of promenade in a fairytale setting. Then visit the Stork Park at the village's base, managed by the association of friends of Eguisheim storks who contributed to reintroducing Alsace's symbol bird to the region.

Take the wine trail toward the Grands Crus Eichberg and Pfersigberg — 2 hours of easy walk between rows of Riesling and Gewurztraminer, with explanatory panels on grape varieties and terroir. Eguisheim is one of the cradles of Alsatian viticulture and its cellars deserve a careful tasting.

map_keywords: Musée Vauban Porte de Belfort Neuf-Brisach
Porte de Colmar Neuf-Brisach pont pierre

visits.text: Neuf-Brisach is the last fortress designed by Vauban and the only one implementing his 'third system' — the most accomplished of his defensive theories. Built from 1698 on Louis XIV's orders after the loss of Breisach in the Treaty of Ryswick, it was constructed from scratch according to an octagonal plan with two concentric enclosures. Louis XIV personally chose, from three projects submitted by Vauban, the most ambitious and costly: 4 million livres. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2008 among Vauban's twelve major sites, Neuf-Brisach is the most complete example of a fortified lowland town of its era. To truly grasp the genius of the star-shaped plan, visit the Vauban Museum in the Porte de Belfort — its relief model is striking.

The town is organized around its Place d'Armes, surrounded by the 18th-century royal church of Saint-Louis. Two defensive enclosures nest together: inside, a security enclosure formed of eight bastioned towers connected by curtain walls 3 meters thick; outside, a combat enclosure composed of counter-guards, tenailles, and demilunes. The moats separating them, now accessible on foot, allow you to measure the works' dimensions. The four monumental gates — Colmar, Strasbourg, Basel, Belfort — are each a masterpiece of military architecture.

activities.text: Walk a quarter of the ramparts with the guided tour offered by the tourist office — guides in period costumes portray historical figures like Vauban or Tarade and recount life in the city during Louis XIV's time. The tour lasts 1h30 to 2h and includes a bastioned tower. Off-season, a self-guided visit with the commented map distributed at the office is also possible.

To appreciate the star-shaped plan from the sky, local operators offer microlight or hot-air balloon flights over Neuf-Brisach — it's by far the best way to appreciate the fortifications' geometry. On the ground, cycling is ideal for exploring the Rhine plain and reaching Biesheim or Breisach on the German side.

map_keywords: Château de Ferrette ruines piton rocheux
Hôtel de Ville Ferrette Renaissance rhénane

visits.text: Ferrette is one of southern Alsace's best-kept secrets. Nestled in a small cluse of the Alsatian Jura, this former capital of the Counts of Ferrette is dominated by the ruins of its castle built in 1105 by Frederick of Montbéliard, first Count of Ferrette. For two centuries, seven counts ruled over a territory that was nearly a sovereign state — the county passed to the Habsburgs in 1324 through the marriage of Joan of Ferrette to Albert II of Austria. Today, Prince Albert II of Monaco still bears the title Count of Ferrette, through a chain of inheritances passing through Mazarin and the Grimaldi family. The ruins are freely accessible year-round — count 10 minutes' climb and 45 to 60 minutes for the entire site.

The upper castle, the oldest, preserves a residential tower carved directly into the limestone on several levels — one of the first of its type in Alsace. From the summit platform at 612 meters altitude, the panorama is exceptional: the rolling hills of Sundgau, the Alsace plain, the Vosges to the north and, on clear days, the Swiss Alps to the south. The lower castle, built from a 12th-century keep, was remodeled in 1488 and has several round towers still standing.

In the lower town, the 1572 Town Hall is an elegant example of Rhine Renaissance with triple-light windows — its small belfry houses a 1592 bell cast in Basel that still rings curfew at 10 p.m. The two coats of arms on the facade tell the story: on the left, the House of Austria; on the right, the two fish of the Counts of Ferrette. The Church of Saint Bernard of Menthon, classified as a Historical Monument since 1902, completes the historic center's heritage.

activities.text: Head out on the trail leading to the Cave of the Dwarves — a widespread legend throughout Sundgau tells of dwarves with webbed feet who inhabited these limestone gorges and helped residents with their chores, until the day the villagers mocked their feet and drove them away forever. The hike to the cave takes 40 minutes from the village. The complete 6 km loop, passing by the castle, cave, and viewpoints over the Jura, is the best discovery route of the site.

If you have energy left, climb to the Rossberg tower — a belvedere a few kilometers from Ferrette offering a 360° view of three countries: the Alsace plain, Swiss Jura, and German Black Forest. The Sundgau's gastronomic specialty is fried carp — several regional inns serve it year-round in a lightly vinegared sauce.

seo.h1_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace
seo.intro_paragraph: From Wissembourg in the north, a border town whose 13th-century abbey church is the second-largest Gothic church in Alsace, to Ferrette in the south, former capital of the Counts of Ferrette whose title the Prince of Monaco still bears, this 5 days itinerary crosses the most beautiful villages of Alsace along the Wine Route. Between Hunspach, voted France's Favorite Village in 2020, and Riquewihr nicknamed Pearl of the Vineyard, between Bergheim's medieval ramparts (2022) and the 1291 Dolder, each stop is a chapter of Alsatian history.
seo.seo_hook: Half-timbering and Riesling from Wissembourg to Ferrette: 15 villages, 800 years of Alsatian architecture, and the Wine Route from end to end.
featured_list: Riquewihr: Pearl of the Vineyard, 1291 Dolder, and 2 million annual visitors
Bergheim: double enclosure from 1311, 40 witch trials, and France's Favorite Village 2022
Kaysersberg: 1514 fortified bridge unique in Alsace, birthplace of Albert Schweitzer (Nobel 1952)
Neuf-Brisach: only example of Vauban's third system, UNESCO-listed in 2008

itineraries.title: Upper Rhine Road Trip: Colmar and the Southern Wine Route
itineraries.subtitle: From Colmar's Little Venice to the battlefields of Vieil Armand, by way of Vauban's fortified city, the vineyards of Guebwiller and the Vosges valleys: 4 days in the Upper Rhine between medieval heritage, gastronomy, and memory.
itineraries.climate: Best time: May-June and September-October, temperatures 15-25°C, ideal for the Wine Route. Avoid July-August (heat waves up to 35°C) and December-February (cold, fog in the plains). Dry climate thanks to the Vosges shield.

visits.text: Little Venice follows the Lauch River for a few hundred meters — half-timbered houses in ochre, rose, and blue reflect in the canal, geraniums spill from every balcony, flat-bottomed boats glide beneath the bridges. It's the most photographed site in Alsace, and the crowds know it. Arrive early in the morning if you want the reflections to yourself.

The Unterlinden Museum occupies a former 13th-century Dominican convent. Its centerpiece is the Isenheim Altarpiece, painted by Matthias Grünewald between 1512 and 1516 for the Antonine commandery at Isenheim — a hospital treating victims of Saint Anthony's Fire. This seven-panel polyptych ranks among the most expressive works in Western painting: the Crucifixion depicts Christ's body with wounds meant to comfort the sick by making them feel understood in their suffering. It survived two world wars hidden in banks and Périgord châteaux. Book your ticket in advance — queues can be long in season.

The Collegiate Church of Saint-Martin has lifted its two unequal spires above the old town since the 13th century — its construction lasted from 1235 to 1365. Look up at the carved west portal and its gargoyles before entering to see the stained glass and the Alsatian Gothic nave.

The Pfister House, built in 1537 for a draper named Ludwig Scherer, is one of the finest Renaissance residences in Alsace. Its corner oriel, wall frescoes, and long carved wooden gallery give it the air of stone lacework. Note that it now houses a wine cellar — you can go inside for a tasting.

Detour through the Tanners' Quarter on rue de la Poissonerie. These narrow half-timbered houses, built in the 16th and 17th centuries, had their upper floors open to the air for drying hides. Also check out the Maison des Têtes at 3 rue des Marchands: its 1609 façade is decorated with over a hundred grotesque faces.

activities.text: Embark on a flat-bottomed boat ride along the Lauch from Little Venice. Operators offer these trips in season — expect about twenty minutes gliding past the colorful façades from the water. Book ahead or wait for a boat at the Poissonerie quay.

practical_info.tip: Arrive early to avoid waiting

activities.text: Wander the lanes of old Colmar hunting for details that go unnoticed: the carved draper figure on a façade along rue des Marchands, the wrought-iron shop signs, the medieval interior courtyards. The tourist office offers themed walking routes that ensure you miss nothing.

Late in the day, push open the door of a winstub — these traditional Alsatian wine taverns — to taste a flammenkueche (tarte flambée) or baeckeoffe paired with a glass of Riesling or Pinot Gris. It's the best moment to catch the local atmosphere away from the tourist rush hour.

visits.text: The Munster Cheese House traces the birth and making of eastern France's only AOP cheese. The story begins in the 7th century when Benedictine monks founded an abbey in the valley — the Monasterium Confluentis — which gave its name to the town, the valley, and the cheese. This soft-paste, washed-rind cheese, rubbed by hand every two days during a 14 to 21-day aging period, has a pronounced nose but remains mild on the palate. Don't miss the guided tasting with a glass of Gewurztraminer — the classic pairing.

The Grand Ballon rises to 1,424 meters, about 16 km from the base town, a 25-minute drive. It is the highest point of the Vosges range. On a clear day the view from the summit stretches over the Alsace plain, the Rhine, the Black Forest in Germany, and sometimes the Swiss Alps. Don't miss the Monument des Diables Bleus at the top, which honors the alpine troops who died on these ridges during the Great War.

Descending via the Route des Crêtes, pause at the Col de la Schlucht at 1,139 meters. This road was built in 1915 for military purposes to supply troops while staying out of range of German lines — it runs for 73 kilometers from Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines to Cernay, mostly above 1,000 meters elevation. The panoramas of the Alsace plain to the east and Lorraine valleys to the west change with every bend.

Eguisheim, which you will spot from the ridges, is tomorrow's stop, about 13 km from the base town, a 20-minute drive. If you have time this evening, take a first stroll through its concentric lanes at the end of the day — the golden light on the half-timbered façades is especially lovely in the early evening.

activities.text: The marcaire meal at a high-altitude farm inn is one of the Upper Rhine's most emblematic culinary experiences. The traditional menu includes soup, valley tourte, sautéed potatoes (röigebrageldi in local dialect), hot Munster, and blueberry tart. Farmhouses in the upland pastures offer these meals typically between 11 a.m. and 3 p.m. Reservations required on weekends.

Hike up to the ruins of the Three Castles that overlook Eguisheim from their ridge, about 13 km from the base town, a 20-minute drive. The castles — Wahlenbourg, Dagsbourg and Weckmund — were built in the 11th and 12th centuries by the counts of Eguisheim. The climb from the village takes 30 to 45 minutes depending on the path and offers a sweeping view down over the vineyards below.

visits.text: Eguisheim arranges itself in concentric circles around its central castle — a unique configuration in Alsace that makes it a genuinely enchanting maze. The octagonal castle at the center of place Saint-Léon dates to 720, when Count Eberhard of Alsace, nephew of Saint Odile, built his residence here. Within these walls in 1002 was born Bruno of Eguisheim, who would become Pope Leo IX in 1049 — one of the rare French popes in history. The Saint-Léon fountain in the square honors his memory. In 2013, Eguisheim was elected France's Favorite Village — the town had already been classified among the Most Beautiful Villages of France since 2003.

The Church of Saint Peter and Saint Paul blends the Romanesque transept with the Gothic nave on a 12th-century foundation raised over the centuries. Its square tower in yellow sandstone is the most visible landmark from the vineyards. Inside, look for the 13th-century opening Virgin — a statue of Mary whose belly opens to reveal a carved Trinity.

Follow rue du Rempart Sud, which traces the old medieval moat. The village's oldest house — dated 1479 — stands on this street. Look at the carved lintels and inscriptions in old Alsatian dialect on the façade beams that tell the names of winemaking families.

At the edge of the village, the Stork Park shelters several active nests. The white stork, emblem of Alsace, had nearly disappeared from the region in the 1980s — a reintroduction program enabled its renaissance. Here you can observe them up close on their nests perched above the enclosures.

activities.text: The Eichberg Grand Cru vineyard trail winds across south-facing limestone slopes. This grand cru has been renowned since Roman times for its Rieslings and Gewurztraminers. Explanatory panels in French and English mark the 3-kilometer circuit and present the seven Alsatian grape varieties as well as the winegrowers' work through the seasons. The panoramic view of Eguisheim and its ramparts from the top of the slope is worth the detour alone.

Push open the door of a winegrower's cellar to taste the local grands crus. Eguisheim has about thirty independent winegrowers — cellars are generally open without appointment during the week. The Grands Crus Eichberg and Pfersigberg are the village's jewels: guided tastings are the occasion to understand why this particular terroir produces age-worthy wines.

map_keywords: Musée Vauban Porte de Belfort Neuf-Brisach

visits.text: Neuf-Brisach is an absolute curiosity: a town created from scratch in 1698 on the Alsace plain after France lost the fortress of Vieux-Brisach following the Treaty of Ryswick. Louis XIV himself chose, among three projects submitted by Vauban, this perfect octagonal plan — which cost him 4 million livres. To transport the pink sandstone from the Vosges, a special canal was dug. The fortifications were completed in 1702, the Church of Saint-Louis in 1736. The ensemble has been listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site since July 2008, as the sole example of Vauban's 'third system.' The best way to grasp it is from the air — operators offer microlight flights that reveal the geometric perfection of the sixteen-pointed star.

The place d'Armes is a large square 120 meters on each side occupying the geometric center of the octagon. Around it, 48 rectangular blocks are organized in a grid of implacable logic: barracks against the ramparts to protect civilians, buildings of power around the central square. Walk to the royal fountain and observe the symmetry of streets converging toward you from all cardinal points.

The Vauban Museum, installed in the Porte de Belfort, traces through models and original plans the construction of this ideal fortress-town. Here you'll understand the genius of the double-wall system: the enceinte de sûreté surrounding the town directly, then the outer works — demi-lunes, counter-guards, bastions — which multiply firing angles to make any enemy approach suicidal.

The Royal Church of Saint-Louis, whose first stone was laid on October 11, 1731 and work completed in 1736, expresses the sober classicism of 18th-century Alsace. Its clean lines survived the American bombing of 1945 that devastated much of the town. The façade of the military hospital built in 1765 to plans by architect Gabriel-Ignace Ritter is also worth a look.

activities.text: Walk the sentry path that makes a complete circuit of the enceinte over 2.4 kilometers. A marked historical route starts from the place d'Armes and guides you through the different military works. Contemporary artworks have also been installed in the ramparts, which since 2013 have housed France's second street art museum (MAUSA).

Operators offer microlight flights from a nearby airfield. From the air, the geometric perfection of Neuf-Brisach's sixteen-pointed star makes complete sense — it's the only angle from which you truly understand Vauban's military genius.

visits.text: The Church of Notre-Dame de l'Assomption is a singular edifice: its construction began in the 11th century in Romanesque style, continued in the 13th and 14th centuries in Gothic, and never really finished — the south tower remained incomplete until 1875 when it was raised in neo-Gothic style. This mixture produces a strange and fascinating result. On your way out, look for vestiges of an old practice: in the chevet, deep notches in the stone — winegrowers once sharpened their pruning knives on the church stone, which was supposed to ensure good harvests. And don't miss the 'Smile of Rouffach': two delicate carved faces — a young woman and a young man — flanking the door of the old sacristy.

The Witches' Tower, last tower surviving from Rouffach's medieval fortifications, is attached to the old town hall. Its round base dates from the 13th century, its square upper part from the 14th and 15th centuries. It served as a prison for centuries, notably for women accused of witchcraft during the Inquisition era — hence its name. A stork's nest tops it today, giving it a more peaceful air.

The Récollets Church, built between 1280 and 1300 by the Franciscans, is one of the very rare mendicant order churches preserved in Alsace with its exterior pulpit. These outdoor pulpits allowed popular preachers to address the crowd directly on the square. Inside, the bareness required by the Franciscan order contrasts with the richness of the neighboring Notre-Dame church.

On place de la République, take time to observe the monumental ensemble: the old 16th-century Halle aux Blés with its characteristic gables, the old town hall with double Renaissance pediment, the houses with stepped gables testifying to the town's golden age under the prince-bishops of Strasbourg. Rouffach was long the capital of the Haut-Mundat, their possession in Upper Alsace.

activities.text: The Vorbourg Grand Cru vineyard trail winds across the limestone slopes above Rouffach, facing south. As you climb, views progressively open over Rouffach, its medieval monuments, the Alsace plain, and on clear days the Black Forest. A marked 4-kilometer trail loops through rows of Gewurztraminer and Riesling.

Climb to the Notre-Dame de Schauenberg sanctuary via the forest path from Pfaffenheim. This pilgrimage site perched among beech trees dominates the valley and vineyards. The path starts in the vineyard, crosses meadows, then enters the woods — the round trip takes about 2h30.

visits.text: Guebwiller is nicknamed 'the town of three churches' — and each represents a different style. The Romanesque Church of Saint-Léger with its two 12th-century towers is the oldest. Its sculpted portal and Gothic choir make it a remarkable example of Rhenish art: take time to examine the historiated capitals before entering.

The Dominican Convent, a listed monument, is another surprise: built from 1294, its ribbed-vault choir dates to 1322. The building was transformed into a hospice then a market hall after the Revolution. In 1838, an industrialist patron had a concert hall built in the choir — Clara Schumann performed there as early as 1862. The acoustics of this nave are reputed among the finest in Europe. Since 2013, the site has hosted exhibitions, concerts, and digital arts.

The Church of Notre-Dame, built between 1765 and 1785 in neoclassical style, completes the trio of three churches. Its Callinet organ resonates beneath the central dome — it became the parish church in 1792 after Murbach Abbey, to which it belonged, transferred its canons there. Continue to the vestiges of Murbach Abbey 4 kilometers away, a masterpiece of Alsatian Romanesque art of which survive the 12th-century choir and transept.

The Théodore Deck Museum traces the work of this ceramicist from Guebwiller born in 1823 who became director of the Sèvres National Manufactory. His enameled earthenware and Art Nouveau creations are displayed in this small municipal museum that preserves the memory of a craftsman of genius.

activities.text: Guebwiller's vineyard is unique in Alsace: it's the only commune in the region to produce four Grands Crus — Kessler, Kitterlé, Saering, and Spiegel. The slopes are vertiginous, some reaching 50 degrees, supported by 50 kilometers of dry-stone walls. Operators offer guided tours in electric 4x4s across these terraces for those who don't want to climb on foot. The tasting that follows helps you understand why these steep terroirs produce wines of exceptional minerality.

practical_info.booking: Guided tour by reservation with estates or the tourist office

activities.text: The marked vineyard trail climbs among the Grands Crus from lower Guebwiller to the overlook dominating the four terroirs. Count on two hours for the complete loop — solid shoes essential on these steep slopes. The view from the top over the Alsace plain and Rhine is worth the effort.

visits.text: The Cité de l'Automobile houses the world's largest car collection in a former woolen mill — and its history reads like a novel. Brothers Fritz and Hans Schlumpf, textile industrialists in Mulhouse, secretly amassed hundreds of cars in their factory from the 1960s onward, sometimes spending their workers' money. In March 1977, when the company went bankrupt and laid-off workers entered the factory to search it, they discovered to their astonishment 500 cars lined up beneath Art Nouveau street lamps. The Schlumpfs had fled to Switzerland. The collection was listed as a monument in 1978. Among the 450 vehicles on display, two of the six Bugatti Royales that exist in the world: Ettore Bugatti's personal limousine (6 meters long, designed by his son Jean at age 20) and the Royale Park Ward. Count on at least two hours.

The Cité du Train spreads across 60,000 square meters Europe's largest railway collection. From 19th-century steam locomotives to TGVs, the route traces 200 years of French rail history. The 'spectacle route' with its animated figures and reconstructed 1900s station sets is particularly successful.

The Temple Saint-Étienne, in the heart of Mulhouse, is the town's most spectacular building. Its neo-Gothic spire rises to 97 meters — the tallest Protestant spire in France. Its 19th-century stained glass illuminates an imposing nave. The town of Mulhouse was long an independent Protestant republican city before joining France in 1798.

The place de la Réunion, in the heart of the old town, is surrounded by some of the best-preserved Renaissance façades in Alsace. The town hall with its trompe-l'oeil frescoes is Mulhouse's emblematic building — its reconstructed wall paintings recount the town's history.

activities.text: The Électropolis Museum traces the adventure of electricity since the late 19th century. The 170-ton Sulzer-BBC machine starts up each day — a striking experience. It once powered Mulhouse's DMC spinning mill. A good way to understand why this town was the cradle of Alsace's industrial revolution.

Mulhouse's zoological and botanical park extends over 25 hectares and shelters 1,200 animals. It's one of France's oldest zoos and one of the rare ones to have maintained a remarkable botanical collection. A green escape in the heart of the industrial city.

visits.text: The Collegiate Church of Saint-Thiébaut is Thann's Gothic jewel and one of the most representative edifices of Rhenish Gothic in Alsace. Its construction lasted over two centuries, from the late 13th century until 1516. The people of Thann like to say: 'Strasbourg has the tallest, Freiburg the biggest, Thann the most beautiful!' — speaking of the bell tower. The stone-lace spire rises to 78 meters. The west portal is carved with three tympana featuring over 500 figures: the Life of the Virgin, the Nativity, and the Crucifixion. Inside, don't miss the 15th-century choir stalls or the stained glass from the same period.

The Witch's Eye watches over Thann from the ruins of Engelbourg castle. In 1673, Louis XIV ordered this fortress dismantled — miners from Giromagny set fire to explosive charges. After three attempts, the great tower broke and a section lifted vertically, forming this cyclopean fragment of stone that resembles an eye scrutinizing the plain. The climb from lower Thann takes twenty minutes and offers a 360° view over the Thur valley, the Rangen vineyard, and the Vosges ridges.

Stroll through Thann's old town among 16th-century houses, their oriels and fountains. The place Saint-Thiébaut at the foot of the collegiate church is the heart of local life. The Museum of the Friends of Thann, installed in a former grain hall from 1519, gathers objects and archives on the town's history and the vineyard.

activities.text: The Rangen vineyard is Alsace's southernmost and steepest, on volcanic slopes facing full south between 350 and 450 meters elevation. It's the only vineyard in Alsace entirely classified as Grand Cru — Riesling and Gewurztraminer acquire a unique mineral character from the basaltic soil. Operators offer guided tours of the vineyard. It's also the southern terminus of the Alsace Wine Route running 170 kilometers from Marlenheim.

practical_info.tip: Southern gateway of the Alsace Wine Route

activities.text: Climb to Engelbourg castle via the trail starting from the Bungert parking lot in Thann. Cross the bridge over the Thur, take rue du Rangen for 150 meters then first right. The climb takes thirty minutes and the ruins site is freely accessible. The panoramic view from the Witch's Eye over Thann, the ridges, and the plain amply rewards the effort.

visits.text: Hartmannswillerkopf — nicknamed Vieil Armand by poilus who couldn't pronounce the Alsatian name — dominates the Alsace plain at 956 meters. In 1915, it became the theater of combat of extreme violence: the summit changed hands repeatedly over a few weeks, both armies digging kilometers of trenches into the Vosges sandstone. An estimated 25,000 French and German soldiers fell here, for virtually no tactical result. The soldiers called it 'the man-eater' or 'the mountain of death.'

The National Monument, built between 1924 and 1932 and inaugurated by President Albert Lebrun, is one of four Great War national monuments along with Douaumont, Notre-Dame-de-Lorette, and Dormans. You access it through an 80-meter honor trench that immediately immerses you in the site's atmosphere. The crypt holds the bones of 12,000 soldiers whose identities were lost. At the entrance, two winged bronze statues are the work of sculptor Antoine Bourdelle. The Altar of the Fatherland, outside, bears the coats of arms of twelve donor cities.

The Franco-German Historial, inaugurated on November 10, 2017 by Presidents Macron and Steinmeier, is the first Great War museum to present events from both countries' perspectives. The scenography follows the evolution of Franco-German relations from the trenches to contemporary reconciliation. Testimonies from soldiers on both sides, archival photographs, and objects from military daily life constitute the bulk of the exhibition.

The battlefield preserves kilometers of trenches carved into the Vosges sandstone, underground shelters, barbed-wire networks, and shell craters. A 4.5-kilometer interpreted route winds through the combat zone. To pay your respects, the Silberloch necropolis, inaugurated in 1922, gathers 1,264 individual graves of French soldiers and six ossuaries.

activities.text: Follow the marked historical trail through the French and German trenches. Explanatory panels at each crossroads situate positions and recount the 1915 offensives. The complete circuit covers about 4.5 kilometers and takes two hours. Bring good shoes — the terrain is irregular and slopes can be slippery in wet weather.

From the Panorama Rock (Aussichtsfelsen), at the ridge's extremity, the view opens over the southern Alsace plain to Mulhouse, across the Belfort Gap, and on clear days to the Bernese Alps. Here you understand why this summit was so fiercely contested — it constituted an exceptional strategic observation point over the entire border.

seo.h1_title: Upper Rhine Road Trip: Colmar and the Southern Wine Route
seo.intro_paragraph: From Colmar's Little Venice and its Isenheim Altarpiece (1512-1516), a masterpiece of Western painting, to the UNESCO-listed fortified city of Neuf-Brisach and the vineyards of the Wine Route, this 4-day circuit crosses the Upper Rhine from end to end. Eguisheim, France's favorite village in 2013, AOP Munster cheese in its valley of origin, Thann's Gothic collegiate church, and the Franco-German memorial at Vieil Armand complete this journey through medieval heritage, Alsatian gastronomy, and the memory of war.
seo.seo_hook: Grünewald's altarpiece in Colmar, Vauban's UNESCO-listed fortifications, terraced vineyards, AOP Munster cheese, and a Great War battlefield: the Upper Rhine in all its depth.
featured_list: Colmar: Grünewald's Isenheim Altarpiece (1512-1516) at the Unterlinden Museum, housed in a 13th-century Dominican convent
Neuf-Brisach: sole example of Vauban's third system, created from scratch in 1698 and UNESCO-listed in 2008
Eguisheim: village elected France's favorite in 2013, founded in 720, birthplace of Pope Leo IX in 1002
Mulhouse: world's largest automobile collection with two of the six existing Bugatti Royales

places_taglines.FR::guebwiller: The only town in Alsace bold enough to claim four Grand Cru vineyards as its own
places_taglines.FR::mulhouse: Where industrial barons hid a fortune in Bugattis and secrets beneath Art Nouveau lamps

highlights: The Isenheim Altarpiece (1512-1516) by Matthias Grünewald at Colmar's Unterlinden Museum, one of the most expressive paintings in Western art
Neuf-Brisach, Vauban's masterpiece created from scratch in 1698 and sole example of his third defensive system, UNESCO-listed in 2008
Eguisheim, village elected France's favorite in 2013, founded in 720 and cradle of Alsatian viticulture around its octagonal castle
Hartmannswillerkopf (Vieil Armand), Great War memorial site where 25,000 soldiers fell and first Franco-German Historial inaugurated in 2017
