itineraries.title: The 10 Most Beautiful Villages of the Haut-Var
itineraries.subtitle: Tufa cliffs, a turquoise waterfall, French formal gardens and hand-painted faience: a 2-day road trip through the Var backcountry, between the Provence Verte and the gateway to the Verdon.
itineraries.notes: Entirely car-based itinerary. In July and August the Sillans waterfall gets very crowded — paid parking from April 1 to September 30. The Vallon Sourn at Correns may be closed during fire-risk periods. The Chateaudouble gorges have been closed to traffic since 2010; the village is reached only by the D51 from Figanieres.
itineraries.climate: Best period: May-June and September-October, temperatures 20-28°C, ideal light for these hilltop villages. Avoid July-August (scorching heat 32-38°C, tourist crowds, drought). Watch for the Mistral wind year-round, especially fierce in winter and spring in the Haut-Var.

visits.text: Cotignac has been listed among France's Most Beautiful Villages since 2022 — and the moment you first catch sight of the tufa cliff, 80 meters high and 400 meters wide, standing over the village rooftops, you understand why. This ochre wall, shaped by the Cassole river in the Quaternary era, is pierced with dwellings hollowed straight out of the rock. A secured path lets you explore these cavities from the foot of the cliff — allow an hour for the full visit. You will find old stables, oil mills and even grain silos, all cut into the tufa by the villagers of the Middle Ages. If you can, take the guided tour offered in summer: the stories about daily life in these caves are worth it.

At the cliff's summit stand the two so-called Saracen towers, built in the 12th century — they're actually the remnants of the feudal castle constructed from 1033 onwards by Boniface de Castellane. Climb up to them via the cobbled paths for a 360° panorama sweeping across the entire plain stretching to Carcès and Entrecasteaux. The medieval village below is equally worth exploring on foot: its 16th and 17th-century stone lanes open onto flower-decked squares, and its 17 fountains — including the famous Cascade fountain — bear witness to the water abundance that built Cotignac's prosperity.

About 1.5 km from the center, the Notre-Dame de Graces sanctuary is worth the detour. In 1519 the Virgin is said to have appeared here to a woodcutter on Mont Verdaille. Louis XIV himself came on pilgrimage on February 21, 1660, with his mother Anne of Austria, to give thanks to Mary for the birth of the Dauphin. The site is quiet, shaded and offers a fine view over the hills.

activities.text: Rise early on Tuesday morning for the Cotignac market, held on Cours Gambetta beneath the centuries-old plane trees. This is one of the most flavorful markets in the Haut-Var: bottarga, lavender honey, hillside olive oil, goat cheese and all-natural soaps. Arrive before 9:30 AM to have your pick and chat with the producers without the crowds.

Head out for an hour's walk in the hills around Cotignac to see the vineyards (Coteaux Varois en Provence appellation) and olive groves encircling the village. Local estates offer tastings — check with the tourist office for opening hours.

visits.text: Sillans-la-Cascade is a medieval village with 11th-century ramparts built with a unique purpose: not to protect a fortress, but to safeguard a spring. The Bresque River, which rises at Fox-Amphoux, feeds the highest waterfall in the department here. The village has a complex castle history: three castles have succeeded one another on its territory — the first medieval one disappeared, the second was erected in 1609 and destroyed during the Revolution, and the third was built in the 19th century and purchased by the commune in 1992 from the Count of Castellane.

The Sillans waterfall is the village's centerpiece — do not miss it on any account. From the parking area, an 800-meter marked trail runs through a shaded stand of old plane trees before reaching the viewpoint, facing the 42-meter fall. The water of the Bresque drops into a pool coloured emerald and turquoise by micro-algae and the limestone bed. Swimming in the main pool is strictly forbidden for safety reasons — rockfalls are possible — but swimming areas can be reached further downstream. Allow 25 to 30 minutes for the round trip, or 45 minutes if you go down to the river. Come early in summer: parking is paid from April to September and fills up fast after 10 AM.

activities.text: After the viewpoint, continue on a longer circuit along the Bresque to discover the small natural pools open for swimming downstream from the waterfall. The water is cool even in midsummer and the shaded banks are ideal for a picnic break. Marked trails let you climb back up to the heights overlooking the village with views across the entire valley.

visits.text: The Chateau d'Entrecasteaux is one of the fine surprises of the Var hinterland. Built on a rocky spur, it has stood 20 meters above the village since the 11th century, but it is above all its 16th- and 17th-century facade that strikes you, with its balanced proportions and its wrought-iron balustrades. Its history is full of scandal and adventure: in 1669 it passed to Francois Adhemar de Castellane, son-in-law of Madame de Sevigne. Le Notre himself is said to have given the marquise the plans of the Orangery garden at Versailles so that her son-in-law could reproduce them here. In 1784 the Marquis Jean-Baptiste de Bruny murdered his wife and fled abroad, ending his life in Portuguese jails. His brother, Admiral Bruny d'Entrecasteaux, born in the castle in 1737 and sent by Louis XVI in search of La Perouse, died of scurvy in 1793 during his expedition in the South Pacific.

The French formal garden, freely accessible year-round, is a gem often overlooked by guidebooks. Designed according to plans inspired by Versailles, it extends below the château's south façade in geometric terraces. Take time to sit and admire the perspective — it's particularly beautiful in late afternoon when golden light strikes the stone façades. Following the village lanes afterwards, you'll discover handsome medieval houses with tall, narrow façades, vaulted passages and Provençal fountains. The fortified church of Saint-Sauveur and the 18th-century Pont Saint-Pierre over the Bresque complete the visit.

activities.text: The Bresque flows through Entrecasteaux for several kilometers before joining Sillans — upstream and downstream from the village, paths following the river offer cool, shaded walks, ideal in summer. Natural swimming spots exist along the river depending on water levels.

visits.text: Salernes is the French capital of the hexagonal tomette — the small red terracotta tile that has paved floors all over Provence since the early 19th century. From 1830 onwards, local factories specialized in this tiling, prized for its thermal inertia: cool in summer, mild in winter. The Terra Rossa museum, housed in a former tile factory converted by the architect Jean-Michel Wilmotte, traces 7,000 years of ceramic activity in the Salernes area. The visit takes in a palaeontology room showing local digs, a full reconstruction of the early 20th-century workshops with their period machinery, and an exceptional collection of more than 2,000 decorated tiles from the Middle Ages to the 19th century, some of them unique in Europe. Allow at least an hour and a half to make the most of it.

The rest of Salernes can be explored leisurely on foot: about fifteen pottery and ceramics workshops are established in and around the village, most open to the public. Step inside two or three to watch artisans at work and understand the techniques that transform the red clay from local hills into tomettes or decorated faience. The old town's lanes, fountains and the Bresque River below complete the stroll.

activities.text: On Sunday morning, the Salernes market is one of the liveliest in the Haut-Var. Local producers sell honey, fresh figs (the white Salernes fig is renowned), olive oil and goat cheeses. It's also an opportunity to find artisan ceramic pieces directly from exhibitors. Arrive between 8 AM and 10 AM for the best selection.

Salernes' old mill and oil press allow you to complete your discovery of traditional local industry. Guided tours combining all three sites — mill, oil press and Terra Rossa — are offered on certain Tuesdays in July and August. Check with the tourist office for dates.

practical_info.booking: Check dates at the tourist office

visits.text: Correns is France's first entirely organic-certified village — a revolution launched in 1997 when its mayor, a winemaker and agronomist, proposed that all farmers convert together to organic agriculture during the height of the wine crisis. Since then, the local economy has thrived on organic Côtes-de-Provence vineyards, chicken and goat farming, honey and olive oil. Wander the cobbled lanes that spiral upward around Fort Gibron, a 12th-century priory of the Abbey of Montmajour in Arles — its 2-meter-thick walls of Correns stone are a fine example of Provençal Romanesque art. The Fort now houses a cultural center with concerts and exhibitions. At the village's base, the 14th-century Porte Saint-Germain with its portcullis gives access to the old quarter — legend has it that Saint Germain stopped here on his return from Rome.

The single-arch stone bridge spanning the Argens connects the old village on the right bank with the suburb on the left. From the bridge, several houses in the center look directly onto the river — the typical image of Correns in summer, with gardens reaching down to the water. The 18th-century baroque church conceals in its choir a gilded wooden high altar topped with a glory, an altarpiece of rare quality for the region.

activities.text: The Vallon Sourn, between Correns and Châteauvert, is one of the Var's most beautiful natural sites. The Argens winds for 4 km at the foot of limestone cliffs renowned for their climbing routes, through protected riparian woodland. Shaded pebble beaches line the river — ideal for family swimming away from crowds. Local outfitters offer canoe trips on the Argens from Correns, descending the valley and passing the Benedictine lock. Check ahead on access conditions during fire-risk periods.

Several organic wine estates in Correns open their cellars for tastings and visits. The white wines of the Côtes-de-Provence appellation are the local specialty. Check with the tourist office for estates that welcome visitors without reservation.

map_keywords: Chapelle Notre-Dame du Bon Secours Fox-Amphoux grotte

visits.text: Fox-Amphoux is a double village: "new Fox" down in the plain holds the school, the town hall and the post office; Old Fox sits perched at 540 meters on a spur and has kept all its medieval character. The remains of the Blacas castle, first mentioned in 1200, stand above the stepped lanes. On the church square, do not miss the hackberry tree, more than 400 years old and 5 meters round — it stays cool there even in the middle of July. The panorama from the viewpoint on rue de la Prison takes in the whole of the Var, as far as the Sainte-Baume and the Alpilles in clear weather. This is also the birthplace of Paul Barras, born here in 1755: this revolutionary viscount voted for the death of Louis XVI, helped bring down Robespierre in 1794 and sat in the Directory before being pushed aside by Napoleon.

Descend from Old Fox on a cobbled path to the Chapel of Notre-Dame du Bon Secours, set within a grotto at the foot of a limestone tufa cliff. The way is marked by several oratories and a peaceful forest atmosphere. Inside the grotto, behind the gates, the altar is adorned with flowers and the vault covered with small ex-votos. A discreet and touching place, off the tourist circuits.

activities.text: At the former cooperative cellar at the village's base, the DinoFox Museo displays fossils and dinosaur bones discovered in the area — notably the Variraptor mechinorum, discovered between 1992 and 1995 by amateur paleontologists, which provided the first proof of a dromaeosaur (velociraptor cousin) in Europe. The visit is free and fascinating for the whole family.

In late afternoon, settle on the Old Fox viewpoint to watch the sun descend over the wooded hills of the Haut-Var. The perched village then stands out as a dark silhouette against the horizon — one of the most distinctive views in the backcountry.

visits.text: Villecroze is first of all an exceptional natural site: a tufa cliff hollowed out by water over 700,000 years, in which cave dwellings have been occupied since prehistory. The Benedictine monks of the Saint-Victor abbey in Marseille took refuge here during the Saracen raids of the 10th century. In the second half of the 16th century the lord of Villecroze turned them into a stronghold, cutting mullioned windows and arrow slits into them — they have belonged to the commune since 1633 and are classified as a Natural Monument of artistic character. The guided tour (booking required) covers 5 levels, passes behind the waterfall and shows the limestone columns formed by seeping water. Note: closed shoes required, open to children from 6 years old.

The 2-hectare municipal park at the cliff's base hosts the 35-meter waterfall descending from Tourtour — its spring, rich in limestone, helped form the tufa cliff from which the caves hang. The park was created in the 1930s and shelters many Mediterranean species: cedars, fig trees, olive trees, palms, magnolias. It's one of the coolest spots in the Haut-Var in summer. After the waterfall and caves, stroll through the old medieval village: its arcades, seven fountains and flower-filled lanes reveal an authentic atmosphere.

The 11th-century Saint-Victor chapel, south of the village, hosts the Villecroze Music Academy. Free concerts of a high standard are given there in summer — check the dates with the tourist office, some are held in the evening in the chapel or in the open-air theater with its clipped cypresses.

activities.text: On Thursday morning, the Villecroze market sets up under the plane trees on the main square. Local producers of black truffle (in season, November through March), olive oil, saffron, honey and goat cheese — all the flavors of the Haut-Var are represented. Don't leave without a piece of fresh goat cheese.

map_keywords: Place des Ormeaux Tourtour huit fontaines
Panorama Tourtour 635 m village dans le ciel

visits.text: Tourtour is nicknamed "the village in the Provençal sky" — and at 635 meters altitude, that's no exaggeration. On clear days, the panorama from Place des Ormeaux embraces the entire Var department all the way to the sea. This central square, shaded by two great elms and crossed by eight fountains, is the village heart where residents gather throughout the day. Its stone houses topped with round tiles, vaulted passages and sun-drenched lanes deserve a long stroll. Art galleries and artisan workshops line the streets — Tourtour has attracted creators for decades.

Tourtour's medieval castle, whose walls date from the Middle Ages, was remodeled in the 17th century. Its outer walls front the square and form the backdrop of Place des Ormeaux. The Church of Saint-Denis, Romanesque in its oldest sections, completes this compact, well-preserved built heritage. From the summit plateau, the view of Sainte-Victoire on clear days is striking.

activities.text: The Tourtour Provençal market is held Wednesday and Saturday mornings — it's one of the most popular markets in the backcountry thanks to the altitude and cool site. Honey, olives, soaps, pottery and local wines are offered in a convivial atmosphere. If you're there Saturday, the selection is more extensive.

Several olive oil mills operate around Tourtour and offer visits and olive oil tastings. Check with the tourist office for addresses open to the public. A walking trail descends from Tourtour to Villecroze passing by the Baume waterfall — allow 2.5 hours round trip.

visits.text: The way into Chateaudouble is a spectacle in itself: the road runs 40 meters through a tunnel cut into the rock before coming out at the perched village. Mentioned as early as 1021 under the name "Castellum Diaboli" — the devil's castle, because of a site the Romans judged impregnable — the village owes its present name to the two castles it had in the Middle Ages, one on each side of the Nartuby. It stands 130 meters above the gorges, and from Place Beausoleil at the top of the village the view over the limestone cliffs and the gorges cut by the river is dizzying. Climb the cobbled lanes to the remains of the 12th-century square keep on the Sainte-Anne plateau — you can also see the ruins of a second castle on the far side of the gorges.

Nostradamus himself mentioned Chateaudouble in one of his prophecies: "Chateaudouble, double castle, the river shall be your tomb", seeing in the Nartuby the natural force able to wear away the cliffs that protect the village. The floods of 2010 did indeed carry off the gorge road. Wander the narrow cobbled lanes between the medieval houses and look at the carved pediments — Templar crosses are still visible on some facades, a reminder of their presence in the 13th century. The church of Notre-Dame de l'Annonciation, built in 1550 and enlarged in 1678, holds three listed altarpieces and 16th-century baptismal fonts.

activities.text: The Nartuby gorges are a classified site and playground for climbing enthusiasts — 5 sites with 350 routes from grade 4 to 8b+. For non-climbers, hiking trails follow the gorge edges from the hamlet of Rebouillon at Châteaudouble's base. Golden eagles and other raptors nesting in the cliffs are regularly spotted.

map_keywords: Lac de Sainte-Croix Gorges du Verdon entrée

visits.text: Moustiers-Sainte-Marie is one of Provence's most striking villages — nestled between two cliffs linked by a 135-meter chain bearing a 115-cm-diameter five-pointed golden star. According to the legend told by Frédéric Mistral, a knight named Blacas, imprisoned by Saracens during the Crusades, had vowed to suspend a star as an ex-voto if the Virgin granted him freedom. Founded in the 5th century by monks from the island of Lérins who had sheltered in tufa cavities, the village developed from the 17th century a faience renowned throughout Europe. The faience museum, with its 300 exceptional pieces, traces this history from the first glazed earthenware of the Middle Ages to contemporary creations.

Climb up to the Chapel of Notre-Dame-de-Beauvoir — count 262 steps on a cobbled path winding up the cliff face from the Notre-Dame bridge. The chapel, built in the 12th century and expanded in 1536, blends Romanesque and Gothic art and has been classified as a Historic Monument since 1921. The Stations of the Cross have been adorned since 1860 with 14 stations in faience tiles. From the esplanade of the chapel at 830 meters altitude, the view plunges over Moustiers' rooftops and, in the distance, to the turquoise waters of Lac de Sainte-Croix. Sturdy-soled shoes recommended — the steps can be slippery after rain.

activities.text: Step into one or two faience workshops in the village lanes — artisans explain traditional techniques and motifs, often in front of an active kiln. Moustiers now counts 8 active workshops. The Friday morning market is held on Place Montelupo, facing the faience museum.

A 10-minute drive away, Lac de Sainte-Croix is the natural culmination of this itinerary. Outfitters offer canoe, pedal boat and electric boat rentals to head up the entrance to the Verdon Gorges from the lake. The water here is a remarkable turquoise color. In June or September, crowds are far lighter than in July–August.

seo.h1_title: The 10 Most Beautiful Villages of the Haut-Var
seo.intro_paragraph: Between the tufa cliff of Cotignac (listed among France's Most Beautiful Villages in 2022) and the star suspended over Moustiers-Sainte-Marie, this 2-day trip crosses the part of the Provence Verte that tourists know least. A 42-meter waterfall at Sillans, the formal gardens of the Chateau d'Entrecasteaux laid out to plans from Versailles, France's first organic village at Correns, the cave dwellings of Villecroze — the Haut-Var opens up to those who leave the beaten track.
seo.seo_hook: Inhabited tufa cliffs, a turquoise waterfall, formal gardens and Verdon faience: the secret Provence of the Haut-Var in 10 stops.
featured_list: Cotignac: an 80-meter tufa cliff pierced with cave dwellings, listed a Most Beautiful Village in 2022
Sillans-la-Cascade: the Var's highest waterfall at 42 meters, emerald lagoon and 11th-century ramparts
Châteaudouble: village perched 130 meters above the Nartuby gorges, mentioned by Nostradamus
Moustiers-Sainte-Marie: a star hanging from a 135-meter chain and faience renowned since the 17th century

tourtour village in the provençal sky

highlights: Cotignac: 80m x 400m tufa cliff, accessible cave dwellings and sanctuary visited by Louis XIV in 1660
Sillans-la-Cascade: 42-meter waterfall fed by the Bresque (source at Fox-Amphoux), emerald pool — paid parking April through September

itineraries.title: Var Road Trip: French Riviera & Green Provence
itineraries.subtitle: From naval ports to island sanctuaries, where lavender hills meet turquoise waters
itineraries.climate: Best time: April-June and September-October, temperatures 18-26°C, ideal sunshine. Avoid July-August (intense heat 30-35°C, massive crowds, high prices). The mistral wind can blow hard in winter and spring, making the coast windy despite mild temperatures (10-15°C).
specialties: AOC Côtes de Provence rosé wines

map_keywords: Musée national de la Marine Toulon
Cathédrale Notre-Dame de la Seds Toulon

visits.text: Behind the monumental 18th-century gateway, the National Maritime Museum showcases ship models, galleys and paintings tracing four centuries of naval tradition. The displays explore the history of the Toulon arsenal and the city's major role in French maritime history.

Board the cable car for a six-minute ride and 378-meter ascent to the summit of Mont Faron. At the top, the Memorial to the Provence Landing and Liberation recounts the August 1944 operation through period artifacts and multimedia exhibits.

Notre-Dame de la Seds Cathedral, founded in the 5th century, blends Romanesque and Gothic elements with a unified Gothic nave, a bell tower crowned by a campanile, and an 18th-century organ. The side chapels house the Chapel of the Virgin and the Corpus Domini chapel.

Listed as a historic monument since 1947, the Tour Royale was begun in 1514 under Louis XII and completed in 1524 under Francis I to defend the entrance to Toulon harbor. Its seven-meter-thick walls and moat make it a rare example of an Italian-style 'torrione'. It hosts cultural events in summer.
The Toulon Opera House, erected over 150 years ago on Place Victor Hugo, seats up to 1,100 spectators. Its classical facade and renowned acoustics make it one of the jewels of the old town.
Step into the Hotel des Arts TPM, a 400 m2 space dedicated to contemporary art. Rotating exhibitions alternate between paintings, sculptures, and installations. Admission is free.

activities.text: Wander through the stalls of the Cours Lafayette market, open Tuesday through Sunday. Herbes de Provence, olives, soaps, and fresh produce line the stands in a typical Provencal market atmosphere.
Embark on a narrated one-hour boat tour of Toulon harbor. You will see military vessels at the quay, the fortifications, the mussel farms of Lazaret Bay, and the naval cemetery.

practical_info.tip: Regular departures from Quai Cronstadt

activities.text: Head to the Mourillon beaches, bordered by landscaped gardens, lawns, and playgrounds. Beyond, the coastal path leads to the coves of Mejean and Magaud, wild inlets at the foot of pine-lined cliffs.

visits.text: Built in the 1920s by architect Robert Mallet-Stevens, Villa Noailles is a masterpiece of modern architecture listed as a historic monument. Gabriel Guevrekian's cubist garden offers a panoramic view of the Golden Islands. The venue hosts exhibitions and fashion and design festivals throughout the year.
Below the villa, Parc Saint-Bernard unfolds its narrow terraces linked by stone staircases. The botanical garden gathers Mediterranean and exotic species: rosemary, wisteria, and rare plants.

Jardins Olbius-Riquier spreads across seven hectares of greenery. An exotic greenhouse shelters palms, bamboo, banana trees, and cacti. The pond and its cascade offer refreshing coolness in summer. Free admission year-round.

Climb up to the Collégiale Saint-Paul, adorned with ex-votos, then wind back down through the steep alleys of the old town. The Templars' Tower, a medieval vestige of the order, can be visited with a treasure hunt for children.

The ruins of the medieval castle crown a rocky peak at the town's summit. Dating from the 11th century, it offers a panorama over Hyères Bay, the Golden Islands, and the Maures massif. Free access via the ruin trail from Villa Noailles.
Visit the archaeological site of Olbia, a Greek trading post founded in the 4th century BCE. Excavations reveal ramparts, dwellings, and Roman baths by the sea.

activities.text: On Saturday mornings, the Iles d'Or market takes over the old town. Seasonal fruit, tapenade, soaps, and local crafts fill the stalls under the plane trees.

practical_info.tip: Arrive early to enjoy the atmosphere

activities.text: Follow the coastal trail around the Giens peninsula. Between salt pans, pine groves, and coves, the route runs along the salt road and its marshes, where pink flamingos and grey herons come to rest.
In the mood for the beach? L'Almanarre beach, a long ribbon of sand between the sea and the salt pans, is renowned for windsurfing and kitesurfing thanks to its steady winds.

visits.text: Fort Sainte-Agathe, strengthened in 1531 under Francis I, has dominated the harbor since Antiquity. Managed by Port-Cros National Park, it hosts exhibitions on the island's marine and terrestrial biodiversity. The view from the ramparts sweeps over the village and Courtade beach.

Notre-Dame beach, voted Europe's most beautiful beach, stretches in a bay bordered by eucalyptus. Its turquoise, shallow waters make it ideal for swimming. Count on 25 minutes on foot or 10 minutes by bike from the village.
Near the fort, the Moulin du Bonheur—a Provençal windmill restored by the National Park—offers a glimpse of island agricultural life. Free guided tours for visitors under 18, from May to September.

Porquerolles village nestles behind the harbor, around the shaded Place d'Armes. Sainte-Anne church and the houses with colorful shutters compose a postcard scene. In the evening, once the ferries have left, calm settles over the village.
Fort de la Repentance, an 1893 buried battery, offers an open view over Notre-Dame Bay and the harbor. The interior can be visited during Heritage Days. The final stretch is steep by bike.

activities.text: Bike rental shops are set up at the harbor. Four trails marked out by the National Park let you cross the island from north to south between vineyards, pine groves, and maquis.

practical_info.tip: Rent upon ferry arrival to avoid sold-out stock

activities.text: Follow the forts circuit: 9.5 km of trails linking Forts Lequin, Alycastre, Repentance, and Sainte-Agathe. The route retraces the stages of the island's military life through four centuries of fortifications.
The island's wine estates devote 70% of their output to AOC Cotes de Provence rose. Tastings are by reservation in a unique island setting, between vines and pine groves.
Two dive centers offer explorations of the seabed around the island, classified as the core of Port-Cros National Park. Posidonia seagrass meadows, groupers, and barracudas populate these waters.

visits.text: A 12th-century medieval village listed among France's Most Beautiful Villages, Bormes unfolds its flowered alleys, its 'cuberts' (vaulted passages), and its ochre-tinted facades. Over 700 plant species color the village, from bougainvillea in summer to mimosa in winter.

Climb up to the 13th-14th-century castle, a historic monument since 1931. From the village's highest point, the panorama takes in Lavandou Bay, the islands of Levant and Port-Cros, Faviere harbor, and Cap Benat.

Saint-Trophyme Church, built in the 18th century in a Provençal Romanesque style, replaced the old church near the castle, which had become too small. In the heart of the village, it stands out for its sober stone façade and typically Provençal atmosphere.

Parc Gonzalez, listed as a Remarkable Garden, brings together across 3,000 m2 plants from Australia and around the world, including 250 species arranged by landscape designer Gilles Augias. The terraces offer views over the Mediterranean.
The Museum of History and Art of Bormes, housed in the former town hall, offers an augmented reality tour via the HistoPad. The rooms reveal the village's secrets through the centuries.

activities.text: Fort de Bregancon, a state residence overlooking the sea, can be glimpsed from the coast. Head down to Cabasson beach below: white sand, crystal-clear water, and a direct view of the fort.
Nine wine estates and one cooperative cellar offer tastings of AOC Cotes de Provence. The Vignobles & Decouvertes label guarantees a quality welcome in the cellars.

practical_info.tip: Ask for the local rosés

activities.text: From Faviere harbor, boat excursions head to Port-Cros, Porquerolles, or offshore to watch dolphins. Departures run from April to October.

visits.text: The Musee de l'Annonciade, housed in a former 16th-century chapel, holds a first-rate collection: Pointillist, Nabis, and Fauvist paintings. Signac, Matisse, Derain, and Marquet are all represented. The place is a reminder that Saint-Tropez was a major center of the pictorial avant-garde.

The Citadel, erected in 1602 under Henri IV, has dominated the harbor for four centuries. The hexagonal keep, a historic monument since 1921, houses the Museum of Maritime History. Models, artifacts, and immersive scenography recount the Tropezian sailors—from whaling to trade with the Ottoman Empire.

Place des Lices, shaded by century-old plane trees, has been the village's beating heart since the 19th century. On Tuesdays and Saturdays, the Provençal market takes over the square. The rest of the time, pétanque games animate the café terraces.

Notre-Dame de l'Assomption church, with its characteristic ochre and pink bell tower, has watched over the village since the 16th century. Inside, the bust of Saint Torpès recalls the founding legend of the town.
On the Citadel ramparts, some thirty peacocks roam freely. The plunging view over the Tropezian rooftops, the naval cemetery, and the gulf makes up one of the finest panoramas on the coast.

activities.text: Follow the coastal path from Graniers beach. This seaside trail runs along the coves and headlands, offering panoramas between pine groves and turquoise water. Swimming is possible in the wild coves.
The old harbor is made for strolling: fishing boats sit alongside yachts, and the colorful facades are reflected in the water. Head to Quai Jean-Jaures for the permanent spectacle.
Carry on to Ramatuelle, a medieval village perched on Paillas hill overlooking Pampelonne Bay. Its spiralling lanes and its ramparts offer a quiet counterpoint to the bustle of Saint-Tropez.

visits.text: Grimaud Castle, built in the 11th century, preserves its three enclosures, two massive round towers, and a medieval keep. Pillaged during the Revolution, its ruins still offer a panorama over the Gulf of Saint-Tropez and the Maures massif. In summer, the ramparts host the Grimaldines festival.

Saint-Michel church, Romanesque and dating from the 12th century, is a listed historic monument. Its typically Provencal architecture contrasts with the Penitents' and Saint-Roch chapels, whose mural paintings have been restored.

Get lost in the village's cobbled lanes: Rue des Arcades houses the Templars' house, a fine 16th-century Renaissance building adorned with three Gothic arches. Mullioned windows and doorways framed with serpentinite punctuate the stroll.

The Saint-Roch mill, a 17th-century windmill restored in 1990 by the Companions of the Tour de France, crowns the village on its hill. On the ground, a large slab was used for threshing wheat; beside it, an old press produced olive oil.

Reach the Pont des Fées via a 3 km loop from the mill. This 15th-century arched bridge spans the Garde and served as an aqueduct to supply the village with water. The trail follows the river through a cool, shaded valley.

activities.text: Port-Grimaud, a lakeside town created in the 1960s by architect François Spoerry, can be explored by boat on its canals. Each house has direct water access and a mooring ring. The 'Provençal Venice' can also be discovered on foot from the village.
The Provencal markets of Grimaud and Port-Grimaud alternate through the week. Local producers and artisans offer fruit, cheese, olive oil, and craft objects.
Several wine estates around the village offer tastings of AOC Cotes de Provence wines. The Grimaud wine cooperative lets you sample the local vintages.

practical_info.tip: Check with the tourist office for schedules

visits.text: The Roman amphitheater, built in the 1st century, could hold 10,000 spectators who came to watch gladiatorial combat. Its tiers, corridors, and vomitoria can be visited freely. The venue still hosts concerts and shows.

Saint-Leonce Cathedral forms, together with the 5th-century Paleo-Christian baptistery, one of France's oldest episcopal complexes. The octagonal baptistery, supported by reused ancient columns, preserves its original baptismal font.

The 13th-century Romanesque cloister is a medieval jewel. Its larch wood ceiling, carved in the 14th century, presents 300 painted panels of fantastic creatures, saints, and scenes of daily life. A bestiary unique in France.

The Roman aqueduct stretched 42 kilometers with a 481-meter drop and 36 aqueduct bridges. At La Roche Taillée, a 50-meter canal was carved directly into the rock. Classified as a historic monument since 1886, its vestiges can be visited on foot from downtown.

The Porte des Gaules, one of the four main entrances to the Roman city, preserves its monumental pillars overgrown with wild capers. Just beside it, a section of Roman paved road testifies to the past of Forum Julii.
The archaeological museum, behind the cloister, displays the results of local excavations. The Hermes Bicephale, a two-faced bust that has become the emblem of Frejus, is its centerpiece.

activities.text: Stroll through the pedestrian lanes of the historic center, between Place Formige with its terraces and Rue Sieyes with its good addresses. The Provencal market brings the squares to life every morning.
Villa Aurelienne and its 24-hectare park offer a green break in town. This Palladian-style residence, surrounded by umbrella pines, hosts temporary exhibitions.
Head to the Roman theater, more modest than the amphitheater but fascinating. Its restored tiers make it possible to picture the comedy and poetry performances of Antiquity.

map_keywords: Basilique Notre-Dame de la Victoire Saint-Raphaël

visits.text: San Rafeu church, a 12th-century Romanesque structure, is a classified historic monument. Its foundations rest on a site occupied since Roman times. The adjoining presbytery houses the municipal archaeological museum, with collections ranging from prehistory to underwater archaeology.

Climb the 129 steps of the San Rafeu Tower, a 13th-century fortified tower standing 25 meters high. From the top, the 360-degree panorama takes in the basilica's domes, the red rocks of the Esterel, the Mediterranean, and the bay of Saint-Tropez.

The Basilica of Notre-Dame de la Victoire, with its Byzantine domes, has dominated the seafront since the late 19th century. Its neo-Romanesque architecture blends golden stone and pink sandstone from the Estérel.
The archaeological museum displays amphorae, anchors, and objects raised from wrecks off the coast. One section is devoted to the Paleolithic, with remains discovered in the region.
The old harbor and its daily Provencal market make up a lively Mediterranean scene. The shaded lanes of the 'village quarter' preserve the atmosphere of an old farming town.

activities.text: Take the Corniche d'Or, a 40 km road between Saint-Raphael and Cannes. Beneath the umbrella pines, the red porphyry rocks of the Esterel plunge into the turquoise Mediterranean. Stops are possible at the coves of Agay, Dramont, and Antheor.
The Agay roadstead, sheltered between Cap Dramont and Pointe de la Baumette, offers calm water ideal for swimming, kayaking, and paddleboarding. The sandy beach is bordered by pines and red rocks.
Several dive clubs offer outings around Cap Dramont, Île d'Or and the wrecks along the coast. Further east, the protected waters of Cap Roux are home to groupers, brown meagres and gorgonians.
Hike in the Esterel massif toward Pic de l'Ours or Mont Vinaigre (614 m, the highest point). The trails wind between red rocks, fragrant maquis, and panoramas over the coast.

map_keywords: Dolmen Pierre de la Fée Draguignan
Musée des Arts et Traditions Populaires Draguignan

visits.text: The Clock Tower, rebuilt in 1662 and classified as a historic monument, rises on the town's central rock. Its 79 steps lead to a campanile offering a panoramic view over the Dracénie landscape. The monument stands 24 meters tall.

The Dolmen de la Pierre de la Fee, dated to 2,500 BCE, is one of the most imposing in Provence: 60 tons, three slabs over 2 meters supporting a 6-meter-long table. Listed as a historic monument since 1889, it backs onto a centuries-old oak.

The Museum of Popular Arts and Traditions of Middle Provence, awarded the Musee de France label, holds one of the country's finest collections of ethnographic objects. Its exhibitions are built in partnership with the greatest museums in the world.

The Museum of Fine Arts, located in the heart of the historic center, displays a collection of artworks and historical artifacts, including the ceremonial armor of François de Montmorency, restored by the Research Center of the Museums of France.
The Rhône American Cemetery and Memorial, established in August 1944, gathers the graves of 861 soldiers who died during the reconquest of southern France. A sober and moving place of remembrance.

activities.text: In Trans-en-Provence, about 12 km southeast of Draguignan, cross the 70-meter footbridge overlooking the Nartuby gorges. The route offers beautiful views of the river, waterfalls and gorges.

practical_info.tip: Park in the village and walk down

activities.text: Climb up to the Malmont orientation table for a 360-degree panorama over the region. The trail starts from the town center and winds between garrigue and pine forest.
Wander the medieval lanes of the old town, between the old houses of the Maison de la Reine Jeanne and the Saint-Hermentaire chapel. Parc Chabran, with its centuries-old trees, invites you to relax.

visits.text: Cotignac's tuff cliff rises 80 meters high and 400 meters wide, sculpted by the ancient Cassole waterfall. Troglodyte dwellings carved into the rock served as refuge in the Middle Ages. Climb the 90 steps to discover the old caves and a panoramic view over the village.

At the top of the rock, two watchtowers known as 'Saracen' once watched the horizon for invasions. An orientation table takes in the rooftops of Cotignac and the terraced hills planted with olive trees and cypresses.

Cours Gambetta, the main street lined with centuries-old plane trees, is the hub of social life. The Fountain of the Four Seasons marks its center. The cafe terraces come alive above all on market days.

The sanctuary of Notre-Dame de Grâces, built in 1519 following apparitions of the Virgin Mary, nestles in the hills 1 km south of the village. King Louis XIV and his mother Anne of Austria made a pilgrimage here in 1660 to give thanks for the king's birth.
Some semi-troglodyte houses, set into the foot of the cliff, are still lived in. The 12th-century medieval lanes reveal ochre and pastel facades, painted shutters, and 17 fountains of clear water.

activities.text: The wine estates around Cotignac produce AOC Cotes de Provence wines. The cooperative cellar in the village center and several estates offer tastings and cellar visits.

practical_info.tip: Ask for the rosé and local olive oil

activities.text: On Tuesday mornings, the Provencal market takes over the Cours. In summer, a farmers' market brings together local producers: wine, oil, honey, truffles, and artisan crafts.

Six kilometers to the north, the Sillans-la-Cascade waterfall plunges 42 meters into a setting of greenery. The access trail crosses an oak forest. Swimming is forbidden at the foot of the falls but possible downstream.
Push open the doors of the craft workshops and galleries scattered through the lanes. Cotignac attracts many artists, painters, and photographers from all over Europe.

seo.h1_title: Var Road Trip: French Riviera & Green Provence
seo.intro_paragraph: Discover Toulon and its harbor, Hyeres and the Golden Islands, Saint-Tropez, Porquerolles island, and Bormes-les-Mimosas. The Var, where Provence meets the Mediterranean.
seo.seo_hook: Toulon, Hyeres and the Golden Islands, Saint-Tropez, Porquerolles: explore the Var, where Provence meets Mediterranean blue beneath the mimosas.
featured_list: Toulon: coastal naval port
Hyeres: palm-lined gateway to the islands
Saint-Tropez: Bohemian soul of the Riviera
Porquerolles: protected island sanctuary

Fréjus: Roman city with amphitheater, aqueduct, and medieval cloister
Cotignac: Troglodyte village at the foot of an 80-meter tuff cliff
Saint-Tropez: Musée de l'Annonciade and citadel overlooking the gulf

itineraries.title: Lake Sainte-Croix and Verdon Circuit
itineraries.subtitle: 2 days around the turquoise waters of Lake Sainte-Croix, exploring drowned villages, Moustiers faience, the Verdon Canyon, and the gateway to Haute-Provence
itineraries.notes: The Musée de la Tournerie sur Bois in Aiguines is only open in July and August. Motorized boats with combustion engines are prohibited on the lake — only electric motors, sailboats, and human-powered craft are allowed. In July and August, beaches and water sports centers get very crowded: plan to arrive early.
itineraries.climate: Best time: May-June and September-October, temperatures 20-27°C, ideal for gorges and lake activities. Avoid July-August (scorching heat up to 35°C, massive crowds, parking nightmare). Mistral winds can blow strong year-round.

visits.text: Les Salles-sur-Verdon is not a village like the others. The old village was pulled down house by house from 1973 to make way for Lake Sainte-Croix; the church itself was dynamited on 5 March 1974 at 4.45 pm, and the last inhabitants were removed by the gendarmerie a few days earlier. The new village, rebuilt on the Bocouenne plateau from 1970, carries the memory of that sacrifice in every stone: the fountain and washhouse in the centre come from the drowned village, and the church bells were saved from the water. Follow the ten-stage heritage trail, where the panels put up by the association Mémoire des Salles sur Verdon recall the vanished buildings with unsettling precision.

The permanent exhibition at the Tourist Office recounts the dam's construction and the story of the submersion. Testimonies from former inhabitants are preserved here — if you're lucky, you might meet one of them still living in the village, since direct descendants of the expelled families still reside here today. The lake itself, France's fourth-largest reservoir at 2,200 hectares, flooded the valley over one year between 1973 and 1974, backed up behind the 95-meter-high double-arch dam.

Head down to the lakeshore to contemplate Costebelle Island, a small wild islet facing the village that you can reach by swimming or pedal boat. In summer, the lake welcomes up to 40,000 tourists per day along its shores — but in spring and September, you'll find rare tranquility here, with the Verdon's turquoise waters at their most spectacular.

activities.text: Take the Toine Nature Trail — an easy 14-station loop through the Provençal garrigue that follows the lakeshore for part of the route. Interpretive panels guide you through the local flora: kermes oaks, rock roses, rosemary, and lavender that perfume the air from spring onwards. Allow 1.5 to 2 hours depending on your pace.

Local providers offer pedal boats, paddleboards, and electric boats from the village's water sports center. Plan to book ahead in July-August — slots fill up fast. Since motorized boats with combustion engines are banned across the entire lake, the atmosphere remains remarkably peaceful.

practical_info.booking: Advance booking recommended in high season

activities.text: Thursday mornings, the Provençal market sets up in the main square. Honey, cheeses, marinated olives, lavender from the nearby Valensole plateau — a delicious stop before hitting the road.

map_keywords: Musée des Tourneurs sur Bois Aiguines

visits.text: Aiguines first reveals itself from the lake: its pepper-pot turrets crowned with polychrome glazed tiles from Moustiers-Sainte-Marie signal the village from afar on its rocky spur. Perched at 800 meters altitude, it dominates the turquoise waters with the Valensole plateau as backdrop — on clear days, you can even make out Mont Ventoux on the horizon. The château, built in the early 17th century by Balthazar de Gauthier during Henri IV's reign, covers 3,300 square meters on a twenty-hectare estate. It remains private but its surroundings and views are freely accessible. Don't try to enter — enjoy it from the small square facing the towers.

Climb up to the Saint-Pierre chapel overlooking the village from its promontory. The orientation table installed on its esplanade lets you identify Lake Sainte-Croix, the Valensole plateau, the Pre-Alps, and the Luberon range. This is one of the widest panoramas in the entire Verdon region — plan to be there in late afternoon for the raking light across the water.

The Musée des Tourneurs sur Bois (Wood Turners' Museum), designated a 'Musée de France', tells an uncommon story: in the 16th century, Aiguines was the largest wood-turning center in southeastern France, using hardwoods from the Verdon cliffs. The most surprising specialty? Studded balls — boxwood spheres turned on lathes and covered with hundreds of tiny nails, ancestors of modern pétanque balls. The museum is only open in July and August. If you visit off-season, artisan workshops carrying on the tradition line the village lanes.

Stroll around the Place de la Fontaine, Aiguines' heart with its wrought-iron bell cage and pastel-hued façades, its sundial and historic fountain. The parish church of Saint-Jean preserves a crucifix classified as a Historic Monument. The village has around 300 winter residents — a number that explodes in summer, but the square retains its authentic Provençal village character.

activities.text: The D71 road known as the 'Balcons du Verdon' (Verdon Balconies) snakes along the corniche between Aiguines and La Palud-sur-Verdon with breathtaking viewpoints over the canyon. The limestone cliffs plunge 300 meters down to the river. Stop at every viewpoint — the Col d'Illoire, the Belvédère de l'Escalès. Allow at least 2 hours for this drive with stops.

Aiguines is the rock climbing capital of the Verdon, with routes for all levels on the limestone walls. The cliffs face east-west, allowing climbing year-round. Local providers offer supervised introductions for beginners and guided outings for experienced climbers.

practical_info.tip: Book a guide for beginners

visits.text: Look up as soon as you arrive in Moustiers: between the two limestone cliffs that squeeze the village, a golden star gleams at the end of a 135-meter chain. Popular legend — recounted by Frédéric Mistral in 1885 — attributes this ex-voto to the knight of Blacas, taken prisoner during the Crusades in 1210 and freed after promising to suspend a star for the Virgin if he returned alive. The mystery remains unsolved. In any case, the star you see dates from 1957, after the previous one fell. The village, classified among France's Most Beautiful Villages since 1983, also takes its name from its founding monastery: monks from Lérins settled here in the 5th century.

The church of Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption is an often-underestimated Romanesque gem. Its 12th-century Lombard bell tower, classified as a Historic Monument since 1913, dominates the village with its sturdy silhouette. Inside, a five-bay nave with pointed barrel vaults and an altar carved from a 5th-century sarcophagus — one of the rare examples of reusing an early Christian piece in a medieval Provençal building.

The Musée de la Faïence presents more than 300 pieces and traces five centuries of an art that made Moustiers famous throughout Europe. It all began in 1668 when Pierre Clérissy obtained the secret of white enamel from a monk at Lérins Abbey — legend has it that Louis XIV's financial crisis, forcing him to melt down his gold tableware, opened the market for luxury faience. The Moustiers workshops subsequently graced the tables of the kingdom's elite. Today, workshops perpetuate the craft in the village center — push open doors when they're open to watch the artisans at work.

activities.text: Climb the 262 steps of the calade (paved path) leading to the Notre-Dame-de-Beauvoir chapel. This chapel blends 12th-century Romanesque with 16th-century Gothic — it was formerly called Notre-Dame-d'Entreroches, 'between the rocks'. Along the way of the cross, the stations are decorated with faience tiles. From the esplanade, the panorama embraces all of Moustiers' rooftops, Lake Sainte-Croix below, and the first buttresses of the Verdon. Avoid the climb at midday in summer — the slope is exposed. Coming back down, take the alternate path passing by the Sainte-Madeleine grotto.

Friday mornings, the market sets up on Place Montelupo, opposite the faience museum. It's a chance to leave with Haute-Provence honey, herb-marinated olives, fresh goat cheese, or a Provençal kougelhopf. Then spend the morning exploring the faience workshops open as boutiques — some offer demonstrations of wheel-throwing.

Providers based 5 km away on the shores of Lake Sainte-Croix offer canoe rentals to paddle up the water corridor at the entrance to the Verdon gorges — a unique experience where the water transitions from the blue-green of the lake to the emerald tint of the canyon. Allow half a day for the round trip.

visits.text: Bauduen cascades in an arc along the Défens hillside, giving every house a frontal view of the lake. It almost resembles a Mediterranean port if not for the Haute-Provence cliffs framing the landscape. Wander the narrow, shaded lanes — you'll find well-preserved Renaissance doorways, mullioned windows, and fragments of medieval ramparts. The ensemble is remarkably authentic for a village that has lived primarily from tourism since the dam deprived it of its agricultural lands in 1973.

The 16th-century Romanesque church of Saint-Pierre is open for visits. Alongside it, the 15th-century Saracen tower is one of the few defensive vestiges of the village still standing. Don't miss the 19th-century sundial — it bears Louis XIV's motto: 'Nec pluribus impar' ('Above all others'). A small irony in this peaceful village, far from any royal court.

The ruins of the medieval château overlooking the bay are worth the climb — from up there, the 180° view across the lake is spectacular. The dam's original plans called for flooding Bauduen like Les Salles, but the presence of the Fontaine-l'Évêque vauclusian spring (which still flows at the bottom of the lake) raised fears of a siphon effect and saved the village. This spring is now invisible beneath the waters, but its story is known to all the residents.

activities.text: Bauduen's large pebble beach and its jetty — which resembles a Mediterranean harbor quay — are the best spots for enjoying the lake. Swimming, sailing, canoeing, kayaking, paddleboarding, and electric boats are all available from the village's water sports center. Providers offer half-day or full-day rentals. Sunday mornings, the market sets up on the lakefront esplanade from 8 AM to 1 PM.

The Circuit du Défens, a marked hiking trail starting from Bauduen, offers a panoramic 20 km loop around the hill and lake. A shorter version of about 8 km is accessible to hikers of all levels. Ask for a map at the local tourist office.

visits.text: Sainte-Croix-du-Verdon perches on a rocky promontory facing the lake at the mouth of the gorges. The village nearly disappeared: the dam's original plans called for flooding it, before the water level was lowered. The stone Provençal houses, flower-filled squares, and tight alleyways retain the character of Haute-Provence's hilltop villages. From the main overlook, the 180° panorama across the lake, the dam to the west, and the Verdon ridges to the east is one of the broadest on the entire circuit.

The 16th-century parish church on the central square is open for visits. The museum and conservatory of Popular Arts and Traditions of Sainte-Croix-du-Verdon traces pre-dam Provençal peasant life — agricultural tools, costumes, everyday objects — and gives a sense of what the valley was like when it lived off lavender, truffles, and honey. It's a moving complement to the visit to Les Salles-sur-Verdon.

Head down to the dam to see up close the structure that changed everything. The double-arch vault, 95 meters high and built with only 55,000 cubic meters of concrete to hold back 760 million cubic meters of water, makes it one of Europe's most 'efficient' dams in terms of concrete-to-water ratio. Though closed to direct visits for security reasons, you can admire it from the D111 bridge spanning the lake just downstream.

activities.text: The Sainte-Croix-du-Verdon water sports center offers windsurfing, kayaking, pedal boats, and sailing on the turquoise waters of the lake. It's one of the best sailing spots on the lake thanks to the wind that regularly rises from the gorges in the afternoon. Providers offer introductory lessons and hourly or half-day rentals.

Hiking the hills overlooking the lake from Sainte-Croix-du-Verdon offers different views at every hour — in the morning, the lake reflects the cliffs in absolute calm; at sunset, the water takes on orange and pink hues. Allow 1.5 to 2 hours for the loop from the village.

Tuesday mornings, a local producers' market sets up on the church square. Honey from the Alpes de Haute-Provence, dried herbs, goat cheeses, local olive oils. A final chance to leave with the flavors of the Verdon before hitting the road.

seo.h1_title: Lake Sainte-Croix and Verdon Circuit
seo.intro_paragraph: Lake Sainte-Croix, France's fourth-largest reservoir at 2,200 hectares of turquoise water, was born in 1973 from the construction of the Verdon dam — at the cost of drowning the village of Les Salles-sur-Verdon. This five-stage circuit loops around the lake through perched medieval villages, the Verdon canyon, Moustiers faience, and water sports on exceptionally clear waters.
seo.seo_hook: Turquoise 2,200-ha lake by the Verdon Canyon, a village drowned in 1973, Moustiers' suspended star, and faience since the 17th century.
featured_list: Moustiers-Sainte-Marie: golden star suspended from a 135-meter chain and faience renowned since 1668
Les Salles-sur-Verdon: village rebuilt after the original site was flooded in 1974
Aiguines: a 17th-century castle with glazed tiles and a museum of wood turning
Bauduen: arc-shaped village on the lake with 15th-century Saracen tower and small Provençal harbor

highlights: Lake Sainte-Croix: 2,200 hectares, France's 4th-largest reservoir, filled 1973-1974
Dam: double-arch vault 95 meters high, 55,000 m³ of concrete holding 760 million m³ of water
Moustiers-Sainte-Marie: classified as one of France's Most Beautiful Villages since 1983, faience renowned since the 17th century
Les Salles-sur-Verdon: village drowned in 1974 — the church was dynamited on March 5, 1974
Navigation: combustion-engine motors prohibited on the entire lake — only sails, electric motors, and human-powered craft allowed
Ideal season: May-June and September to avoid summer crowds (40,000 tourists/day in July-August)
