itineraries.title: Burgundy's 15 Most Beautiful Villages
itineraries.subtitle: From Chablis to Paray-le-Monial, a road trip through classified vineyards, thousand-year abbeys, hilltop villages, and Burgundian Romanesque art
itineraries.notes: The itinerary crosses Burgundy from north to south. Departure is possible from Auxerre or Tonnerre station (close to Chablis). It ends in Paray-le-Monial, connected by TER regional trains to Mâcon and Lyon. Check the opening times of Ancy-le-Franc and Châteauneuf castles.
itineraries.climate: Best period: May-June and September-October, temperatures 15-25°C, ideal for village visits. Avoid July-August (heat often exceeding 30°C, peak tourist crowds) and December-February (frost, frequent valley fog). Moderate rainfall year-round.

visits.text: Start with the Collégiale Saint-Martin, built between 1160 and 1220 in early Gothic style inspired by Sens Cathedral. Look closely at the south portal: 111 horseshoes are nailed to the oak doors. Tradition held that riders would invoke Saint Martin's protection for their mounts. Legend has it that Joan of Arc also nailed a horseshoe here in 1429.

Just behind the collegiate church, step through the door of the Obédiencerie - a house dating from the 15th to the 17th centuries that served as a residence for representatives of the canons of Tours. Inside, you will discover a 15th-century lever press, one of the oldest in Burgundy.

Wander through the narrow streets of the lower town among winegrowers' houses and remnants of the 15th-century ramparts, financed by a tax on wine—the winegrowers had to surrender 10% of their harvest for eight years. The Porte Noël, with its two round towers rebuilt in 1775, is the last vestige of the fortifications that once included 29 towers. Don't miss the nine-arched washhouse from 1840 on the banks of the Serein.

activities.text: Climb up to the Aire des Clos for a panorama over the Chablis vineyard—5,800 hectares planted exclusively with Chardonnay, the largest white wine region in Burgundy. From this viewpoint, you can take in all seven Grands Crus in a single glance. If you're visiting in October, don't miss the Chablis Wine Festival.

Follow the Serein downstream through footbridges and small bridges. The river, whose name means "calm," flows through Chablis below the hillsides. The path is flat and shaded—perfect for late afternoon after sightseeing. Wine cellars offer tastings throughout the year.

visits.text: Pass through the Porte de Tonnerre and plunge into the Middle Ages: Noyers-sur-Serein boasts 78 buildings classified or registered as Historic Monuments, most dating from the 15th century and little altered since. Half-timbered houses stand alongside stone mansions, arcades, and squares with evocative names: Place du Marché-au-Blé, Place de la Petite-Étape-aux-Vins. Voted 7th Favorite Village of France in 2014.

Walk along the ramparts with their 19 defense towers still partially visible. The fortifications, originally flanked by 24 towers, protected a prosperous town built on wine and timber trade. Film buffs will recognize the Hôtel du Globe: this is where Bourvil and Louis de Funès shot the inn scene in La Grande Vadrouille in 1966. More than twenty films have been made in this village.
Visit the Museum of Naive and Popular Arts. Three floors and 1,500 m² of exhibition space present works by craftspeople and popular artists.

activities.text: Walk around the village along the riverside path beside the Serein. Noyers is built within a meander of the river that almost completely encircles the town—a natural defense that gives it its island-like character. From the small bridge downstream, you'll have the finest overall view of the rooftops, towers, and reflections in the water.
The trails around the village traverse the meurgers—those typical Burgundian dry stone walls—and old vine huts. Allow 1.5 hours for the hillside loop offering views over the Serein valley.

visits.text: The Château d'Ancy-le-Franc is a masterpiece of Italian Renaissance architecture in Burgundy. Designed around 1542 by architect Sebastiano Serlio for Antoine III de Clermont, brother-in-law of Diane de Poitiers, it's the only French château to adopt a perfectly square plan with four identical wings. The interior frescoes, created by artists from the Fontainebleau school (including Primaticcio and Nicolò dell'Abate), cover more than 4,000 square meters—a unique ensemble in France. Allow 1.5 hours for the guided tour.

Take time to stroll through the château's park: formal parterres, canal, and classical perspectives. The estate has been recently restored and the gardens replanted in Renaissance spirit. From the terraces, the view over the village rooftops and the Auxois countryside is restful.

Head down to the Canal de Bourgogne, which runs through the village. The lock and the plane-tree-lined canal sections create a landscape typical of Burgundy's waterways. If you see a barge maneuvering through the lock, stop and watch—it's always a small spectacle.

activities.text: Hop on a bike along the Canal de Bourgogne cycle route—the section between Ancy-le-Franc and Tonnerre is flat, shaded, and virtually car-free. Rental shops offer bikes near the lock. Allow 1.5 hours for the round trip.

If you have time, push on to Château de Tanlay, 10 km northwest. Another Renaissance jewel, it preserves a trompe-l'oeil gallery in the Tour de la Ligue where Admiral de Coligny gathered Protestant leaders during the Wars of Religion.

visits.text: Climb the Grand'rue to the Basilica of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Built in the 12th century, it was the starting point of the Second Crusade preached by Bernard of Clairvaux in 1146 before Louis VII and an immense crowd. The narthex and its carved capitals are among the finest examples of Romanesque art. Viollet-le-Duc restored the basilica in the 19th century when it was in danger of collapse.

From the esplanade behind the basilica, the panorama embraces the Morvan and the Cure valley. This is the "eternal hill"—one of four starting points for the Way of Saint James in France. Pilgrims still depart from here every spring. If you arrive late afternoon, the light on the nave is spectacular: at summer solstice, the patches of light from the stained glass windows align perfectly down the center of the nave.

Walk back down through the ramparts and ancient gates. The golden stone houses along the Grand'rue shelter art galleries, craftsmen's workshops, and bookshops. Vézelay has 400 inhabitants but attracts nearly a million visitors annually—arrive early morning or late afternoon to appreciate it in peace.

activities.text: Walk down to Saint-Père-sous-Vézelay (2 km below). The village has a beautiful 13th-century Gothic church and old washhouses by the Cure river. The marked trail connecting the two villages crosses through vineyards and offers lovely perspectives on the hill.

Take the loop of viewpoints around the hill (marked trail, 1.5 hours). You'll pass through sunken lanes bordered with boxwood, viewpoints over the valley, and remnants of old vineyards. This circuit partly follows pilgrimage routes—you might encounter pilgrims with their scallop shells.

visits.text: Semur-en-Auxois sits on a pink granite spur encircled by the Armançon gorges. The four round 13th-century towers—including the Tour de l'Orle d'Or, standing 44 meters high—dominate the town and are visible from afar. Climb up to the walkway for a plunging view over the river 30 meters below.

Step through the door of the Collégiale Notre-Dame, built in the 13th and 14th centuries. It preserves remarkable stained glass windows, including one donated by the drapers' guild depicting the stages of cloth manufacture. Outside, linger over the sculpted portals. The Place du Terreau just in front is the heart of the town.

Walk down to the Pont Joly, below the town. From here you'll have the most photographed view of Semur: the towers and ramparts reflected in the Armançon, with medieval houses clinging to the cliff face. Come late afternoon for the best light.

activities.text: Walk around the ramparts then descend to the banks of the Armançon via the marked trail. The river carves deep gorges here—a striking natural setting for a Burgundian town. Allow 1.5 hours for the complete loop.
Every year in late May, Semur hosts France's oldest horse race—documented since 1639. If your dates coincide, don't miss this popular festival that takes over the town for three days.

visits.text: Upon arrival in Flavigny, a sweet scent of anise welcomes you. Anis de Flavigny candies have been made since the 16th century in the former Benedictine abbey—an anise seed coated for 15 days in flavored sugar syrup. Visit the factory housed in the abbey's Carolingian crypts: it's free and you'll leave with pockets full of dragées flavored with rose, violet, or lemon.

Wander the cobbled streets of this hilltop village, classified among France's Most Beautiful Villages. Medieval ramparts, fortified gates, Renaissance houses with ornate facades—Flavigny served as the setting for the film Chocolat with Juliette Binoche and Johnny Depp. The 13th-century Saint-Genest church, with its carved choir stalls, deserves a detour.

Walk around the ramparts to discover views over the valleys of the Ozerain. The village sits on an isolated plateau at an altitude of 400 meters, offering 360-degree panoramas over the Burgundian countryside.

activities.text: Take the rural trail that descends toward the Ozerain valley and climbs back through the orchards. Along the way, you'll cross the Alesia archaeological site—the plateau where Vercingetorix surrendered to Julius Caesar in 52 BC is just 8 km away. If the subject fascinates you, the MuséoParc Alésia is worth the detour.
In the evening, settle onto the ramparts with a glass of Crémant de Bourgogne. The sunset over the hills of Auxois is one of the most beautiful along the route.

visits.text: The source of the Bèze springs forth right in the village center in a spectacular resurgence—water emerges from an underground network stretching several kilometers. It's one of the most beautiful springs in Burgundy. Stop by the basin: the water is translucent blue-green, surrounded by lush vegetation.

Descend into the Grottes de Bèze, accessible by boat on an underground river. The navigable gallery ventures beneath the village—the experience is unique in Burgundy. Check opening hours; the caves are only accessible in season (April to October).

Stroll through the village: vestiges of the Abbey of Saint-Pierre founded in the 7th century (one of the oldest in Burgundy), washhouses, alleyways lined with gardens, and limestone houses. Bèze has a discreet charm—it's the quietest stop along the route.

activities.text: Follow the Bèze river on foot downstream from the village, between wet meadows and pastures. The path runs alongside the water for 3 km—guaranteed bucolic atmosphere, with occasional grey herons fishing in the shallows.

If you're traveling by car, make a detour through the vineyards of Marsannay or Fixin, at the gateway to the Côte de Nuits, 30 minutes south. A tasting at a winemaker's is a good way to prepare for the next part of the journey toward the Route des Grands Crus.

visits.text: You'll spot Châteauneuf from afar—the village and its fortress perch on a rocky spur visible from the A6 motorway. Classified among France's Most Beautiful Villages, the town has preserved its 14th-century medieval castle, one of the last remnants of Burgundian military architecture in its original state. Climb the keep for views over the Auxois valley and the Canal de Bourgogne, 200 meters below.

Explore the cobbled streets lined with 15th-16th century merchants' houses. The Maison Bichot, Maison du Mouton, and their sculpted facades testify to the prosperity of Burgundian merchants at the end of the Middle Ages. In summer, the village hosts contemporary artists in the old residences—don't be surprised to stumble upon an art installation in a 15th-century courtyard.

activities.text: Walk down to the Canal de Bourgogne via the trail that leaves from the village. The towpath follows the reaches and locks—a flat, soothing walk after climbing to the château. Pleasure barges pass regularly, especially in summer.

If you've rented bikes, the Canal de Bourgogne makes for beautiful rides. The stretch between Châteauneuf and Vandenesse-en-Auxois is particularly pretty, passing flower-decked locks and rolling countryside.

visits.text: The Hospices de Beaune—or Hôtel-Dieu—is Burgundy's most famous monument. Founded in 1443 by Nicolas Rolin, chancellor to Duke Philip the Good of Burgundy, this hospital for the poor operated until 1971. The polychrome glazed tile roofs (diamond patterns in yellow, green, red, and black) have become the image of Burgundy. Inside, don't miss Rogier van der Weyden's polyptych of the Last Judgment. Arrive at opening time—it's the most visited site in Burgundy.

Don't overlook the Collégiale Notre-Dame, built in the 12th century: it houses five tapestries of the Life of the Virgin, woven in the 15th century. Less famous than the Hospices, it's nevertheless well worth the visit. Take time to sit in the adjacent cloister—a haven of calm in the heart of town.

Walk around the ramparts—Beaune has preserved virtually all of its medieval walls, punctuated by bastions and towers. The rampart walk has been landscaped as a tree-lined promenade. In November, the Hospices wine auction attracts buyers from around the world and sends bids into the millions of euros.

activities.text: Explore the cellars of Beaune. The town rests on a network of underground galleries carved into the limestone—some cellars descend 10 meters deep. Wine houses offer guided tastings year-round. Allow 1 to 1.5 hours per cellar.

The market takes place on Saturday morning. Époisses cheeses, Burgundy mustard, snails, parsleyed ham and gougères bring Burgundy's gastronomy together in one place. Arrive around 8 a.m. for the best selection.

visits.text: La Rochepot Castle rises above the forest like a fairytale castle, with polychrome glazed-tile roofs identical to those of the Hospices de Beaune and instantly recognizable. Dismantled during the Revolution, it was then restored in the 19th century by the son of President Sadi Carnot.

Walk down to the tiny but charming village below—a few stone houses, a church, and above all an open view over the vineyard slopes. Look for public viewpoints where the château's polychrome tiles stand out against the sky.

activities.text: Follow the vineyard paths that lead from the village toward the hillsides. You're here on the edge of the Côte de Beaune—plots of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay climb in terraces between murgers (dry stone walls), clos, and cabottes (small vine huts). The landscape is classified as a UNESCO World Heritage site under the Climats of Burgundy Vineyards.
Walk on to the hamlet of Evelle for a panorama over the entire wine-growing area. The trail crosses landscapes of "ribbons"—the long, narrow plots that shape the geography of Burgundy's appellations.

visits.text: You're now in the heart of Burgundy's great white wines. Begin at the Place de l'Hôtel de Ville, with the Gothic spire of the Saint-Nicolas church (15th century), then explore streets lined with massive carriage doors concealing winegrowers' courtyards and centuries-old cellars—push those that are ajar; nearly every house is connected to the vine.

Tour the historic clos on the village outskirts—Clos des Perrières, Les Charmes, Les Genevrières. These "Climats" of the Côte de Beaune have been inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 2015. Each parcel, bordered by stone walls, produces a distinct wine. Panels along the paths explain this system unique in the world.

activities.text: Walk the vineyard trail connecting Meursault to Volnay or Auxey-Duresses—an hour's stroll among walls, cabottes, and rows of vines. The landscape changes with the seasons: intense green in spring, golden in autumn. This may be the most beautiful vineyard walk in Burgundy.

Several estates offer cellar visits and guided tastings. Ask the tourist office for a list of domains open to the public—some have vaulted cellars from the 14th century. La Paulée de Meursault in November is one of the world's most celebrated wine feasts.

visits.text: Brancion is a medieval ghost village—not in a frightening sense, but in the sense that time has stood still. The fortified town, clinging to a ridge, preserves its market hall, stone streets, and 12th-14th century houses. The motto of the lords of Brancion, the "Gros" family, was "Into the thick of battle"—quite a program. The village is pedestrian; park below.

Walk to the Romanesque church of Saint-Pierre, perched at the village end with its cemetery. The view plunges over the Grosne valley. Inside, look up: 14th-century frescoes were discovered beneath the whitewash. The light entering through the narrow windows creates a striking atmosphere.

Climb to the château (11th-14th century) for the panorama over the Mâconnais hills. The ruins are impressive—keep, curtain walls, and lord's residence. Admission is charged, but the ticket includes an interpretive route recounting the history of the site.

activities.text: Take the loop to the Romanesque chapel of Lancharre through bocage paths—1.5 hours' walk through meadows, hedgerows, and woodland. The chapel, isolated in the countryside, is a 12th-century jewel of Romanesque art.
The ridgetop trail above Brancion offers views over the Mâconnais hills and the Pouilly-Fuissé vineyards to the south. If you have vertigo, stick to the lower path—both are marked.

visits.text: Prepare for a shock: for five centuries, Cluny Abbey was the largest Christian building in the world—187 meters long—and was surpassed only by the reconstruction of St. Peter's Basilica in Rome in the 16th century. Founded in 910 by William I of Aquitaine, it headed a network of 1,400 monasteries across Europe. Only one tenth of it remains today after its destruction during the Revolution, but what survives—the south arm of the transept and the Clocher de l'Eau Bénite—is enough to inspire awe. Don't miss the 3D film in the museum, which reconstructs the abbey church in all its splendor.

Explore the medieval town around the abbey. Cluny preserves an exceptional density of 11th-12th century Romanesque houses—some rank among the oldest civilian dwellings in France. The Tour de l'Horloge and the Farinier (former monks' grain storehouse, with a 13th-century chestnut timber frame) complete the visit.
The Haras National has occupied the former monastic quarters since 1806. If you love horses, visit the stables and riding arena—equestrian shows are regularly scheduled during the season.

activities.text: The Cluny-Mâcon greenway follows a former railway line converted to a cycle path. Flat, shaded, and car-free, it crosses the Mâconnais countryside for 22 km. Rental shops offer bikes at Cluny station. At least cycle the first section to Berzé-le-Châtel (10 km) to see the château dominating the valley.

The circuit of the abbey's former towers is marked through the town. It reveals the colossal footprint the monument once had: you'll literally walk on the foundations of the vanished nave, marked on the ground.

visits.text: Climb to the Château Saint-Hugues, considered the oldest castle in Burgundy. Hugues de Semur was born here around 1024; he later served as Abbot of Cluny for 60 years and launched the construction of the great abbey church. From the ruins of the keep and curtain walls, you overlook a panorama of hedged farmland and valleys that seems unchanged since the 11th century.

The Collégiale Saint-Hilaire, built in the 12th century, is one of the last great Romanesque structures in Burgundy. Its octagonal bell tower with eight arcades and columns has become the village emblem. Classified as a historic monument since 1862, it blends Cluniac Romanesque art with early Gothic elements. Step inside and look up at the sculpted capitals.

Stroll through the hilltop village—the houses with almost pink walls (local limestone) and cobbled streets make this one of France's Most Beautiful Villages. Below, the Romanesque church of Saint-Martin-la-Vallée glows in rosy tones at sunset—a bucolic spectacle.

activities.text: The Brionnais concentrates a hundred Romanesque churches and chapels within a 30 km radius. Take the car and do a mini-circuit of the three finest: Anzy-le-Duc (remarkable sculpted tympanum), Montceaux-l'Étoile, and Bois-Sainte-Marie. Allow half a day.

The bocage trails around Semur cross hedgerows, meadows with Charolais cattle, and small ridge roads. The Brionnais is the birthplace of the Charolais breed—you're never far from a white herd in the pastures.

visits.text: The Basilica of the Sacred Heart in Paray-le-Monial is a miniature replica of the abbey church of Cluny—it's the best way to imagine what the vanished great church looked like. Built between 1090 and 1109 under Abbot Hugues de Semur (the one you encountered in Semur-en-Brionnais), it's considered a masterpiece of Cluniac Romanesque art. The play of light in the nave at sunrise alone is worth the visit.

Stop by the Musée du Hiéron, right next to the basilica. Its collection of sacred art spans from the 12th to the 20th century. Look for the white marble Romanesque tympanum from the former Abbey of Anzy-le-Duc—it's the centerpiece, one of the finest in Burgundian Romanesque art. Admission is inexpensive and the museum is rarely crowded.

The Hôtel de Ville of Paray, a former Renaissance mansion, deserves a look for its turreted facade and sculptures. Continue to the banks of the Bourbince for a shaded stroll—a lovely way to end this Burgundian road trip.

activities.text: Treat yourself to a final walk along the Bourbince and the Canal du Centre. Pleasure barges, flower-decked locks, and reflections of the basilica in the water—the loop covers 4 km, it's flat, and it's a beautiful way to conclude the journey.

If you have a bit more time, visit the Chapelle des Apparitions within the grounds of the Visitation convent. This is where Marguerite-Marie Alacoque had her visions of the Sacred Heart in the 17th century—an event that made Paray a major pilgrimage site. Even without religious conviction, the place has a particular atmosphere.

seo.h1_title: Burgundy's 15 Most Beautiful Villages
seo.intro_paragraph: From Chablis and its thousand-year-old vineyards to Cluny Abbey via Vézelay, Semur-en-Auxois, Flavigny-sur-Ozerain, and the Route des Grands Crus, this 5-day road trip crosses Burgundy from north to south. Hilltop villages, Renaissance châteaux, Romanesque churches, centuries-old cellars, and hills planted with Chardonnay and Pinot Noir punctuate the route.
seo.seo_hook: From Chablis to Cluny: Vézelay, Beaune, hilltop villages, and classified vineyards. 15 stops to discover 2,000 years of Burgundian heritage.

Noyers-sur-Serein: 78 historic monuments in a meander of the Serein, setting for La Grande Vadrouille
Beaune: 15th-century Hospices with polychrome roofs, capital of Burgundy wines
Cluny: vestiges of the largest abbey church in Christendom before the reconstruction of Saint Peter's in Rome

itineraries.title: Burgundy Road Trip: Cathedrals, Vineyards & Medieval Villages
itineraries.subtitle: From Sens to Dijon via Vézelay, Beaune, and the most beautiful villages of Yonne and Côte-d'Or
itineraries.notes: The Route des Grands Crus between Beaune and Dijon is narrow and winding—avoid harvest weekends in September. Several châteaux close between November and March. Book cellar tastings in advance during high season.
itineraries.climate: Best time: May-June and September-October, temperatures 15-25°C ideal for vineyards and villages. Avoid July-August (intense heat up to 35°C) and December-February (cold, frequent frost, many cellars closed). Moderate rainfall year-round.

visits.text: Begin your road trip at the Cathedral of Saint-Étienne in Sens—quite simply the world's first Gothic cathedral. Construction began around 1135 under Archbishop Henri Sanglier, even before Notre-Dame de Paris. The exceptionally wide nave (50 feet across) is covered with sexpartite vaults similar to those in Paris. In 1234, Saint Louis married Marguerite of Provence here. Don't miss the Flamboyant transept designed by Martin Chambiges in the late 15th century, or the stained-glass window depicting the assassination of Thomas Becket—the Archbishop of Canterbury had taken refuge in Sens before being murdered in 1170.

Right next door, the Cathedral Treasury occupies the former chapel of the archbishop's palace. You'll see remarkable pieces: 15th-century Flemish tapestries, Thomas Becket's chasuble, and the Sainte Châsse, an ivory reliquary casket. This is one of France's richest cathedral treasuries—allow 30 to 45 minutes.

Wander through old Sens by following the "Circuit de Brennus" (named after the Gallic chieftain of the Senones who captured Rome in 390 BC). Arrows on the ground guide you through narrow streets, half-timbered houses, and the banks of the Yonne River. Pick up the guidebook at the Tourist Office before you set out.

activities.text: If you arrive on a Wednesday or Saturday morning, explore the Sens market—it's the best place to sample regional products from the Yonne: goat cheeses, Gâtinais honey, and Burgundy snails.

visits.text: Stop in Joigny along the way—this little town on the Yonne conceals beautiful 15th- and 16th-century half-timbered houses. If you look up at the so-called "Maison de l'Arbre de Jessé," you'll discover a carved wooden façade depicting the genealogy of Christ. It's understated yet striking.

In Auxerre, head for the Cathedral of Saint-Étienne, whose 13th-century Gothic choir contains some of France's oldest stained-glass windows. The 11th-century Romanesque crypt preserves an exceptional fresco of Christ on horseback—unique in Western Romanesque art. Climb to the top of the north tower if it's open—the view over Auxerre's rooftops and the Yonne River is superb.

Step inside the Abbey of Saint-Germain, founded in the 5th century. The 9th-century Carolingian crypt contains France's oldest known wall frescoes—paintings from the 9th century depicting scenes from the life of Saint Stephen. You'll descend into a dark, moving space 20 feet underground.

Head back up toward the old center—you'll pass Auxerre's 15th-century Clock Tower and half-timbered houses. The pedestrian quarter between Place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville and the cathedral is particularly pleasant.

activities.text: Late in the day, walk down to the banks of the Yonne—this is where you'll find the most beautiful view of Auxerre. The skyline—cathedral, Abbey of Saint-Germain, and Church of Saint-Pierre aligned in succession—is one of the finest in Burgundy, especially when the light warms the stonework.

visits.text: On your way to Vézelay, stop at the Caves of Arcy-sur-Cure—an underground network inhabited for 200,000 years. The cave paintings, dating back 28,000 years, are among the oldest in Europe. The guided tour lasts about an hour. Book in advance during summer, as slots fill up quickly.

You'll spot the Basilica of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine from a distance—it crowns Vézelay from the "eternal hill." A UNESCO World Heritage site since 1979, this 12th-century abbey church is a masterpiece of Burgundian Romanesque art. Saint Bernard preached the Second Crusade here in 1146 before King Louis VII and Eleanor of Aquitaine. In 1190, Richard the Lionheart and Philip Augustus met here before departing for the Third Crusade. The tympanum of the narthex, depicting the Mission of the Apostles, is unique in Romanesque art. If you're here around June 21st, watch for the solstice phenomenon: the southern windows project a line of light down the center of the nave.

The village of Vézelay itself is worth a stroll—only 450 residents live here, and it's classified as one of the Most Beautiful Villages in France. Walk up the main street lined with art galleries and medieval houses, follow the ramparts, and continue to the esplanade for the panorama over the Morvan. Take your time.

If you still have time, detour to the Château de Bazoches, a 10-minute drive away. Vauban purchased it in 1675 with spoils from the capture of Maastricht and made it his design office—this is where he conceived most of his fortification plans.

activities.text: From the esplanade behind the basilica, you'll have the finest panorama over the Morvan. It's the ideal spot for a late-afternoon picnic—bring Époisses cheese and white Burgundy wine.

visits.text: Avallon demands a bit of effort: the old town perches on a granite spur overlooking the Cousin valley. Enter through the Clock Tower—if you can climb it, the view plunges over the town's rooftops and the surrounding countryside. The ramparts, which still encircle much of the city, date from the 12th century.

The Collegiate Church of Saint-Lazare features a carved Romanesque portal reminiscent of Vézelay's—both were created around the same time by related workshops. The portal suffered during the Revolution, but you can still make out the signs of the zodiac and the labors of the months on the archivolts.

If you detour to Pierre-Perthuis (4 miles south), you'll discover a tiny village famous for its two superimposed bridges—a 12th-century Romanesque bridge spanned by an 18th-century road bridge. The Roche Percée, a natural rock formation, overlooks the Cure River. It's wild and rarely crowded.

activities.text: Walk the circuit of Avallon's viewpoints—you'll take in the Cousin valley from three or four vantage points accessible on foot from the center below. Allow an hour for a leisurely walk with no difficulty.

visits.text: Start with the Château d'Époisses—you'll find a moat-ringed fortress 15 minutes from Semur, inhabited by the same family since the 17th century. Legend has it that Madame de Sévigné often stayed here—she wrote some of her most famous letters in this very place. The park and exterior grounds can be visited without reservation.

You're going to love Semur-en-Auxois, one of Burgundy's most beautiful small towns. It wraps around a pink granite spur encircled by a meander of the Armançon River. Four round towers from the 13th-century keep dominate the town. The Pont Pinard offers the most photographed view—ramparts and towers reflected in the river below. Head down there in late afternoon for the best light.

The Collegiate Church of Notre-Dame, dating from the 13th century, boasts a remarkable carved portal and, inside, stained-glass windows donated by butchers' and drapers' guilds—you'll recognize the tools of each trade depicted in the glass.

activities.text: Late in the day, walk down to the banks of the Armançon at the foot of the ramparts. The path follows the river below the cliffs—it's quiet, shaded, and offers a unique perspective on the medieval towers. Allow 45 minutes for the loop.

visits.text: The Abbey of Fontenay, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1981, is the world's best-preserved Cistercian abbey. Founded in 1118 by Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, it has retained its cloister, austere abbey church, hydraulic forge, and gardens in remarkable condition. The entire complex nestles in an isolated valley—the silence is arresting. Allow at least 90 minutes for your visit, longer if you stroll through the park.

In Montbard itself, climb up to the Parc Buffon—naturalist Georges-Louis Leclerc, Count of Buffon, lived and worked here in the 18th century. He designed this terraced park above the Brenne River. You'll find the remains of the medieval castle. The Tour de l'Aubespin and Tour Saint-Louis offer beautiful views over the town and the Canal de Bourgogne.

activities.text: Walk or cycle along the Canal de Bourgogne from Montbard—the towpath is flat, shaded, and you'll pass pleasure boats. Allow an hour for a round trip to the next lock.

visits.text: Take the Route des Grands Crus (D122) between Beaune and Dijon—37 miles of UNESCO-listed vineyards (the "Climats of Burgundy," inscribed in 2015). You'll pass through Pommard, Volnay, Meursault, Nuits-Saint-Georges, Vosne-Romanée, and Gevrey-Chambertin. Stop at the Clos de Vougeot: this 125-acre walled estate was created by Cistercian monks in the 12th century. The road is narrow and winding—take your time.

In Dijon, head for the Palace of the Dukes and States of Burgundy, which dominates the Place de la Libération (designed by Hardouin-Mansart between 1681 and 1686). The Musée des Beaux-Arts, housed in the palace, is one of France's oldest museums—and it's free. If you have the stamina, climb the 316 steps of the Tour Philippe le Bon (15th century, 150 feet high) for panoramic views over the entire city.

Don't miss the Church of Notre-Dame in Dijon—you'll see the Jacquemart, an automaton stolen from Courtrai in 1382 by Philip the Bold. In 1651, the people of Dijon added a wife (Jacqueline), then a son in 1714 (Jacquelinet) and a daughter in 1884 (Jacquelinette). On a buttress of the church, stroke the little carved owl with your left hand while making a wish—it's been a tradition since the 15th century.

activities.text: Follow the Owl Trail—22 stages marked on the ground by bronze plaques that guide you through Dijon's protected heritage district (240 acres, UNESCO-listed). You'll pass the private mansions of Rue des Forges, the 15th-century Maison Millière, the Law Courts, and Saint-Bénigne Cathedral. Pick up the guidebook at the Tourist Office. Allow an hour of walking.

visits.text: Second day in Dijon—start with Saint-Bénigne Cathedral. You'll descend into the 11th-century Romanesque crypt, one of the few of its type still standing in France. Three levels descend into the ground around a columned rotunda. It's austere and powerful.

Head to the Dijon Market Halls, built in a metal style attributed to Gustave Eiffel (opinions differ, but the structure is typical of his work). The Tuesday, Friday, and Saturday morning market is spectacular: Époisses cheeses, mustard, gingerbread, snails, blackcurrants. If you're not here on a market day, the permanent shops beneath the halls are still worth a visit.

Visit the Cité Internationale de la Gastronomie et du Vin—you'll discover the Gastronomic Meal of the French (inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2010) through interactive exhibitions, cooking workshops, and a tasting cellar. Opened in 2022 in the former General Hospital. Allow at least 90 minutes.

If you love sculpture, continue to the Chartreuse de Champmol, a former monastery founded by Philip the Bold in 1383. Only the church portal (with statues by Claus Sluter) and the Well of Moses remain—six life-size prophets carved in stone, with astonishing realism for the 14th century.

activities.text: End the day with a tasting of crème de cassis—you'll learn that Dijon has been the birthplace of blackcurrant liqueur since the 19th century. Try a kir (Aligoté white wine + crème de cassis): it was Canon Kir, former mayor of Dijon, who popularized this cocktail in the mid-20th century.

map_keywords: Hôtel des Ducs de Bourgogne Beaune

visits.text: On your way to Beaune, stop at the hilltop village of Châteauneuf-en-Auxois. This fortified village overlooks the Canal de Bourgogne from a promontory—the 12th-century castle offers views that reach all the way to the Morvan on clear days. The narrow streets are lined with 14th- and 15th-century merchants' houses.

The Hôtel-Dieu in Beaune (the Hospices) is the monument you won't forget. Founded in 1443 by Chancellor Nicolas Rolin and his wife Guigone de Salins in the midst of the Hundred Years' War, this "palace for the poor" remained in operation until 1971. The exterior façade is austere, but once you step into the courtyard, the polychrome glazed-tile roofs (red, green, black, and yellow diamond patterns) will astound you. The Salle des Pôvres (Paupers' Ward) measures 165 feet long, 46 feet wide, and 52 feet high, with an inverted ship's hull timber ceiling. Don't miss Rogier van der Weyden's Last Judgment polyptych. Allow at least 90 minutes.

After the Hospices, walk the ramparts of Beaune on foot—you can follow nearly the entire circuit, which still encircles the historic center. The 12th-century Collegiate Church of Notre-Dame houses 15th-century tapestries depicting the life of the Virgin.

activities.text: Book a tasting in one of Beaune's historic cellars—the town has dozens, carved into the limestone beneath the houses. You'll sample appellations from the Côte de Beaune: Pommard, Volnay, Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet. Allow 60 to 90 minutes.

practical_info.tip: Reservations recommended

map_keywords: Place du Grenier à Sel Noyers

visits.text: Noyers-sur-Serein is classified among the Most Beautiful Villages in France—and deservedly so. This walled medieval village bathed by the Serein River has preserved its half-timbered houses, arcades, and Place du Grenier à Sel intact. Park outside the walls and enter on foot. The silence is absolute.

Climb up to the ruins of the Château de Noyers—you'll have a magnificent view from the hilltop above the village. Only wall fragments and towers remain. The view over the loop of the Serein and the village rooftops below is worth the climb. In summer, the village hosts an early music festival in courtyards and cellars.

activities.text: Stroll along the banks of the Serein below the ramparts. The water is crystal-clear, light filters through the trees, and you'll likely have the path to yourself. It's one of the most peaceful spots in all of Burgundy.
On your way to Noyers, stop in Joux-la-Ville for a gourmet break at an artisanal biscuit shop—you'll sample Burgundian specialties (gingerbread, blackcurrant cookies). Allow 30 minutes.

visits.text: You'll be surprised by the Château d'Ancy-le-Franc—one of the purest examples of the Renaissance in Burgundy. Designed around 1546 by Italian architect Sebastiano Serlio for the Count of Clermont-Tonnerre, it presents a perfectly symmetrical façade around a square courtyard. Inside, the 16th-century Italian frescoes are remarkable—some attributed to Primaticcio and the Fontainebleau School. Allow 90 minutes for a visit with the audio guide.

In Tonnerre, head down to see the Fosse Dionne—you'll stand transfixed before this deep blue-green karst spring, surrounded by an 18th-century washhouse. No one has ever reached the bottom of this resurgence (divers have stopped at 230 feet). It's hypnotic and slightly unsettling.

Step inside the Hôtel-Dieu of Tonnerre—you'll discover a 295-foot-long ward for the sick, founded in 1293 by Marguerite of Burgundy. It's one of the largest in medieval Europe. The broken-barrel timber ceiling is impressively vast. The tomb of Marguerite of Burgundy stands inside.

activities.text: Walk along the Canal de Bourgogne in Ancy-le-Franc before getting back on the road. The towpath passes a lock and offers a peaceful view of the Tonnerre countryside.

visits.text: Chablis is a compact wine town—you can tour it in an hour. Start with the 13th-century Collegiate Church of Saint-Martin, whose horseshoe-arch portal reveals Burgundian influence. Pass through the Porte Noël, the only remnant of the medieval fortifications. The real spectacle is outside: the Kimmeridgian limestone slopes, a soil of fossilized oysters 150 million years old, which gives Chablis its distinctive mineral taste.

Explore the vineyards around Chablis by car or on foot—the Grands Crus (Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur, Vaudésir) occupy a single southwest-facing slope. From the path overlooking the parcels, you'll understand why each climat bears a different name: exposure, slope, and soil change with every step.

activities.text: Book a tasting at one of the Chablis cellars to compare appellations: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru, Grand Cru. You'll sense the difference in minerality and length on the palate from one climat to another. Allow 60 to 90 minutes depending on the cellar.

practical_info.tip: Reservations recommended in summer

visits.text: Return to Sens to complete the loop. If you didn't do it on the first day, climb the south tower of the cathedral (open in summer, by reservation)—the view from the top embraces the town and the Sénonais countryside. Otherwise, revisit the nave with fresh eyes after seeing all the Romanesque and Gothic churches along the route—you'll appreciate its pioneering status all the more.

End at the Jardins de l'Orangerie, behind the cathedral—you'll find a formal garden that has recaptured its 19th-century appearance. Horticultural beds, shaded paths, view of the cathedral's rear. It's a peaceful, free conclusion to your journey.

activities.text: If you're leaving on a market day (Wednesday or Saturday), make your last Burgundy purchases—cheeses, mustard, gingerbread, Gâtinais honey. Sens has a TGV station with connections to Paris in one hour, making for an easy return.

seo.h1_title: Burgundy Road Trip: Cathedrals, Vineyards & Medieval Villages
seo.intro_paragraph: This 5 days Burgundy circuit loops from Sens to Dijon, passing through the eternal hill of Vézelay, the ramparts of Semur-en-Auxois, the Cistercian Abbey of Fontenay, and the cellars of Beaune. The Route des Grands Crus traverses UNESCO-listed vineyards between Pommard, Nuits-Saint-Georges, and Gevrey-Chambertin. The route alternates Gothic cathedrals, fortified medieval villages, and cellar tastings.
seo.seo_hook: World's first Gothic cathedral in Sens, UNESCO Vézelay, Beaune's polychrome Hospices, Grand Cru vineyards: 5 days through Burgundy's heritage and flavors.
featured_list: Sens: world's first Gothic cathedral, begun around 1135, predating Notre-Dame de Paris
Vézelay: UNESCO Romanesque basilica where Saint Bernard preached the Second Crusade in 1146
Beaune: Hospices founded in 1443, with glazed-tile roofs and Van der Weyden's polyptych
Dijon: Palace of the Dukes, Owl Trail, and UNESCO-listed Cité de la Gastronomie
