itineraries.title: Complete Tour of Corsica
itineraries.subtitle: 13 days circling the Isle of Beauty: red porphyry cliffs, perched Genoese villages, laricio pine forests, and white sand beaches from Porto-Vecchio to Bonifacio.
itineraries.notes: Self-drive itinerary departing and returning to Ajaccio (Napoléon Bonaparte Airport, AJA). Corsica in July–August is very busy: book accommodations and boat excursions 2 to 3 months in advance. Some mountain roads (Col de Bavella, Gorges de la Restonica) are narrow and winding—plan on a small car. Access to Scandola is by boat only from Porto or Calvi.
itineraries.climate: Best time: May-June and September-October, temperatures 20-26°C, both coast and mountains accessible. Avoid July-August (intense heat up to 35°C, coastal roads overcrowded). Mountain roads (Corte, Évisa) sometimes closed December-March.

visits.text: Start at the Maison Bonaparte on rue Saint-Charles—this is where Napoleon was born on August 15, 1769, in a family home that came into Bonaparte ownership in 1743. The tour begins on the second floor with Corsica's history and portraits of Charles and Letizia, then descends to the birth chamber on the first floor. The Directoire furniture purchased by Letizia Bonaparte in Marseille in 1798 is still there, including Milanese commodes gifted by Joseph. Listed as a historic monument in 1923 and opened as a national museum in 1967, the house is open daily except Mondays. Arrive in the morning to beat the cruise ship crowds.

The Cathedral of Our Lady of the Assumption, steps away from the Maison Bonaparte, is where Napoleon was baptized on July 21, 1771—nearly two years after his birth, which was common practice at the time. The 16th-century building houses a Virgin of the Sacred Heart said to have belonged to Letizia Bonaparte. The polished marble floors and light filtering through the stained glass make for a calm interlude between visits.

Climb up to the Place d'Austerlitz at the top of town to see the artificial grotto built under Napoleon III on the spot where young Bonaparte used to retreat as a child. A statue of the Emperor crowns a monumental staircase. The view from the esplanade over the Gulf of Ajaccio and the Sanguinaires Islands is one of the finest in the city.

Make the detour to Pointe de la Parata, 12 km west of Ajaccio—from the parking area, a 10-minute trail leads to a 16th-century Genoese tower overlooking the Sanguinaires archipelago. In late afternoon, the setting sun ignites the pink granite rocks and the water turns orange—this is one of Corsica's most photographed sunsets.

activities.text: The Ajaccio market takes place on Place Foch and along the waterfront every morning (until 1 PM). Corsican cheese shops, butchers, smoked figatellu, maquis honey—take your time; the producers love to chat. It's the best place to assemble a picnic or bring home island specialties.

The Musée Fesch, housed in the palace of Cardinal Joseph Fesch—Napoleon's uncle—holds France's second-largest collection of Italian paintings after the Louvre: Botticelli, Titian, Bellini, Veronese. Allow at least 90 minutes. Open Tuesday through Sunday; closed Mondays.

Tour operators offer boat excursions from Ajaccio harbor to the Sanguinaires Islands. The trip lasts about two hours and follows the coast out to the archipelago. Book the day before in summer—boats depart in the morning between 9 and 10 AM.

visits.text: Cargèse is a village unlike any other—its origins go back to 1676, when Greek refugees fleeing Ottoman occupation first settled at Paomia before founding the present village in 1774 after being driven out by the Corsicans. This past is still visible in the two churches facing each other across the main road. The Greek Orthodox church, built in 1852, preserves Byzantine icons brought by the founders—including an icon of the Virgin reputed to be miraculous. Across the way, the Latin church dates from 1828. For a long time the two communities celebrated their masses at different hours in the same bell tower. Step inside the Greek church—the contrast with the Corsican exterior architecture is striking.

Climb above the village for views over the Gulf of Sagone—one of Corsica's widest, with a 25 km opening. On a clear day you'll glimpse the Piana calanques to the north. The panorama is worth the few minutes' walk from the center.

activities.text: The beach at Chiuni, 3 km north of the village, is one of the finest on the west coast: 700 meters of white sand in a cove framed by two granite promontories, with water that turns turquoise in good weather. Arrive before 10 AM in summer—the parking is small and fills quickly.

Peru beach, to the south, is wilder and less crowded than Chiuni. The access road from the main route is a bit bumpy but the fine sand and clear waters are worth the detour—ideal for a quiet late afternoon.

visits.text: Don't miss the Calanques de Piana under any circumstances—listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1983 along with the Gulf of Porto and the Scandola reserve. These 250-million-year-old red porphyry formations rise up to 400 meters above the sea across 11,800 hectares. The D81 road between Porto and Piana winds through them for 2 sinuous kilometers: stop at the viewpoints to make out the wind-sculpted silhouettes—a fortress, a bishop, petrified lovers. Maupassant crossed these same rocks in 1880 and wrote: "these are the marvels of Corsica, one might say one of the marvels of the world." By car or on foot, plan to be there late in the day when the sun sets the rock ablaze.

Girolata is a fishing hamlet accessible only by boat or by a 2.5-hour trail from the Col de la Croix—no roads, no cars, just colorful houses on the edge of a green gulf. Also inscribed within the UNESCO perimeter, it counts barely a few dozen year-round residents. If you take the boat from Porto, you'll glimpse it while passing the Scandola reserve.

Porto's Genoese tower—square and red like the rocks—has dominated the harbor since the 16th century. It was built to watch for Barbary raids and alert the inland villages. The climb takes 10 minutes and the view over the gulf from its summit is worth it, especially at golden hour.

activities.text: The boat excursion from Porto to Scandola, Girolata, and the Calanques de Piana is the trip's essential outing. The Scandola nature reserve—France's first marine reserve, created in 1975 and listed by UNESCO in 1983—is home to peregrine falcons, ospreys, and giant groupers you'll see diving beneath the hull. The cruise generally lasts 3 to 4 hours. Tour operators depart from Porto harbor every morning. Book the day before in high season—it's often sold out.

Hike the calanques trail starting from Roches Bleues: from the parking area on the D81, a marked trail winds through the red porphyry formations for 3 to 4 km. The route offers views the road doesn't allow—count on 2 hours round-trip. Closed shoes required; no flip-flops on these sharp rocks.

visits.text: The Gorges de Spelunca connect Evisa to the village of Ota via a 5 km mule track carved into the gorges of the Porto and Tavulella rivers. The descent winds between orange granite walls and crystal-clear pools. Along the way you'll cross the Zaglia bridge—a 15th-century Genoese arch listed as a historic monument, built of pink granite over the river. It's one of Corsica's most beautiful low-mountain trails; count on 2.5 hours descending. Bring water and a swimsuit.

If you still have energy after the gorges, climb up into the Aïtone forest above Evisa: laricio pines 40 to 50 meters tall, centuries old, filtering the light into a green and gold checkerboard. A marked trail follows the waterfalls and natural pools of the torrent—the water is icy even in mid-August. It's the most frequented swimming spot in the region, so avoid Sunday morning.

activities.text: Swimming in the natural pools of the Gorges de Spelunca: midway along the trail between Ota and Evisa, several basins carved in granite allow you to plunge into transparent water. It's a popular family picnic spot on weekends—come during the week or arrive early in the morning for peace and quiet.

Hike in the Aïtone forest from the village of Evisa: the trail gradually climbs under the pines to viewpoints over the Gulf of Porto. The forest is cool even in midsummer—ideal if you're looking for an alternative to the coastal heat. Count on 2.5 hours for a complete loop.

visits.text: Take the road that climbs the Fango valley for 15 km from Galéria—a forest of cork oaks and chestnuts descending from the heights of Monte Cinto (2,706 m, Corsica's highest point) down to the sea, classified as a UNESCO biosphere reserve. Solitude is almost total on weekdays. The Fango's waters are among the island's most transparent, shifting from blue to green depending on depth and light.

Don't leave without stopping at the Fango's natural pools—a series of basins and potholes carved in granite between two Genoese stone bridges. The main swimming spot is about 5 km from the village, past the old bridge. The water is cool and limpid even in August.

activities.text: Rental companies offer sea kayaks and canoes in Galéria for paddling up the lower Fango in season (April–October). The section between the sea and the first pools takes about 90 minutes. Best in the morning, before the offshore wind picks up.

practical_info.booking: On-site rental, arrive early in July–August

activities.text: Picnic beside the Fango pools: bring your provisions from Galéria (the village grocery is the only option in the valley). Set up on the flat rocks by the water—the shade's coolness and the torrent's sound do the rest. The spot is quiet on weekdays; packed on July Saturdays.

visits.text: Calvi's citadel dominates the bay from its granite spur—a 15th-century Genoese fortress whose motto inscribed on the ramparts, "Semper Fidelis," says everything about the city's attachment to Genoa. In the paved lanes of the upper town, a plaque on some ruins claims "Christopher Columbus was born here in 1441." Historians agree the explorer was probably Genoese, but the Calvais won't hear anything else—the legend is far more entertaining. Also visit the Saint-Jean-Baptiste cathedral in the citadel's center, which houses an organ and artworks from the Genoese period.

Notre-Dame de la Serra, 5 km from Calvi via a road climbing through the maquis, is a chapel perched on a rocky peak at 200 meters altitude. The view from its forecourt embraces the entire Bay of Calvi, the citadel below, Monte Cinto in the background, and on clear days the Ligurian coast on the horizon. The walk up from the road takes 20 minutes.

The Revellata peninsula, beyond the beach, contains a lighthouse and several wild coves accessible on foot or by kayak. It's also one of Balagne's best diving spots, with posidonia meadows and rocky bottoms down to 30 meters. Tour operators offer diving outings from Calvi harbor.

activities.text: Calvi's beach stretches 4 km of white sand between the harbor and the Revellata peninsula. It's well equipped with lifeguard stations, water sports rental, and beach bars. Arrive before 9:30 AM to get space; in July–August the parking fills in an hour.

The Bonifatu forest, 18 km east of Calvi, is the trailhead for hikes toward Balagne's high peaks. An easy 2-hour trail follows the Figarella river to natural pools for swimming. The pine and oak forest offers welcome coolness after the beaches.

visits.text: Sant'Antonino is one of France's most beautiful villages—and one of Corsica's oldest, perched at 500 meters altitude on a granite outcrop since the 9th century. The lanes are so narrow you can barely pass. The view from the summit over the Balagne beaches and sea is breathtaking. Count on 45 minutes to walk around—cars stay below in the parking lot.

Occi is a ghost village: abandoned in the 1950s by its inhabitants who left for the coast, it sleeps on its spur facing the sea with its roofless houses overgrown by maquis. The trail from Lumio takes 45 minutes each way. It's a silent and slightly melancholy place that neatly sums up 20th-century Corsican inland depopulation.

Speloncato, at 600 meters altitude in the heart of Balagne, is a belvedere village overlooking the plain on one side and the ridges on the other. Cardinal Pietro Casini hailed from here. Twice a year, at sunset on the spring and autumn equinoxes, the sun's rays thread precisely through a church window portal—a spectacle announced in advance and much anticipated by locals.

activities.text: The Balagne village loop by car is a day in itself: Lumio, Lavatoggio, Zilia, Montemaggiore, Cateri follow one another on the hillsides. Stop in Zilia for its olives and reputed spring water, in Montemaggiore for the church perched above the vineyards. Local producers sell olive oil, honey, and figatellu directly.

visits.text: Île-Rousse was founded from scratch in 1758 by Pascal Paoli to compete with the Genoese port of Calvi—he wanted to give independent Corsica its own maritime outlet. Place Paoli, with its cafés under the plane trees, is the heart of local life. The 1850 covered market comes alive from 8 AM with Corsican cheese makers, butchers, and market gardeners: this is where you'll find the region's best fresh brocciu.

Walk around the Pietra peninsula, linked to the town by a 300-meter causeway: its red porphyry rocks are the same volcanic stone as the Piana calanques, in a more discreet version. An automatic lighthouse occupies the point. The trail that circles it takes 30 minutes and gives beautiful views of the town, the open sea, and the Balagne reliefs—a simple, car-free stroll to take at dusk.

activities.text: Bodri beach, 3 km west via the D81, is a wild beach at the foot of the maquis—less crowded than Île-Rousse's central beach, with access via a small dirt path. The water is clear and the sand fine. Ideal for late afternoon when tourists have returned to the center.

Bike or walk the cycle path that follows the coast south from Île-Rousse toward Lumio—8 km of coastal road with views over the sea and Balagne hills. Bike rental shops are set up near the harbor. Ideal in late afternoon to avoid the heat.

map_keywords: Plage du Lotu Désert des Agriates

visits.text: Saint-Florent is nicknamed the Corsican Saint-Tropez—an upscale marina on the Gulf of Saint-Florent, with its white yachts, waterfront restaurant terraces, and evening buzz. The 15th-century Genoese citadel dominates the harbor from the hill. It's well preserved and you can walk its ramparts. Below the harbor, wander the old town's lanes before joining the evening promenade.

The Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta del Nebbio, 1 km from Saint-Florent on the Bastia road, is one of Corsica's finest examples of Pisan Romanesque architecture: built in the 12th century in white limestone with an apse in cul-de-four and sculptures of serpents and animals on the capitals. The sober, cool interior contrasts with the heat outside. Take 20 minutes to walk around.

The beaches of Saleccia and Lotu, in the Désert des Agriates, rank among the Mediterranean's most beautiful wild beaches—white sand, turquoise water, and not a building on the horizon. Accessible only by shuttle boat from Saint-Florent harbor (30-minute trip) or by a 2-hour walking trail from Chjera. Shuttles run several times daily from May to October. Don't miss Saleccia: a kilometer of white sand surrounded by umbrella pines.

activities.text: Stroll through Saint-Florent's lanes and enjoy an aperitif on the harbor in late afternoon: the waterfront terraces come alive around 6 PM. It's a chance to taste Cap Corse, the local aperitif made from macerated Corsican wines that the Italians copied to make their Martini.

Tour operators offer day sea kayak rentals to reach the Désert des Agriates beaches from Saint-Florent. The sea route follows a coast virgin of any construction—count on 2 hours of paddling each way, with swimming stops along the way. Ideal for travelers who like getting away from crowds.

map_keywords: Musée de Bastia Palais des gouverneurs

visits.text: Climb up to Bastia's citadel—the Terra Nova quarter, founded in 1380 by Genoese governor Leonello Lomellini on a rocky spur. It's from this fortress called "bastiglia" that the city takes its name. Paved lanes wind between tall houses with laundry drying at the windows, opening onto the Place du Donjon with the Palais des Gouverneurs—a 15th-century crenellated tower building, now the Bastia museum. The view from the esplanade over the old harbor and sea is magnificent.

Inside the citadel, step through the door of Sainte-Marie Cathedral: built between 1604 and 1619, it holds a little-known treasure—the silver statue of the Virgin of the Assumption that Bastiais have carried in procession every August 15 since the 17th century. Inside, the Assumption of the Virgin by Leonoro d'Aquila (1512) is Bastia's oldest painting. The cathedral was the seat of the Genoese governor—this is where the passing of power between two viceroys of the island took place.

Descend to Bastia's old harbor—the Portu Vecchju—to see Italian-style houses in fawn colors stacked in an amphitheater around the cove. It's one of Corsica's most beautiful old harbors, often overlooked in favor of Ajaccio. In the evening, fishermen unload their catch directly on the wharf, and restaurants set up their tables right to the water's edge.

activities.text: The Bastia museum in the Palais des Gouverneurs presents the city's and Corsica's history since the Genoese era: paintings, sculptures, maps, and models of the original bastiglia. The citadel tower is accessible by climbing the palace staircase—the view from the summit over the sea and Cap Corse is Bastia's finest.

Place Saint-Nicolas—280 meters long, one of France's largest seaside squares—is Bastia's living room. The terraces are wide, the palm trees provide shade, and the Sunday market is one of the island's liveliest. An evening aperitif on this square, with views over the boats returning to harbor, is a Bastiais ritual worth adopting.

map_keywords: Nonza plage galets noirs Cap Corse

visits.text: Macinaggio is the port at Cap Corse's northern tip—the end of the end. Tour operators offer narrated cruises to the Giraglia islets and the cape's limestone cliffs, accessible only from the sea. The crossing follows a coast almost virgin of construction, with cliffs plunging directly into the water.

Nonza, on Cap Corse's west coast, is one of the island's most photographed villages: a 17th-century Genoese tower perched on a black cliff, and below a beach of black pebbles—colored by the mountain's schist. It's at Nonza that a lone woman, Catarina Gentili, defended the tower against the French in 1768 by making them believe an entire garrison was entrenched inside. Come in late afternoon for the light on the cliff.

If you still have time, push on to Erbalunga, 10 km north of Bastia—a small Genoese fishing village with houses clustered around a tower collapsed into the sea. It's one of the east coast's most picturesque spots on the cape, often photographed as a backdrop to the seafood terraces, among the region's finest.

activities.text: The sentier des douaniers (customs officers' path) between Macinaggio and Barcaggio is a 12 km one-way hike along Cap Corse's northern corniche, between maquis and sea cliffs. It's Corsica's wildest coastal trail—count on 4 hours round-trip or do it one way with a return shuttle. Bring water: no supply points along the route.

The Patrimonio wine route crosses Corsica's first AOC vineyards (the appellation dates from 1968) at the cape's foot. Cap Corse muscat and red nielluccio are the two pillars of this black schist terroir. Estates offer tastings without appointment, particularly around Patrimonio village.

map_keywords: Citadelle Corte musée de la Corse

visits.text: Corte is the only inland city—and Corsica's former capital between 1755 and 1769, when Pascal Paoli made it the seat of his government and founded a university there. The citadel, perched on a rocky spur 100 meters above the confluence of the Restonica and Tavignano, is the only one of Corsica's seven citadels built inland. Climb to the belvedere for the 360° view over both valleys and the triangular bell tower of the Annunciation church. The Museum of Corsica, in the Serrurier barracks at the citadel's heart, houses 3,000 objects of traditional Corsican ethnography collected by Father Doazan—opened in 1997, it's the island's best museum for understanding insular culture. Your Corte train ticket entitles you to a discount.

Place Gaffory, in the old town, contains the house of General Jean-Pierre Gaffory—the man who liberated Corte from the Genoese before being assassinated in 1753. The bullet impacts visible on his house's façade aren't decoration: they date from the 1750 Genoese siege, when Gaffory was defending his own home with his wife while the Genoese held his son hostage.

The Gorges de la Restonica begin 2 km from Corte's center via a narrow mountain road. In summer, a shuttle runs from the town parking lot (the road is often closed to cars in July–August). The pools and natural basins between the gorges and the Grotelle shepherds' hut are among Corsica's finest—the water is icy even in full heat wave.

activities.text: Lake Melo hike from the Grotelle shepherds' hut: from the Restonica valley terminus parking lot (1,375 m), count on 1 hour each way to reach Lake Melo at 1,711 m. Rocky marked trail, 300 m elevation gain. The lake is framed by cliffs and its water is an intense cold blue. In summer, the local shepherds sell their tomme cheese directly at the hut—don't miss this break.

Swimming in the Restonica's pools on the return from Grotelle. The best basins are mid-valley, accessible from parking areas on the D623. The water descends directly from Lake Melo—count on 10°C in midsummer.

map_keywords: Plage de Fautea tour génoise Solenzara

visits.text: Fautea beach, 15 km north of Solenzara, has a silhouette you won't see anywhere else: a round 16th-century Genoese tower stands directly on the beach, its feet in white sand. Built to watch for Barbary raids, it's now a listed historic monument. The beach in front is uncrowded—tourists rarely stop.

Make a detour to the Étang de Diane, accessible by track from the national road: a natural lagoon exploited for oyster farming since Antiquity—the Romans already appreciated its oysters. The site remains wild, bordered by tamarisks. Go early in the morning: the raking light on the water and mountains behind is one of the east coast's finest.

activities.text: The Côte des Nacres between Fautea and Solenzara is a string of undeveloped beaches with translucent waters and polished granite bottoms. Stop at Canella beach—white sand, no beach bar, no paid parking—for a no-frills afternoon.

Solenzara is the starting point for the Gorges du Solenzara, 10 km west: a mountain road follows the river between granite walls to a series of pools and waterfalls. Ideal for a late-afternoon swim before returning to the village.

visits.text: Porto-Vecchio's old town, perched on its Genoese ramparts above the gulf, is more pleasant in the morning before the heat and midday tourists. The paved lanes and granite arches from the Genoese era are well preserved. Wander to the old Genoese gate overlooking the gulf—the view over the umbrella pines and turquoise water below explains Porto-Vecchio's reputation.

Palombaggia beach is regularly cited among Europe's most beautiful: 2 km of pink sand at the foot of century-old umbrella pines, with water in 50 shades of turquoise and blue. It's genuinely exceptional—and a victim of its own success in July–August. Arrive before 8:30 AM or after 5 PM. Outside these windows, the parking is full and the beach towels are touching.

Rondinara beach, between Porto-Vecchio and Bonifacio, is an almost circular bay enclosed by two hills—one of Corsica's most photographed. The natural amphitheater shape means the wind almost never disturbs it: the water is always glassy. Bring water and provisions because the only on-site service is minimal.

activities.text: The Cavu valley, 15 km west of Porto-Vecchio via the D368, contains natural pools carved in pink granite with translucent water. The site is classified Natura 2000. The walk from the parking lot takes 20 minutes. Avoid going on a Sunday in August—it's every Porto-Vecchio vacationer's favorite excursion.

Santa Giulia beach, in its shallow lagoon 8 km south of Porto-Vecchio, is ideal for families with children: the water is warm, calm, and transparent, and the sandy bottoms let you walk far from shore. Canoe and paddleboard rentals are set up there in season.

map_keywords: Point de vue baie Porto-Vecchio Ospedale

visits.text: Climb to the Ospedale forest, at 900 meters altitude above Porto-Vecchio: an oasis of coolness among laricio pines and holm oaks, with an artificial lake built in the 1960s shimmering at the basin's bottom—a surprising image at this altitude. From the forest road you'll have some of the finest views over the Bay of Porto-Vecchio. Stop at the viewpoints on the village road.

The Piscia di Gallo waterfall—"rooster piss" in Corsican, which gives an idea of local poetry—is Corsica's highest waterfall at 60 meters. It's 30 minutes on foot from the forest parking lot. Only catch: it's spectacular in spring and after autumn rains, but can reduce to a trickle in August.

activities.text: Two-hour round-trip hike to Piscia di Gallo waterfall from the forest parking lot: well-marked trail in the pines, moderate 200 m elevation gain. Hiking shoes required—the path is rocky.
From the Ospedale forest belvedere, the Bay of Porto-Vecchio spreads below with its islets and green waters. Stop there in late afternoon: the declining light turns the gulf to gold.

visits.text: The Aiguilles de Bavella are the postcard of Corsican mountains: seven jagged granite peaks surge to 1,840 meters above a pass planted with laricio pines and a statue of Notre-Dame-des-Neiges. The road from Zonza or Solaro climbs through switchbacks to the pass at 1,218 meters—one of Corsica's most spectacular. Arrive early in the morning to see them in the pink light of sunrise before clouds envelop them.

The Trou de la Bombe is a tafone—an oval hollow carved by erosion in a granite block—8 meters in diameter, perched in equilibrium on the needles' crest. To reach it, a marked 1.5-hour trail climbs from the Col de Bavella. You'll pass through a light via ferrata (cables and rungs in place) and the passage under the arch gives a plunging view over the gorges.

activities.text: Hike at Col de Bavella: from the pass, several marked trails head toward the needles. The most accessible, "the tafoni hike," is 5 km round-trip and follows the hollow granite formations—count on 2.5 hours. For the more adventurous, climbing the needles (with required guide) offers views to the sea.

Dinner in Zonza village before tackling Bavella the next morning: the village restaurants offer Corsican charcuterie, wild boar, and milk-fed veal—Alta Rocca specialties. Ask locals for their favorite trail for the next day; they know dozens beyond the marked circuits.

visits.text: Bonifacio sits on a limestone plateau plunging in 60 to 80-meter cliffs directly into the sea—the limestone is a geological anomaly on an island essentially made of granite. The upper town's houses seem ready to topple into the void, house foundations sometimes extending beyond the cliff edge. The Genoese citadel dates from the 12th century; in 1420, King Alfonso V of Aragon besieged it for five months without managing to take it. The Bastion de l'Étendard, at the upper town's entrance, houses a museum and offers the best view over the harbor below and the Bouches de Bonifacio—the 11 km strait separating Corsica from Sardinia.

The Escalier du Roy d'Aragon is carved right into the limestone cliff: 187 steps cut in the rock, descending to the cliff base. Legend says Aragonese troops carved it in a single night during the 1420 siege—reality is more prosaic; it's probably a Genoese construction to access a freshwater source. Listed as a historic monument. Walk down it: the view climbing back up of the houses overhanging the cliff is vertiginous.

Petit Sperone beach, accessible by trail from the Pertusato lighthouse, is a white sand cove at the limestone cliffs' foot—crystalline water, reduced crowds because the walk is dissuasive. Plan on 30 minutes walking each way. The Pertusato lighthouse has watched over the strait since the 19th century.

activities.text: The cruise around Bonifacio from the harbor is the essential excursion: from the sea, the 60 to 80-meter cliffs take on an entirely different dimension, and marine caves carved in limestone open beneath the upper town. Boats pass the "Grain de sable"—a building-sized rock block that broke away from the cliffs. Tour operators offer 1-hour or half-day trips to the Lavezzi Islands.

The Lavezzi Islands—a protected archipelago 10 km south of Bonifacio, beyond the Bouches—are granite islets polished by the sea with pristine white sand beaches and water transparent down to 10 meters. Boats depart mornings from Bonifacio harbor. The nature reserve prohibits camping and picking: you come just to swim and observe monk seals in winter.

map_keywords: Église Sainte-Marie Sartène place de la Libération

visits.text: Sartène is the most Corsican town in Corsica, according to Prosper Mérimée's phrase. Its black granite houses squeeze into the old town's steep lanes like nowhere else on the island—not a painted façade, not a tourist garland, just stone and silence. Every Good Friday evening, the Catenacciu procession crosses the town since the 14th century: a chained penitent carries a 30 kg cross through the lanes, his identity kept secret. Place de la Libération, at the center, is surrounded by arcades under which the elders play cards.

The Departmental Museum of Corsican Prehistory and Archaeology, installed in an 18th-century former convent, houses Corsica's most important prehistoric collection: sculpted Bronze Age menhirs, Neolithic ceramics, warrior statue-menhirs with eyes and sword. Count on 1 hour. The megalithic site of Filitosa, 20 km away, is its natural extension.

activities.text: Sartène's old town is better discovered with the tourist office's small guide than with apps: the lanes still bear their Corsican names and the oldest houses date from the 16th century. Count on 90 minutes for a complete walking tour—start from the square and descend toward the Santa-Anna quarter.

Make a detour to Sainte-Lucie-de-Tallano, 12 km east, an Alta Rocca village perched above chestnut groves. The village has a 15th-century Franciscan convent and a church housing a 16th-century marble Entombment. They also sell the region's best charcuterie here—several producers have shops in the village.

visits.text: Campomoro, 18 km south of Propriano, is one of the Corsican coast's most preserved natural sites: a round 16th-century Genoese tower watches over a pebble and sand beach facing the Gulf of Valinco. The coastal trail starting from the tower follows the cliffs and coves for 7 km—a 2.5-hour walk through maquis with sea views at every turn. Not a building on the horizon.

The prehistoric site of Filitosa, 20 km north, is Corsica's most important: Bronze Age warrior statue-menhirs (2000–1200 BC) rise among thousand-year-old olive trees—some have carved faces with a sword and helmet still recognizable. The site is listed. Plan on 90 minutes to walk it with the audio guide.

activities.text: Portigliolo beach, 3 km north of Propriano, is wild and uncrowded: 700 meters of sand at the back of the Gulf of Valinco, without a beach bar or paid parking. The water is warm and calm because the gulf is sheltered from offshore winds. The region's best spot for a quiet morning.

Tour operators offer boat trips from Propriano harbor to the Calanques de Piana or the Sanguinaires Islands—day excursions that let you revisit sites already seen by road from the sea, from another angle. Book in advance.

visits.text: This last day in Ajaccio before the airport road is a chance to wander the neighborhoods you didn't see on arrival. The Quartier des Cannes, above Cours Napoléon, is the Ajaccio of Ajacciens—far from the Napoleonic circuit, with its Corsican groceries, bakeries, and neighborhood cafés. Walk up to the Notre-Dame-de-la-Miséricorde cathedral for the view over the gulf.

If time permits before the airport, revisit Pointe de la Parata for a final view of the Sanguinaires Islands—the morning light is different from the sunset and the site is nearly deserted before 9 AM. A simple way to close the island loop at the same starting point, but from a different angle.

activities.text: Final tasting at Ajaccio market, Place Foch and Quai Napoléon: figatellu, lonzu, coppa, brocciu, arbutus honey, citron jam, canistrelli with white wine. If you haven't yet tasted Corsican charcuterie, this is the last moment. The producers selling directly in the morning aren't the same as the evening tourist shops.

Corsican wine tour from Ajaccio: the Ajaccio region wine route follows the hillsides north of the city for 30 km. Corsica has 9 AOCs—Ajaccio, Patrimonio, Muscat du Cap Corse, Porto-Vecchio, Sartène, Figari, Corse, Calvi, Corse-Coteaux-du-Cap-Corse. Estates offer tastings; prefer those producing white vermentino, very floral and typical of the island.

seo.h1_title: Complete Tour of Corsica
seo.intro_paragraph: Over 13 days, this complete circuit loops around Corsica clockwise from Ajaccio: UNESCO-listed Piana calanques, the Scandola nature reserve accessible only by boat, Genoese citadels of Calvi and Bastia, the Aïtone forest, Corte with its glacial gorges, white beaches of Porto-Vecchio, and Bonifacio's limestone cliffs. The itinerary combines the wild west coast, authentic Cap Corse, mountainous interior, and the Mediterranean's deep south.
seo.seo_hook: 13 days to circle the Isle of Beauty: Piana's red calanques, Genoese citadels, glacial Lake Melo, and Bonifacio's cliffs.
featured_list: Calanques de Piana: 400-meter red porphyry cliffs UNESCO-listed since 1983
Bonifacio: Genoese citadel on 60 to 80-meter limestone cliffs, withstood a 5-month Aragonese siege in 1420
Corte: former capital of independent Corsica, Lake Melo at 1,711 m altitude
Scandola: France's first marine reserve, accessible only by boat from Porto

itineraries.title: From Marseille to Aix-en-Provence: Calanques, Hilltop Villages and Provençal Light
itineraries.subtitle: 4 days between the Phocaean city, Cassis calanques, the birthplace of cinema in La Ciotat, Le Castellet vineyards, and Aix's elegance.
itineraries.notes: Access to the calanques is regulated in summer (fire risk)—check the National Park website before departure. Book calanques cruises and Eden-Théâtre guided tours in advance during high season.
itineraries.climate: Best time: April-June and September-October, temperatures 18-26°C, perfect for calanques and hilltop villages. Avoid July-August (scorching heat 30-35°C, strong mistral winds, massive crowds). Mild winter (10-15°C) but frequent mistral.

visits.text: Start with La Bonne Mère—that's what locals call Notre-Dame-de-la-Garde, and it's the first thing you should do upon arrival. Perched at 154 meters atop a limestone outcrop, this Romano-Byzantine basilica consecrated in 1864 dominates everything. The gilded statue of the Virgin at the summit measures 11.20 meters and weighs nearly 10 tons—it was crafted by the Christofle house and requires regilding every 25 years. Inside, the walls are covered with 1,200 m² of gold-backed mosaics and sailors' ex-votos: suspended ship models, thank-you plaques, and naïve paintings. Go up in the morning for the light and avoid weekends.

Head back down to the Old Port and climb up into Le Panier district, Marseille's oldest neighborhood—this is where Greek settlers from Phocaea landed 2,600 years ago. Today, narrow alleys are covered in street art, hidden squares shelter artists' workshops and improvised terraces. Don't look for a precise route: get lost, that's the whole point. Place des Moulins, the district's highest point, makes a good landmark if you lose your bearings.

Leaving Le Panier toward the sea, you'll encounter La Major cathedral. Built between 1852 and 1893 in neo-Byzantine style, it's massive—142 meters long, the largest religious building constructed in France during the 19th century. The contrast between white Carrara marble and green Florence stone gives it a striking striped appearance. Glance inside at the choir mosaics, then exit on the sea side for views over the port of La Joliette.

End the day with a stroll along the Old Port. It's been Marseille's beating heart for 26 centuries. In the morning, the fish market on quai des Belges is a spectacle—fishermen sell their catch directly from boats, shouting in Provençal. By late afternoon, the terraces take over. The Vieux-Port ombrière, Norman Foster's immense polished steel structure, acts as a mirror reflecting the crowds—it's become one of modern Marseille's symbols.

activities.text: Walk up to Notre-Dame-de-la-Garde on foot from the Old Port via Saint-Victor Abbey—one of France's oldest, founded in the 5th century, with crypts and early Christian sarcophagi. Allow 30 minutes uphill. Alternatively, bus 60 departs from the Old Port and drops you at the basilica's foot.

Late afternoon, walk along Corniche Kennedy heading south. It's a 25-minute walk from the Old Port to reach Vallon des Auffes, a tiny fishing harbor wedged between two concrete cliffs. This is postcard Marseille, with colorful pointus (traditional boats) and little bouillabaisse restaurants. The spot is perfect for an aperitif facing the sunset.

visits.text: Devote the morning to MuCEM—this concrete cube wrapped in an openwork lattice facing the sea was designed by Rudy Ricciotti. Opened in 2013 when Marseille was European Capital of Culture, it entered the world's 50 most visited museums the following year. Collections cover anthropology, archaeology, and contemporary art around the Mediterranean. Even if exhibitions don't appeal, head to the rooftop terrace: the view over the Old Port and the open sea is free and spectacular.

Cross the 130-meter footbridge linking MuCEM to Fort Saint-Jean—suspended above the harbor basin, it offers a vertiginous view of the sea. The fort, built on Louis XIV's orders from 1668 onward, dominates the Old Port entrance from its 20-meter height. It served as much to protect Marseille as to watch over it—cannons were aimed at the city in case of revolt. Free entry, it houses the Garden of Migrations, a 12,000 m² Mediterranean botanical space with lavender, rosemary, and orange trees. Look for the Fanal tower (17th century) that served as a lighthouse and King René's tower (15th century), whose terrace offers plunging views over the port.

Return landward via the second footbridge leading directly into Le Panier district. Take rue du Petit-Puits to La Vieille Charité, a former 17th-century hospice built by Pierre Puget around an arcaded courtyard and oval chapel. Today, the building houses the Museum of Mediterranean Archaeology and the Museum of African, Oceanic, and American Indian Arts. Even without entering the museums, the courtyard is magnificent and free.

activities.text: If you enjoy contemporary art and alternative spaces, make a detour to Friche Belle de Mai—a former tobacco factory converted into a 45,000 m² cultural center. Galleries, artists' studios, concert hall, rooftop skatepark, restaurants. This is creative Marseille, far from tourist circuits. Take bus 49 from the Old Port.

Late afternoon, head down to Prado beaches or Escale Borély for a seaside walk. Parc Borély is Marseille's largest green space, with its 18th-century château, botanical garden, and lake. The atmosphere is relaxed—joggers, families, pétanque players. Grab a drink on a terrace facing the sea before heading to Cassis the next day.

visits.text: Arrive early in Cassis—parking lots fill up quickly in season. The harbor is charming, with pastel façades, terraces, and aligned pointus. From there, look up toward Cap Canaille to the east: at 394 meters, it's France's highest sea cliff (and some say Europe's). The ochre-red color of the rock at sunset is a spectacle in itself.

Head on foot toward Port-Miou calanque, 20 minutes from the center. This long 1,400-meter fjord, bordered by remains of an old limestone quarry operated from the 18th century until 1981, now serves as a natural harbor for hundreds of sailboats. In Provençal, "Port-Miou" means "good harbor"—it's the perfect shelter on windy days.

Continue on the GR98 trail to Port-Pin—allow 40 minutes from Port-Miou. You'll recognize it by its small sand and pebble beach framed by Aleppo pines (hence its name). The water is translucent, turquoise—you'd think you were in the Caribbean. If you're there early morning, you'll have the beach almost to yourself.

For motivated hikers, push on to the En-Vau belvedere—170 meters above the sea, aligned with the canyon. En-Vau is considered the massif's most beautiful calanque: vertical white cliffs 100 meters high plunge into impossibly blue water. Warning: the descent to the beach is steep and technical (Portalet passage, fixed rope), bring good shoes. Allow 1h30-2h from central Cassis.

activities.text: If hiking doesn't appeal, board a cruise from Cassis harbor. Boats depart every 30 minutes in season for a calanques tour—3, 5, or 8 calanques depending on the formula. You'll see Port-Miou, Port-Pin, and En-Vau from the sea, which lets you appreciate the cliff heights. Allow 45 min to 2h depending on the route.

practical_info.booking: Frequent departures, but book ahead in summer

activities.text: Late afternoon, take the Route des Crêtes between Cassis and La Ciotat (D141). Over 15 km, this cliff road winds along the top of the Soubeyranes cliffs with viewpoints offering plunging views over Cassis on one side and La Ciotat bay on the other. Warning: the road closes in strong wind (mistral over 60 km/h). Best time is late afternoon for the light.

visits.text: First, step through the doors of Eden-Théâtre at 25 boulevard Clemenceau. Built in 1889, it's the world's oldest cinema still in operation. The Lumière brothers organized a private screening here as early as September 21, 1895—weeks before Paris—and the first paid public screening took place here on March 21, 1899. The Lumière family spent vacations in La Ciotat at their Clos des Plages château, and the town's streets were where they filmed their first movies, including the famous "Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat Station." The building, listed as a historic monument, was saved and renovated by passionate volunteers. Guided tours on Wednesdays and Saturdays afternoons.

Next, head down to La Ciotat's Old Port. The quays are lined with 17th-century houses in colorful façades. At the quay's end, the old Town Hall (1864) houses the Ciotat museum with maritime history and Lumière brothers memorabilia. Did you know pétanque was invented here in 1907 or 1910, depending on sources? A monument commemorates it near the port.

Continue on foot to Parc du Mugel, 20 minutes from the port. This 12-hectare botanical park nestles in a red-rock calanque, sheltered by the Bec de l'Aigle. Climb to the belvedere at 82 meters elevation: the view of ochre cliffs plunging into turquoise Mediterranean is probably La Ciotat's finest. The vegetation is lush—pines, eucalyptus, palms. Bring proper shoes for the trails.

Right next to Mugel, stop at Figuerolles calanque. Smaller and more intimate than those near Cassis, it's distinguished by strangely shaped rocks sculpted by erosion and crystalline waters. If you're there late afternoon, the grazing light on the red rocks is superb.

activities.text: To extend the day seaside, take a shuttle from the port to Île Verte, the only wooded island on the coast between Marseille and Toulon. The crossing takes 10 minutes. On site: hiking trails, small beach, and restaurant—a peaceful escape facing the mainland. Allow half a day.

Stroll the waterfront in the evening. In summer, the port comes alive with nighttime artisan markets and open-air concerts. Try the local bouillabaisse—each restaurant has its own recipe, and locals claim theirs is better than Marseille's.

visits.text: Enter Le Castellet village through the Grand Portail, one of only two fortified gates pierced in the ramparts—there's no other access. Listed among France's Most Beautiful Villages, this perched medieval village dominates Bandol vineyards 360°. Sloping lanes climb toward the 15th-century château (now town hall, interior not open to visitors). Marcel Pagnol filmed "The Baker's Wife" here in 1938 with Raimu—you can still see Place de l'Ormeau where scenes were shot.

Look for the "Trou de Madame"—an opening in the ramparts, left of the château. It's a discreet but spectacular viewpoint: the entire Brûlat wine plain spreads before you, bordered by olive groves and pine forests, with the white line of the Sainte-Baume massif as backdrop. On clear days, the contrast between golden garrigue and blue sky is striking.

Push on to La Cadière-d'Azur, 5 minutes by car. This hilltop village, also labeled a Var Village of Character, is less touristy than Le Castellet but equally charming. Its orientation table offers a panorama over vineyards, the distant sea, and Var hills. Lanes are quiet, stone façades golden—this is Provence in its authentic form.

In Le Castellet, take time to browse artists' workshops—potters, ceramicists, painters, leatherworkers. The village has specialized in art crafts, and the Parcours des Arts lets you discover them shop by shop. Saint-Sauveur church, built in 1030 by the Marseille bishopric and oriented toward Jerusalem, deserves a look for its three-arch bell tower and campanile.

activities.text: Take advantage of your visit for a tasting at a Bandol AOC wine estate. Vineyards spread at Le Castellet's foot on sunny terraces. Mourvèdre dominates the reds—powerful, tannic wines that age remarkably well. Several estates offer visits and tastings without reservation in off-season, but call ahead in summer.

Late afternoon, drive down to Bandol (15 minutes). The small marina is lined with terraces where you can grab a final drink facing the boats. The Tuesday morning Provençal market is worth the detour if your schedule allows. Bandol is also the departure point for shuttles to the Embiez islands—if you have half a day ahead, the island walk is pleasant.

visits.text: Begin with Cours Mirabeau, 440 meters long and 42 meters wide, lined with century-old plane trees forming a vegetal tunnel overhead. Four fountains punctuate the promenade, including the Mossy Fountain—covered in thick green moss, it's fed by a thermal spring at 18°C. At no. 55, look for Paul Cézanne's childhood home. At the Cours's upper end, the King René fountain shows the good king holding the Muscat grape he introduced to Provence—an 1819 statue by David d'Angers.

Dive into the old town north of the Cours. Aix counts over a hundred fountains and dozens of 17th-18th century private mansions—wrought-iron balconies, sculpted doors, atlantes and caryatids. Place d'Albertas, with its fountain framed by Baroque façades, is among the finest. At Place de l'Hôtel de Ville, the Saturday morning flower market is a feast for eyes and nose.

Visit Saint-Sauveur Cathedral, an astonishing building mixing five architectural styles from the 5th to 17th centuries: Merovingian baptistery, Romanesque nave, Gothic nave, Romanesque cloister, and Renaissance portal. Nicolas Froment's Burning Bush triptych (1476), in the Gothic nave, is the collection's jewel—ask the guardian to open it if the panels are closed.

If you have time and desire for a powerful moment, head to the Camp des Milles Site-Memorial, 8 km southwest of Aix. This former tile factory served as an internment and deportation camp between 1939 and 1942—over 10,000 people were detained here, including artists and intellectuals who left poignant wall murals. The memorial, demanding but necessary, takes about 2h to visit.

activities.text: Follow the "In Cézanne's Footsteps" walking route through Aix. Brass studs embedded in the ground guide your steps from Cours Mirabeau to the Lauves Studio, where the painter worked from 1902 until his death in 1906. The studio has been preserved as it was—easels, brushes, skulls and objects he painted in his still lifes. From the terrace, you have views of Mont Sainte-Victoire, which he painted over 80 times. Allow 1h30 total.

End the trip with a calisson d'Aix, the local specialty—an almond and candied melon paste covered with royal icing. You'll find them in downtown confectioneries, some even offer production workshops. If you prefer savory, the Provençal markets (Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday on the Cours) overflow with tapenade, anchoïade, and local goat cheeses.

seo.h1_title: From Marseille to Aix-en-Provence: Calanques, Hilltop Villages and Provençal Light
seo.intro_paragraph: 4 days between Marseille, Cassis, La Ciotat, Le Castellet, and Aix-en-Provence. This itinerary crosses coastal Provence from its turquoise calanques to hilltop villages nestled in garrigue, passing through the birthplace of cinema and Bandol vineyards. It begins at Marseille's Old Port and ends in Aix's elegance, among fountains, plane trees, and Cézanne's studio.
seo.seo_hook: Turquoise calanques, world's oldest cinema, hilltop villages among Bandol vines, and Aix's elegance under its plane trees.

Cassis: three calanques on foot via GR98, turquoise water and white cliffs
La Ciotat: Eden-Théâtre from 1889, birthplace of the Lumière brothers' cinema
Aix-en-Provence: 440-meter Cours Mirabeau, Cézanne and over 100 fountains

itineraries.title: The Great Museums of Paris
itineraries.subtitle: A complete tour of Paris's 21 essential museums, from the medieval world of Cluny to the avant-garde at Beaubourg, passing through the Water Lilies at the Orangerie and the world cultures at Quai Branly.
itineraries.notes: Fixed-base itinerary in Paris. Hotels should be booked according to your neighborhood preferences—each museum is accessible by metro from any arrondissement. Online booking strongly recommended for the Louvre, Orsay, and Centre Pompidou during high season (July-August).
itineraries.climate: Best time: April-June and September-October (15-25°C), ideal for museum visits without summer crowds. Avoid July-August (intense heat up to 35°C, tourist rush) and rainy winter. Bring an umbrella year-round.

map_keywords: Dame à la Licorne Musée de Cluny

visits.text: Start with the Musée de Cluny, nestled in the heart of the Latin Quarter within a Gothic mansion built in 1510 by Burgundian monks from Cluny Abbey—on the ruins of Gallo-Roman baths whose remnants you'll still see on the façade. The highlight of your visit: the six Lady and the Unicorn tapestries, woven around 1500 and rediscovered by chance by Prosper Mérimée and George Sand in 1841 in a château in Creuse. Five tapestries illustrate the five senses; the sixth, titled "À mon seul désir" (To my only desire), remains the most debated enigma in French medieval art. Allow 90 minutes for a leisurely visit—avoid Wednesday mornings, which are packed with school groups.

activities.text: After Cluny, wander through the narrow streets of the Latin Quarter around Place de la Sorbonne—the museum sits just steps from the main entrance of the university founded in 1257. The bouquinistes (used-book sellers) along Boulevard Saint-Michel and the nearby Fontaine Saint-Michel are worth a detour before heading to your next museum.

visits.text: The National Museum of Natural History, founded in 1635 under Louis XIII as the Royal Garden of Medicinal Plants, sprawls across the Jardin des Plantes in the 5th arrondissement. Don't miss the Grande Galerie de l'Évolution: inaugurated in 1994 in an 1889 building, it stages a procession of thousands of taxidermied animals—the giraffe, African elephants, a suspended whale—in a scenography that takes your breath away. The basement houses the hall of threatened and extinct species, sober and haunting. Allow 2 hours.

activities.text: While you're in the Jardin des Plantes, take a tour of the tropical greenhouses built between 1834 and 1936—one of the oldest collections of living plants in Europe. On your way out, the menagerie founded in 1794 is the world's oldest zoo still in operation, just a few steps farther.

visits.text: The Musée d'Orsay has occupied the former train station built by Victor Laloux between 1898 and 1900 for the Universal Exposition since 1986—the painter Édouard Detaille said as early as 1900: "The station is superb and looks like a fine arts palace." It took 86 years for the prophecy to come true. Here you'll find the world's most important collection of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist paintings: more than 1,100 canvases, including 72 Monets, 64 Renoirs, plus Degas, Van Gogh, Cézanne, and Gauguin. You absolutely must climb to the 5th level for the Impressionist Gallery, which runs along the Seine quays—the light streaming through the great gilded clocks is incomparable. Book your ticket online: lines at the ticket office can exceed 45 minutes.

activities.text: Leaving Orsay, cross the Pont Royal to reach the Tuileries—you can grab coffee on a terrace facing the garden before continuing. If you have the energy, the Musée de l'Orangerie is a 10-minute walk from the Left Bank: the two can be combined in the same half-day.

visits.text: The Louvre is the world's largest art museum: 72,735 m² of rooms and galleries, 35,000 works on display out of 460,000 in total—spanning from prehistory to 1848, from Europe to Iran via Egypt. The building itself is a 12th-century fortress transformed into a royal palace over 800 years before opening as a museum on August 10, 1793, with 537 paintings. I.M. Pei's glass pyramid, inaugurated in 1989, sparked as much scandal as the Eiffel Tower did in its day. Come with a strategy: in 2 hours, you'll see the Mona Lisa, Venus de Milo, and Winged Victory of Samothrace. In a full day, you'll traverse the Egyptian antiquities and the painting department. Arrive at opening time (9 a.m.) for the Mona Lisa—an average of 15,000 people visit the museum each day.

activities.text: After the Louvre, stroll through the Jardin des Tuileries, which Napoleon III had landscape architect Édouard André design—the garden connects the museum to Place de la Concorde over 1 km of perspective. Modern sculptures scattered throughout the pathways serve as an open-air museum.

visits.text: The Musée des Arts Décoratifs occupies the Rohan wing of the Louvre palace, on the Rue de Rivoli side. Its collection spans seven centuries of French decorative arts: from medieval furniture to Hector Guimard's Art Nouveau interiors, passing through 18th-century table arts and Belle Époque posters. An entire section is devoted to fashion and textiles—more than 100,000 pieces of clothing. Less crowded than its neighbors, it offers a more peaceful visit just meters from the Louvre. Allow 90 minutes.

activities.text: After the museum, the arcaded Rue de Rivoli leads you directly to the Palais Royal—its interior gardens, open to the public, are one of the best-kept secrets of the 1st arrondissement: a tree-lined courtyard surrounded by shopping galleries, sheltered from the noise of the city.

visits.text: The Orangerie is one of Paris's smallest museums—and one of its most mesmerizing. On the ground floor, two oval rooms built according to Monet's own plans house the eight Water Lilies panels, given to France in the aftermath of the November 11, 1918 armistice. Each panel measures 1.97 m tall; the total length of the canvases installed here reaches 91 meters. Natural zenithal light, filtered through a fabric veil according to the painter's instructions, makes the colors vibrate with the rhythm of the sky. André Masson called this ensemble the "Sistine Chapel of Impressionism." Come on an overcast day if possible—diffuse light works better than direct sun. In the basement, the Walter-Guillaume collection brings together 144 paintings by Renoir, Cézanne, Matisse, Picasso, and Modigliani.

activities.text: Leaving the museum, cross the Jardin des Tuileries to Place de la Concorde—the 23-meter Luxor Obelisk, gifted by Egypt in 1830, marks the geometric center of the Parisian historical axis. From there, the Champs-Élysées climbs toward the Arc de Triomphe over 1.9 km.

map_keywords: Musée des Beaux-Arts Petit Palais Paris

visits.text: The Petit Palais, built by Charles Girault for the 1900 Universal Exposition, houses the City of Paris's Museum of Fine Arts—and permanent admission is free. The architecture itself is worth the visit: a trapezoidal plan around an interior garden with colonnades, a central rotunda crowned by a dome, mosaics and Belle Époque murals. The collections span 5,000 years of history: Greek and Egyptian antiquities, medieval enamels, paintings by Courbet, Monet, and Cézanne, sculptures by Carpeaux. Allow 90 minutes at your own pace—the rooms are rarely crowded.

activities.text: The Petit Palais faces the Grand Palais—the two buildings connected by Avenue Winston Churchill form a cohesive architectural ensemble from the 1900 era. Stroll between the two to observe their façades: the allegorical sculptures, glass canopies, and friezes from the period testify to the decorative ambition of the Third Republic.

visits.text: The Grand Palais—240 meters long, a nave 45 meters high topped with 15,000 m² of glass canopy—is one of Paris's largest exhibition spaces. Built in 1897-1900 for the Universal Exposition, it hosts major temporary exhibitions at the Galeries Nationales and significant cultural events. Its central nave, the largest in France, is open to the public during certain events. Check the current program before coming—exhibitions change every two to three months and require advance booking.

activities.text: Walk or rent a bike up the Champs-Élysées to the Arc de Triomphe—1.9 km of perspective from Place de la Concorde. The panorama from the top of the Arc (284 steps, open daily) embraces the 12 radiating avenues and, on clear days, the towers of La Défense on the horizon.

visits.text: The Palais de la Découverte, installed in the west wing of the Grand Palais since its creation in 1937 by physicist Jean Perrin, is an interactive, participatory science museum. Planetarium, static electricity demonstrations, atomic reconstruction: here science is touchable, hands-on, explained by live demonstrators. If you're visiting Paris with children or teenagers, this is the museum not to miss in the 8th arrondissement. Allow 2 hours to enjoy the demonstrations.

activities.text: After the Palais de la Découverte, head down Avenue Montaigne to glimpse the façades of the great fashion houses—Dior at no. 30, boutiques of Parisian labels. A terrace café on the avenue remains one of the most classic spots for people-watching in the 8th.

map_keywords: Fée Électricité Musée d'Art Moderne Paris

visits.text: The Musée d'Art Moderne de Paris—free permanent admission—occupies the east wing of the Palais de Tokyo, built for the 1937 International Exposition. Its collections cover the major movements of the 20th century: Fauvism, Cubism, abstract art, Nouveau Réalisme, through to contemporary creations. The highlight of the visit: Raoul Dufy's La Fée Électricité (The Electricity Fairy) from 1937, a 600 m² fresco installed in a large ground-floor room—the world's largest painting, commissioned by the Parisian Electricity Distribution Company for the 1937 Expo. Allow 90 minutes to 2 hours.

activities.text: Steps away, the Palais de Tokyo hosts Paris's most experimental contemporary art exhibitions—regularly renewed programs, often open until midnight. The terrace of its restaurant with views of the Eiffel Tower is one of the best vantage points from the Trocadéro.

map_keywords: Musée national arts asiatiques Guimet Paris

visits.text: The Musée Guimet, created by Lyon industrialist Émile Guimet in 1879 and donated to the state in 1888, is one of the world's largest Asian art museums outside Asia. Its 45,000 works cover India, China, Japan, Southeast Asia, Central Asia, and Afghanistan, from prehistory to the 20th century. Don't miss the Buddhist rotunda at the museum's heart and the Khmer collections from Angkor—among the most complete outside Cambodia. The Hôtel d'Heidelbach annex, 200 meters away, houses Japanese arts in reconstructed salons. Allow 2 hours.

activities.text: You're steps from the Trocadéro—the terrace of Palais de Chaillot offers the most frontal view possible of the Eiffel Tower, and it's photographers' favorite spot at sunrise and sunset. Descend the stairs to the Champ-de-Mars if you want to get closer.

map_keywords: Cité de l'Architecture et du Patrimoine Paris
Galerie des Moulages Cité Architecture Paris

visits.text: The Cité de l'Architecture et du Patrimoine, in the east wing of Palais de Chaillot, is a surprising museum: its gallery of plaster casts presents life-size reproductions of cathedral portals, sculptures, and frescoes from great French monuments—from Chartres to Vézelay, from Conques to Notre-Dame de Paris. You literally walk through the façade of Chartres at 1:1 scale. The gallery of murals and stained glass, contemporary architecture collections, and a direct view of the Eiffel Tower from the windows complete the ensemble. Allow at least 2 hours.

activities.text: Palais de Chaillot, built for the 1937 Universal Exposition on the site of the former Trocadéro, also houses the Maritime Museum and the Museum of Mankind—plan a second visit if these themes interest you. The central terrace between the two wings offers the most perfect view of the Eiffel Tower and the Champ-de-Mars.

map_keywords: La Porte de l'Enfer Rodin Paris

visits.text: The Musée Rodin occupies the Hôtel Biron, an 18th-century mansion that Rodin inhabited from 1908 until his death in 1917. He bequeathed his works to the state on the condition that the house become a museum—which happened in 1919. In the 3-hectare garden, you'll find The Thinker, The Burghers of Calais, and The Gates of Hell—an ensemble of 180 bronze figures that Rodin worked on for 37 years without ever considering it finished. Inside, the plasters, marbles, and work notebooks reveal the sculptor's creative process. The collections also include 300 paintings by Eugène Carrière, Van Gogh, and Monet bequeathed by Rodin. Allow 90 minutes to 2 hours.

activities.text: Lunch or picnic in the Musée Rodin garden—one of the most pleasant addresses in the 7th arrondissement, sheltered from the city. The museum café in the garden's orangery is open to visitors without an entrance ticket for the terrace.

map_keywords: Musée du Quai Branly Jacques Chirac Paris
Collections arts premiers Quai Branly Paris

visits.text: The Musée du Quai Branly - Jacques Chirac, designed by Jean Nouvel and inaugurated in 2006, is dedicated to the arts and civilizations of Africa, Asia, Oceania, and the Americas. Its façade is greened by Patrick Blanc—an 8,000 m² wall covered with 15,000 plants of 150 different species. Inside, the scenography in semi-darkness highlights ritual masks, African statues, musical instruments, and textiles from around the world: 370,000 objects in total, of which 3,500 are in permanent exhibition. The approach is not encyclopedic but sensory—Chirac wanted these objects treated as artworks, not ethnographic curiosities. Allow 2 hours.

activities.text: The Quai Branly borders the Seine with a direct view of the Eiffel Tower—a stroll along the banks between the two is ideal in late afternoon. If you visit in the evening (Thursday through Saturday until 9 p.m.), you'll see the light show on the tower from the museum garden.

map_keywords: Fondation Louis Vuitton Paris Bois de Boulogne
Collections art contemporain Fondation Vuitton Paris

visits.text: The Fondation Louis Vuitton, built by Frank Gehry and inaugurated in 2014 in the Bois de Boulogne, is one of Paris's most spectacular buildings: 12 glass sails blown around an iceberg structure of white concrete, comprising 3,600 curved glass panels across 11 galleries. The foundation exhibits a permanent collection of modern and contemporary art—Basquiat, Richter, Hirst, Koons—and organizes major temporary exhibitions. The terrace at the top offers a 360° view of the Bois de Boulogne, the Eiffel Tower, and La Défense. Book your ticket online. Free shuttles depart from Porte Maillot every 20 minutes.

activities.text: The Bois de Boulogne surrounds the foundation—take advantage of it for a walk or bike ride around the Lac Inférieur after your visit. The Bagatelle gardens, a 10-minute walk away, are renowned for their rose garden with 1,200 varieties in bloom from May to July.

map_keywords: Cité des Sciences et de l'Industrie Paris Villette

visits.text: The Cité des Sciences et de l'Industrie, inaugurated in 1986 in the former La Villette slaughterhouses transformed by Adrien Fainsilber, is Europe's largest science museum: 30,000 m² of permanent and temporary exhibitions, a planetarium, a real submarine to visit, and the Géode—a steel sphere 36 meters in diameter with a 1,000 m² hemispherical screen. The interactive exhibitions are calibrated for all age groups. If you're coming with children, block out the entire day. Without children, 2 hours allows you to see the essentials.

activities.text: Parc de la Villette (55 hectares), Paris's largest urban park, surrounds the Cité des Sciences. It houses the Philharmonie de Paris, the Grande Halle, red follies designed by Bernard Tschumi, and themed gardens. In summer, the outdoor cinema is free. A walk from the Cité to the Canal de l'Ourcq takes 30 minutes.

visits.text: The Musée de Montmartre occupies the oldest house in the neighborhood: a 17th-century building where Renoir, Suzanne Valadon, Maurice Utrillo, and Raoul Dufy all lived in turn. The museum traces the artistic history of the Butte since the 19th century—posters by Toulouse-Lautrec, paintings by the Nabis, photos of Pigalle's nightlife. The Renoir Gardens, recently restored according to period documents, recreate the garden that Renoir painted in several of his canvases between 1875 and 1877. In summer, the view from the terrace over the Montmartre vineyards is one of the gentlest in Paris.

activities.text: Montmartre is best explored on foot: Place du Tertre with its street painters, the Sacré-Coeur whose dome marks the horizon from almost everywhere in Paris, Rue Lepic and its food shops. If you're there on Saturday morning, the market on Rue Lepic is one of the liveliest in northern Paris.

map_keywords: Musée national d'Art moderne Pompidou Paris

visits.text: The Centre Pompidou—inaugurated in 1977 by President Giscard d'Estaing, three years after the death of Georges Pompidou who dreamed of it—is the enfant terrible of Parisian architecture: exterior pipes in blue (water), green (air), yellow (electricity), and red (circulation), exposed metal structure, caterpillar escalators climbing diagonally on the façade. Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers won it against 681 projects in an international competition in 1971. Inside, the National Museum of Modern Art houses Europe's foremost contemporary art collection: 100,000 works—Matisse, Picasso, Kandinsky, Duchamp, Warhol, Boltanski. Ride the escalator to the 6th level for the view over Paris—free without a museum ticket. Note: Centre Pompidou has been undergoing renovation work since late 2025 until 2030—check the current program before your visit.

activities.text: The Piazza Beaubourg in front of Centre Pompidou is one of Paris's liveliest squares year-round: acrobats, street musicians, sketch artists. Head down Rue Rambuteau toward the Marais to reach Rue des Francs-Bourgeois and the neighborhood galleries.

map_keywords: Musée des Arts et Métiers Paris
Pendule de Foucault Arts et Métiers Paris
Avion Clément Ader Arts et Métiers Paris

visits.text: The Musée des Arts et Métiers, installed since 1794 in the former Saint-Martin-des-Champs priory, is one of Paris's strangest and most fascinating museums. At the center of the large choir hall, hanging from the vault: Foucault's pendulum—the original pendulum that demonstrated the Earth's rotation at the Panthéon in 1851, transferred here after physicist Léon Foucault's death. On the nave walls, Clément Ader's Avion III—the first airplane to take off in 1897, three years before the Wright brothers. The collection traces the history of technical and scientific inventions since the 17th century: automata, steam engines, measuring instruments. A museum for the curious of all ages. Allow 2 hours.

activities.text: The museum is two minutes' walk from the Marché des Enfants Rouges—visiting both in the same half-day is natural. The Marais neighborhood around Rue de Bretagne deserves a stroll: art galleries, designer boutiques, and cafés have succeeded one another here since the neighborhood's rehabilitation in the 1980s.

visits.text: The Musée Picasso, installed in the Hôtel Salé in the Marais—a mansion from 1659 nicknamed for its owner who made his fortune from the salt tax—brings together the world's largest collection of Pablo Picasso's works: 5,000 pieces bequeathed by the family in payment of inheritance taxes in 1973. Paintings, sculptures, ceramics, collages, sketchbooks, correspondence: the museum traces 80 years of creation through all his periods, from the Rose to Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, from Cubism to Guernica. If you've never seen this much Picasso assembled, the impact is real. Allow 2 hours.

activities.text: The Marais is the ideal neighborhood to end the afternoon: Place des Vosges, Paris's first royal square built by Henri IV in 1612, is a 5-minute walk. The arcades surrounding it house art galleries and a few cafés—sit under the vaults for a final Parisian drink.

map_keywords: Marché des Enfants Rouges Paris Marais

visits.text: The Marché des Enfants Rouges, opened in 1615 on Rue de Bretagne in the Marais, is Paris's oldest covered market—its name supposedly comes from children at the neighboring hospice who wore red clothes, the uniform of charity orphans at the time. Closed and fallen into disrepair in the 20th century, it was classified as a historic monument in 1982 and reopened in 2000 after restoration. Today a dozen stalls offer Moroccan, Japanese, Lebanese, Creole, and French cuisine under the original metal and glass canopies. It's a place to eat on-site, standing or sitting on benches, like Parisians from the neighborhood.

activities.text: Lunch at the Marché des Enfants Rouges—choose your dish at one of the counters, settle on the communal benches under the arcades. The neighborhood market atmosphere, between onlookers and regulars, nicely sums up what's lively and informal about Paris far from the museums. It's a fitting way to end this cultural tour.

seo.h1_title: The Great Museums of Paris
seo.intro_paragraph: Paris concentrates the world's greatest art collections within just a few square kilometers: the Louvre with 35,000 works displayed across 72,735 m², the Musée d'Orsay and its Impressionist collection of 1,100 canvases, the Orangerie and its 91 meters of Water Lilies, Beaubourg and Europe's foremost contemporary art collection. This 21-stage itinerary over 6 days guides visitors through every era and every continent, from the Lady and the Unicorn tapestries at Cluny to the 1615 Marché des Enfants Rouges.
seo.seo_hook: 21 Parisian museums in 6 days: from the Louvre to Beaubourg, from Cluny to the Fondation Vuitton, art in all its forms in the world capital of museums.
featured_list: Louvre: 35,000 works displayed in the former royal palace, the world's most-visited art museum with 8.7 million visitors in 2024
Musée d'Orsay: more than 1,100 Impressionist paintings in the former Victor Laloux train station built in 1900
Musée de l'Orangerie: 91 meters of Monet's Water Lilies in two oval rooms designed by the painter himself in 1927
Centre Pompidou: Europe's foremost contemporary art collection, building by Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers inaugurated in 1977
