itineraries.title: Bordeaux to Toulouse Road Trip: Ocean, Pyrenees and Heritage
itineraries.subtitle: 6 days through Bordeaux vineyards, the Dune du Pilat, Landes surf beaches, Basque villages, the hot springs of Dax and the pink-brick streets of Toulouse.
itineraries.notes: The Dune du Pilat staircase is open from Easter to All Saints' Day. The La Rhune rack railway runs from March to November — booking ahead is strongly recommended in summer.
itineraries.climate: Best time: May-June and September-October, temperatures 18-26°C, optimal sunshine and fewer crowds. Avoid July-August on the Basque coast (overcrowding, high prices) and in Toulouse (intense heat 32-36°C). Autumn and winter bring heavy Atlantic rains, mountain roads occasionally closed in winter.

visits.text: Place de la Bourse and Miroir d'Eau — Start your visit to Bordeaux at the Place de la Bourse, the city's first grand urban showcase, built in 1730. Facing it, the Miroir d'Eau (Water Mirror), unveiled in 2006: 3,450 m² of granite slabs covered with just 2 cm of water that reflect the classical façades opposite. It's the largest water mirror in the world. Go in the late afternoon — the reflection at sunset is stunning. In summer, children love splashing around in it.

Place des Quinconces and Monument aux Girondins — At 12 hectares, this is the largest public square in France. Built between 1810 and 1828 on the site of the former Château Trompette fortress, it takes its name from the staggered rows of trees planted across it. In the centre, the Girondins Column rises 43 metres, a tribute to the deputies who fell victim to the Reign of Terror. The two bronze fountains at its base are worth a closer look. On the riverside, spot the two rostral columns dedicated to Trade and Navigation.

Grand Théâtre de Bordeaux — Step inside this neoclassical masterpiece by architect Victor Louis, opened in 1780. Its façade features 12 Corinthian columns topped with 12 statues. The grand staircase is said to have inspired the one at the Opéra Garnier in Paris. Guided tours are available outside performance times.

Old Bordeaux and Porte Cailhau — Lose yourself in the narrow streets of the Saint-Pierre quarter. Golden limestone façades, carved doorways, wrought-iron balconies. The Porte Cailhau (1494), a Renaissance triumphal arch built to celebrate Charles VIII, marks the entrance to the old quarter. Climb its floors for a rooftop view. Just nearby, the Grosse Cloche, a 13th-century medieval belfry, is one of the few still standing in France.

Cathédrale Saint-André and Tour Pey-Berland — On Place Pey-Berland, this UNESCO-listed cathedral was built between the 12th and 16th centuries. Unusually, its bell tower stands separate from the nave. If you have the energy, climb the 231 steps of the tower for a 360° panorama over Bordeaux.

Cité du Vin — End your day at this interactive museum, opened in 2016 and ranked the 7th best museum in the world by National Geographic. The decanter-shaped building rises to 55 metres. Inside, 3,000 m² of exhibition space with 19 interactive modules. Allow 2 to 3 hours. Head up to the 8th-floor belvedere to enjoy a glass of wine (included in your ticket) with a 360° view over Bordeaux and the Garonne.

activities.text: Wine tasting at the CIVB wine bar — To carry on the wine experience, stop by the bar run by the Bordeaux Wine Council on Cours du XXX Juillet, near the Quinconces. You'll taste hand-picked Bordeaux wines in an elegant setting, on the 3rd floor of a prow-shaped building designed by Victor Louis in 1789.

visits.text: Dune du Pilat — The tallest dune in Europe stands at roughly 104 metres (its height shifts from year to year). It stretches 2.9 km long and 616 m wide, holding 60 million m³ of sand some 4,000 years old. From Easter to All Saints' Day, a 160-step staircase makes the climb easier. Get there early — over 2 million people visit every year. From the top, the view spans the Atlantic, the Banc d'Arguin sandbar, Cap Ferret and the vast Landes pine forest. Be warned: in summer the sand surface can reach 55°C.

Ville d'Hiver, Arcachon — This neighbourhood was created under Napoleon III in the 1860s and is packed with Belle Époque villas in every style you can imagine: neo-Gothic, neo-Moorish, Swiss chalets. Stroll beneath the pines along the shaded lanes. The Parc Mauresque has a lookout point over the bay.
Arcachon seafront — Walk along the Jetée Thiers pier. The marina (2,600 berths) is the largest in Aquitaine. Carry on to the Moulleau quarter for its café terraces and canelés.

activities.text: Boat trip on the Arcachon Bay — Sail out to the Île aux Oiseaux (Bird Island) and its famous cabanes tchanquées — wooden huts perched on stilts ('tchanquées' means 'on stilts' in the local Gascon dialect). The island, a Natura 2000 site, is home to over 150 species of migratory birds. Several operators run cruises lasting 1.5 to 3 hours, passing the oyster beds along the way.

Oyster tasting in an oyster village — Make a detour to the waterfront shacks at Gujan-Mestras harbour or L'Herbe on the Cap Ferret side. Sit at a wooden table, order a dozen oysters with a glass of dry white wine — it's the local ritual.

visits.text: Hossegor beaches — Europe's surf capital, with 7 km of coastline. Four beaches are lifeguard-patrolled in summer: the Centrale (family-friendly), La Gravière and La Nord (big-wave spots and a stop on the world championship tour), and La Sud. Even if you don't surf, watching the pros ride is a show in itself. Behind the Place des Landais, look for the 'La Vague' (The Wave) mural.

Lac d'Hossegor and Basque-Landes villas — This saltwater lake is connected to the ocean and rises and falls with the tides. A 7.4 km trail loops around it. Along the way, admire the 1920s–1930s villas designed by Robert Maurice and Louis Lagrange. The Sporting Casino, a listed Historic Monument, is a fine example of the neo-Basque style from the late 1920s. At the far end of the lake, oyster shacks serve locally farmed Hossegor oysters.

Port de Capbreton — The only harbour on the Landes coast, just a stone's throw from Hossegor. Walk along the pier to watch the fishing boats come in. Offshore, the Gouf de Capbreton — a submarine canyon 300 km long and up to 4,000 m deep — creates the unique wave conditions that make this stretch of coast famous for surfing.

activities.text: Beginner surf lesson — Dozens of surf schools cater to all levels. A 1.5- to 2-hour group lesson is enough to get you standing on a foam board. The Centrale and Sud beaches are the best spots for beginners.

visits.text: Église Saint-Jean-Baptiste — This is where Louis XIV married the Spanish Infanta Maria Theresa on 9 June 1660, sealing the Treaty of the Pyrenees. The gilded wooden baroque altarpiece (1669), the most monumental in the Basque Country, features 20 statues arranged across three tiers. The ceiling, shaped like an upturned ship's hull, is typical of churches in the Labourd province. Look for the bricked-up door on the right — it was sealed after the royal couple walked through it.

Maison Louis XIV and Maison de l'Infante — On Place Louis XIV, the Lohobiague-Enea house (1643–1649), where the Sun King stayed for a month, is open to visitors. Across the harbour stands the Maison de l'Infante (c. 1640), with its pink-brick façades and Italianate galleries. Both mansions are a testament to the wealth of Basque shipowners who made their fortune from whaling.

Fishing harbour and Rue Gambetta — Head down to the harbour to see the tuna boats come in. Saint-Jean-de-Luz was nicknamed 'The Vipers' Nest' by the English because of its notorious privateers. Walk up Rue Gambetta, a pedestrian street lined with red half-timbered houses and shops selling Basque linen. Don't leave without trying the macarons or the mouchous pastries.

activities.text: La Rhune rack railway from Sare — A 30-minute drive away, hop on the little cog railway built in 1924, which climbs to 905 metres in 35 minutes. From the top, the view stretches across the Basque coast, the Pyrenees and into Spain. Allow about 2.5 hours for the round trip. In summer, pottoks (wild Basque ponies) graze around the summit. Book ahead.

practical_info.booking: Advance booking strongly recommended in summer

visits.text: Fontaine Chaude (Nèhe Fountain) — In the heart of Dax, this hot spring gushes out at 64°C with a flow of 2.4 million litres a day. Touch the water at the lion-head taps — but not for too long, it really does burn. The Romans called the town 'Aquae Tarbellicae'. Legend has it that a legionary threw his ailing dog into these waters, and the animal came out cured.

Arènes de Dax — Built in 1913 in an Andalusian style, the arena hosts the Feria every summer. Even out of season, the arcades are reminiscent of the plazas of Seville. Dax is at the heart of the course landaise tradition, where the écarteur faces a cow without any killing involved.

Musée de Borda — Open since 1807, the museum is named after the Dax-born scientist Jean-Charles de Borda. It houses collections of Gallo-Roman archaeology, natural history, and exhibits covering 2,000 years of thermal bathing. Remains of the Gallo-Roman ramparts can be seen in the surrounding streets.

Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Dax — Built in a neoclassical neo-Greek style between the 17th and 19th centuries. Fine stained-glass windows and a remarkable organ. Nearby, stop by the Halles de Dax covered market for local Landes produce: foie gras, duck, asparagus and Chalosse beef.

activities.text: Thermal spa experience — France's leading spa town (60,000 cure-goers a year). Several establishments offer half-day wellness packages: hot-water baths and applications of péloïde — a unique thermal mud made from Adour river silt, 64°C spring water and a blue micro-algae. The relaxing effect is almost instant.

visits.text: Jardin Massey and Musée des Hussards — This 11-hectare garden, classified as a 'Jardin remarquable', was laid out in the 19th century by Placide Massey, landscape gardener to the king and former director of the Kitchen Garden at Versailles. Rare tree species, two lakes, a 15th-century cloister and a monumental greenhouse. At the centre stands the Massey Museum — the world's first museum dedicated to the Hussars — displaying 17,000 items spanning four centuries. The 130 mannequins dressed in uniforms from 30 countries are a remarkable sight. Upstairs, the Fine Arts gallery holds Italian works from the 16th and 17th centuries.

Haras National de Tarbes — Founded by Napoleon in 1806, this national stud farm covers 8 hectares of parkland and stables. The Maison du Cheval traces the history of horse breeding. From April to November, guided tours and demonstrations are available.

Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes — 20 km from Tarbes. Since the apparitions reported by Bernadette Soubirous in 1858, Lourdes has welcomed 5 million visitors a year. The Grotto of Massabielle, the Basilica of the Immaculate Conception and the Rosary Basilica form a monumental ensemble. The underground Basilica of Saint Pius X (1958) can hold 25,000 worshippers. Even without religious conviction, the sheer scale of the site is awe-inspiring.

activities.text: Market and Bigorre specialities — If you're here on a Thursday or Saturday, head to the Brauhauban market. Try the haricots tarbais beans (IGP-certified), porc noir de Bigorre and the gâteau à la broche — a distinctive cone-shaped cake baked by rotating the batter on a spit over an open flame, recognisable in every bakery window in the area.

visits.text: Place du Capitole — The beating heart of the 'Pink City'. The neoclassical façade stretches 128 metres, housing both the city hall and the opera house. Step inside to see the Salle des Illustres and its painted ceilings. Under the arcades, look up at the ceiling paintings. Grab a coffee on the terrace to soak in the city's rhythm.

Basilique Saint-Sernin — The largest Romanesque church in France, built between the 11th and 13th centuries. Its octagonal bell tower is a layered mix of brick and stone, and the church contains 250 carved capitals and a crypt holding the relics of Saint Saturninus (a 3rd-century martyr). It is UNESCO-listed as part of the Routes of Santiago de Compostela. Free entry.

Couvent des Jacobins — A gem of Southern Gothic architecture from the 13th century. Its famous 'palm tree' vault — a single 22-metre column from which the ribs fan out like fronds — is unique in Europe. The convent also houses the relics of Saint Thomas Aquinas. The cloister, with its paired columns, is a haven of calm. Go in the early afternoon when sunlight pours through the stained glass.

Garonne riverbanks and Pont Neuf — Toulouse's oldest bridge (16th–17th century). From the bridge, enjoy the classic Toulouse sunset view: the Dôme de la Grave and the Hôtel-Dieu reflected in the river. Cross over to the Saint-Cyprien side for the left bank.
Musée Aeroscopia — In Blagnac, 15,000 m² devoted to aviation. Climb aboard a Concorde, explore an A300B, see the Super Guppy. Over 30 historic aircraft on display. Allow about 2 hours.

Cité de l'Espace — On the eastern outskirts, this space centre features a full-scale replica of the Ariane 5 rocket, a replica of the Mir space station, a planetarium and immersive exhibitions. Ideal for families — allow half a day.

activities.text: Halles Victor Hugo — Toulouse's largest covered market. On the ground floor, fresh produce from the South-West: foie gras, Toulouse sausage, crystallised violets. Upstairs, restaurants cook with the ingredients from the stalls below. This is the best place in town for an authentic Toulouse cassoulet.

seo.h1_title: Bordeaux to Toulouse Road Trip: Ocean, Pyrenees and Heritage
seo.intro_paragraph: 6 days from the vineyards of Bordeaux to the pink-brick streets of Toulouse. Scale the Dune du Pilat (104 m, the tallest in Europe), catch a wave in Hossegor, relive the royal wedding of Louis XIV in Saint-Jean-de-Luz (1660), dip your feet into the 64°C waters of Dax and step aboard a Concorde at the Aeroscopia museum. A road trip across two regions and a thousand flavours of France's South-West.
seo.seo_hook: Bordeaux to Toulouse: Dune du Pilat, Atlantic surf, Basque harbours, Roman hot springs and aerospace capital. Six days, endless flavours.

itineraries.title: The Grand Tour of France in 5 Weeks, Car-Free
itineraries.subtitle: This itinerary takes you through the most beautiful places in France — the world's most visited country — without ever getting behind a wheel. Culture, heritage, landscapes and coastlines: the road trip of a lifetime.
itineraries.notes: The route in brief: 8 days in Paris to cover everything (museums, historic neighbourhoods, the Marais, Montmartre, Père-Lachaise), with two day trips to Versailles and Chartres. Then south to the Loire Valley for 2 days in Blois (Chambord and Chenonceau). East: 2 days in Nancy (with a side trip to Metz), 2 days in Strasbourg (with Colmar), then a day in Dijon. South again: 2 days in Lyon, 2 days in Avignon (Pont du Gard and Arles), 2 days in Marseille (with the Cassis calanques), 2 days in Nice (with Villefranche-sur-Mer and Cimiez). The itinerary's only flight connects Nice to Toulouse — 2 days in the Pink City (with Carcassonne), then 2 days in Bordeaux (with the Pilat Dune and Arcachon Basin). Back north along the Atlantic: 2 days in Nantes, 2 days in Rennes (with Dinan), then a day in Saint-Malo. A mandatory stop at Mont-Saint-Michel (overnight for the atmosphere after the day-trippers leave). Return via Normandy with Rouen, then 2 days in Lille before the 1-hour TGV back to Paris. Total: 22 stopovers, 5 UNESCO sites, three coastlines (Mediterranean, Atlantic, English Channel), one domestic flight — everything else by train or bus.
itineraries.climate: Best time: May-June and September-early October, with temperatures between 15-25°C across most of the route. Avoid July-August: scorching heat in the South (35-40°C in Marseille, Avignon), tourist crowds, inflated prices. Northern and western regions remain rainy year-round, pack a raincoat.

visits.text: Start at the Trocadéro on the Right Bank. This is where you get the best straight-on view of the Eiffel Tower, especially in the morning when the light hits the ironwork head-on. The terraced gardens descend to the fountains, and the esplanade of the Palais de Chaillot frames the classic postcard panorama you've seen a thousand times.

Cross the Pont d'Iéna and head for the Eiffel Tower. Standing 330 metres including its antenna, it was built by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 World's Fair and was originally meant to be dismantled after 20 years — it survived only because of its usefulness as a radio antenna. Book online several weeks ahead, or expect a two-hour queue. The second floor (115m) offers the best balance between views and vertigo.

Take metro line 8 to Concorde. The square covers 8.6 hectares — the largest in Paris. The Luxor Obelisk at its centre dates from the 13th century BC (the reign of Ramesses II) and was gifted by Mehemet Ali, Viceroy of Egypt, in 1830 and erected on the square in 1836. Louis XVI was guillotined here in 1793. So was Marie-Antoinette.

Walk up the Champs-Élysées to the Arc de Triomphe — 1.9 km of avenue. Napoleon commissioned the arch in 1806 after Austerlitz, but never saw it completed in 1836. There are 284 steps to the top. Under the vault, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and its flame, rekindled every evening at 6:30pm.

activities.text: In the evening, head back to the Eiffel Tower for the light show — every hour on the hour after dark, 20,000 LED bulbs flash for five minutes. Spread out on the Champ-de-Mars with a picnic: it's a proper Parisian ritual.

For dinner, try Rue Cler in the 7th — a lively pedestrian market street with solid bistrots in the evenings. Budget €25–40 for a main and a glass of wine at a classic spot like Café Constant or Le Petit Cler.

visits.text: Arrive at the Louvre the moment it opens at 9am sharp. Use the Carrousel entrance (the underground passage on the Rivoli side) rather than the pyramid — the queue is shorter. The world's largest museum holds 380,000 works, with 35,000 on display across 73,000 m². Prioritise the Mona Lisa (Denon wing, 1st floor, room 711), the Venus de Milo, the Winged Victory of Samothrace, and the Napoleon III apartments.

Walk through the Tuileries Garden to Place de la Concorde — 25 hectares, created in 1564 for Catherine de' Medici, the oldest garden in Paris. The green metal chairs scattered around the central pond are one of the city's best-loved details.

At the far end of the Tuileries, step into the Orangerie for Monet's Water Lilies. Eight monumental compositions totalling 91 metres, housed in two oval rooms designed by architect Camille Lefèvre following Monet's own instructions. He offered the gift to the French state on 12 November 1918, the day after the armistice; the deed was signed on 12 April 1922, and the rooms inaugurated in May 1927, a few months after his death. The Walter-Guillaume collection downstairs features Renoir, Cézanne, Utrillo, and Soutine.

Head up towards the Palais-Royal via Rue de Rivoli. The inner courtyard contains Buren's Columns (1986) — 260 black and white marble cylinders. The rear gardens, lined with arcaded galleries of antique shops and cafés, are an unexpected haven of calm right in the city centre.

Finish at the Opéra Garnier. Completed in 1875, 11,000 m², 2,000 seats. Its Italian-style red-and-gold auditorium, ceiling painted by Chagall in 1964, and grand staircase in 30 different marbles are among the great theatrical interiors of Europe. Self-guided visit €15.

activities.text: Stop at Angelina, 226 Rue de Rivoli, for a L'Africain hot chocolate — the thickest in Paris since 1903, served with homemade whipped cream. €9. Proust and Coco Chanel were regulars.
Dinner in the Palais-Royal neighbourhood — Le Grand Colbert (a grand 1900s brasserie), Le Gabriel, or Le Soufflé, a restaurant devoted to sweet and savoury soufflés since 1961. €40–60.

visits.text: Île de la Cité — the historic cradle of Paris. Notre-Dame reopened in December 2024 after five years of post-fire restoration following the blaze of 15 April 2019. The new spire is a faithful recreation of Viollet-le-Duc's 1859 design. Entry is free; booking a time slot is not mandatory but strongly recommended on notredamedeparis.fr to avoid the queue.

Two hundred metres away, the Sainte-Chapelle. Saint Louis had it built in seven years (1242–1248) to house the Crown of Thorns. The upper chapel: 15 stained-glass windows standing 15 metres tall, depicting 1,113 biblical scenes, with 90% of the original 13th-century glass still in place. When the sun is out, the kaleidoscope effect is breathtaking. €13.

Cross to the Latin Quarter. Shakespeare & Company, the English-language bookshop opened in 1951 by George Whitman — Hemingway, Fitzgerald, and Ginsberg all slept here. Climb to the Panthéon, a former church converted into a national mausoleum in 1791: Voltaire, Rousseau, Hugo, Zola, Curie, and Joséphine Baker (2021) are all interred here. Foucault's pendulum has been demonstrating the Earth's rotation since 1851.

Descend to the Luxembourg Garden — 25 hectares, created by Marie de' Medici in 1612 on the model of the Boboli Garden in Florence. It is laid out around the Luxembourg Palace, seat of the French Senate since 1799. Children rent toy sailboats to race on the octagonal pond.

The Musée d'Orsay, a former railway station built for the 1900 World's Fair and converted into a museum in 1986. Monumental clock, 138-metre nave. The world's finest Impressionist collection: Monet, Renoir, Van Gogh, Manet, Degas, Cézanne, Gauguin. Allow at least two hours. €16, closed Mondays.

activities.text: For lunch, try Polidor on Rue Monsieur-le-Prince — a workers' soup kitchen open since 1845, still serving honest food at honest prices (€15–20), with checked tablecloths and numbered cloth napkins. Hemingway, Joyce, and Verlaine all ate here.

End the day on the Left Bank quays, UNESCO-listed since 1991. Between the Pont Neuf and the Pont des Arts, the bouquinistes have been setting up their 900 green boxes since the 16th century. The bridges are illuminated after dark.

visits.text: Metro to Abbesses — the deepest station within Paris proper (36 metres), surpassed since January 2025 by Villejuif-Gustave Roussy on line 14. Original Art Nouveau Guimard canopy. Walk up to the Wall of Love: 612 declarations in 311 languages on blue ceramic tiles. Then Rue Lepic, where Amélie Poulain worked at the Café des 2 Moulins (no. 15).

Climb via Rue Tholozé to the Moulin de la Galette, the last surviving original windmill of Montmartre (17th century). Renoir painted his Bal du moulin de la Galette here in 1876. Rue Girardon and Rue Norvins bring you to the Place du Tertre, the historic heart of the village.

The Sacré-Coeur basilica, completed in 1914, crowns the top of the Butte at 130 metres. Its Château-Landon limestone actually whitens in the rain. The dome (€7) offers the second-highest viewpoint in Paris — but the view from the steps in front is already exceptional. The basilica itself is free.

Descend on the north side past the Montmartre Vineyard — 2,000 vines planted on Rue des Saules in 1933, with a festive harvest in early October. Le Lapin Agile, a cabaret open since 1860 where Picasso, Modigliani, and Utrillo used to drink. The Moulin Rouge on the Boulevard de Clichy, open since 1889.

Afternoon: metro to République for the Canal Saint-Martin. 4.5 km dug by Napoleon in 1825 to supply Paris with drinking water. Iron swing bridges painted dark green, 9 working locks, pedestrianised banks at weekends. This is the Paris of bobos and intellectuals — cocktail bars, vintage shops.

activities.text: In Montmartre, skip the Place du Tertre — it's a tourist trap. Head instead to Rue des Abbesses or Rue Lepic: Le Relais Gascon does a generous warm goat's cheese salad for €14; Pink Mamma is the go-to for trendy Italian.

Evening on the Canal Saint-Martin. Le Verre Volé (a cult wine bar and bistrot in the 10th), Holybelly (brunch and coffee), or head to Place Sainte-Marthe — a small, almost secret cobblestoned square with a genuinely local feel.

visits.text: Metro to Saint-Paul for the Marais, the best-preserved neighbourhood in old Paris — largely spared by Haussmann in the 19th century. The Place des Vosges, inaugurated in 1612 by Henri IV, was Paris's first royal square: 36 identical pavilions in red brick and white stone. Victor Hugo lived here for 16 years, at no. 6.

The Musée Picasso, on Rue de Thorigny, occupies the Hôtel Salé — a private mansion from 1659. Some 5,000 works by Picasso: paintings, sculptures, ceramics, engravings. The collection came to the state as a donation from his heirs in lieu of inheritance tax. €16, closed Mondays.

Lunch on Rue des Rosiers, the heart of the historic Jewish quarter. L'As du Fallafel (or Chez Hanna directly opposite) — €7–9 for a stuffed pitta. Lenny Kravitz and Scarlett Johansson both stop here whenever they're in Paris.

The Centre Pompidou closed on 22 September 2025 for a five-year renovation, with reopening scheduled for 2030. The exterior architecture remains spectacular: the Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers building (1977) with its colour-coded pipework (blue=air, yellow=electricity, green=water, red=circulation). The Place Beaubourg attracts street performers and musicians. During construction, the collections are touring via the Constellation programme (Centre Pompidou-Metz, the Grand Palais, and the Tripostal in Lille for temporary shows); a new Centre Pompidou Francilien is due to open in Massy between late 2026 and 2027.

Metro to Père-Lachaise. 44 hectares, Paris's largest cemetery, 70,000 graves since 1804. Notable tombs: Jim Morrison (division 6), Edith Piaf (97), Oscar Wilde (89, covered in lipstick kisses), Chopin (11), Molière (25), Apollinaire (86). Free map at the entrance.

activities.text: End of the day at Place de la Bastille. The July Column commemorates those who died during the Three Glorious Days (1830), not the storming of the Bastille in 1789. Have a drink on Rue de Lappe, or on the quieter Rue de la Roquette.

Dinner in the Marais. Breizh Café for gourmet Breton crêpes (€16–22), Chez Janou for a Provençal bistrot with unlimited chocolate mousse, or Miznon on Rue des Écouffes for Israeli-style pittas. €35–50.

visits.text: The Musée Rodin, on Rue de Varenne, is housed in the Hôtel Biron (1732), where Rodin had his studio at the end of his life. In 1916 he bequeathed to the state 6,600 sculptures, 8,000 drawings, and his personal collection including works by Van Gogh and Monet. The three-hectare garden holds The Thinker, The Burghers of Calais, and The Gates of Hell. €14, closed Mondays.

Les Invalides. Commissioned by Louis XIV in 1670 to house wounded soldiers — still a functioning hospital today. The gilded dome rises to 107 metres and shelters the church of Saint-Louis and Napoleon's tomb, a sarcophagus of red porphyry placed here in 1861. The Army Museum covers 12 centuries of French military history. €15.

Metro to Bercy (line 14). Bercy Village, a 19th-century wine warehouse complex converted into a cobblestoned shopping and dining promenade in 2001. The Parc de Bercy is right next door — 14 hectares with three themed gardens, and the original railway tracks preserved in the ground.

Metro to Buttes-Chaumont (line 7bis). This 25-hectare park was inaugurated in 1867 by Napoleon III — one of the four great Haussmann parks. Built on a former gypsum quarry, it plays on the terrain with artificial cliffs, a stalactite cave, a lake with a central island topped by a Temple of the Sibyl, and a suspension bridge designed by Gustave Eiffel. Completely unlike any other park in Paris.

Walk down towards Belleville and Ménilmontant. Belleville is Paris's second-highest point after Montmartre. Street art, world cuisine (the best Asian neighbourhood in Paris on Rue de Belleville). The Cité Fleurie, with its pedestrian lanes, offers a glimpse of the Paris that escaped Haussmann.

activities.text: If you still have energy: Parc de la Villette in the 19th — 55 hectares, Paris's largest park, designed by Bernard Tschumi in 1987. Cité des Sciences, the Géode, the Philharmonie de Paris, the Zénith. Free outdoor cinema in summer.

Farewell dinner in Paris at a bistrot in the 11th or 10th. Le Chateaubriand on Rue Parmentier remains one of the best tables in the city at €75 (book a month ahead). Budget option: Bouillon Pigalle, with dishes from €4 to €15.

visits.text: Leave early on RER C from Saint-Michel, Musée d'Orsay, Invalides, or Champ-de-Mars. Direction: Versailles Château Rive Gauche, 40 minutes, €8 return. Book your entry slot online — the 9am–10am windows are the least crowded.

The Palace of Versailles has 2,300 rooms across 63,000 m². Louis XIV moved the court here in 1682, after 21 years of construction. Walk through the King's Grand Apartments (seven drawing rooms dedicated to the planets, ceilings by Le Brun) to the Hall of Mirrors. Seventy-three metres long, 357 mirrors opposite 17 arched windows, completed in 1684. The Treaty of Versailles was signed here on 28 June 1919.

The Queen's Apartments are as impressive as the King's. Marie-Antoinette's restored four-poster bed, the Salon des Nobles, the Antichambre du Grand Couvert where the royal family ate in public. Don't miss the Royal Chapel completed in 1710, with Corinthian columns on two levels and a vaulted ceiling painted by Antoine Coypel.

The gardens, designed by André Le Nôtre: 800 hectares in total, 93 of which are formal French gardens. Geometric parterres, hidden groves, 400 sculptures, and up to 1,400 fountains in Louis XIV's time (around 670 today, including 55 main basins). Tuesdays and weekends from April to October: the Grandes Eaux Musicales, fountains choreographed to music by Lully and Rameau. €10–12 supplement.

Walk to the Grand Trianon (20 minutes on foot) or take the small train (€8). A pink marble palace built by Mansart in 1687. The Petit Trianon was given by Louis XVI to Marie-Antoinette in 1774. Behind it, the Queen's Hamlet: a fake Norman village built in 1783 with a farm, a mill, and a dairy — Marie-Antoinette's pastoral retreat.

activities.text: Lunch at La Flottille in the gardens (on the edge of the Grand Canal, €30–40). Alternative: Angelina inside the palace, or head out to the Place du Marché Notre-Dame.

Back in Paris by late afternoon. Dinner in an unexplored neighbourhood — the 9th arrondissement (South Pigalle) has been one of the city's top dining destinations for the past decade: Hôtel Amour, Buvette, Le Pantruche. €40–60.

visits.text: TER train from Paris Montparnasse to Chartres, a direct 1h–1h15, around €21 full fare (from €7 with the Rémi card). Aim to arrive around 9:30–10am to see the cathedral in the morning light — its two mismatched spires dominate the Beauce plain and are visible from 30 kilometres away.

The Notre-Dame Cathedral of Chartres, UNESCO-listed since 1979, was built almost entirely between 1194 and 1220 — a remarkable pace. Its 176 stained-glass windows from the 12th and 13th centuries cover 2,600 m², the majority original. The famous Chartres blue came from a manufacturing secret that has since been lost.

In the middle of the nave, the Labyrinth — 13 metres in diameter, 261.5 metres of path, inlaid in the floor since 1205. Pilgrims once walked it on their knees. Visible on one Friday per month outside liturgical periods.

Descend into the crypt, the third largest in Europe — 220 metres long. It houses the Veil of Our Lady, a relic gifted by Charles the Bald in 876. The Well of the Strong Saints dates from the Gallo-Roman era. Guided visit only, €3.

Head down to the lower town via Rue des Écuyers. The banks of the Eure: half-timbered houses, stone bridges, medieval washhouses, converted mills. The Maison Picassiette is worth the detour — a house covered entirely in mosaic by a visionary worker between 1938 and 1962. €6.

activities.text: Lunch in the old town — Le Saint-Hilaire on Rue du Pont-Saint-Hilaire at €25–35. Alternative: La Picoterie on Rue du Bourg, lunch menu at €16. Local specialities: pâté de Chartres, cochelins, mentchikoff.
April to January: Chartres en Lumières after dark — 22 sites lit up with video mapping every evening until 1am. Completely free. Otherwise, catch the TER back to Paris (last train around 10pm).

visits.text: Direct TER from Paris Austerlitz to Blois-Chambord, 1h25 to 1h40, €16–35 depending on how far ahead you book (OUIGO Train Classique from €16, full-fare TER/Intercités around €34). Trains every 1–2 hours. Blois town centre is a 10-minute walk from the station. Drop your bags near the Place Louis XII — you'll be right in the thick of things. Head straight for the royal château that towers over the town.

The Royal Château of Blois is a rare thing: four châteaux in one, built around a single courtyard across different eras. Start with the Louis XII wing (1498–1501) in red brick and stone, flamboyant Gothic with Italian touches. Inside, the Fine Arts Museum displays works by Rubens, Ingres, and Boucher. €15, allow 2 hours.

The François I wing (1515–1524) is the showpiece. Its monumental open spiral staircase, placed on the façade like a stage set, is a pure Renaissance invention. Look for crowned salamanders everywhere — the emblem of François I. It was at Blois that he launched his great architectural ambitions before Chambord.

The Salle des États Généraux — the oldest part of the château, 13th century. A vast Gothic civic hall measuring 30 × 18 metres, one of the largest surviving in France. The Estates General met here in 1576 and 1588. On 23 December 1588, Henri III had the Duke of Guise assassinated in this very room for threatening his throne.

Across the square, the Maison de la Magie Robert-Houdin. Every half hour, six giant mechanical dragons emerge from the windows and breathe steam. Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin (1805–1871), a native of Blois, is considered the father of modern magic — Houdini took his stage name as a tribute. €12.

Walk down towards the Loire. The Saint-Louis Cathedral, rebuilt after a hurricane in 1678, preserves a 10th-century Carolingian crypt. Behind it, the Jardins de l'Évêché — a formal terraced garden with a sweeping view over the town and the river. The Denis-Papin staircase, 120 steps, leads down to the square and its statue.

activities.text: Dinner in the old town. L'Orangerie du Château, next to the monument, serves gastro cuisine at €45–70 in an 18th-century setting. More affordable: Le Castelet (Rue des Trois Marchands, €18–25). Try rillettes de Tours, Selles-sur-Cher AOP goat's cheese, and tarte Tatin — invented at Lamotte-Beuvron, 45 km away, in 1889.

April to September: son et lumière show at the Royal Château after dark. 45 minutes of projections across the four façades of the inner courtyard — 1,500 projectors, original score. Off-season: an evening stroll along the illuminated Loire embankment and over the Pont Jacques-Gabriel (1724, listed).

visits.text: Rémi bus (line 2) from Blois-Chambord station to Chambord in about 35 minutes, €2 per journey (Rémi fare). Arrive at opening time, 9am. Chambord reveals itself along a 4.5 km approach: a cascade of turrets, chimneys, and pinnacles. 426 rooms, 77 staircases, 282 fireplaces. UNESCO World Heritage Site. €16.

François I began Chambord in 1519. The largest Loire château was originally a hunting lodge — he spent only 72 nights here in his entire life. The central double-helix staircase is attributed to Leonardo da Vinci, who died just a few months before construction began. Two interlocking spirals: two people can go up and down simultaneously without ever crossing paths.

Climb to the rooftop terraces. The forest of 800 sculpted pinnacles evokes the skyline of an oriental city — historians have identified Leonardo's Italian influence throughout. The Greek cross floorplan was inspired by St Peter's Basilica in Rome. Views over the 5,440-hectare enclosed estate.

Back to Blois around midday. Quick lunch, then TER to Chenonceaux — about 1h20 total with a change at St-Pierre-des-Corps (the TGV hub for the Tours area), €14–29. Chenonceaux station is 400m from the château, five minutes on foot.

Chenonceau, the Ladies' Château. Built between 1513 and 1517 by Katherine Briçonnet on a fortified mill. Given by Henri II to Diane de Poitiers in 1547, reclaimed by Catherine de' Medici in 1559. The gallery spanning the River Cher — 60 metres long, 18 windows, built 1570–1576 — makes it the world's only château-bridge. €17.

Inside: the Chamber of the Five Queens, the Guard Room, the Chapel, and the Green Study from which Catherine de' Medici governed France as regent. Flemish tapestries, paintings by Rubens, Primaticcio, Correggio, and Van Dyck. In 1914–1918, Gaston Menier (of the chocolate fortune) converted the gallery into a military hospital, treating 2,254 wounded soldiers. In 1939–1945, it was the only crossing point between the Occupied Zone and the Free Zone.

The gardens are equally remarkable. Diane de Poitiers' garden (12,000 m²) was laid out in 1559. Catherine de' Medici's garden is more intimate. A 1,500 m² maze of 2,000 yew trees. The flower garden supplies 70 bouquets a day to the rooms inside. In November, pumpkins take over for Halloween.

activities.text: Return to Blois by TER in the late afternoon, about 1 hour via St-Pierre-des-Corps. Last connections around 7–8pm — check on SNCF Connect. In winter, Chenonceau closes at 4:30pm, so plan accordingly.

Last dinner in Blois. Cheverny or Touraine wine on a terrace. To extend your Loire stay by a day: Cheverny (10 km, the château that inspired Tintin's Moulinsart), Amboise (Clos Lucé, where Leonardo da Vinci died in 1519), and Chaumont-sur-Loire (garden festival) are all reachable by TER or shuttle.

visits.text: From Blois, take the TER to Paris Austerlitz (1h30), cross Paris by metro to Gare de l'Est (20–30 minutes), then a direct TGV to Nancy (1h30). Total journey around 4h30 with the Paris changeover — you can grab lunch in Paris between the two trains. From Nancy's central station it is a 10-minute walk to Place Stanislas.

Place Stanislas: 106 × 124 metres, UNESCO World Heritage since 1983. The work of Stanisław Leszczyński — a deposed Polish king who became Duke of Lorraine in 1737 thanks to his son-in-law Louis XV. Completed in 1755 by Emmanuel Héré. Jean Lamour's gilded wrought-iron gates flanking the Neptune and Amphitrite fountains are considered a pinnacle of 18th-century Rococo ironwork.

Place de la Carrière, 124 metres long, lined on both sides with clipped rows of trees and uniform 18th-century façades. Once used for jousting tournaments. Together, the Stanislas-Carrière-Alliance ensemble is the finest example of 18th-century classical town planning in France.

The Fine Arts Museum, founded in 1793 — one of the oldest in France. Rubens, Caravaggio (The Annunciation, 1608–1610, one of the master's late works in France, donated by Henri II, Duke of Lorraine, to Nancy's primatial church), Delacroix, Manet, Monet, Modigliani, Picasso. In the basement, remains of 16th-century fortifications and the Daum collection — 600 pieces of Art Nouveau and Art Deco glasswork. €7, closed Tuesdays.

Old town via Rue Saint-Jean. Basilique Saint-Epvre: a neo-Gothic spire rising 87 metres, built between 1864 and 1871 in Euville limestone. Emperor Franz Joseph I of Austria co-funded its construction. Inside: 70 Art Nouveau windows by the Viennese Geyling studios, amounting to 2,300 m² of stained glass. Free entry.

activities.text: Dinner: Le V Four (Rue Saint-Dizier), modern gastronomy at €45–65. Le Capu (Rue Stanislas), a classic brasserie serving quiche lorraine and baba au rhum, €25–35. Local specialities: Nancy macarons (recipe from the Soeurs Macarons, 1793) and bergamotes de Nancy (translucent bergamot-flavoured boiled sweets, created in 1850, IGP protected since 1996).

June to mid-September: the Rendez-vous Place Stanislas sound and light show — free projection on the façades at nightfall, 15 minutes, repeated in a loop. Out of season, the cafés stay open late — the Grand Café Foy is a 19th-century institution.

visits.text: Morning spent in Art Nouveau Nancy. Nancy is France's capital of the movement, thanks to the École de Nancy founded in 1901 around Émile Gallé, Louis Majorelle, Daum and Victor Prouvé. Musée de l'École de Nancy, 36–38 Rue du Sergent Blandan: 400 pieces on display including the fully reconstructed Masson dining room. €7, open Wednesday to Sunday 10am–6pm, closed Monday and Tuesday.

Villa Majorelle, 1 Rue Louis-Majorelle. Designed by Henri Sauvage in 1901 for the cabinet-maker Louis Majorelle — the first Art Nouveau residence built in Nancy. Ironwork by Jean Lamour, windows by Jacques Gruber, stoneware by Alexandre Bigot. A hundred pieces of signed Majorelle furniture. €6, open Wednesday to Sunday (2–6pm for individual visitors).

Afternoon in Metz as a day trip. Direct TER Nancy–Metz every 30 minutes, 40-minute journey, €11 return. Metz, former historic capital of Lorraine. Saint-Étienne Cathedral: 41 metres to the vault (the third-highest Gothic nave in France), nicknamed the Lantern of God for its 6,500 m² of stained glass — the largest expanse of glazing in all French Gothic cathedrals. Chagall's windows (1960) in the ambulatory.

Centre Pompidou-Metz, the Paris Pompidou's sister venue, opened in 2010. Spectacular architecture by Shigeru Ban and Jean de Gastines: a roof in the form of a woven Chinese hat, 8,000 m² of laminated timber covered in a fibreglass membrane. Temporary modern and contemporary art exhibitions only. €13, closed Tuesdays.

On the way out, take a moment for Metz railway station, right next door — a listed monument and one of France's most beautiful stations. Built 1905–1908 during the German era, a masterpiece of Rhenish neo-Romanesque style. Kaiser Wilhelm II wanted it as a showcase of German power. A 300-metre façade, a 40-metre bell tower, 150 sculpted capitals.

activities.text: Lunch in Metz on Place Saint-Louis or Place de Chambre, €18–30. Try Lorraine hotpot, quiche lorraine (the real thing — no cheese), mirabelle plums in September–October, and tarte flambée in a winstub. Local cheese: Carré de l'Est.

Walk around the Outre-Seille district of Metz — the oldest, with medieval lanes, Renaissance mansions, Place Saint-Louis and its 13th-century arcades. The Temple Neuf (Protestant, 1904) rises in pink sandstone at the water's edge on the Moselle, its Rhine-valley silhouette visible from the Moyen-Pont.
Return to Nancy by TER in the late afternoon — last services around 10pm. Get ready for an early start the next morning for Strasbourg.

visits.text: TER Nancy to Strasbourg: 1h30 direct, €25–35. Strasbourg station has been wrapped since 2007 in a contemporary glass bubble designed by Jean-Marie Duthilleul. The UNESCO-listed historic centre is a 15-minute walk or a 5-minute tram ride (lines A or D).

Strasbourg Cathedral (Notre-Dame), completed in 1439 after 250 years of construction — at 142 metres, it was the world's tallest building until 1874. Victor Hugo called it a prodigy of the gigantic and the delicate. The west façade, in pink Vosges sandstone, is carved like lacework. Goethe, studying in Strasbourg in 1770, called it his revelation of Gothic architecture. Free entry, €8 for the rooftop platform.

The Astronomical Clock (1842, Jean-Baptiste Schwilgué): a procession of apostle automata every day at precisely 12.30pm. Arrive by 11.45am, presentation at noon, procession with a crowing cock at 12.30. €3. At the top: 330 steps, a 360° view over the Alsace plain, the Vosges and the Black Forest.

Palais Rohan, former palace of the Prince-Bishops. Built 1732–1742 by Robert de Cotte. Louis XV, Marie-Antoinette, Napoleon and Joséphine all stayed here. Three museums under one roof: Decorative Arts (18th-century apartments, Hannong faience), Fine Arts (Giotto, Raphael, Rubens, Goya, Delacroix) and Archaeological. €7.50 combined ticket, closed Tuesdays.

La Petite France, former quarter of tanners, millers and fishermen. Half-timbered houses from the 16th and 17th centuries lean over the canals of the Ill. The steep roofs with open attic floors were used to dry animal hides. Avoid 2–5pm in summer — the crowds are oppressive.

The Ponts Couverts — actually uncovered since the 17th century. Three bridges span the arms of the Ill, with four square 14th-century towers, remnants of the old fortifications. Just beyond, the Vauban Dam (1690): a free panoramic terrace with the classic postcard view — covered bridges, cathedral spire in the distance.

activities.text: Dinner in a traditional Alsatian winstub. Winstub Le Clou (Rue du Chaudron, since 1884), Chez Yvonne (Rue du Sanglier), or Fink'Stuebel (Rue Finkwiller). On the menu: choucroute garnie au riesling with four cuts of pork, tarte flambée, baeckeoffe (a three-meat stew marinated for 48 hours). Riesling or gewurztraminer by the jug. €30–45.

After dinner, walk the illuminated Ill quays. A full loop of the Grande Île on foot is about 3 km — UNESCO listed since 1988. Storks nest on certain chimneys. In December: the Christkindelsmärik, running since 1570 and among the oldest Christmas markets in the world.

visits.text: Morning in the Neustadt — the German imperial quarter. From 1871 to 1918, Alsace-Moselle was German following the defeat at Sedan. The Kaiser massively expanded Strasbourg as a showcase of Prussian power. One and a half square kilometres of monumental boulevards, neo-Renaissance and neo-Baroque façades, Jugendstil. UNESCO listed since 2017. Place de la République (1884) at the centre — war memorial, Rhine Palace, National Library.

The European Parliament, the official seat since 1999, is free to visit. The building takes the form of an incomplete ovoid (Architecture Studio). Twelve plenary sessions a year bring together the 705 MEPs. Free audio guide, 1-hour visit, advance booking required at europarl.europa.eu. Tram E, stop Parlement Européen.

Musée Alsacien, Quai Saint-Nicolas. Three 16th–17th-century half-timbered houses connected by courtyards and staircases. A labyrinthine journey through 30 rooms: traditional costumes, painted peasant furniture, wooden toys, Christmas cribs, reconstructed Alsatian farmsteads. €7.50, closed Tuesdays.

Afternoon in Colmar. Direct TER from Strasbourg every 30 minutes, 30-minute journey, €13 return. Like a miniature Strasbourg. La Petite Venise, the former market-gardeners' quarter: half-timbered houses in blue, green and yellow lining the canals of the Lauch. The Tanners' Quarter, Rue des Marchands, Place de la Cathédrale with the Collegiate Church of Saint-Martin (13th–14th century).

Musée Unterlinden, a Dominican convent founded in 1252, renovated by Herzog & de Meuron in 2015. Centrepiece: the Isenheim Altarpiece by Matthias Grünewald (1512–1516). A nine-panel polyptych devoted to Saint Anthony. The Crucifixion panel is of a physical violence that has fascinated generations of artists. €13, closed Tuesdays.

activities.text: Lunch in Colmar — Caveau Saint-Pierre (on the inner canal) or Wistub Brenner. Quick alternative: a giant bretzel and a glass of Pinot Blanc. The Wine Route begins right here — Riquewihr, Ribeauvillé and Kaysersberg are all reachable by regional bus.

Back to Strasbourg by TER. Last evening: Maison Kammerzell at the foot of the cathedral (a half-timbered house from 1427, one of the finest Renaissance façades in Alsace), €40–60. Or Buerehiesel in the Orangerie Park, Michelin-starred, €95–150.

visits.text: TGV Strasbourg to Dijon: around 2 hours direct via Mulhouse and Besançon Franche-Comté TGV, €25–60 depending on booking lead time. Dijon-Ville station is a 10-minute walk from the centre. Dijon was the capital of the Duchy of Burgundy (14th–15th centuries, when the Valois Dukes rivalled the King of France himself) and serves as the gateway to Burgundy's wine country — the Grands Crus route begins in the southern suburbs.

The Palace of the Dukes and States of Burgundy, the historic heart of the city. Built from the 14th to the 17th century, it houses the town hall and the Fine Arts Museum — one of the oldest in France, founded in 1787. In the Guards' Room: the monumental black marble and alabaster tombs of Philip the Bold (died 1404) and John the Fearless, their recumbent figures surrounded by 82 weeping mourners. Free admission. Closed Tuesdays.

Place de la Libération (formerly Place Royale), laid out in 1685 by Jules Hardouin-Mansart. A semicircular space with uniform façades, pools and fountains. Climb the Tour Philippe le Bon (46 metres, 316 steps) for the panorama: rooftops covered in multi-coloured glazed Burgundian tiles — yellow, green, red and black in geometric patterns. Free with the museum ticket.

Notre-Dame Church (13th century). A façade unique in Europe: three tiers of arcaded galleries decorated with 51 purely ornamental carved gargoyles. On the north wall, the Owl — a small sculpture worn smooth by seven centuries of rubbing. Tradition holds that if you stroke it with your left hand while making a wish, it will come true. The owl is Dijon's symbol, with 22 marked stops on the city's self-guided Owl Trail.

The Owl Trail — 22 signposted stops, 1h30 through the historic centre. Renaissance and classical private mansions (Rue Vauban, Rue des Forges), half-timbered houses on Rue Verrerie and Rue Chaudronnerie, hidden interior courtyards. Free trail map available from the tourist office on Place Darcy.

activities.text: The Halles de Dijon, an 1873 iron market hall by a student of Gustave Eiffel. Market on Tuesdays, Fridays and Saturday mornings. Époisses AOP and soumaintrain cheeses, jambon persillé, artisan mustards (Edmond Fallot since 1840), snails, pain d'épices.

Classic Burgundian dinner: boeuf bourguignon simmered in pinot noir, oeufs en meurette, jambon persillé, coq au vin. Chez Léon (Rue des Trois Forgerons), €30–40. Pair it with a Chablis, Pommard or Gevrey-Chambertin. The Cité Internationale de la Gastronomie et du Vin (2022, near the station): 1,750 m² of exhibitions, 250 wines to taste. €14.

visits.text: TGV Dijon to Lyon Part-Dieu: 1h40 direct, €35–60. From Part-Dieu, take metro B then change at Saxe-Gambetta to line D for Bellecour (around 15 minutes). Stay in the Presqu'île (between Bellecour and Les Terreaux) to have everything within walking distance. Lyon deserves two full days: France's third city, former capital of the Gauls, and home to one of Europe's largest Renaissance ensembles.

Place Bellecour — 62,000 m², one of Europe's largest pedestrian squares. Louis XIV on horseback since 1825. In the south-east corner, a bronze statue of Saint-Exupéry and his Little Prince (2000) — the aviator-writer was born in Lyon in 1900. This is the city's kilometre zero.

Vieux Lyon, UNESCO World Heritage since 1998 along with the Fourvière hill — one of Europe's largest Renaissance districts. Thirty hectares of 15th–16th-century buildings put up by Italian merchants who came for Charles VII's trade fairs. Saint-Jean Cathedral (1175–1480) blends Romanesque and Gothic over 80 metres. A 14th-century astronomical clock, one of the oldest in Europe. Henri IV married Marie de' Medici here in 1600.

Traboules — around 500 in Lyon, 200 in the Vieux Lyon alone. Covered passages running through buildings and courtyards to connect parallel streets. The earliest date from the 4th century, when the people of Lugdunum came down from Fourvière for water. During the Second World War, the Resistance used them to move unseen. A golden lion-head plaque marks each entrance. La Longue Traboule (54 Rue Saint-Jean) passes through four buildings and five courtyards.

Funicular F1 from Vieux-Lyon up to Fourvière — 2 minutes, €2. The Basilica of Notre-Dame de Fourvière (1896) dominates Lyon from 130 metres. Architect Pierre Bossan wanted a building inspired by Palermo and Byzantium — a unique neo-Byzantine style. The interior explodes in gold-ground mosaics, stained glass and sculpture. At the top of the bell tower, a gilded Virgin (5.60 m, by sculptor Joseph-Hugues Fabisch, 1852). Free entry.

Fourvière Esplanade: panorama over the whole of Lyon, the Presqu'île between the two rivers, the Part-Dieu tower, the Croix-Rousse, and on clear days the Alps with Mont-Blanc. The Roman theatres of Lugdunum: Grand Théâtre (15 BC, 10,000 seats, the oldest in Roman Gaul) and the Odeon (1st century). Nuits de Fourvière festival every summer. Free access, Lugdunum museum €12.

activities.text: Dinner in a lyonnais bouchon. Tablier de sapeur (breaded tripe), andouillette sausage, pike quenelle in Nantua sauce, salade lyonnaise, gâteau de foies blonds, cervelle de canut, pink praline tart. Accredited Bouchons Lyonnais: Daniel & Denise, Les Lyonnais, Café des Fédérations. €30–45. Reservation essential.

Walk back down through the Jardin du Rosaire — a winding path under century-old chestnut trees with views over an illuminated Vieux Lyon. Via Montée des Chazeaux and Place Saint-Paul. The funicular runs until midnight. The Saône quays are beautifully lit — Lyon confirms its status as City of Light every 8 December with the Fête des Lumières.

visits.text: Place des Terreaux, at the foot of the Croix-Rousse. The Bartholdi Fountain (1892) represents the Garonne and its tributaries — originally destined for Bordeaux, which refused it. Embedded in the square, 69 ground-level water jets by Daniel Buren (1994). The Town Hall (1672) stands to the east. To the west, the Palais Saint-Pierre houses the Fine Arts Museum in a 17th-century former convent.

The Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon, the second-most important in France after the Louvre. Collections spanning five millennia: Egyptian antiquities (the finest in France outside Paris), Rubens, Rembrandt, Veronese, Zurbarán, Delacroix, Monet, Degas, Van Gogh, Picasso, Matisse, Soulages. €12, closed Tuesdays. The cloister garden is free and one of the finest places to pause in the city centre.

The Croix-Rousse hillside — former working-class quarter of the canuts, silk weavers who made Lyon's fortune from the 16th to the 19th century. The buildings have 4-metre ceilings and monumental windows to accommodate the giant Jacquard looms (invented in 1801 by Joseph-Marie Jacquard, a Lyon native). The canut uprising of 1831 was one of the first workers' insurrections of the modern era. Their motto: Live working or die fighting.

Mur des Canuts, boulevard des Canuts: Europe's largest trompe-l'œil, 1,200 m² painted since 1987 by CitéCréation and updated every ten years. Look for Guignol, the Lyon puppet created in 1808, and the Jacquard loom. Free. Opposite, the Maison des Canuts on rue d'Ivry gives weaving demonstrations on period looms. 8 euros, 45 minutes.

Descend via the Croix-Rousse traboules — less touristy than those in Vieux Lyon. Cour des Voraces (9 Place Colbert): an exterior staircase six storeys high, used to bring down silk bales quickly. A canut hideout during the uprisings of 1831 and 1848. The Grande Côte descent to the Presqu'île — eight centuries of Lyon's history compressed into 800 metres.

Les Halles de Lyon Paul Bocuse — 13,500 m², 60 traders. Lyon's first covered market in 1859, renamed in 2006 in honour of the three-Michelin-starred chef who died in 2018. La Mère Richard's aged Saint-Marcellin and Saint-Félicien cheeses, Giraudet quenelles, Sibilia charcuterie, Pralus pink pralines, brioche aux pralines. Allow at least an hour.

activities.text: Lunch at Les Halles. Les Garçons Bouchers (côte de boeuf), Chez Léon de Lyon (oysters, seafood platters), Maison Rousseau (charcuterie sandwiches, €8–12). Pair with a Mâcon, Beaujolais or Condrieu.

The Confluence district — at the southern tip of the Presqu'île, where the Rhône and Saône meet. A former industrial area redeveloped since 2003. Musée des Confluences (Coop Himmelb(l)au, 2014, the crystal cloud), Cube Orange (Jakob + MacFarlane), Raymond-Barre footbridge. Musée des Confluences €12, 2 hours.

Last evening in Lyon. Try a starred restaurant: Les Apothicaires (creative cuisine, €75–130), Prairial (lunch menu €55). Traditional option: Brasserie Georges on Rue des Marronniers, open since 1836, seating 900 at each service — an absolute institution.

visits.text: TGV Lyon Part-Dieu to Avignon TGV: 1h10 direct, €40–75. The TER shuttle (la Virgule) connects Avignon TGV to Avignon Centre in 5 minutes for €1.60 (or included if your TGV ticket arrives at Avignon Centre). The walled old town is barely 1 km across. Staying intra-muros is worth it for the atmosphere at night.

The Palais des Papes, the world's largest Gothic palace at 15,000 m². Between 1309 and 1377, seven successive popes ruled from Avignon after Clement V relocated the papacy from Rome — the Hundred Years' War and the insecurity of Rome explain the move. Twenty-five rooms to visit: chapels with frescoes by Matteo Giovannetti (1343–1348), private apartments, the Great Audience Hall. €12, combined ticket with the Bridge €14.50.

Pont Saint-Bénézet — the Pont d'Avignon of the famous song. Originally 920 metres long with 22 arches, built 1177–1185 by the Frères Pontifes. According to legend, the shepherd Bénézet built it on divine orders. Repeated flooding of the Rhône (notably in 1668) swept away most of the arches. Only four remain today, along with the two-storey Chapel of Saint Nicholas. €5.

Rocher des Doms, a three-hectare garden on the limestone spur overlooking the Rhône. Neolithic traces were found here. A formal French garden with a pond, ducks and peacocks. The panorama: Pont Saint-Bénézet below, Villeneuve-lès-Avignon across the river (where the cardinals had their residences), Mont Ventoux in the distance, the Alpilles on clear days. Free access, magical at sunset.

Musée du Petit Palais, former 14th-century archbishops' palace. Three hundred medieval Italian and Provençal paintings and sculptures — one of the finest collections of early Italian masters outside Italy. Botticelli, Sienese and Florentine altarpieces, the Avignon School (Enguerrand Quarton). €6, free on the first Sunday of the month. Closed Tuesdays.

Rue des Teinturiers — well off the tourist trail. It follows a canalized stretch of the Sorgue and retains four old waterwheels, remnants of the 14th-to-19th-century dye mills. Centuries-old plane trees, penitents' chapels, weathered façades, bohemian cafés. Pierre Boulle — author of Bridge over the River Kwai and Planet of the Apes — lived here.

activities.text: Dinner: avoid Place de l'Horloge (too touristy). Head instead to Rue de la Bonneterie, Rue des Teinturiers or Place des Corps-Saints. La Fourchette (Rue Racine), €35–50. L'Épicerie (10 Place Saint-Pierre), Provençal cuisine. Specialities: Avignon-style daube, soupe au pistou, aïoli. Wines: Côtes du Rhône, Châteauneuf-du-Pape (15 km away), Tavel rosé. €35–55.

Walk the 14th-century ramparts — 4.3 km with towers and gates, a rare survival in France (most towns demolished their walls in the 19th century). In July, the Festival d'Avignon takes over courtyards, cloisters and squares. Book well ahead if you plan to visit then.

visits.text: Morning at the Pont du Gard. Bus liO line 115 from the PEM interchange next to Avignon Centre station: 40 minutes to 1 hour depending on stops, €2 payable on board. Timetables vary by season (school term, holidays, summer) — check lio.laregion.fr before setting out, as services are limited (a handful of buses per day). The aqueduct is one of the most impressive monuments of ancient Gaul — built in the 1st century AD (40–60 AD) to supply Nîmes with water from Uzès, 50 km away, with an average gradient of just 24 cm per kilometre.

The Pont du Gard: 275 metres long, 48 metres tall (the highest Roman aqueduct bridge ever built), three tiers of arches in local limestone, some blocks weighing 6 tonnes, all assembled without mortar. The masons' technical marks are still visible (FR for Frons Dextra). UNESCO since 1985. Five kilometres of footpaths, an archaeological museum, swimming in the Gardon in summer. €11.50 site + museum.

Back to Avignon by around 1pm, quick lunch, then TER from Avignon Centre to Arles: 20 minutes, €8. Arles is 40 km south. Founded in 46 BC by Julius Caesar as a Roman colony, it became one of the largest cities in the Empire in Gaul. Eight UNESCO-listed monuments in the Arles Roman and Romanesque Monuments ensemble, listed since 1981.

The Arles Amphitheatre, built around 90 AD under Domitian — 25,000 spectators, one of the largest in Gaul (136 × 107 m). Converted into a fortress in the Middle Ages, with 200 houses built inside and four towers added. Cleared from 1825 onwards. Bullfights during the Easter Feria and the Rice Feria (September). €9.

The Ancient Theatre of Arles, built around 25 BC under Augustus, with 10,000 seats. Used as a quarry for stone over the centuries, leaving only a partial façade with two Corinthian columns known as the Two Widows. The Venus of Arles (1st century, discovered in 1651) is now in the Louvre. Combined ticket with the amphitheatre: €12.

Arles town centre: Place du Forum with its statue of Frédéric Mistral (Nobel Prize for Literature 1904, champion of the Provençal language), and the vividly yellow Café Van Gogh (the subject of Terrasse du café le soir, painted in 1888 — Van Gogh lived here for 15 months and produced 300 works). Place de la République: the Saint-Trophime Cathedral (12th-century Romanesque, UNESCO) with its spectacular sculpted portal and cloister. The underground cryptoporticos beneath the town hall.

activities.text: For photography enthusiasts: the Fondation Vincent Van Gogh (35 Rue du Docteur Fanton) in a 15th-century mansion. No permanent collection but excellent temporary exhibitions. €10. Or LUMA Arles — the Maja Hoffmann foundation in a former railway yard, anchored by Frank Gehry's spectacular tower (2021, 56 m, 11,000 steel panels). Park free, exhibitions €18.

Return to Avignon by TER in the early evening. Provençal dinner intra-muros — tapenade, brandade de morue (from Nîmes), courgette-flower fritters in season, a goat's cheese board with a Gigondas or Vacqueyras.

visits.text: Direct TER from Avignon Centre to Marseille Saint-Charles: 1h05, €15–25 (TGV 35 minutes at €25–45). Marseille Saint-Charles station has a monumental staircase from 1925 with statues by Henri Allouard. Metro M1 or M2 to the Vieux-Port in 5 minutes. Stay in the Vieux-Port or Le Panier area.

La Bonne Mère — Notre-Dame-de-la-Garde. Perched at 154 metres on a limestone pinnacle, this Romano-Byzantine basilica was consecrated in 1864. The gilded Virgin at the summit: 11.20 m tall, 9.8 tonnes, sculpted by Eugène-Louis Lequesne and cast by the Christofle workshops (copper electroforming with gold leaf). Major restoration 2001–2008. Inside: 1,200 m² of gold-ground mosaics and ex-votos left by sailors (model ships, plaques, naïve paintings). Free.

Abbaye Saint-Victor — one of France's oldest abbeys, founded in the 5th century by John Cassian. Underground crypts with 4th–5th-century sarcophagi and a 13th-century Black Virgin. €2 for the crypts. Fortified in the 14th century against Barbary Coast raids.

The Vieux-Port, beating heart of the city for 2,600 years. Greek settlers from Phocaea landed here around 600 BC and founded Massalia. From early morning until 1pm: the fish market on Quai des Belges — fishermen sell directly from their boats, shouting in Provençal. Norman Foster's Ombrière (2013), a 46 × 22 metre sheet of polished steel that reflects the port below.

Le Panier, Marseille's oldest quarter and original urban nucleus. Narrow lanes, hidden squares, designers' studios, street art on every wall. Place des Moulins at the highest point. La Vieille Charité (Rue de la Charité): a 17th-century almshouse by Pierre Puget, with arcaded courtyards on three levels and a baroque oval chapel. Mediterranean archaeology museum and African arts museum inside. The courtyard is free to enter.

La Major Cathedral — 142 metres long, the largest religious building erected in France in the 19th century (1852–1893). Neo-Byzantine style, striped domes (Carrara white marble and Florence green stone). Golden-mosaic interior. Free. The forecourt overlooks the Joliette docks.

activities.text: Dinner, Marseille-style. Bouillabaisse: a thousand-year-old dish protected by a charter since 1980 (minimum four rock fish — scorpionfish, weever, John Dory, tub gurnard). Chez Fonfon at the Vallon des Auffes, €65–80. More affordable: Chez Madie Les Galinettes on Quai du Port, or Le Café des Épices on Rue Fort-Notre-Dame, €35–55.

After dinner, the Palais du Pharo (1858, Napoleon III had it built for Empress Eugénie) offers views over the port entrance and the Saint-Jean and Saint-Nicolas forts. Nightlife: Cours Julien and Rue d'Aubagne (bars, concerts, bohemian atmosphere). Marseille is France's rap capital — if a concert is on, it's worth discovering.

visits.text: Morning at the MuCEM — Museum of European and Mediterranean Civilisations. A cube of black concrete wrapped in a pierced concrete lacework screen, facing the sea, designed by Rudy Ricciotti (2013). Opened when Marseille was European Capital of Culture. The architecture alone is worth the trip. €11; rooftop terrace free.

A 130-metre suspension walkway above the dock connects the MuCEM to Fort Saint-Jean — with open water 20 metres below your feet. The fort (Louis XIV, 1668) commands the entrance to the Vieux-Port. Its cannons were aimed at the city as well as at enemies — it served to protect Marseille and keep an eye on it simultaneously. Free. The Migration Garden (12,000 m² of Mediterranean plants), the Tour du roi René (15th century) and the Tour du Fanal (17th-century lighthouse).

Afternoon in the Calanques — a national park created in 2012. Twenty kilometres of coastline between Marseille and Cassis. Sheer white limestone cliffs dropping 400 metres to turquoise water. TER from Marseille Saint-Charles to Cassis (20–25 minutes direct, €7–10) then a local bus to the port (Cassis station is 3 km from town), or a boat from the Vieux-Port (2h30 return trip, €30).

From Cassis, boat trips from the port (3, 5 or 8 calanques, €18–32, 45 minutes to 2 hours). Port-Miou (the largest), Port-Pin (pebble beach), En-Vau (the most spectacular — 200-metre cliffs, translucent water). On foot: trail from La Gardiole in Cassis to Port-Pin, 1 hour, easy. Towards En-Vau: 1h30 over rocks.

Return to Cassis around 5–6pm. A small fishing town of 35,000 residents with an authentically Provençal atmosphere. Pastel façades, colourful fishing boats, Place Baragnon, cafés along the quays. If the weather holds and you have a designated driver: the Route des Crêtes to Cap Canaille — 394 metres, the highest sea cliff in France. A 180° view over Cassis, La Ciotat and the calanques.

activities.text: Lunch or dinner options from Marseille. The Vallon des Auffes: a tiny fishing harbour tucked between two cliffs, 25 minutes on foot from the Vieux-Port. Chez Fonfon (mythical bouillabaisse, €75) or L'Épuisette (Michelin-starred). More affordable: Chez Étienne on Rue de Lorette, Marseille-style pizza (thin crust, anchovies, Gruyère) €15–25, no reservation needed. Eddie Barclay, Mick Jagger and Gérard Depardieu have all eaten here.

Aperitif on the seafront in Cassis. Cassis AOC white wine (France's oldest wine AOC, 1936), tapenade, anchoïade, brandade. Return TER to Marseille Saint-Charles around 9–10pm. Check the last timetable carefully before committing.

visits.text: TGV from Marseille Saint-Charles to Nice-Ville: 2h30–2h40 direct, €25–60 depending on how far ahead you book. The station is a 15-minute walk or 5 minutes by tram T1 from the centre. Hotel between the station and Vieux-Nice. Prices double in summer.

The Promenade des Anglais: what started as a 2-metre-wide footpath was funded in 1822 by the English pastor Lewis Way to give work to Nice's day labourers, ruined by the 1820 frost that killed the orange groves. Nice was then part of the Kingdom of Sardinia (it joined France in 1860). Seven kilometres of palm trees along the Baie des Anges, with the characteristic smooth round pebbles.

Place Masséna, Nice's geometric centrepiece — a black-and-white chequered esplanade from 1844 with Italian ochre-red arcaded façades. Seven luminous figures by Jaume Plensa (2011) change colour through the night. The Sun Fountain with its monumental white marble Apollo.

Vieux-Nice: Baroque façades in ochre and terracotta — a reminder of the centuries under Italian rule. Sainte-Réparate Cathedral (1650–1699), dedicated to a 15-year-old martyr whose headless body reportedly floated to Nice on a boat guided by angels. A Baroque interior overloaded with stucco, polychrome marble and 17th-century paintings. Place Rossetti: Fenocchio ice cream, 90 flavours (olive, lavender, tomato-basil).

Palais Lascaris, Rue Droite — a 17th-century Baroque palace of the Lascaris-Vintimille family. Museum of musical instruments: 500 instruments including 18 historic harps. A monumental staircase and trompe-l'oeil painted ceilings. Free, closed Tuesdays.

Castle Hill. The castle was demolished in 1706 by Louis XIV after resisting sieges in 1543 and 1691. In 1822 the King of Sardinia turned it into a public park with 320 trees. Access by staircase from Quai des États-Unis (300 steps) or by free lift near Quai Rauba-Capeù. Panoramic views.

activities.text: Dinner: Niçoise cuisine is distinct from Provençal cooking. Socca (chickpea galette) at Chez Pipo (Rue Bavastro, since 1923) or Lu Fran Calin. Pissaladière, pan-bagnat, Niçoise daube, stockfish, farcis niçois. La Merenda (4 Rue Raoul Bosio, no phone, no reservations) is the cult address — Dominique Le Stanc, formerly two-starred, now cooks his grandmother's recipes. Queue from 7pm.
Cours Saleya in the evening: craft market (Tuesday–Sunday), bars on Rue du Pont-Vieux or Rue de l'Abbaye. A terrace facing the sea with a gin-tonic or pastis looking out over the Baie des Anges.

visits.text: Morning in Cimiez — the chic hilltop neighbourhood, 10 minutes by bus (line 15 or 17 from Place Masséna, €1.50). The Matisse Museum in the Villa des Arènes, a 17th-century Genoese villa in the middle of an olive grove amid Roman ruins. Matisse settled in Nice in 1917, drawn by the light, and died here in 1954; he is buried in the monastery cemetery nearby. Six hundred works — from his early Impressionist portraits to the great late blue paper cut-outs. €10, closed Tuesdays.

The Marc Chagall Museum, a 10-minute walk away. A rare national museum created during the artist's lifetime and inaugurated in 1973 in his presence. Seventeen large canvases on the Biblical Message: blues and greens on themes from Genesis, Exodus and the Song of Songs. Three monumental stained-glass windows in the concert hall. A mosaic of the Prophet Elijah in the pond. €10, closed Tuesdays.

The Cimiez arenas: remains of the ancient city of Cemenelum, capital of the Roman province of Alpes-Maritimes in the 1st century. The amphitheatre was built in the 2nd century for 5,000 spectators. The adjacent baths are among the best-preserved in Roman Gaul. Free access. The Cimiez Monastery (9th century) next door: a kitchen garden with climbing roses, citrus trees and cypresses, and views over the Paillon valley.

Quick lunch, then Villefranche-sur-Mer by TER: 6 minutes from Nice-Ville, €2.20. The Villefranche bay is one of the deepest in the Mediterranean (95 metres at its centre) and regularly hosts US Navy aircraft carriers. Colourful old town lanes. The Chapel of Saint-Pierre, entirely decorated by Jean Cocteau in 1957 as a tribute to the local fishermen. Charlie Chaplin was at the opening. €3.

The Citadelle Saint-Elme (1554) above the harbour. Built by Henri II, Duke of Savoy, against Barbary raids and French territorial ambitions. Several free municipal museums inside (Volti, Goetz-Boumeester, Roux). The Plage des Marinières below is one of the best beaches for snorkelling — crystal-clear water thanks to the sheltered bay.

Èze village, perched at 429 metres between Nice and Monaco. Bus 82 or 112 from Villefranche (or direct from Nice), 30–40 minutes. Èze is entirely pedestrian and entirely vertiginous. Medieval cobbled lanes, artisans, perfumeries (Fragonard, Galimard) with free guided tours. The Exotic Garden (1949) on the ruins of the medieval castle, with cacti and feminine terracotta sculptures. On a clear day, Corsica is visible 170 km away. €6 for the garden.

activities.text: For the energetic: descend from Èze village to Èze-sur-Mer on the Nietzsche Path — 400 metres of descent, 1 hour. Nietzsche used to walk this coastal trail in 1883; it is said he conceived the final sections of Thus Spoke Zarathustra here. Wear proper shoes, bring water, check TER times at Èze-sur-Mer. Otherwise, catch the direct bus back.

Dinner in Nice for your last Côte d'Azur evening. La Réserve (Boulevard Franck Pilatte), fish with sea views, €55–90. More affordable: Acchiardo on Rue Droite in Vieux-Nice, a family bistrot since 1927, €30–45. Tourton de blettes (a sweet-savoury tart of Swiss chard, pine nuts, raisins and cheese) — a medieval Niçoise recipe.

visits.text: Flight Nice Côte d'Azur to Toulouse Blagnac: 1h05–1h15, €50–150 depending on advance booking (direct flights with EasyJet and Volotea; Air France goes via Paris-Orly in 3–4 hours, no direct option). The only domestic flight in the whole itinerary — it replaces 6 hours of train travel via Marseille. Book 2 months ahead. Tram T2 airport to the city centre: 30 minutes, €2. Hotel around the Capitole or the Carmes for everything within walking distance.

Place du Capitole, the city's heart since the 12th century. A 135-metre neo-classical façade with 8 marble columns — town hall and opera house combined in a single building. An Occitan cross in marble on the ground, with four branches each bearing three roundels (12 in total, variously interpreted as the 12 months or the signs of the zodiac). Free open access to the Capitole interior: the Salle des Illustres with Jean-Paul Laurens's monumental frescoes on Toulouse's history, and the Salle Henri-Martin with Pointillist paintings.

The Basilica of Saint-Sernin, the largest Romanesque church still standing in Europe. Built 1080–1220 for pilgrims on the Way of Saint James, UNESCO listed. The octagonal bell tower at 64 metres is the signature of the Toulouse school. A 115-metre nave, sculpted capitals, ambulatory. Shrine of Saint Saturninus, who evangelised the city in the 3rd century and was martyred in 250. Free entry, €4 for the crypt.

Couvent des Jacobins (13th century, work begun in 1230). Southern Gothic style, with its stone palm tree: a central column 22 metres tall whose ribs unfurl like palm fronds under the vault — the pinnacle of Languedoc Gothic. The relics of Thomas Aquinas have rested here since 1369. Between 11am and 3pm, light through the windows illuminates the painted walls. €5.

Hôtel d'Assézat, 1555, built by Pierre d'Assézat, a merchant who made his fortune in woad — the dye plant that enriched Toulouse in the 16th century before Indian indigo ruined the trade. The Renaissance inner courtyard: three tiers of arcaded galleries, mullioned windows. Houses the Bemberg Foundation — Cranach, Canaletto, Gauguin, Bonnard. €12.

activities.text: The Garonne quays at end of day. The Pont Neuf (paradoxically the oldest bridge in Toulouse, 1544–1632): seven unequal arches spanning 220 metres. Lit up in gold in the evening. The pink bricks glow orange at sunset — hence the Ville Rose. Restaurants on Quai de la Daurade.

Cassoulet — THE dish of Toulouse. White Tarbais beans, duck confit, Toulouse sausage IGP, pork rind. Its origin has been endlessly disputed with Castelnaudary and Carcassonne, and never settled. Chez Émile (Place Saint-Georges, since 1942) serves a benchmark version at €28. Au Père Louis (Rue des Tourneurs, since 1889). Le Bibent (Place du Capitole, Belle Époque listed interior). Pair with a Fronton or Gaillac red.

visits.text: TER Toulouse to Carcassonne: 45 minutes direct, €15. Several trains per hour. Leave your bags at the hotel in Toulouse and travel light — you'll be back for a second night. The station is in the lower town (Bastide Saint-Louis), a 25-minute walk from the Cité (2 km) or a €1 shuttle bus (line 4). Wear comfortable shoes — cobblestones and steep climbs ahead.

Enter through the Porte Narbonnaise — late 13th century, built under Philip III the Bold, two massive towers. The Cité has been UNESCO-listed since 1997: 52 towers and a double ring of walls, whose foundations from the 3rd–4th-century Gallo-Roman period are still clearly visible. Four to five million visitors per year, with barely 50 permanent residents. The lices — the strip of ground between the two rings of walls — made a crossed-fire approach impossible to breach.

The Château Comtal, a fortress within the fortress. 12th century, built by the Trencavel viscounts — lords who patronised troubadours and sheltered the Cathars. In 1209, Raymond-Roger Trencavel was imprisoned here, defeated by Simon de Montfort after a 15-day siege during the Albigensian Crusade. He died in his own dungeon a few months later, aged 24. The rampart walk (1.3 km, 35 towers) starts from the castle: views over the Pyrenees and the Montagne Noire. €12.

The Basilica of Saint-Nazaire inside the Cité. Free. Begun in 1096 by the Trencavels, it combines a restrained Romanesque nave with a soaring 14th-century Gothic choir. The 13th-century windows are among the oldest and best-preserved in the South. The 17th-century organ still gives concerts. Visit in late afternoon for the light through the stained glass.

The Pont Vieux (1315–1320), 12 semi-circular arches over the Aude, fully pedestrian. Descend into the Bastide Saint-Louis, founded in 1260 by Saint Louis to rehouse the inhabitants expelled from the Cité after the rebellion of 1240. A medieval grid plan. Place Carnot paved in red marble from Caunes-Minervois (20 km). Saturday morning market, the most animated in the Aude. Neptune Fountain (1771).

The Canal du Midi runs alongside the Bastide from 1810 (a century after the canal's inauguration in 1681, when Carcassonne was finally linked to it). Designed by Pierre-Paul Riquet under Louis XIV: 241 km from the Atlantic to the Mediterranean, UNESCO since 1996. Walk the towpath between the station and Square André Chénier under century-old plane trees. A 1-hour canal cruise (€12) from the port, including passage through a lock.

activities.text: Lunch in the Cité. Cassoulet (Carcassonne is one of the three cities that claim its invention). Le Jardin de la Tour (Rue Porte d'Aude) serves a refined version at €22 in a peaceful courtyard setting. Avoid Rue Cros-Mayrevieille — pure tourist trap. Alternative: Brasserie Donjon (Place du Grand Puits), shaded terrace.

Before leaving, return to the Pont Vieux at sunset — the finest viewpoint for the illuminated Cité reflected in the Aude. Photographers love it. Take the last TER back to Toulouse in the evening (last service around 9pm). Free evening in Toulouse.

visits.text: Intercités or TGV INOUI direct from Toulouse Matabiau to Bordeaux Saint-Jean: 2h–2h25 (no high-speed line between the two cities, LGV currently planned), from €10 on OUIGO, €15–40 on average. Tram C to the city centre (15 minutes). Hotel near Pey-Berland, the Triangle d'Or or the Garonne quays for everything within walking distance. Bordeaux in two days: the city plus one excursion — either Saint-Émilion or the Arcachon Basin. The entire city centre has been UNESCO-listed since 2007: 1,810 hectares, the largest urban World Heritage site in France after Paris.

Place de la Bourse, an 18th-century jewel.
