Designed 1730–1755 by Jacques Gabriel then Ange-Jacques Gabriel — France's first open square in urban planning history, a revolution compared with the closed royal squares of the past. Three identical curved façades, Fountain of the Three Graces (1869). Facing it, Michel Corajoud's Water Mirror (2006): 3,450 m², the world's largest reflecting pool, cycling through a mist-water-dry sequence every 15 minutes, mirroring the façades like a painting.

Saint-André Cathedral, begun in the 11th century, enlarged through the 15th — 124 metres long, 41 metres to the vault. Eleanor of Aquitaine, duchess of the entire south-west, married the future Louis VII here in 1137, a foundational union that brought the crown of France closer to the Duchy of Aquitaine. The 13th-century Royal Portal. Tour Pey-Berland alongside: 66 metres, 231 steps, €6. A detached bell tower from 1440. Panoramic views over the Bordeaux rooftops.

The Grand Théâtre on Place de la Comédie. Victor Louis, 1773–1780 — one of Europe's most beautiful theatres. Twelve monumental Corinthian columns, twelve statues of the Muses and goddesses. Its grand Italian-style staircase directly inspired Charles Garnier when he designed the Paris Opéra a century later. Blue, white and gold interior, 1,114 seats; guided tour €11 (check availability). Perfect proportions from the outside.

Rue Sainte-Catherine, Europe's longest pedestrian street at 1.2 km. The Grosse Cloche, a 15th-century medieval belfry with two 40-metre towers — its 7,800 kg bronze bell (1775) rings only six times a year. Former Porte Saint-Éloi and town prison for centuries. Behind it, the Saint-Pierre quarter: cobbled lanes, small squares, cafés, restaurants and independent shops.

activities.text: The Garonne quays in the late afternoon. 4.5 km of riverside promenade redesigned since 2009. The Pont de Pierre (1822), 17 brick-and-stone arches — legend has it that there are 17 letters in Napoléon Bonaparte, which historians have disproven, but the story remains charming. Sunset over the Water Mirror: magical.

A classic Bordelais dinner: entrecôte à la bordelaise (in a red wine and bone-marrow sauce), lamprey à la bordelaise (a fossil fish, medieval recipe), Arcachon oysters, duck magret, cannelés (invented by the Annonciades nuns in the 18th century). La Tupina (Rue Porte de la Monnaie, since 1968), solid terroir cooking €50–80. Chez Dupont (Rue Notre-Dame), whole duck from the oven. Saint-Émilion, Pessac-Léognan, Médoc — you're at the source.

visits.text: Marché des Capucins, the belly of Bordeaux. Every day except Monday, 5am–2pm. A Bordeaux institution since 1749, in a 1950s market hall. Arcachon oysters, Bordelaise entrecôte, cannelés, aged cheeses, local fruit and vegetables. A dozen oysters at Chez Jean-Mi (the iconic oyster bar) with a glass of dry white wine, €12. A hearty breakfast at 10.30am.

The Cité du Vin, opened June 2016 on the Garonne waterfront. Not a conventional museum but an immersive experience on the world of wine. A glass and anodised aluminium building by XTU Architects — a twisted vine shoot or a swirling carafe in motion. 3,000 m² across 8 floors. Twenty interactive modules in 2 hours with audioguide. Eighth-floor belvedere with an included tasting of a wine from anywhere in the world. €22.

Light lunch, then the Arcachon Basin by TER: Bordeaux Saint-Jean to Arcachon, 50 minutes direct, €11. At Arcachon, take Baia bus 1 or Autocars Citram to the Dune du Pilat (30–40 minutes, €1). Europe's highest sand dune: 100–110 metres depending on the year (it moves), 2.9 km long, 616 m wide, 60 million cubic metres of sand. It advances inland by 1 to 5 metres per year. Parking €4–6.

A 160-step wooden staircase (March–November, dismantled in winter to protect the sand from storms) or 20 minutes on foot through the sand. From the summit: the Atlantic with its surf (a world-famous surf destination), the Landes Forest behind (Europe's largest man-made forest, planted in the 19th century to stabilise the dunes), the Banc d'Arguin bird reserve, and Cap Ferret opposite. On a clear day, 25 km out to sea.

Oyster village. Le Canon on the Cap Ferret peninsula (boat shuttle from Arcachon, 20 minutes, €12 return) or Gujan-Mestras on the southern shore. Wooden sheds serve oysters straight from the basin, with a glass of dry white wine (Entre-Deux-Mers, Graves), buttered rye bread. Simple, fresh, best value of the trip. €12–18 per dozen. The tchanquées huts — houses on stilts built in the 19th century to watch over the oyster beds, named after the Gascon word for stilts — are visible from these villages.

activities.text: If the weather is kind: a trip in a pinasse (the traditional basin fishing boat) around the Île aux Oiseaux and its tchanquées huts. Two hours from Arcachon port, €25–35.

Back to Bordeaux by TER in the late afternoon. Evening in the Darwin Quarter, on the Right Bank (a 15-minute walk across the Pont de Pierre). A former military barracks converted into a 10,000 m² eco-alternative hub: indoor skatepark, urban farm, craft brewery (Les Brasseurs de Darwin), organic restaurants, second-hand shops. This is the Bordeaux that moves — very different from the classical left bank.

map_keywords: Château des Ducs de Bretagne Nantes

visits.text: Direct TGV INOUI from Bordeaux Saint-Jean to Nantes: 2h06–2h12 (fastest option), €40–75. Alternative: direct Intercités via La Rochelle, Rochefort and Saintes, 4h10–4h30, €25–50 (longer but scenic along the Atlantic coast). Nantes station is 15 minutes' walk or 5 minutes by tram from the centre. Hotel in the Bouffay, quayside or Feydeau areas.

The Château des Ducs de Bretagne — allow at least 2 hours. Built in the late 15th century by François II, the last independent Duke of Brittany, then by his daughter Anne of Brittany (twice Queen of France through her marriages to Charles VIII and Louis XII). A striking contrast: on the town side, a granite fortress with 500 metres of rampart walks and 7 towers; on the courtyard side, a white tuffeau stone residential palace of Italian Renaissance refinement.

The History Museum of Nantes (since 2007), 32 rooms, 1,150 objects. An entire room on the Edict of Nantes of 1598 — where Henri IV signed the guarantee of religious tolerance for Protestants. Sections on the Atlantic slave trade: Nantes was France's leading slaving port between 1700 and 1830, responsible for the deportation of 550,000 people — these sections are considered an international reference for their historical honesty. Courtyard and ramparts free, museum €8, closed Mondays.

Passage Pommeraye, one of the most spectacular covered passages in Europe. Built 1840–1843 by Louis Pommeraye, an ambitious young notary. It solved a simple problem with a brilliant solution: connecting the lower and upper town by absorbing a 9-metre difference in elevation across three levels, via a monumental central staircase in wrought iron and wood. Sixty-six luxury boutiques at its inauguration in July 1843. Jacques Demy filmed Lola and The Umbrellas of Cherbourg here. Listed 1976. Free.

The Bouffay quarter, the historic heart of Nantes. Half-timbered houses from the 15th century, cobbled lanes, Renaissance façades. Place du Bouffay, once the site of public executions. Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Paul Cathedral: a nave 37.5 metres tall — among the highest Gothic naves in France. The tomb of François II by Michel Colombe (1507), a masterpiece of French Renaissance sculpture, in the north transept.

activities.text: Dinner. A dynamic food scene. L'Océanide (Rue Fouré), ultra-fresh fish (Nantes is 50 km from the sea), €40–60. Lulu Rouget (Rue Saint-Léonard), Michelin-starred, €80 menu. More casual: Le Bougainville on Place du Bouffay, or Le Nid (restaurant at the top of Tour Bretagne, 360° views). Specialities: beurre blanc (invented in Nantes in the late 19th century by Clémence Lefeuvre), Muscadet sur lie AOC, far breton with prunes.

The green line painted on the ground — the Voyage à Nantes public art trail since 2012 (Jean Blaise). Twelve kilometres across the city. In the evening the lighting makes it particularly easy to follow. The Loire quays or the illuminated Île de Nantes — the Hangar à Bananes (a 1930s industrial warehouse converted into a bar and restaurant) right on the river.

visits.text: Les Machines de l'Île — a unique attraction in France, installed in the former Dubigeon shipyard (closed 1987). Three areas: the Grand Elephant, the Gallery of Machines, the Carousel of Sea Worlds. BOOK ONLINE IN ADVANCE — the Grand Elephant is often fully booked several days ahead. Allow 3–4 hours for all three. Combined ticket €25 at lesmachines-nantes.fr. Tram 1, stop Chantiers Navals.

The Grand Elephant, a mythical colossus — 12 m tall, 8 m wide, 21 m long, 48 tonnes. It walks, moves its ears and trunk, trumpets and occasionally sprays the crowd with water. It roams the Parc des Chantiers for 30 minutes per session, carrying 50 passengers on 3 levels. Wood, leather, steel — designed by François Delarozière and Pierre Orefice in 2007, inspired by the automatons of Jules Verne (a Nantes native, born 1828). If the engineer aims the trunk your way, step back.

The Carousel of Sea Worlds (2012). Twenty-five metres tall, 36 animated marine creatures on 3 levels (seabed, ocean, surface). Giant squid, jellyfish, octopus, ray, flying fish, Nautilus. Winner of the 2014 Thea Award for the world's most original attraction. You're in control: arms, fins and tentacles respond to your movements. Seven-minute sessions. The Gallery of Machines next door displays prototypes in live demonstration.

Lunch near the Machines (guinguettes, food trucks), then walk across to Île Feydeau — a former island on the Loire, absorbed into the city after land reclamation in the 19th century. Eighteenth-century mansions belonging to shipowners enriched by the triangular trade. Façades with sculpted grotesque masks, wrought-iron balconies, characteristic tilting (the buildings rest on piles and have leaned over time).

The Memorial to the Abolition of Slavery (2012), Quai de la Fosse — the very quay from which the slave ships departed. Moving and essential. By Krzysztof Wodiczko and Julian Bonder. Three hundred and sixty metres along the Loire. Two thousand glass plaques engraved with the names of Nantes's slave ships, ports of trade, and passages from abolitionist texts (Condorcet, Schoelcher) in 47 languages. An underground exhibition space. Free.

Jardin des Plantes, next to the SNCF station. Seven hectares, created 1687. Ten thousand species, tropical greenhouses, pond, camellias (Nantes is France's camellia capital). Since 2013, works from the Voyage à Nantes trail have been integrated: giant courgette benches, a metal heron-tree, and the sculpture Le Nid perched in a tree. Free — one of France's most beautiful public gardens.

activities.text: Last dinner in Nantes. Bouffay quarter: La Cigale (Place Graslin, a Belle Époque brasserie from 1895, listed Art Nouveau building, seafood), Le Bistrot du Bouillon for simple food at good prices, or a traditional crêperie such as La Pierre Chaude (100% organic buckwheat galettes, €10–16).

If the evening is mild: La Nef, a former shipbuilding hangar converted into a bar-restaurant on the Île de Nantes, with a direct view over the Loire. DJ sets in summer. Or Tour Bretagne (32 floors, 144 m — Nantes's tallest building): Le Nid at the top, a bar-restaurant with giant egg-shaped furniture and 360° views. Cocktail €12–15, magical at sunset.

visits.text: TGV Nantes to Rennes: 1h15 direct, €25–45. Tram A or B to the centre (8 minutes). Hotel in Vieux-Rennes, around Place du Parlement and Place des Lices. Rennes has been Brittany's capital since the 15th century — 220,000 inhabitants, a lively university city.

The Parlement de Bretagne. Built 1618–1655 by Salomon de Brosse (the same architect as the Palais du Luxembourg in Paris) — one of the finest 17th-century civic buildings in France. Brittany's highest court until the Revolution. Devastated by fire in February 1994 (sparked during fishing industry protests, a tragedy still keenly felt), restored to its original state by 1999. Guided tours only, 1h30 (€8, Tourist Office) to see the Grand'Chambre with its painted ceilings by Ferdinand Elle.

The medieval streets of Vieux-Rennes. The Great Fire of December 1720 burned for six days and destroyed 945 houses but spared this quarter — the colourful 15th–17th-century half-timbered houses survived. Rue Saint-Michel (known as the Rue de la Soif — the Street of Thirst — by students), Rue du Chapitre, Rue Saint-Guillaume, Rue Psalette. The half-timbered house at 3 Rue Saint-Guillaume (15th century) is one of the oldest. Stop for a galette and cider in one of the crêperies.

Place des Lices, the heart of popular Rennes. Two identical iron market halls from 1870, known as the Martenot halls. Saturday morning only: one of France's largest food markets — around 250 to 300 stalls, 10,000 visitors. 7.30am–1.30pm. Sausage-galette eaten standing up, crêpes, salted butter, Guémené andouille sausage, Cancale oysters.

Saint-Pierre Cathedral, rebuilt in the 19th century after the Gothic chancel collapsed in 1754. The neo-classical façade from 1704 — salvaged from the previous cathedral and grafted onto the new building. A lavish interior with polychrome marbles and an 1874 organ. A 16th-century Flemish altarpiece in the Lady Chapel, a survivor of the Revolution, and the cathedral's greatest treasure. Free entry.

Parc du Thabor — 10 hectares of botanical garden at the heart of Rennes, created from 1860 by the Bühler brothers. One of France's finest public gardens. Rose garden with 2,000 roses in 200 varieties, formal French garden, exotic bird aviary, fountains, a 1881 bandstand, listed glasshouse. Sunday open-air concerts in summer. Free. Highly photogenic in May and June.

activities.text: Dinner at an authentic crêperie. Crêperie Sainte-Anne (Place Sainte-Anne), an institution since 1920. La Saint-Georges (11 Rue du Chapitre), creative menu. €18–30 for a savoury galette, sweet crêpe and a bowl of cider AOP. Try kouign-amann (invented in Douarnenez in the 19th century) and far breton with prunes.

Rennes is a student city (70,000 students), with a lively nightlife on Rue Saint-Michel and surrounding streets. Local beers (Lancelot, Britt, Breizh Cola), live concerts, Irish pubs. Les Transmusicales in December — a rock and electronic music festival since 1979.

visits.text: TER Rennes to Dinan: 1 hour direct or 1h15 with a change at Dol-de-Bretagne, €15. Limited departures (around ten per day) — check SNCF Connect. Leave your bags at the hotel in Rennes. Dinan is one of the best-preserved medieval towns in Brittany, with 10,000 inhabitants, 2,800 metres of ramparts, and the Ville d'Art et d'Histoire designation. Perched on a rocky spur 75 metres above the Rance, it once controlled a strategic crossing between Normandy and Brittany.

The medieval ramparts — 2,800 metres, among the most complete in France. Built between the 13th and 15th centuries, reinforced by Bertrand du Guesclin (Constable of France, a native of Dinan) during the Hundred Years' War. Fourteen towers and four gatehouses still standing. The rampart walk takes 1h30, with plunging views over the Rance, the countryside and the half-timbered houses below. Free.

The Château de Dinan, built 1382–1387 by Duke Jean IV of Brittany, houses the Musée de Dinan. The keep alone — 34 metres tall — is one of the most massive in Brittany, with five storeys. Exhibitions on the town, medieval weapons, religious sculpture, traditional Breton costumes. Views from the top. €7. The Porte du Guichet alongside is the medieval main entrance, complete with portcullis and machicolations.

Rue du Jerzual and Rue du Petit-Fort — the picture-postcard of Dinan. A 25% gradient, uneven cobblestones, 15th–16th-century half-timbered houses with craftsmen's workshops at street level (glassblowers, sculptors, turners, weavers). This lane connected the upper town to the port on the Rance. The craft workshops are still running — glassblowing, tapestry, leather — push the door and look in. Four hundred metres that deserve thirty minutes at the very least.

The medieval port on the Rance — a working trading port until the 19th century (salt, wine and linen to England). Now a peaceful pleasure harbour, with colourful houses, houseboats, summer guinguettes. The 1852 viaduct (40 m high, 225 m long) soars above the valley. Lunch in the sun is possible here — galettes and seafood.

Walk back up the towpath, then visit the Basilique Saint-Sauveur (12th century, originally Romanesque, extended in Gothic style in the 16th century). Inside, the heart of Bertrand du Guesclin, the great Breton hero of the Hundred Years' War, who died in 1380 on campaign. His body is at Saint-Denis, his entrails at Le Puy-en-Velay, his flesh at Montferrand, his heart at Dinan, his native city. Free entry. The Tour de l'Horloge (15th century, 45 m) next door for the panorama.

activities.text: Lunch. Crêperie Ahna (Rue de la Cordonnerie), an institution since 1926, galettes €8–14 in a medieval setting. La Fleur de Sel (Rue de la Poissonnerie), bistro €25–40. Pommeau (a Breton apple aperitif, 17%) or a local farm cider.

Return to Rennes by TER in the late afternoon. Last evening in Rennes. Rue Saint-Michel, Rue Vasselot, Rue Saint-Georges for drinks. Or wind down at the Halles Centrales on Place des Lices — a bar-restaurant in the Art Nouveau market hall, open late.

visits.text: TER Rennes to Saint-Malo: 55 minutes direct, €16. The station is a 10–15-minute walk from the walled old town. Staying intra-muros is the experience, though it is expensive in summer (€120–180). Saint-Malo was 80% destroyed by American bombing in August 1944 and rebuilt faithfully over 15 years — what you see is a meticulous reconstruction in local granite.

Enter the walled city through the Porte Saint-Vincent. Walk the full rampart circuit — 1.8 km, free. Built between the 12th and 18th centuries, reinforced by Vauban from 1689. Clockwise: Bastion Saint-Philippe, Tour Bidouane (north viewpoint), Bastion de la Hollande, Plage du Sillon facing the open sea. Views over the water, the Grand Bé and Petit Bé islets, Dinard opposite, the offshore forts.

Tour Bidouane, the highest point of the ramparts, looks out over the sands at low tide. Grand Bé — a rocky islet accessible on foot at low tide, where Chateaubriand has lain since 1848. Born in Saint-Malo in 1768, he wanted to be buried facing the sea on this wind-battered rock. His tomb is of absolute simplicity: a granite slab, a cross, nothing else — not even his name. Accessible only at low tide; allow 30 minutes return and always check the tidal tables.

The Château de Saint-Malo, 15th century, built by the Dukes of Brittany Jean V and François II. The History Museum of Saint-Malo is in the Great Keep. Corsairs, the great figures of Saint-Malo (Jacques Cartier who discovered Canada in 1534 and named the Saint Lawrence, Duguay-Trouin, Surcouf, Chateaubriand), naval history, colonisation. Magnificent views from the rooftops. €6, closed Mondays.

The intra-muros lanes — all at right angles (rebuilt to a plan), tall houses in blue-grey local granite. Saint-Vincent Cathedral at the centre: Romanesque-Gothic, 12th–18th century, destroyed in 1944 then restored with contemporary windows by Jean Le Moal and Bernard Allain. The Maison de la Duchesse Anne (a timber-framed gable, a rare survivor, 15 Grande Rue).

Plage du Sillon — 3 km of fine sand from Saint-Malo to Paramé. A bracing breeze, waves (kite-surfing spot), and tides among the strongest in Europe with amplitudes of up to 13 metres. German Atlantic Wall blockhouses still emerge at low tide. Swimmable in summer (18–20°C maximum). In winter: a typically Breton windswept walk.

activities.text: Dinner: avoid Rue Saint-Vincent (tourist trap). Try Rue Jacques Cartier or Rue Sainte-Barbe instead. Le Cambusier (3 Rue Porcon de la Barbinais), excellent seafood €40–60, produce from the Cancale and Saint-Malo auction markets. L'Ancrage (Rue du Grout Saint-Georges): seafood platters (12 Cancale oysters €18, spider crab, langoustines). Muscadet sur lie or Breton cider.

Walk the illuminated ramparts at night — spectacular and far less crowded than during the day. The lights pick out blockhouses, bastions, slate rooftops, the sea glittering under the moon. One of the finest nocturnal scenes in Brittany. Le Corps de Garde (4 Montée Notre-Dame): a bar inside a former rampart tower, looking out over the harbour.

visits.text: Keolis Armor bus from Saint-Malo to Mont-Saint-Michel: ~55 minutes to 1h15 direct, around €15 single. One to three departures per day depending on season — check keolis-armor.com. Alternative: TER Saint-Malo to Pontorson (1 hour with a change at Dol-de-Bretagne) then Nomad shuttle Pontorson to Mont (15 minutes). From the mainland car park, free Le Passeur shuttles run, or walk the causeway on foot (35 minutes — the new road-dike opened in 2014).

Grande Rue, the only route to the abbey. Four hundred metres, steep climb, uneven cobblestones, medieval houses now converted to shops (many tourist traps, a few good addresses). The Escalier du Gouffre leads up to the abbey. The 15th-century ramparts encircle the mount — built during the Hundred Years' War, Mont-Saint-Michel withstood the English for 30 years despite several sieges. The only place in Normandy never to fall into English hands.

The Abbey of Mont-Saint-Michel, 80 metres tall. Founded in 709 by Bishop Aubert of Avranches after three appearances of the Archangel Michael. Enlarged in the 11th century (Romanesque abbey), then in the 13th century with La Merveille — a three-storey Gothic building constructed on the cliff face, a feat of medieval engineering. UNESCO since 1979. Allow 1h30–2h: the abbey church, the suspended cloister, the refectory, the Guests' Hall, the Knights' Hall, the crypt of the Great Pillars. €13.

The suspended cloister — the jewel of the visit, seemingly floating between earth and sky. A double arcade of 220 small Caen limestone columns with individually carved capitals. A kitchen-garden courtyard in the centre. Looking down through the arcades onto the bay. The abbey church above blends Romanesque (nave) and Flamboyant Gothic (choir rebuilt after it collapsed in 1421). The monks of the Fraternités Monastiques de Jérusalem, who still live in the abbey, may be at prayer.

The rampart walk covers almost the full circuit of the mount. West Terrace: spectacular panoramas over the ever-changing bay. The tides here are the strongest on the continental European coastline — amplitude up to 14 metres, the sea retreating 15 km then surging back at the speed of a galloping horse, according to Victor Hugo (reality: the pace of a brisk walker). Check the posted tidal times. The greatest show is at the equinox tides (March and September).

activities.text: Lunch: be wary on the Grande Rue — prices are inflated. La Mère Poulard (since 1888), famous for its soufflé omelette (beaten for 7 minutes in copper bowls over an open fire), €40 — pricey. Alternative: restaurants on the mainland at La Caserne, cheaper and often better. Or a picnic on the ramparts, with supplies from the intra-muros grocery shop.

Sleeping intra-muros (20 hotels, €120–250, book 2 months ahead): the Mont is magical after the last day-trippers leave around 6pm. Illuminated ramparts, complete silence, empty lanes — the real experience. Otherwise Pontorson (9 km, €50–80) or La Caserne (€80–150). July–August: nocturnal abbey visits Monday to Saturday evenings, €15, classical music and dramatic lighting.

visits.text: From Mont-Saint-Michel, the journey is complex: shuttle to Pontorson, then TER direct Pontorson to Caen (2h30, four departures per day), then TER Caen to Rouen (1h30–2h). Total 5 to 5h30, €40–60. Alternative: bus back to Saint-Malo or Rennes, then TGV via Paris. Rouen Rive-Droite station is a 10-minute walk from the cathedral. Hotel near the Vieux-Marché or the cathedral.

Rouen Cathedral (Notre-Dame), the city's emblem. Begun in 1145, completed in the 16th century. The cast-iron spire at 151 metres was the world's tallest structure between 1876 and 1880. The Flamboyant Gothic façade is of breathtaking complexity — Monet painted it 30 times between 1892 and 1894 at different hours and in different seasons, working from a window in a lingerie shop across the street. The series is now scattered (Orsay, the Metropolitan, the Getty). Free entry. Tombs of the Norman Dukes, including Richard the Lionheart — his heart is here, his body at Fontevraud.

The Gros-Horloge, 200 metres away. A 16th-century Gothic arch spanning a pedestrian street, with a 2.50-metre astronomical clock face. A single hand (hours only, as was medieval practice), the hour hand shaped as a golden lamb. The dial shows the moon phase and day of the week. The mechanism dates from 1389 — one of the oldest still functioning in Europe. Museum €7, with panoramic views from the belfry over the rooftops.

Place du Vieux-Marché, heavy with history: on 30 May 1431, Joan of Arc was burned at the stake here at the age of 19, following a heresy trial conducted by Bishop Cauchon and the English. A 20-metre cross marks the exact spot of the pyre. The Church of Saint-Joan-of-Arc (1979), designed by Louis Arretche, has a contemporary form evoking a flame or an upturned keel. Thirteen stained-glass windows from 1520 (rescued from the bombed Saint-Vincent church in 1944). The square hosts a covered morning market.

The Aître Saint-Maclou, five minutes on foot. One of Europe's rare surviving medieval ossuaries. Built in the 14th century during the Black Death to pile up the dead, converted into a gallery-cemetery in the 16th century (1526–1533). A rectangular courtyard surrounded by half-timbered galleries carved with skulls, bones and funerary symbols. Home to the École des Beaux-Arts until 2014, restored 2019–2020. Free. The Church of Saint-Maclou next door (15th-century Flamboyant Gothic) is also worth a look.

The medieval streets around the cathedral: Rue Saint-Romain, Rue Damiette, Rue Martainville. Rouen has more than 2,000 half-timbered houses — the highest concentration in Europe (Strasbourg has only 130). Leaning façades, ancient carvings, polychrome beams. Musée des Beaux-Arts on Place Verdrel: one of the finest art museums in France outside Paris — Caravaggio, Velázquez, Rubens, Poussin, Fragonard, Monet, Sisley, Pissarro, Duchamp (a Rouen native). Permanent collections free.

activities.text: Dinner. La Couronne (Place du Vieux-Marché, founded 1345 — claiming to be France's oldest inn), classic Norman cuisine €40–60 (Rouen-style duck, Dieppe sole, Norman tart). More casual: Gill Côté Bistro (Rue Saint-Étienne-des-Tonneliers), the relaxed version of the starred Gill restaurant. Normandy AOC cheeses: Camembert, Livarot, Pont-l'Évêque, Neufchâtel (heart-shaped), farmhouse cider from the Pays d'Auge, Calvados.

June to mid-September: Cathédrale de Lumière — free video projection on the cathedral façade every evening at nightfall. Twenty minutes, with different shows in different years. One of Europe's finest light spectacles. Otherwise: walk the Seine quays as far as the Pont Gustave-Flaubert (2008, Europe's tallest bascule bridge at 86 metres when raised).

visits.text: Rouen to Lille: direct TER from Rouen Rive-Droite to Lille-Flandres (6 departures per day), 2h38–3h, from €30. Alternative with one change at Amiens (TER, 3h30, €35–55). Faster via Paris: TGV Rouen–Paris Saint-Lazare 1h15 + metro across to Gare du Nord + TGV Paris–Lille 1h, total 3 hours including the Paris crossing, €70–100. Hotel near the Grand'Place or in Vieux Lille. Lille is the capital of the Hauts-de-France region, 230,000 inhabitants, right on the Belgian border — warm, carnival-spirited Northern atmosphere.

The Grand'Place (officially Place du Général-de-Gaulle, but nobody calls it that). The Colonne de la Déesse (1845), commemorating Lille's successful resistance to the Austrian siege of 1792. Flemish façades from the 17th and 18th centuries in red brick and white stone with scroll gables. La Voix du Nord (the regional newspaper) occupying a 1936 Art Deco building. Christmas market in December — among the finest in France.

The Vieille Bourse, an architectural gem. Built 1652–1653 during the Spanish era (Lille was Spanish until 1667, when Louis XIV annexed it). A masterpiece of Flemish architecture — 24 houses arranged as a quadrilateral around an inner courtyard. A sculpted façade: caryatids, garlands, grotesque masks, coats of arms. Second-hand booksellers fill the courtyard every afternoon (except Mondays). Chess and draughts players. Listed monument. Free.

Vieux Lille — the quarter that escaped Haussmannian planning, entirely pedestrianised. Cobbled lanes, brick-and-stone façades, 17th-century Flemish mansions. Rue de la Monnaie, Rue Esquermoise, Rue Basse. Designer boutiques, concept stores, chocolate shops (Meert, since 1761 — a Lille institution, serving a waffle filled with Madagascar vanilla favoured by De Gaulle). Notre-Dame-de-la-Treille Cathedral with its contemporary translucent marble façade (2000).

The Opéra de Lille (1913, monumental neo-classical) and the Chamber of Commerce with its 76-metre belfry flank Place du Théâtre. The Beffroi de l'Hôtel de Ville (1929–1932): France's tallest belfry at 104 metres, UNESCO since 2005 as part of the Belfries of Belgium and France. Lift then 100 steps (€7) for a 360° panorama over Lille, the Flemish plain and — on a clear day — Belgium. The legendary giant figures Lydéric and Phinaert carved into the belfry.

activities.text: Dinner. Estaminet Chez la Vieille (Rue de Gand): carbonade flamande (beef stewed in beer), waterzooi, potjevleesch (a 3-to-5-meat terrine in aspic), moules-frites in season. La Chicorée (26 Rue de Béthune), open 24 hours, cult address. €25–40. Local beers: Goudale, Jenlain amber, Ch'ti blonde. Meert waffle for dessert.

Rue Royale, Rue de la Barre, Place Louise-de-Bettignies for bars and cocktails. Le Barbue d'Anvers, an estaminet and live-music bar on Rue Saint-Étienne. Festive: Rue Solférino and Rue Masséna for students — Lille has 120,000 of them. First weekend of September: the Braderie de Lille, Europe's largest flea market since 1127, two million visitors, 10,000 sellers spread across 100 km of pavements.

practical_info.tip: Braderie first September weekend — book your hotel 6 months in advance

visits.text: Palais des Beaux-Arts, Place de la République. The second-largest museum in France after the Louvre, inaugurated in 1892. A monumental neo-Renaissance building. Five centuries of collections: Donatello, Raphael, Rubens (Descent from the Cross), Van Dyck, Goya, David, Courbet, Monet, Renoir, Degas, Toulouse-Lautrec, Picasso. Basement: relief maps — 15 military scale models of French fortified towns commissioned by Louis XIV in the 17th century to plan sieges. €7, closed Tuesdays. Allow 2 hours.

Sunday morning (or Wednesday/Friday/Saturday): the Wazemmes market — Lille's largest and most popular, an emblem of the cosmopolitan city. Covered 1869 market hall plus outdoor stalls. Three hundred vendors, produce from around the world. Music, florists, cheesemongers, rotisserie, Maghrebi, Italian and Portuguese specialities. Roast chicken with chips to take away, €9, a local institution. 7am–2pm. Metro Gambetta.

Afternoon in Roubaix for La Piscine — one of the most memorable visits in France. Art and industry museum installed in a 1932 Art Deco municipal swimming pool, converted into a museum in 2001. The main pool with its original mosaics, zenithal lighting and a sunset stained-glass window serves as the main gallery — sculptures facing one another in the still, reflecting water. Paintings, sculptures and textiles (Roubaix was France's textile capital). Metro Gare Jean-Lebas then 10 minutes. €11, closed Mondays.

The Vauban Citadel, a masterpiece of the great military architect. Built 1667–1670 after Louis XIV's annexation of Lille. Known as the Queen of Citadels for its perfect pentagonal shape with five bastions, it is still operational as a military barracks. The surrounding 70-hectare park is free and popular with Lille joggers. The Lille Zoo is inside (free, 70 species).

The birthplace of Charles de Gaulle (9 Rue Princesse, Vieux Lille) — a museum in the house where the General was born on 22 November 1890. A late-19th-century bourgeois home, restored and furnished as it was. A biographical trail, 1,500 personal objects. €7, closed Mondays and Tuesdays. Worth visiting even for non-Gaullists, for the atmosphere of a Flemish Catholic bourgeois childhood.

activities.text: Last dinner of the tour. Bloempot by Florent Ladeyn (Rue des Bouchers): a bistronomic table that is resolutely locavore, a single set menu at €48, 100% regional produce. Or T-Rex Café (Rue Saint-André) for a Northern burger and craft beer. Welsh rarebit is unmissable (bread, melted Cheddar, beer, fried egg) — caloric but iconic. Genièvre as digestif (a Flemish juniper berry spirit, 40%).

Last night of the grand tour. A drink in a rooftop bar or a signature cocktail. Le Comptoir Volant (Rue Esquermoise), creative cocktails in a cosy room. Open Gallery (Place du Lion d'Or) for something trendier. Or go back to the hotel and get ready for tomorrow's return to Paris — 1 hour on the TGV, arriving at Gare du Nord in the morning.

visits.text: Direct TGV from Lille-Flandres to Paris Gare du Nord: 1 hour, €40–75. Many departures. You arrive in the heart of Paris, with the metro everywhere. If your train or flight departs in the afternoon or evening, you have the morning for one last neighbourhood. If you have an international flight during the day, allow a generous buffer — at least 2h30 before an international departure.

Saint-Germain-des-Prés, which you may not have explored at the start of the trip. The Church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, the oldest in Paris (6th century, rebuilt in the 11th), where Descartes is buried. Café de Flore and Les Deux Magots (Boulevard Saint-Germain) — the bastions of existentialism where Sartre, Beauvoir and Camus held court. Coffee €6–8, but the atmosphere is unchanged. Rue Jacob, Rue de Buci, Rue de Seine: galleries, boutiques, covered market.

Alternative: Place Vendôme and Rue Saint-Honoré for the Paris luxury experience. The Vendôme Column (1810) erected by Napoleon from the bronze of cannon captured at Austerlitz, a copy of Trajan's Column in Rome. Classical façades by Mansart (1702). The Hôtel Ritz at no. 15 (Coco Chanel lived here for 37 years; Proust and Hemingway were regulars). Boutiques of Chanel, Dior, Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels. Place de la Madeleine with the neo-classical Madeleine church (1842) and the luxury food shops (Fauchon, Hédiard, Maille).

A final Parisian lunch to match the occasion. Le Grand Véfour (Palais-Royal, an institution since 1784, frequented by Napoleon, Victor Hugo and Colette; chef Guy Martin — the setting is a listed monument and still sumptuous, €75–135 at lunch). Bouillon Chartier (Rue du Faubourg-Montmartre, a popular institution since 1896, dishes from €5 to €15). Or Clamato (Rue de Charonne, oyster bar and small plates, €35–55). Or the simplest and most genuine: a baguette-tradition, Paris ham, a wedge of cheese and a glass of wine on a bench in the Tuileries.

activities.text: If your train or flight is in the evening: one last hour on the Pont des Arts, the Pont Neuf or the Seine quays. A final look at Notre-Dame, the Louvre, the Eiffel Tower in the distance. Thirty-seven days ago you were discovering Paris for the first time on this trip. You have made a complete loop around the hexagon. This time you look at Paris carrying everything you've been through — Loire, Alsace, Alps, Mediterranean, Atlantic, Brittany, the North. You have seen the whole of France: it will never look the same again.

Airports: Charles de Gaulle (RER B from Gare du Nord direct, 35 minutes, €12; taxi €55–65 from the centre, 45 min–1h depending on traffic), Orly (Orlyval from Antony or tram T7, 30–40 minutes, €12; taxi €40–50). Allow 3 hours before international non-Schengen flights, 2 hours for domestic or Schengen flights. Gare du Nord for the Eurostar. Gare de Lyon for the south-east, Montparnasse for the west, Austerlitz for the centre.

seo.h1_title: The Grand Tour of France in 5 Weeks, Car-Free
seo.intro_paragraph: A full month to cross France without a steering wheel — from Paris back to Paris via the Loire châteaux, Alsace, the French Riviera, the Pyrenees, the Atlantic, Brittany and the North. TGV, regional trains, local buses, and a single domestic flight from Nice to Toulouse. Six days in Paris to see it all, 22 city stopovers, 5 major UNESCO sites, three coastlines (Mediterranean, Atlantic, English Channel).
seo.seo_hook: A month-long journey across France by train: Paris, Loire châteaux, the Riviera, Mont-Saint-Michel. 22 cities, 5 UNESCO sites, 3 coastlines.
featured_list: Paris for 6 days: Louvre, Orsay, the Marais, Montmartre, Père-Lachaise, Buttes-Chaumont
Loire: the royal Château of Blois, Chambord and Chenonceau in a single day
Alsace: Strasbourg Cathedral (142 m) and the Isenheim Altarpiece in Colmar
Lyon: UNESCO Vieux Lyon, the traboules, the Halles Paul Bocuse
Provence: Palais des Papes in Avignon, the Pont du Gard, the Arles amphitheatre
French Riviera: Promenade des Anglais, Cimiez, Èze village perched at 429 m
South-West: the Cité de Carcassonne UNESCO, Place de la Bourse in Bordeaux
Brittany: the Machines de l'Île in Nantes, the ramparts of Saint-Malo
Mont-Saint-Michel: a thousand-year-old UNESCO abbey in the heart of its bay
The North: Lille's belfry (France's tallest at 104 m) and La Piscine in Roubaix
