itineraries.title: Indre Road Trip: Secret Berry and the Vallée Noire
itineraries.subtitle: From Talleyrand's châteaux to George Sand's villages, journey through intimate Berry between medieval valleys and literary landscapes
itineraries.climate: Best period: May-June and September-October, temperatures 15-25°C, ideal for heritage sites and nature. Avoid November-March (cold, grey, frequent rain). July-August can be warm (up to 30°C) but remain bearable in this rural countryside.

visits.text: Château de Valençay. This Renaissance residence once hosted Prince de Talleyrand, one of France's greatest diplomats. The château has retained its original Empire furniture, and its salons bear witness to the refinement of the Napoleonic era. The kitchens, pantry, and wine cellars illustrate the importance of gastronomy for Talleyrand, whose table was renowned throughout Europe. The First Empire theater, a jewel from 1810, still preserves its period sets and painted backdrops.

Château gardens and grounds. The estate extends over 130 acres with formal French gardens, the terraced Duchess's garden, and Antonin's garden showcasing 300 species of aromatic plants in tribute to Antonin Carême. The Princes' Forest offers a 2.5-mile woodland trail with seven historical points. For children: a petting zoo, scent game, children's château, and Napoleon's Grand Labyrinth.

Valençay town center. The heritage trail follows medallions set into the ground and leads you to the covered wheat market, the former textile mill, Saint-Martin church, and Talleyrand's tomb. The town boasts two AOC designations bearing its name: the pyramid-shaped Valençay goat cheese and Valençay wine.

activities.text: Valençay cheese and wine tasting. Local producers offer tastings of Valençay AOC goat cheese in its distinctive truncated pyramid shape, along with Valençay AOC white and red wines. A winemaking and cheesemaking tradition stretching back centuries.

Valençay Automobile Museum. A remarkable collection of over 60 vintage cars, all in working order, traces the history of the automobile. The museum also displays fire trucks, motorcycles, bicycles, period garage signs, and vintage posters.

Bas-Berry tourist train. This historic railway line offers scenic journeys through the Berry countryside. The train winds through bucolic landscapes and typical villages at a pace that allows you to savor every detail of rural Berry.

visits.text: Old bridges and Creuse riverbanks. Nicknamed the Venice of Berry, Argenton features houses with galleries suspended above the Creuse River. The old bridges offer the finest views of this architectural ensemble. A developed promenade along the right bank allows you to walk past picturesque mills and discover ancient alleyways.

Bonne-Dame Chapel. Perched on the heights, this chapel crowned with a gilded statue of the Virgin Mary offers a remarkable panorama over the town's rooftops and the Creuse valley. The site provides the best vantage point for appreciating Argenton's urban ensemble.

Saint-Sauveur Church. This 19th-century neo-Gothic church dominates the town center. Its bell tower-porch is visible from afar, and the interior houses a remarkable organ. The building testifies to the town's development during the industrial era.

Shirt-making and Masculine Elegance Museum. From 1860 onwards, Argenton became a major center for textile manufacturing. The museum traces this epic story through modern scenography presenting the expertise of shirt-makers, great fashion houses, and local working-class history. Collections of catalogs, stylists' engravings, and vintage machines illustrate this industry that formed the economic heartbeat of the town.

activities.text: Argentomagus archaeological site in Saint-Marcel. A neighboring Gallo-Roman city, Argentomagus testifies to the ancient town's major role on Gaul's commercial routes. The museum built over monumental remains presents a domestic altar unique in Gaul and immersive reconstructions. Outside, you can wander among the ruins: temples, houses, theaters, and ancient roads.
Greenway. This former railway line turned cycle path runs through Argenton and lets you reach Le Blanc. The route crosses the Creuse valley through green countryside, perfect for walking or cycling.

Traditional market. On Tuesday and Saturday mornings, the market animates the town center with Berry regional produce. Goat cheeses, local wines, seasonal vegetables, and artisanal specialties come together in a convivial atmosphere.

visits.text: Medieval village. Classified among France's Most Beautiful Villages, Saint-Benoît-du-Sault perches on a rocky spur overlooking the Portefeuille valley. The village has preserved its proud medieval character with winding cobbled streets, houses from the 15th and 16th centuries, and fortification remnants. The 14th-century portal, the belfry with its still-functioning clock, and the Demi-lune square bear witness to this past.

Church and priory. The 11th-century Saint-Benoît church features a remarkable inverted boat-hull timber frame. The priory, founded at the end of the 10th century by the Abbey of Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire, constituted an advanced outpost in Aquitaine territory. The current building dates from the 18th century and regularly hosts art exhibitions.

Argentier's House. This dwelling listed as a Historic Monument presents a remarkable medieval façade. The finely carved door lintel features two warriors' heads with helmets, a geometric rosette, and two hearts. This architecture constitutes a historical enigma that fascinates visitors.

Valley viewpoint. From the church terrace, a stunning view extends over the verdant Portefeuille valley. The colors change with the seasons and create a natural tableau that has captivated numerous artists over time.

activities.text: Le Temps Suspendu Festival. Each summer in August, this baroque music festival pays tribute to the village's exceptional heritage. Concerts take place in the church and its surroundings, creating an intimate experience between musicians and audience. Open-air dinners and aperitif concerts punctuate the festival.

Photography Encounters. In early August, the priory hosts photography exhibitions by established artists for about ten days, along with conferences, portfolio reviews, workshops, and concert-projections. A photo contest open to all completes the program.

Portefeuille Gorges. This fast-flowing river runs below the village in a steep-sided valley. Hiking trails allow you to explore this preserved natural environment where flora and fauna thrive freely. The contrast between the perched medieval village and the verdant valley creates a remarkable landscape.

visits.text: Gargilesse village. Classified among France's Most Beautiful Villages, Gargilesse nestles in the verdant Creuse valley. Its houses with steep roofs covered in brown tiles are harmoniously grouped around the Romanesque church and château. This village captivated George Sand, who owned a retreat house here, then numerous Impressionist painters like Armand Guillaumin and Léon Detroy.

Notre-Dame Church and its crypt. Built in the 12th century, this Romanesque church reveals 120 superb historiated capitals where the 24 Elders of the Apocalypse and carved biblical scenes coexist. A small staircase leads down to the crypt adorned with 13th and 16th-century frescoes illustrating the instruments of the Passion and episodes from the lives of Christ and Mary.

Villa Algira. George Sand discovered Gargilesse one June evening in 1857 during a walk with Alexandre Manceau, who gifted her this small house. The writer stayed here regularly between 1857 and 1864, finding inspiration for several novels in this romantic refuge. The museum presents naturalist collections, drawings by Maurice Sand, and everyday objects that tell the story of George Sand's life in Berry.

Gargilesse Castle. Built in the 13th and 14th centuries, the château was expanded in the 16th and 18th centuries. Access to the estate is through the ancient 12th-century gate flanked by two towers, the sole remnant of the old fortress. The square tower dates from the 17th century and originally served as a tomb for the lords of Gargilesse.

activities.text: International Harp Festival. Gargilesse has become the world capital of the harp thanks to Pierre Jamet, who founded this festival in 1968, now directed by his daughter Marie-Claire. Concerts, courses, and masterclasses take place throughout the year, with a particularly prestigious summer festival in August. The international harp academy offers workshops in April and August.

Creuse riverside trails. Hiking paths follow the banks of the Creuse and reveal the landscapes that inspired so many artists. The changing reflections on the water, lush vegetation, and viewpoints over the village create a uniquely romantic atmosphere.

Art galleries and artisan workshops. The village perpetuates its artistic tradition with several galleries exhibiting paintings, sculptures, and art crafts. Open workshops, depending on the season, allow you to meet creators and discover their works in a simple, warm atmosphere.

visits.text: Saint-Étienne Basilica. Listed as UNESCO World Heritage as part of the Routes of Santiago de Compostela, this 11th and 12th-century Romanesque basilica presents an architectural design unique in France. The building combines a central nave with side aisles and a three-level rotunda with ambulatory, modeled after Jerusalem's Holy Sepulchre. The rotunda, 72 feet in diameter, is supported by 11 columns representing the eleven apostles.

Rotunda and relics. The rotunda evokes Jerusalem's Holy Sepulchre and was built by Eudes de Déols in the 11th century. In 1257, Cardinal Eudes de Châteauroux gifted three drops of Christ's Precious Blood, initiating an important pilgrimage celebrated each Easter Monday. Each column is adorned with carved capitals depicting the battle between forces of Good and Evil.

Saint-Pierre Church in Dampierre. Three miles from town, this village possesses a 12th-century Romanesque church listed as a historic monument. Beautiful in its proportions, it is characterized by its bell tower clad in chestnut shingles. The right chapel contains the tombstone of Pierre de Muzard, lord of Chanlebon.

activities.text: Multimedia guided tour. A smartphone app allows you to discover the basilica independently. The great figures who marked the monument's history tell the story: Eudes de Déols the founder, Eudes de Châteauroux donor of the relics, Viollet-le-Duc who saved it from ruin. This audio tour of 8 stops is enriched with anecdotes, photos, and unpublished documents.

Summer concerts. The basilica regularly hosts sacred and classical music concerts that showcase the site's exceptional acoustics. The Romanesque atmosphere and circular rotunda create a unique sonic experience for music lovers.

visits.text: La Châtre historic center. A three-flower town, La Châtre astonishes with the quality of its heritage. The 15th-century keep, which became a prison then museum, dominates the old town. The mysterious lantern of the dead and the picturesque tanners' quarter with its half-timbered houses plunge you into the medieval atmosphere. History-laden streets follow a 20-stage marked route.

Chauvigny Keep. This massive tower stands out above the old town of La Chatre. Once the fortress of the local lords, it long served as a prison before housing collections devoted to George Sand. The building can no longer be visited, but its mass of stone remains the landmark of the historic center and the best place to understand the town's defensive position above the Indre.

Parish church. The town center's religious building presents characteristic architecture and testifies to La Châtre's spiritual history. Its belfry is visible from afar and serves as a landmark in the urban landscape.

activities.text: George Sand's estate at Nohant. A few miles away, George Sand's house is open year-round. This 18th-century residence preserves the famous writer's furniture and belongings. The salon and dining room welcomed Balzac, Chopin, Delacroix, Flaubert, and Liszt. The 15-acre park, classified as a Remarkable Garden, features a rose garden, meadow-orchard, and vegetable garden. The puppet theater created by the family completes the visit.

practical_info.hours: Open year-round except January 1, May 1, November 1 and 11, December 25
practical_info.visit_type: Guided tour required for the house, free access to gardens
practical_info.interest: Essential site for understanding George Sand's work and 19th-century artistic life

activities.text: Saint-Martin Church in Vic. In Nohant-Vic, this 11th-century Romanesque church houses remarkable 12th-century frescoes, preserved thanks to George Sand and Prosper Mérimée's intervention in 1851. The biblical scenes with striking colors and expressions constitute a unique testimony to Berry Romanesque art.

Saturday market. The weekly market animates the town center with regional produce stalls. Goat cheeses, seasonal vegetables, honey, Berry wines, and local culinary specialties create a typically Berry convivial atmosphere.

visits.text: White Tower. Erected in 1195 at Richard the Lionheart's request and completed in 1202 under Philip Augustus, this 89-foot tower has dominated the town for over 830 years. Never conquered despite numerous attacks, it returned to the Kingdom of France with Blanche of Castille's dowry. The new 2014 scenography presents a video projection on the first level about the history of this unjustly forgotten queen. From the summit, remarkable panorama over the town and surroundings.

Saint-Roch Hospice Museum. Housed in the former Hôtel-Dieu beside the Théols, this museum contains exceptional heritage. The 15th-century chapel presents decoration unique in France, and the patients' wards testify to hospital history. Gallo-Roman and medieval archaeological collections, 17th and 19th-century apothecary, and a splendid carved Tree of Jesse enrich the tour. A modern extension hosts prestigious contemporary art exhibitions.

Belfry and Clock Gate. The 12th-century belfry testifies to medieval communal independence. The Clock Gate, rebuilt after the Wars of Religion, presents remarkable Renaissance decorations. Two round towers connected by a vaulted passage, one adorned with a clock and bell, constitute this ensemble that served as a prison until World War I.

Saint-Cyr Church. This Gothic church dominates the historic center with its splendid 15th-century stained glass window. The interior architecture testifies to the town's religious importance in the Middle Ages.

activities.text: Ramparts promenade. The Boulevard Champion runs along the ancient ramparts and offers a remarkable viewpoint over the château quarter, town hall, and White Tower. A panoramic elevator installed in a cleft in the ramparts allows easy access to François Mitterrand Park.

François Mitterrand Park. This five-acre green space extends on both sides of the Théols. Children's playground, benches, and landscaping that changes with the seasons make it a popular walking spot. At night during the season, the park and ramparts benefit from artistic lighting: the Paysages de Lumières.

Saturday market. A stronghold of fairs since the Middle Ages, Issoudun perpetuates this tradition with its weekly market. Regional produce, goat cheeses, seasonal vegetables, and Berry specialties animate the town center in a convivial atmosphere.

visits.text: Bouges Castle. At the end of a 1.2-mile riding avenue bordered by two-hundred-year-old plane and chestnut trees appears this 18th-century château, nicknamed the Petit Trianon of Berry. The elegant residence has remained furnished and decorated with refinement, giving the impression that the owners have just stepped out. The salons, dining room, and bedrooms illustrate the French art of living during the Age of Enlightenment.

French formal gardens. Designed by the celebrated landscape architects Duchêne, these formal gardens present boxwood and yew borders trimmed into cones, surrounded by a double row of lime trees. The basin vista leads to the nymphaeum water buffet, while at the center of the lawn rises a white marble group representing Hercules.

Bouquetier garden. This flower garden created by Renée Viguier in the early 20th century draws inspiration from the Belle Époque spirit. Organized along two main axes around a circular basin, it offers a diversity of annual flowers intended for the bouquets that adorn the château's rooms. The reproduction greenhouses cultivate plants for floral displays. Best viewed June through October, with full bloom in July-August.

English park and stables. The 200-acre park presents a thinned forest landscape with colorful plantings: sweetgums, tulip trees, purple beeches, American red oaks, and sumacs set the lake ablaze with golden reflections in autumn. The stables house a museum of horse-drawn carriages and testify to the importance given to horses in the 19th century.

activities.text: Family activity booklet. A free playful trail allows children to discover the gardens while having fun. Puzzles and treasure hunts adapted for ages 6-12 punctuate the walk through the park and gardens.

Park stroll. The 200 acres of greenery offer multiple walking possibilities. The Remarkable Tree Collection label rewards the exceptional quality of the centuries-old trees. The lake constitutes a soothing focal point for a contemplative pause.

visits.text: Château Raoul. Founded in the 10th century by Raoul the Large, who gave the town its name, this castle rises above the ramparts and the Indre valley. Rebuilt in stone in the 12th century after two fires, it was the seat of power in Lower Berry. Seven lords bearing the name Raoul succeeded one another here. Now owned by the Indre department, the castle can be seen on guided tours in summer and during the European Heritage Days.

Bertrand Museum. Housed in the mansion of General Henri-Gatien Bertrand, Napoleon's faithful companion, this museum presents highly diverse collections across 26 rooms. The aviary brought back from Saint Helena, the Aboukir saber carried by Bonaparte, the original plaster cast of Sakuntala by Camille Claudel, a cabinet of curiosities and Egyptology, Flemish and Dutch paintings, Gallo-Roman and medieval works compose an exceptional ensemble. The Empire collections testify to the Napoleonic epic.

Cordeliers Convent. This former medieval convent now houses cultural spaces and testifies to the town's religious past. The building's Gothic architecture contrasts with the contemporary installations within.

Historic center. From Château Raoul to rue des Pavillons, from place Monestier to place de la République, Châteauroux reveals a thousand years of history. The medieval quarter preserves numerous ancient half-timbered dwellings. Place Sainte-Hélène and place Napoléon evoke the town's connection with the Imperial epic.

activities.text: Indre riverbanks and Saint-Gildas meadow. Below Château Raoul, this 42-acre natural space harbors remarkably rich fauna and flora. A marked discovery trail allows you to observe European pond turtles, kingfishers, beavers, marsh fritillary butterflies, and numerous other species. The four-flower garden city well deserves its title.

Saturday market. The weekly market animates the town center with Berry products. Goat cheeses, local wines, seasonal vegetables, and artisanal specialties create a convivial atmosphere typical of the Berry prefecture.

Art Deco and Belle Époque architecture. Châteauroux has preserved several buildings testifying to its development during the Belle Époque. The Art Deco architecture of certain public facilities illustrates the urban modernization of the early 20th century and contrasts with the medieval heritage.

seo.h1_title: Indre Road Trip: Secret Berry and the Vallée Noire
seo.intro_paragraph: Discover authentic Berry between Renaissance châteaux and literary villages. Visit Valençay Castle with its 130-acre estate. Explore Argenton-sur-Creuse, the Venice of Berry, and its gallery houses. Climb to Saint-Benoît-du-Sault, classified as one of France's Most Beautiful Villages. Follow George Sand's footsteps through La Châtre and Nohant. Between medieval heritage and preserved nature, Berry cultivates its identity with discretion.
seo.seo_hook: Talleyrand's chateaux, George Sand's villages, romantic valleys. Intimate Berry reveals its gallery houses and remarkable gardens.

itineraries.title: Jura Road Trip: Lakes, Waterfalls & Mountains
itineraries.subtitle: From Arbois wine cellars to Salins underground galleries, from Chateau-Chalon cliffs to Chalain's turquoise waters: the Jura unfolds its terroirs, UNESCO heritage and reculee landscapes.
itineraries.climate: Best time: May-June and September-October, temperatures 15-25°C, waterfalls at their peak after snowmelt. Avoid winter (December-March): snowy roads, closed sites. Summer (July-August) remains mild but frequent afternoon thunderstorms.
specialties: Comté cheese aged in traditional cooperatives
Vin Jaune matured six years under veil
Vin de Paille sweet dessert wine

visits.text: Chat Perché Circuit: a 4-kilometer trail through 35 waypoints spanning eight centuries of Dole's history. Brass plaques depicting a cat guide your steps through cobbled lanes. You'll discover the Collégiale Notre-Dame dominating the skyline, Renaissance townhouses, the tranquil Tanners' Canal with its still reflections, and Rue du Collège de l'Arc. The circuit offers a free map at the Tourist Office, also available as an audio guide.

Louis Pasteur's Birthplace, located at 43 Rue Pasteur along the Tanners' Canal. Louis Pasteur was born here on December 27, 1822, in his tanner father's family home. The visit reveals the life of this scientist who revolutionized microbiology and hygiene. One room displays his pastel portraits created as a teenager, testament to his little-known artistic talents. His private laboratory is preserved exactly as he used it during his regular visits.

Collégiale Notre-Dame, the religious edifice dominating the town, built between the 13th and 18th centuries. Its imposing yellow stone bell tower can be seen from several kilometers away. The interior houses three naves with galleries and richly decorated side chapels. The church testifies to Dole's prosperity when it served as capital of Franche-Comté until 1678. The stained glass windows and liturgical furnishings tell the story of the city's religious history.

Tanners' Canal and river port. This historic quarter has kept the three-storey houses of the tanners, with cellars opening onto the pavement through a trapdoor. The passage Raynaud conceals an architectural surprise. Renaissance façades are reflected in the still water of the canal, where dozens of pleasure boats are moored.

Fine Arts Museum with a non-conformist approach to art history. Collections from the 16th to 19th centuries sit alongside contemporary artworks that break chronology. The Barbizon school and Comtois masters like Courbet, Pointelin, Brun, and Adler occupy pride of place. Dole's prosperity as capital of Franche-Comté shines through in the richness of Burgundian and Comtois art collections from the Renaissance to the 18th century.

activities.text: Walk along the Doubs and Loue rivers. The landscaped banks offer a bucolic setting for walking or cycling. The confluence of the two rivers creates a rich ecosystem observed by anglers and naturalists. The towpaths lead away from the city center toward preserved countryside landscapes.

Covered market halls on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays. The unique atmosphere of this market offering a wide choice of food stalls attracts both locals and visitors. Local producers sell Comté cheese, Morteau sausages, Jura wines, and fresh farm products. Conversations between vendors and customers create a warm atmosphere conducive to gastronomic discoveries.

visits.text: Saint-Just Church, visible from afar thanks to its ocher-yellow stone bell tower reaching 60 meters. The Romanesque building consists of three naves with galleries and numerous side chapels. The architecture testifies to Arbois's rich wine-growing past. The warm stone color gives this monument dominating the wine town its distinctive character.

Louis Pasteur's House, preserved in the state the scientist knew it. Pasteur returned here regularly throughout his life and set up a private laboratory where he developed the famous pasteurization process. The museum presents his research work and his connection to the region. Fun science workshops for families are organized during school holidays, making science accessible to the youngest visitors.

Wine and Vine Museum at Château Pécauld, a medieval building that was part of the old fortifications. The visit begins in the vineyards planted around the château. The rooms trace the work of the vine, the social history of winemakers, and the vinification of Jura grape varieties: Poulsard, Trousseau, Chardonnay, Vin de Paille, Macvin, and Vin Jaune. The collections explain why Arbois became France's first AOC in 1936.

Fruitière Vinicole d'Arbois at Château Béthanie. This cooperative founded in 1906 during the wine crisis testifies to the collaborative work of winemakers. It contributed to improving Jura wine quality and obtaining the AOC designation. The 14th-century cellars host tastings of Arbois and Côtes du Jura wines. The venue also organizes vineyard walks with audio guides via QR codes.

Cascade des Tufs at Planches-pres-Arbois, at the foot of a vast reculee. A family-friendly walk leads to this marvel gushing in an invigorating environment. Water cascades over tufa limestone formations covered with mosses and lush vegetation. The forest trail offers immersion in Jura nature just moments from the village.

Pont des Capucins, an 18th-century pedestrian bridge under which flows the Cuisance. Locals also call it the lovers' bridge. The view of the town from this tranquil spot reveals the Gloriette Tower, a square fortification from the 13th to 17th centuries standing 17 meters high. The bucolic setting invites contemplation away from the bustle of the center.

activities.text: Cellar visits and Jura wine tasting. Winemakers open their doors to introduce Savagnin, Chardonnay, Poulsard, Trousseau, and local specialties like Vin Jaune aged six years and three months under veil, Vin de Paille with its candied fruit aromas, and Macvin, a typical aperitif. The centuries-old vaulted cellars create the ideal atmosphere for understanding these exceptional wines.

practical_info.tip: Arrange for a designated driver

activities.text: Walk through the vineyards to Pupillin, 3 kilometers away. This village boasts an impressive concentration of winemakers per square kilometer and is considered the world capital of Poulsard. The south-west-facing slopes offer magnificent panoramas over plots that turn green, yellow, and russet with the seasons. The belvedere above the village opens a striking view over the vineyard and Bresse Comtoise.

Exploring Arbois's alleyways on foot. The yellow-ocher stone of the old town gives it a distinctive character perfect for wandering. Welcoming squares, beautiful winegrowers' houses, private mansions, romantic gardens, and arcades compose the scenery. The Cuisance bubbles and winds through the alleyways, adding a refreshing touch to the stroll.

visits.text: Maison du Comté, an interpretation center completely rebuilt in 2021 with modern architecture reimagining the traditional farm buildings of Haut-Doubs. The 3,000-square-meter interactive journey offers a sensory voyage discovering that there isn't just one Comté but multiple varieties with ever-changing flavors. Films, sensory games, and testimonies from industry actors tell of terroirs, know-how, and production techniques. The visit concludes with a guided tasting.

Collégiale Saint-Hippolyte from the 15th century, whose first stone was laid in 1415 by the Archbishop of Besançon. The church, enriched by donations from wealthy Poligny lords, owes its renown to Claus de Werwe, sculptor to the Duke of Burgundy. The building testifies to the Burgundian golden age with its sculptures and imposing architecture. The stained glass windows and furnishings tell the religious history of the capital of Comté.

Circuit de la Tour, marked on the ground, traversing Poligny's heritage. The itinerary reveals vestiges of the old Château de Grimont ramparts, the wine-growing quarter of Charcigny with its traditional houses, the Jacobins' crypt, and the Ursulines' Courtyard. Monasteries, cloisters, and churches unfold like hidden treasures. A free map and audio guide are available at the Tourist Office.

Old Pharmacy of the Hôtel-Dieu on the ground floor of the current hospital. This prestige room built in the late 17th century preserves its wood paneling, pharmacy jars, and period furniture. It testifies to Poligny's level of medical development at that time. Apothecaries prepared remedies and potions here according to doctors' prescriptions.

activities.text: Ascent of Croix du Dan, a 12-meter-high cross dominating Poligny and visible from the town center. The trail winds through forests and meadows to the summit offering panoramic views over the valley, vineyards, and first Jura plateaus. On clear days, the view extends to the foothills of Burgundy. The effort of the climb is rewarded by this 360-degree spectacle.

Walk through the vineyard between the Monts Martin, Grands Roussots, and Chevraudes terroirs. The trail crosses these three entities with different soils beneath the limestone cliff that generates the gravels characterizing Poligny's terroirs. Panoramas unfold over the town, the Collégiale Saint-Hippolyte, and the wine-growing slopes. In the Charcigny quarter, traditional wine-growing housing with trappon cellars tells the local story.

Visit to Comté cheese dairies. Poligny concentrates an impressive number of dairies and creameries dedicated to France's first AOC cheese by tonnage. Dairies like Poligny-Tourmont offer tours of aging in their cellars and the production of this cheese—1.65 million wheels produced annually. Tasting reveals the differences between young and aged Comté.

visits.text: Village of Château-Chalon, one of France's Most Beautiful Villages, perched on a rocky spur at 400 meters altitude overlooking the Seille valley. Cobbled lanes wind between blonde stone winegrowers' houses and tiled roofs. Vestiges of the old Benedictine abbey and medieval keep recall that in the 7th century, the nuns planted the first Savagnin vines that gave birth to Vin Jaune. The vaulted cellars tell the wine-growing story through the centuries.

Saint-Pierre Church, an 11th-century Romanesque edifice located in the village heart. The simple yet elegant architecture testifies to the influence of the abbey that dominated the site. The stones weathered by time and austere vaults create an atmosphere conducive to contemplation. The church houses several sacred artworks and offers a viewpoint from its parvis.

Maison de la Haute-Seille in a historic village mansion. This fun and interactive discovery of the Jura vineyard presents through video projections, audio testimonies, and touch screens the Château-Chalon AOC reserved exclusively for Vin Jaune. The 60 hectares of steep vineyards spread across four communes produce approximately 35 hectoliters per hectare of this rare wine aged a minimum of six years and three months.

Four belvederes offering different perspectives on the vineyard and valley. From these strategic viewpoints, the gaze embraces the steep slopes planted with Savagnin protected by limestone cliffs from northern and eastern winds. The south-southwest orientation provides maximum sunshine. The wine-growing villages of Domblans, Ménétru-le-Vignoble, and Nevy-sur-Seille compose the appellation with their abrupt slopes.

activities.text: Hike through the Sous-Roche and Puits-Saint-Pierre vineyards at the mouth of the Baume-les-Messieurs cirque. The trail meanders through these two emblematic terroirs where everything is difficult for the vines and winemakers. These constraints and an exceptional environment create the outstanding wine that is Château-Chalon. The route passes beneath the famous yellow rock and offers plunging views over the Seille valley.

Vin Jaune tasting at winemakers' estates. The 62-centiliter clavelin contains this wine ranked among the world's five best whites. After a minimum of six years and three months in oak barrels without racking or topping up, the yeast veil protects the wine and gives it its characteristic aromas of walnuts, spices, curry, and dried apples. Passionate winemakers explain this unique and ancestral process.

Lunch at a village restaurant with views over the vines. Terraces come alive on sunny days for savoring regional specialties like chicken with Vin Jaune and morels, or morel croûte. The pairing of Vin Jaune with an aged slice of Comté creates a perfect marriage. The peaceful atmosphere of this belvedere village invites you to linger over your meal.

visits.text: Imperial Abbey of Baume-les-Messieurs, a Cluniac site founded in the 9th century by Abbot Bernon before the creation of Cluny Abbey. The abbey church of Saint-Pierre preserves an exceptional 16th-century Flemish altarpiece made of carved oak wood decorated with gold leaf. This masterpiece ranks among the most remarkable in Europe with its profuse details. The three courtyards, tomb chapel, and abbot's lodging can be visited to understand monastic life.

Caves of Baume-les-Messieurs winding 120 meters underground with a 70-meter entrance worthy of a church nave. The hour-long guided tour crosses a succession of chambers with ceilings 20 to 80 meters high shaped by the Dard, an underground river. Stalactites and stalagmites adorn the galleries developed over 600 meters. The constant temperature of 11 degrees requires warm clothing even in summer. Some chambers serve for exceptional acoustic concerts.

Tufa Waterfall of Baume-les-Messieurs at the back of the cirque. The Dard emerges after its underground journey creating a magical spectacle in the midst of verdant landscape. Crystal-clear water cascades over mosses and limestone rocks in a luminous environment with sumptuous colors. A small trail allows you to pass above the waterfall to witness the crystalline purity of the water. The lush vegetation adds to the enchanting character of the place.

Reculée of Baume-les-Messieurs, a geological cirque over 200 meters high typical of limestone rock collapse. The vertical cliffs dominate the village nestled at the confluence of three valleys. This particularity offers a natural setting enhancing the abbey and houses with flagstone roofs. The belvederes of Granges-sur-Baume and Crançot overlook this grandiose landscape inscribed in the network of remarkable sites of Bourgogne-Franche-Comté.

Village of Baume-les-Messieurs, one of France's Most Beautiful Villages and doubly labeled as a Cité de Caractère. Picturesque lanes wind between blonde stone houses vying in charm. The village of 200 inhabitants has preserved its authenticity far from modern bustle. The soothing atmosphere protected by the rock invites wandering between gardens, fountains, and covered passages.

activities.text: Hike to the belvederes overlooking the cirque. The trail climbs via the Échelles de Sermu, steep but secured stairways, to spectacular viewpoints. From atop the cliffs, the plunging view reveals the village, abbey, and three cirques converging on this unique site. The route crosses deciduous forests and undergrowth before descending toward the caves. Count on a half-day for the complete loop.

Échappée Jurassienne trail crossing the site. This emblematic 300-kilometer itinerary links Dole to Les Rousses station passing through the major sites of the Jura. The portion near Baume allows hikes suited to walkers of all levels through landscapes of cirques, forests, and high-altitude meadows. The marked trails regularly offer panoramas over the surroundings.

visits.text: Grande Saline of Salins-les-Bains, UNESCO site inscribed on the World Heritage list since 2009. The mandatory hour-long guided tour descends into underground galleries built in the 13th century in the image of a cathedral, extending 165 meters long and 10 meters high. The two saltwater extraction wells are protected by majestic vaults. France's last salt pan, the tools, carts, and timbers impregnated with salt testify to 1,200 years of operation until closure in 1962. The Salt Museum completes the visit.

Fort Saint-André watching over Salins since the 17th century on the heights of the town. Rebuilt by Vauban after 1674 following Franche-Comté's attachment to France, this fort of medieval origin can be visited with a guide. The view from the ramparts embraces the entire Furieuse valley and the rooftops of the spa town. The visit concludes with a tasting of wines, Comté, and cured meats in the old vaulted rooms.

Old town and its private mansions testifying to past prosperity. Salins counted 8,500 inhabitants on the eve of the French Revolution, the second city of Franche-Comté thanks to white gold. Transverse lanes hide architectural treasures: fountains, covered passages, Renaissance houses, terraced gardens. The Collégiale Saint-Anatoile dominates the heights with its imposing architecture. The city stretches along the Furieuse between the two forts.

ThermaSalina spa, a thermal establishment completely renovated in 2017 over 2,800 square meters. The naturally salty waters denser than those of the Dead Sea provide a unique sensation of weightlessness. The richness in trace elements like magnesium, iron, and zinc plays a therapeutic role for rheumatism and joint flexibility. The wellness area open Monday to Saturday offers pools, hammam, caldarium, and water jets for passing visitors.

activities.text: Hike to Mont Poupet culminating at 851 meters altitude. The trail climbs through forests and meadows to the summit offering an exceptional panoramic view. On very clear days, you can even glimpse Mont Blanc. It's also the favorite spot for regional paragliders who launch from the summit. The descent allows observation of the cirque, forts, and Jura plateaus from different angles.

Hidden Treasures of the Salt City trail offered by the Tourist Office. Join Léa, Léo, and Lucas to discover how Salins developed thanks to its white gold. Historical anecdotes, prestigious monuments, beautiful viewpoints, and secret places unfold throughout the walking circuit. The elevation gain and stairs on the route provide access to the heights to admire the town.

Relaxation at the spa with saltwater treatments. The wellness area accessible without a cure offers hydro-baths, jet showers, mud applications, underwater saltwater massages, and scrubs. The water temperature between 30 and 34 degrees and exceptional salt content create a soothing floating experience. Half-day or full-day packages allow you to enjoy the therapeutic benefits.

practical_info.tip: Children under 12 not accepted

visits.text: Royal Saltworks of Arc-et-Senans, masterpiece by Claude-Nicolas Ledoux inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1982. This unique monument built between 1775 and 1779 commissioned by Louis XV was Europe's first monumental factory. The 11 buildings arranged in a semicircle within a 13-hectare park housed places of production and habitation according to a rational and hierarchical organization. The neoclassical architecture reflects the Enlightenment ideal of progress with its columns, pediments, and harmonious proportions.

The Ledoux Museum presents 60 models of projects built or dreamed up by this visionary architect. Theatres, mansions, toll houses, the ideal city of Chaux with its cemetery, house of pleasure, schools, prisons and industrial buildings reveal the scale of his utopian vision. The works, with their futuristic roundness, show a mind ahead of its time.

Lumières Center in the Berne Est, a 1,500-square-meter hall where the extraction boilers were located. Eight 3D films projected continuously transport visitors to UNESCO sites around the world through digital modeling. Palmyra, Leptis Magna, and other threatened or inaccessible treasures come to life in this immersive experience inaugurated in 2023. The impressive framework evokes that of an overturned ship.

Salt Stories exhibition tracing salt's origins, production, trade, and uses. The extremely rich and well-designed permanent exhibition explains how brine was extracted at Salins-les-Bains then transported 21 kilometers by wooden salt pipeline to Arc-et-Senans between 1780 and 1895. The Chaux forest provided fuel to evaporate the saltwater in the pans. Salt, the white gold of the 18th century, generated considerable revenues via the salt tax.

Un Cercle immense, a 13-hectare landscape development completing Ledoux's project. No fewer than 400 trees planted, 10 educational gardens on themes of seeds, soil, climate, recycling, vegetable garden, and biodiversity, plus 10 permanent gardens compose this second plant-filled semicircle. The harmonious dialogue between stone and vegetation restores to the monument the spirit of its creator. The garden festival transforms the site each summer with ephemeral creations.

activities.text: Stroll through the landscape and vegetable gardens bordering the buildings. The shaded paths invite contemplation of the architecture in its plant setting. Themed gardens illustrate different approaches to cultivation and biodiversity. Strategically placed benches allow admiration of the perfect arc of buildings from different angles. The harmony between nature and construction illustrates Ledoux's global vision.

Break at the café with a view of the hemicycle. The terrace offers an unbeatable perspective on the architectural ensemble. The exceptional setting transforms a simple coffee into a privileged moment. The local products served recall the territorial anchoring of this classified monument. The peaceful atmosphere of the park invites you to extend your stop.

visits.text: Lake Chalain, about 13 km from the stopover town, 20 minutes by road, the largest natural lake in the Jura with its 232 hectares of turquoise, lagoon-like water. This glacial lake at the foot of the first Jura plateau spreads its green reflections between Fontenu, Marigny and Doucier, lined with limestone cliffs and conifer forests. The fine sandy beaches offer a change of scene worthy of an exotic destination. The Neolithic site has revealed remains of lake dwellings 5000 years old. Waymarked footpaths go all the way round the lake.

The Hérisson waterfalls, about 16 km from the stopover town, 24 minutes by road, a listed natural site in the Grands Sites de France network, in the Hérisson valley and the Plateau of the 7 lakes. The lively torrent fed by the lakes of Bonlieu and Ilay creates 31 successive drops over 3.7 kilometres, including 7 main waterfalls. The Éventail waterfall takes its name from its very distinctive shape, 60 metres high. The Grand Saut majestically dominates the route. Pure water gushes out in a magical green setting.

The Maison des Cascades, about 16 km from the stopover town, 24 minutes by road, an audiovisual and museum space plunging into the heart of the valley's heritage. The geological origins of the site, its history and its legends are presented in a playful way. Entry is free with the car park ticket. The explanations help to understand how these spectacular falls were formed and the fragile ecosystem around them.

Joux Forest, one of Europe's most beautiful fir forests extending over several thousand hectares. The president firs, remarkable trees over 45 meters high and 4 meters in circumference, impress with their majesty. Forest trails wind beneath the dense canopy creating a plant cathedral atmosphere. The filtered light and silence conducive to wildlife observation invite contemplation.

activities.text: Full walk of the Hérisson waterfalls from the Maison des Cascades, about 16 km from the stopover town, 24 minutes by road. The 7-kilometre round trip takes about 3 hours and remains accessible all year. The well-laid-out path climbs alongside the torrent with steps and footbridges to admire the falls from different angles. The less sporty can opt for the easy 1.6-kilometre stroll from the Ilay car park. Bring good shoes, as it is slippery in winter.

Swimming at Lake Chalain on the laid-out beaches, about 13 km from the stopover town, 20 minutes by road. The clear water is inviting on hot summer days. The gentle terrain around the lake and the chance to combine walking and swimming make it a perfect family destination. Pedalos, kayaks and windsurf boards can be hired for water sports fans. Supervised swimming areas ensure safety.

practical_info.tip: Arrive early in high season for parking

activities.text: Tour of Lake Chalain on foot or by bike on the waymarked paths, about 13 km from the stopover town, 20 minutes by road. The full route of about 10 kilometres follows the shore through forests and meadows. The viewpoints offer varied perspectives over the turquoise water and the cliffs. The relatively flat path suits families with children. Picnic stops at the laid-out areas make the most of the natural setting.

visits.text: Saint-Pierre Cathedral dominating the town nestled in the Bienne gorge. The imposing religious edifice testifies to Saint-Claude's historical importance as a religious center. The architecture blends different construction periods with its Gothic choir and remodeled nave. The 15th-century carved choir stalls rank among the finest in Franche-Comté. The treasury contains remarkable pieces of religious goldwork.

Pipe and Diamond Museum tracing the two industries that made Saint-Claude's renown. The town was the world capital of pipes until the decline of smoking, with hundreds of workshops producing millions of briar pipes. Diamond cutting developed there thanks to local artisan know-how. The collections present tools, techniques, and exceptional pieces. Demonstrations allow understanding of the precision of these art crafts.

Bienne Gorges carved by the river between spectacular limestone cliffs. The impressive natural site can be discovered from the road or via hiking trails. The vertical walls dominate the tumultuous watercourse creating wild landscapes. Developed belvederes offer plunging views over the gorges and valley. The vegetation clinging to the rocks adds to the dramatic character of the place.

Fort des Rousses, about 19 km from the stopover town, 29 minutes by road, one of the largest forts in France, built between 1840 and 1862 under Louis-Philippe. The underground galleries run for several kilometres into the mountain. Part of them now houses the Comté maturing cellars, where 100000 wheels age in ideal conditions of temperature and humidity. The guided tour reveals the imposing military architecture and includes a tasting of the cheese matured in these unusual surroundings.

Lake des Rousses at 1060 metres altitude in the heart of the village resort, about 19 km from the stopover town, 29 minutes by road. This peaceful stretch of water surrounded by fir forests offers a rural setting made for relaxing. The flat path around the lake suits families. In winter the frozen lake turns into a natural ice rink. The laid-out shores offer picnic areas and supervised swimming zones in summer.

Les Rousses resort, a mountain village on the Swiss border, about 19 km from the stopover town, 29 minutes by road. The alpine feel comes through in the chalet architecture and the lively streets. In winter the French-Swiss ski area offers downhill runs and 200 kilometres of cross-country tracks. In summer, walking and mountain-bike trails criss-cross the high plateaux. The village keeps its authenticity despite tourist development.

activities.text: Hike to the Flumen waterfalls. The forest trail leads to these impressive falls gushing in a rocky amphitheater. Water cascades over several levels creating a striking sound and visual spectacle. The coolness released by the spray provides welcome relief on hot days. The route crosses varied landscapes between dense forests and flowery clearings.

Hike to Lake Lamoura in a preserved mountain cirque. The trail climbs through alpine pastures flowering in summer offering panoramas over the surrounding mountains. The high-altitude lake with cold waters reflects the surrounding peaks. The high mountain atmosphere contrasts with the cirque landscapes of the lower Jura. Montbéliarde cows graze in the meadows bordering the path.

Mountain biking in the Haut-Jura forests on numerous marked trails. The varied routes adapt to all levels from family trails to technical singletracks. Playful descents alternate with sustained climbs rewarded by open views. Electric mountain bike rentals allow less athletic riders to enjoy the itineraries. Themed circuits like the GTJ VTT cross the massif over several days.

Visit diamond-cutting workshops perpetuating century-old know-how. Artisans explain faceting techniques that reveal the stone's brilliance. The millimeter precision of the gesture and necessary patience impress. Contemporary creations sit alongside historical pieces testifying to the evolution of styles. Possibility to purchase directly from the cutters.

seo.h1_title: Jura Road Trip: Lakes, Waterfalls & Mountains
seo.intro_paragraph: Explore the wine valleys and landscapes of the Jura. Discover Dole and its historic center. Journey through the Arbois vineyards. Follow the valley around Poligny. Climb to Chateau-Chalon, perched on its hillside. Experience the springs and heritage of Salins-les-Bains.
seo.seo_hook: Lakes with emerald reflections, vineyards clinging to the slopes, high meadows carpeted with flowers. The Jura, between peaks and grape varieties.
featured_list: Arbois: tradition of the wine valley
Château-Chalon: a hilltop village crowned with vineyards
Salins: heritage of the salt springs
Baume: monastery of the limestone gorges

itineraries.title: Nièvre Road Trip: Morvan and Ducal Heritage
itineraries.subtitle: From Nevers to Decize, between the Loire River and the Morvan woodlands
itineraries.climate: Best time: May-June and September, temperatures 15-25°C, ideal for the Morvan hills. Avoid November-February (cold, damp, thick fog in the massif, 2-8°C). Frequent rainfall year-round, bring a windbreaker.

map_keywords: Faïence and Fine Arts Museum Nevers

visits.text: The cathedral boasts two opposing choirs, bearing witness to fifteen centuries of history. The 11th-century Romanesque choir features a fresco depicting Christ in Glory, while the 14th-century Gothic choir blazes with 1,052 square meters of contemporary stained glass.
Climb the Bohier Tower to discover panoramic views of the Loire and Nevers' slate rooftops.

Completed in 1491, the Ducal Palace is considered the first Loire château. Its Renaissance façade is adorned with sculptures inspired by Sebastiano Serlio's architectural treatise. Two medieval round towers dominate the Place de la République.
The Ducal Palace Heritage Centre traces the town's history through Nevers stone, Loire waters, and traditional crafts. An aquarium showcasing Loire fish species completes the visit.
The Faïence Museum houses 1,950 pieces of Nevers pottery from the 16th to 20th centuries, plus a collection of enameled glass on loan from the Louvre. The museum gardens provide a peaceful setting.
Saint-Étienne Church stands as one of France's best-preserved Romanesque churches. Built in the 11th century, it belonged to the Abbey of Cluny. Listed as a historic monument in 1840.
The Espace Bernadette Soubirous occupies the former Saint-Gildard convent where Bernadette lived from 1866 to 1879. Her body has rested intact in a glass shrine in the chapel since 1925.

activities.text: Follow the Faïence Route, a blue line traced on the sidewalks that connects historic pottery workshops to the town's monuments.
Stroll along the Loire quays, complete with an urban beach in summer. The royal river offers views of the Ducal Palace and cathedral.
Explore the Gardens of La Baratte, a centuries-old site with vegetable gardens, fountains, and wash houses. Restored former market gardeners' houses dot the landscape.

practical_info.tip: Free admission, peaceful walk

visits.text: Founded in 1059 by the Cluniac order, La Charité's priory earned the nickname "eldest daughter of Cluny." In the 12th century, the church stretched 120 meters long with over 400 dependencies across Europe.

Notre-Dame Church, inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage list in 1998 as a major stop on the Way of St. James, displays a radiating chapel apse and two carved tympana. The ambulatory capitals illustrate Cluniac inspiration.
The conventual buildings, rebuilt in the 18th century, preserve two cloister wings and staircases with ornate railings. They host exhibitions and cultural events year-round.
The Monks' Garden offers magnificent views of the church's chevet. Excavations have unearthed the foundations of buildings that preceded the current church.
The 14th-century medieval ramparts encircle the town. Two towers and several fortified gates survive, testifying to La Charité's strategic importance along the Loire.

activities.text: La Charité holds the "Book Town" label, with some fifty secondhand bookshops and bouquinistes. Browse through the shelves—each shop has its specialty.

practical_info.tip: Book fair in spring

activities.text: Wander along the Loire quays, redesigned for pedestrians. The royal river once served to transport goods from the Nivernais forges.
The Centre Culturel de Rencontre hosts concerts and exhibitions. The medieval town comes alive with cultural events.

visits.text: The Loire Museum occupies the former Augustinian convent, a historic monument listed in 1977. Its collections trace the history of traditional river trades: boatmen, fishermen, washerwomen, sand dredgers.
The museum's fine arts collection brings together works by renowned artists. The museum holds the "Musée de France" designation.
Founded in 1735 by Pierre Babaud de La Chaussade, the royal forges produced anchors and cannons for the Royal Navy. They employed 3,500 workers in the 18th century before closing in 1871.

The "Sévigné" portal, the entrance gate to the former forges dating from the late 17th century, bears a plaque citing Madame de Sévigné's visit in 1677. The riverside site has retained its historic façades.
Saint-Agnan Church dominates the town. Built in the 12th century, it preserves Romanesque and Gothic elements. Its bell tower serves as a visible landmark from the quays.

activities.text: Stroll along the Quai du Maréchal Joffre by the Loire. The river once facilitated transport of goods produced at the forges.
Discover the Eden Cinema, listed as a historic monument. Its Art Deco façade and Briare enamel sign make it an unmissable photo stop on the old N7 road.
Walking tour through town: former medieval castle with its keep (Rue Duguet), remnant rampart tower (Rue Chollet), boatmen's quarter.

practical_info.tip: Booklet available at Tourist Office

visits.text: The Museum of Art and History occupies the birthplace of Romain Rolland, winner of the 1915 Nobel Prize for Literature, and the 17th-century Hôtel du Duc de Bellegarde. It holds the "Maisons des Illustres" label.
The log-floating room evokes the activity that supplied Paris with wood from the Morvan for 400 years. In 1804, over 3,500 timber rafts arrived in Paris from Clamecy.
The museum preserves 6,000 posters by Charles Loupot, a 20th-century advertising giant—the world's most complete collection. Clamecy earthenware and Gallo-Roman archaeology round out the collections.

The Collegiate Church of Saint-Martin, built between the 13th and 16th centuries, dominates the town with its two towers. Its Flamboyant Gothic portal and ancient stained glass windows are worth the detour.
Bethlehem Church, a fortified Romanesque building, once served as the parish church for log floaters. Its square bell tower and thick walls recall its defensive role.

activities.text: Walk along the Nivernais Canal, opened in 1841 after three tunnels were cut. The towpath offers a shady stroll between locks and unspoiled landscapes.

practical_info.tip: On foot or by bike

activities.text: Visit the Log Floating Ecomuseum where enthusiasts teach you how to build a timber raft. Discover the epic of the floaters who descended the Yonne to Paris.
Relax in Parc Vauvert, a green haven in the heart of Clamecy. Its century-old trees and paths invite relaxation after the museum visit.

map_keywords: Mission of the Apostles tympanum Vézelay

visits.text: Inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage list in 1979, the Basilica of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine crowns the "eternal hill." Founded in the 9th century, it became a major pilgrimage site to Compostela in the 11th century when belief spread that it held Mary Magdalene's relics.
The inner portal tympanum depicts the Mission of the Apostles, a unique masterpiece of Romanesque art. Christ in Glory blesses the apostles and assigns them the mission to convert the nations.

The Romanesque nave (1120-1140) displays grand semicircular arches with two-tone voussoirs. Its sculpted capitals illustrate biblical and hagiographic scenes plus secular allegories in exceptional style.

The Gothic choir (late 12th century) floods the building with light. At the summer solstice, the southern windows project a line of luminous points down the center of the nave, symbolizing divine light.

The Monastic Fraternities of Jerusalem have animated the basilica since 1993. Saint Bernard preached the Second Crusade here in 1146; Richard the Lionheart and Philip Augustus departed for the Third in 1190.
The 14th-century medieval ramparts encircle the hill. The Porte Neuve and its towers protected the town from crowds of pilgrims.

activities.text: Wander the medieval village streets. Honey-stone houses, artisan workshops, and galleries punctuate the climb to the basilica.
Visit the Maison du Visiteur to discover the art and secrets of the basilica's builders through exhibitions and models.

practical_info.tip: Perfect complement to basilica visit

activities.text: From the hilltop heights, take in panoramic views of the Morvan, the Cure valley, and Burgundy hills. The landscape has remained unchanged since the Middle Ages.

map_keywords: Claude de La Porte cellar Tannay

visits.text: Listed as a historic monument in 1840, the Collegiate Church of Saint-Léger marries a 13th-century Gothic choir to a 15th-century Flamboyant Gothic nave. Eight buttresses pierced with arches support the building; the square bell tower adorned with gargoyles culminates with a rooster atop its cross.
The polychrome stone statue of Saint Roch from 1522 adorns the interior. The five bays of the nave are flanked by side aisles the same height as the main vault.
The Claude de La Porte cellar is one of Tannay's oldest known cellars. It once housed the communal wine press and oven.
Tannay preserves numerous towers that dominate the roofs, an architectural peculiarity of the village. Eight châteaux are listed in the area, witnesses to its aristocratic past.
The Coteaux de Tannay vineyard received PGI designation in 2011. Planted by the collegiate's monks as early as 1207 on clay-limestone soil, it now covers 25 hectares farmed by seven winemakers.

activities.text: Taste Coteaux de Tannay wines at local producers. Whites made from Chardonnay and Melon de Bourgogne, reds from Pinot Noir or Gamay perpetuate a thousand-year winemaking tradition.

practical_info.tip: Seven winemakers share the appellation

activities.text: Walk or bike along the Nivernais Canal. The towpath runs through Tannay, offering a shaded stroll between the Yonne valley and wooded hills.
Follow a section of the GR654, the Way of St. James from Vézelay. A reception center reserved for pilgrims marks this historic stage.

practical_info.tip: Stage toward Compostela

visits.text: Built from 1754, Saint-Léonard Abbey towers over Corbigny in all its height. A listed historic monument, it opens broadly to the sky, with light flooding its galleries.

The abbey hosts contemporary art and artist companies in residence. Krijn de Koning's blue room, Lawrence Weiner's works, and Vincent Mauger's wooden sphere dialogue with the centuries-old architecture.
The relics of Saint Leonard, a monk who died in 570, were transported to Corbigny in 882. The abbey took his name, as did the town that grew around it.

Saint-Seine Church, in Flamboyant Gothic style with three naves, was built in the early 16th century and consecrated in 1537. The high altar in pink and white marble comes from the former abbey church.
Ancient choir stalls line the choir, while cast iron holy water fonts and 18th-century baptismal fonts marry pink marble and copper.
The remains of the abbey's former fortified entrance on Rue de l'Abbaye protected the dependencies in the Middle Ages. The site served as a military hospital during World War I.

activities.text: Attend performances and artistic residencies by the La Transverse Association. The "Scène Ouverte aux Arts Publics" project transforms the entire town into a living stage.

practical_info.tip: Cultural program June to September

activities.text: Stroll along the Anguison, a tributary of the Yonne that flows through Corbigny. The peaceful banks invite relaxation at the gates of the Morvan Regional Natural Park.
Follow the Route Buissonnière, the Way of St. James. Corbigny was one of the first stops for pilgrims departing from the Basilica of Vézelay.

map_keywords: Niki de Saint Phalle fountain Château-Chinon

visits.text: Le Calvaire rises to 609 meters on the site of the former castle destroyed during battles between Charles the Bold and Louis XI in 1475. Three mission crosses dominate the site.
The panorama offers 360° views of the Morvan mountains, the Bazois plain, and the Yonne valley. The orientation tables were inaugurated in 2014.
The François Mitterrand Memorial, set in an oak forest facing the Bazois plain, is a place of remembrance dedicated to the former president. He loved to contemplate the horizon opening westward.
The Septennat Museum, housed in the former 18th-century Sainte-Claire convent, displays official and personal gifts received by François Mitterrand during his two presidential terms (1981-1995).
The Porte Notre-Dame, built in the 16th century with stones from the destroyed castle, remains the sole witness to the era when the castle overlooked the town.
The Château-Chinon Fountain, a monumental work by Niki de Saint Phalle and Jean Tinguely inaugurated in 1988, numbers among the five examples worldwide.

activities.text: Walk the 4.4-kilometer François Mitterrand trail, the former president and mayor of Château-Chinon's (1959-1981) regular route. Fifteen points of interest mark the itinerary.

practical_info.tip: Map available at Place Notre-Dame

activities.text: Hike in the Morvan from Château-Chinon, the massif's capital. Marked trails wind through oak and beech forests, valleys crossed by rushing streams.

practical_info.tip: Various circuits from town

activities.text: Discover the "From Earth to Sky" project at Le Calvaire: exhibition on meteorites and Morvan minerals, weather station history since 1934, climate evolution.

visits.text: The Thermal Baths, inaugurated in 1855, display neoclassical architecture with 1900 windows adorned with Briare enamels. The establishment opens onto a century-old six-hectare park.
Three springs feed the baths: "Romains," "Crevasse," and "Garenne." These chlorinated, sodic, and mildly sulfurous springs treat rheumatism and respiratory ailments.
The thermal park displays century-old oaks, plane trees, and cedars. Benches, basins, and stairways in Briare enamels take up the springs theme in Art Deco style, in Morvan colors: yellow and green.
Belle Époque villas adorned with carved fretwork, decorative red brick bands, and wrought-iron canopies dot the town. The bourgeoisie and aristocracy had them built in the 19th century.

The Château de La Montagne (16th century), entirely remodeled in the 18th by Jean-Baptiste Caristie, occupies a 25-hectare hamlet listed as a Historic Monument. Félix Duban redecorated the interiors in 1840.

activities.text: Enjoy the thermal SPA for a moment of relaxation: essential oil massages, hydrotherapy treatments, beauty rituals in a preserved natural setting.
Follow the heritage trail punctuated with markers discovering Belle Époque monuments linked to spa tourism: villas, casino, classified resort infrastructure.

practical_info.tip: Booklet available at Tourist Office

activities.text: Hike 10 kilometers between Bazois and Morvan, mainly through open landscapes with beautiful scenery and charming hamlets. Departs from the Tourist Office.
Relax at the Étang des Sources with its accessible fishing dock and "Family Fishing" label. Playground and picnic area complete the 8-hectare space.

visits.text: Built on a rocky island, Decize is nicknamed "little Venice." You must cross five bridges to go from one end to the other: Nivernais Canal, Aron, Vieille Loire, Loire, and lateral canal.

The confluence brings together the Nivernais Canal, Aron, Vieille Loire, and Loire at the end of the Promenade des Halles. This waterway crossroads offers magnificent views of the Saint-Léger-des-Vignes dam.
Saint-Aré Church honors the former Bishop of Nevers who wished to be placed in a boat at his death. It miraculously sailed up the Loire to Decize where he was buried.
The ramparts (12th century) preserve a watchtower, two towers, and a former drawbridge gate. The ruins of the former château of the Counts of Nevers are topped by a statue of the Virgin.
The Vieille Loire bridge (1777) allows the D981 to cross the waterways. One arch was demolished by the retreating French army on June 18, 1940, then repaired.

The Promenade des Halles, created in the late 18th century and extended in 1810, stretches nearly a kilometer. Three rows of century-old plane trees and lindens run along the confluence between town and waterways.

activities.text: The Port de la Jonction, awarded the Blue Flag label, accommodates 80 boats. This crossroads connects all French navigable waterways: Nivernais Canal, Loire, and lateral canal.

practical_info.tip: Quality services and harbor master

activities.text: Walk the Vieille Loire interpretive trail with its twenty educational panels. Quizzes and mini-games explore the Loire ecosystem and South Nivernais natural heritage.
Follow the EuroVelo 6 along the Loire or the Nivernais Canal bike route. Decize is a hub for river and cycling tourism.

practical_info.tip: Marked routes

activities.text: Fish in the waterways that earned Decize the nickname "Fisherman's Paradise." Pike-perch, chub, perch, pike, and catfish frequent these fish-rich waters.

practical_info.tip: Fishing license required

seo.seo_hook: The Morvan hills, pilgrimage basilicas such as Vézelay, the peaceful Loire. The Nièvre is a ducal and sacred land, between heritage and nature.
featured_list: Vézelay: pilgrimage basilica on the eternal hill
La Charité-sur-Loire: Cluniac abbey by the Loire
Nevers: cathedral with two choirs and faïence capital
Cosne-Cours-sur-Loire: royal forges town by the river
