itineraries.title: Loire-Atlantique Road Trip: Nantes and the Côte de Jade
itineraries.subtitle: From Nantes' urban creativity to the salt marshes of Guérande, passing through Clisson's vineyards and the wild coastline of the Guérande Peninsula.
itineraries.climate: Best season: May through September, with temperatures of 18–25°C and optimal sunshine along the coast. Avoid November through March: frequent rain, Atlantic winds, and damp chill. Summer can be windy by the sea.

map_keywords: Castle of the Dukes of Brittany Nantes

visits.text: The Castle of the Dukes of Brittany deserves at least two hours of your first day. Built in the late 15th century by Francis II and then his daughter Anne of Brittany, it presents a striking contrast: on the town side, a fortress of rough granite with 500 meters of wall walk punctuated by seven towers; on the courtyard side, a residential palace in white tuffeau stone of almost Renaissance refinement. Since 2007, the Nantes History Museum has unfolded its exhibition across 32 rooms and presents over 1,150 objects. An entire room is dedicated to the 1598 Edict of Nantes, and the sections on the Atlantic slave trade—Nantes was France's leading slave-trading port between 1700 and 1830—are considered international benchmarks. The courtyard and ramparts are freely accessible.

Don't miss the Pommeraye Passage, one of Europe's most spectacular covered galleries. Built between 1840 and 1843 by Louis Pommeraye, an ambitious young notary, it solves a simple problem with an ingenious solution: connecting lower town to upper town by absorbing a 9-meter elevation change across three levels via a monumental central staircase in wrought iron. At its inauguration in July 1843, 66 luxury boutiques had set up shop. The developer went bankrupt as early as 1849 despite the commercial success, an irony you'll appreciate as you walk the galleries. Jacques Demy filmed scenes from Lola here. Classified as a historic monument in 1976, renovated in 2015. Free entrance.

Lose yourself in the medieval maze of the Bouffay district, Nantes' historic heart. Half-timbered houses from the 15th century, cobbled streets, and Renaissance facades follow one after another. Place du Bouffay was once the site of public executions—details the well-restored facades no longer hint at. Continuing on, Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Paul Cathedral is worth a stop: its flamboyant Gothic interior rises 37 meters high, and the tomb of Francis II by Michel Colombe, a masterpiece of late-15th-century sculpture, stands in the north transept arm.

activities.text: Absolutely reserve your ticket online before visiting the Grand Elephant of the Machines de l'Île—performances often sell out several days in advance, especially in summer. This colossus of wood, leather, and steel stands 12 meters tall, 8 meters wide, and 21 meters long, weighing 48 tons. It roams the Parc des Chantiers, the former Dubigeon shipyards closed in 1987, for 30 minutes. If the operator sprays the crowd with the trunk, step back—fair warning. The Carousel of the Marine Worlds, inaugurated in 2012, is worth the trip on its own: 25 meters tall, 36 animated sea creatures across three levels. It won the prize for the world's most original attraction at the 2014 Thea Awards. Budget 3 to 4 hours for all three spaces (Grand Elephant, Machines Gallery, Carousel).

practical_info.booking: Online booking essential for the Grand Elephant

activities.text: As evening approaches, follow the green line traced through the streets to discover the Voyage à Nantes, a contemporary art route connecting works scattered throughout the city. Continue toward the Island of Nantes and its converted former shipyards. The Banana Warehouse, facing the Loire, houses galleries and restaurants in a 1930s industrial building. The view over the river from the redesigned quays, especially at sunset, is well worth the detour.

visits.text: Clisson Castle has watched over the Sèvre Nantaise from its height since a wooden castle stood here in the 9th century—the stone fortress you see today was built over five centuries, from the 12th to the 17th. This is where two great figures of Breton history were born: Olivier V of Clisson, Constable of France, and Francis II, the last Duke of Brittany and father of Anne of Brittany. Burned during the Vendée Wars, the castle was bought in 1807 by the sculptor Lemot, who turned it into a romantic setting for his artist friends. Its ruins, today preserved across four hectares, offer a remarkable panorama over the town below.

Then cross the old stone bridge over the Sèvre and wander the cobbled streets: ochre houses, Roman-style barrel tiles, umbrella pines, and round arches make you forget you're in Loire-Atlantique. After the destruction of the Vendée Wars, Clisson was rebuilt in the 19th century in a neoclassical style of Italian inspiration, driven by the Cacault brothers and the sculptor Lemot—one of a kind in France. Notre-Dame Church, rebuilt in the 19th century on the model of an Italian Romanesque church, is the most striking example, with its Tuscan campanile.

The wooden medieval market halls, built in the 14th century, rank among France's largest and oldest. They still host a market on Tuesday and Friday mornings—if you're there, it's the best place to buy local produce. Then venture into the Garenne Lemot Estate on the opposite bank: an English-style landscape park, temple, follies, and views of Clisson create a tableau of romantic beauty.

activities.text: The Clisson vineyard produces one of the most renowned Muscadets of the Nantes region. The Clisson communal cru, recognized in 2011, comes from old vines on granite—the Armorican bedrock, weathered into granite sand, gives the wines their smoky notes, candied citrus, and sweet spice. Head to the cellars of the local estates to taste this Muscadet made for keeping, aged on its lees for at least two years. Plan to book your tasting in advance.

Follow the Sèvre Nantaise on foot or by canoe from the Pont Caffino site. The river winds between granite cliffs, water mills, and vineyards: a setting that changes at every bend. If you're there in June, check the dates for Hellfest, the metal festival that turns Clisson into the world capital of the genre for several days and has drawn hundreds of thousands of festivalgoers since 2006.

practical_info.timing: Hellfest in June—verify dates on the official website

visits.text: Pornic reveals itself first from the Gourmalon corniche, opposite the castle and the old harbor: the finest vantage point over the town. Pornic Castle, whose origins date back to the 10th century, dominates the old harbor from its cliff. Its present silhouette, with romantic turrets, is chiefly the result of a 19th-century restoration—it is privately owned and cannot be visited, but the view of it from the quays is worth a look. Below, stroll the old harbor lined with colorful fishermen's houses. At low tide, the boats tip over onto the mud while the quayside restaurants come alive.

Noëveillard Beach, sheltered near the pleasure port, is Pornic's most family-friendly: it remains accessible even at low tide. To discover some of the wilder coves dotting the coast toward La Bernerie-en-Retz, take the coastal path from the Gourmalon gardens—the scenery shifts at every turn.

activities.text: The great walk of Pornic is the Customs Officers' Path. Within the municipality it runs 14 kilometers of coastline, from Saint-Michel-Chef-Chef to Les Moutiers-en-Retz. The stars of the route are the pêcheries: wooden huts on stilts, set above the water, used for carrelet fishing—a 25-square-meter square net the fisherman hauls up at high tide with a winch. They are entirely private and cannot be visited, but watching them from the path is a sight in itself. Bring water and good shoes; the route is easy but long.

Head to Pointe Saint-Gildas, some twenty kilometers north of Pornic. This rocky headland, classified as a Regional Nature Reserve, offers a panorama over Bourgneuf Bay and the island of Noirmoutier on clear days. The Customs Officers' Path passes here too: allow 7.5 km for the loop around the point, easily accessible.

visits.text: Piriac-sur-Mer is classified a Petite Cité de Caractère, and the label is deserved. The village has kept its Breton stone lanes with rare coherence. Set off on foot from the harbor: white houses with blue shutters, fishing pots stacked on the quays, pleasure boats in the basin. Saint-Pierre-ès-Liens Church (1766), its square tower clearly visible from the sea, deserves a look inside—the ex-votos and hanging ship models recall that Piriac was a deep-sea fishing port bound for Newfoundland as early as the 17th century. Émile Zola stayed here in 1876 while writing L'Assommoir, and Alphonse Daudet spent two consecutive summers here, in 1874 and 1875.

Castelli Point, at the far end of the municipality, is a geosite of major interest: its outcrops of mica schist and gneiss, 477 million years old, rank among the geological curiosities of the Armorican Massif. From the rocks you'll spot Dumet Island—the only maritime island in Loire-Atlantique, owned by the Coastal Conservancy since 1990 and now a bird reserve. A wild-coast panorama worth the detour.

activities.text: The coastal path from Piriac toward La Turballe is one of the finest walks on the peninsula. Over 5 kilometers, ochre mica-schist cliffs alternate with sandy coves, and you pass close to the famous Tombeau d'Almanzor, a granite block that stays above water even at high tide and around which a medieval legend has grown. It is in fact a geological curiosity, with holes drilled during 19th-century tin mining. The walk is easy, there and back or as a loop.
Fishermen sell their daily catch each morning on the quays, facing the boats. Fish and shellfish at their freshest—your chance to put together a good picnic before setting off on the coastal walk.

visits.text: Le Croisic harbor comes alive early in the morning: if you're there when the fish auction opens, you'll see sea bass, sole, and langoustine sold straight off the boats. As early as the 16th century, proud ship owners and captains secured the prosperity of this town, today one of the most architecturally beautiful on the peninsula. The Ministry of Culture has listed several 15th- to 17th-century houses lining the granite quays. Take time to stroll before the day's tourist crowds arrive.

The Océarium du Croisic grew out of a family story in 1968, when a fish wholesaler set up an aquarium to keep his customers occupied while they waited. It has since become one of France's largest private aquariums, with over 4,000 animals across 56 tanks. From Australian sharks to penguins, by way of an 800,000-liter Pacific ray tank—unique in Europe according to its designers—there's enough for 1.5 to 2 hours. The daily events (penguin feeding, shark presentations) are included in the ticket. No reservation required, but come early in peak season.

Climb Mont Esprit to take in the whole peninsula at a glance. This artificial mound was formed by the stone ballast that foreign ships dumped on arriving in port to load their cargo of salt—over time, the stones built up into a hill. The 360° panorama over the salt marshes, the ocean, and Le Croisic harbor is worth the climb.

The Côte Sauvage stretches south of Le Croisic, between granite cliffs and wind-swept heath. A maintained path follows the ocean from the Vigie parking lot to Pen Bron Point: allow about 2 hours there and back to enjoy the views over the coves and rocks. One of the peninsula's best spots, quiet outside weekends.

activities.text: Cycle the Guérande Peninsula between ocean and salt marshes. Bike paths connect Le Croisic, La Baule, and Guérande on a 25–30-kilometer loop. The route between the marsh basins is particularly beautiful in late afternoon when the sun catches the water mirrors. Bike rentals are available on-site.

visits.text: Saint-Guénolé Church in Batz-sur-Mer can be spotted from far off thanks to its 60-meter tower, built between 1660 and 1677 to replace a wooden bell tower struck twice by lightning. Climb the 184 steps of the spiral staircase: on clear days, the panorama sweeps from the island of Noirmoutier to Belle-Île. The Breton Gothic interior is also worth the detour—the organ, whose case dates from the 17th century, is among the oldest in the Pays de la Loire region. The tower is open from April to September. Access is managed by a local association.

The Salt Marshes Museum, founded in 1887 by Adèle Pichon, a nun and daughter of a salt worker, ranks among Brittany's oldest museums of popular traditions. Closed in 1970, it reopened in 1984 with 800 square meters of exhibits in former salt granaries. You'll find scale models of marshes, salt workers' tools entirely of wood, and a recreation of a 19th-century Batzien interior. A helpful context before wandering the marshes.

The Notre-Dame-du-Mûrier Chapel, steps from the church, deserves a stop. Its name comes from the Breton word murié, meaning brine—not from the mulberry tree, contrary to a local legend about a castaway guided to shore by a statue in a mulberry. Built in the 15th century, it features a beautifully sculpted porch. Then head to La Govelle Beach for a break facing the Atlantic.

activities.text: Walk the salt marshes between Batz and Guérande. The tourist office offers several marked trails, including a 4.3-kilometer salt worker village circuit crossing Kervalet, a hamlet of tall terraced houses in white stone that seems frozen in the 19th century, complete with its own Saint-Marc chapel where mass was held in high summer to spare salt workers the trek to town. Informational signs along the trails explain the ecosystem and harvesting techniques.

visits.text: Guérande's ramparts are among the best preserved in France—1,300 meters of intact walls, six towers, and four fortified gates, listed as a historic monument since 1877 and built mainly in the 15th century under Francis II. A third of the wall walk can be visited, via the stretch between the Saint-Jean tower and the Sainte-Anne tower. Enter through the Saint-Michel gate, the main entrance: this fortified 15th-century residence now houses the Guérande castle museum, which traces the town's history from its origins. From up there, the view over the slate roofs and the Guérande countryside is worth the admission.

Saint-Aubin Collegiate Church has stood at the heart of the town since the 12th century—the Romanesque base, burned in 1342, was raised by a flamboyant Gothic rebuilding in the 15th and 16th centuries. The feature is a rare one: five centuries of construction layered and legible in a single building. Listed as a historic monument in 1840. The 19th-century stained glass is remarkable, including the windows depicting Margaret of Antioch. Free access.

Wander the cobbled lanes of the medieval center, lined with half-timbered houses and private mansions. The market is held Wednesday and Saturday mornings inside the ramparts, under the market halls and on the Collegiate Church square—around 200 producers and traders. If you're there on a Saturday morning, it's one of the liveliest markets on the peninsula. A daily fish market (except Monday and Thursday) rounds out the offering.

Five kilometers north of Guérande, Careil Castle preserves Renaissance furnishings and 15th-century timber framing in remarkable condition. Its water-filled moats reflect the fortified silhouette of the manor house, built between the 14th and 15th centuries by the Careil family. Guided tours, arranged by the owners, grant access to still-furnished interior rooms.

activities.text: Join the salt workers in the pans to observe the harvest. From June through September, they rake coarse salt and gather precious fleur de sel from the water's surface with a wooden scoop—a gesture passed down since the Middle Ages essentially unchanged. The 2,000-hectare salt marsh around Guérande produces one of Europe's most renowned fleur de sel. Guided visits with a salt worker are organized; book ahead in peak season.

Cycle the trails between basins and dikes of the salt marshes. Light is especially beautiful in late afternoon when water mirrors reflect the sky. Bike rentals are available in town. The circuit connecting Guérande, Saillé, and Le Croisic spans roughly 15–20 km and remains accessible to all.

visits.text: La Baule's Grande Plage stretches 9 kilometers of fine sand in a crescent between Pornichet and Le Pouliguen—one of the longest in Europe. The resort was born in 1879 when two representatives of the Paris-Orléans Railway Company had the bright idea of building a seaside resort on what was then just a marshy spot called La Bôle. The pine forest, planted as early as 1849 by a Nantes ship owner to stabilize the dunes, made the town's reputation. The seafront esplanade gradually filled with villas between 1880 and the Roaring Twenties: the town counts more than 4,000 today, in Art Deco, neo-Breton, neo-Basque, and Belle Époque styles. The bay has belonged to the Club of the World's Most Beautiful Bays since 2011.

To appreciate the architectural heritage, stroll residential neighborhoods set back from the seafront. Themed guided tours of villas and architecture are offered by the tourist office (roughly 1.5 hours). Fifteen villas are distinguished as exceptional heritage in the architectural heritage protection zone. The Sainte-Anne Chapel, built between 1880 and 1904, regularly hosts exhibitions and concerts—check the program on-site.

La Baule's market runs every morning along the seafront and in covered halls. Regional oysters, Guérande fleur de sel, and Loire terroir products mingle here. An unmissable market for assembling a beach picnic or bringing edible souvenirs home.

activities.text: La Baule Bay is ideal for water sports thanks to regular westerly winds. Local operators offer lessons and rentals of sand yachts, kitesurfing, catamaran, and stand-up paddleboard directly on the beach. If you're a beginner, try sand yachting—the sport emblematic of La Baule, practiced on the beach at low tide.

visits.text: Go down into the submarine Espadon, moored in the fortified lock of the submarine base—the only submarine in France that can be visited afloat. 77 meters long and commissioned in 1960, the Espadon became famous in May 1964 when it became the first French submarine to cross the Arctic Circle beneath the ice pack, together with its sister ship Le Marsouin. The visit lasts about 45 minutes and takes you through every compartment: torpedo room, control room, quarters for the 65 crew members. Book ahead in peak season.

Escal'Atlantic, housed in the submarine base built by the German Army between 1941 and 1942 to shelter its U-boats, is a 3,500-square-meter museum-liner. The scenography immerses you in legendary transatlantic liners: luxury cabins, engine room, bar, promenade deck—you step into the 1930s and cross the Atlantic in imagination. Plan 1.5 hours on timed slots. Reservation advised.

Climb to the fortified lock's panoramic terrace for a 360° view of the entire site: port, Atlantic Shipyards, Loire estuary, and the Saint-Nazaire Bridge spanning the river 3.356 kilometers—France's longest suspension bridge at its inauguration in 1975. From the terrace, you'll also see works by Felice Varini painted on concrete bunkers, a large-scale contemporary installation.

activities.text: The Atlantic Shipyards, founded in 1862, sprawl across 100 hectares assembling the world's largest cruise ships. Bus tours allow you to traverse the yard and observe thousands of workers and technicians at work. The guide explains the entire process, from steel plate cutting to block assembly. A unique experience to grasp the industrial scale of contemporary ship construction. Booking required through the tourist office.

The Saint-Nazaire Ecomuseum traces the city's industrial and port history: post-war reconstruction (the city was 85% destroyed in 1942–1943), shipbuilding history, working life. A more intimate museum than technical sites, yet useful for understanding Saint-Nazaire's human context.

visits.text: Paimboeuf was Nantes' outer port in the 17th and 18th centuries: deep-draft vessels could not sail up the river to Nantes, and it was here, 50 km from the mouth, that goods changed ships. The town numbered nearly 9,000 inhabitants on the eve of the Revolution, while Saint-Nazaire had only 700—the roles were reversed in the 19th century. Stroll the redesigned quays: the colorful facades of fishermen's houses alternate with elegant ship owners' residences with wrought-iron balconies and dormer-windowed roofs. The Chaussée Neuve lighthouse, erected in 1854, is the only lighthouse on the Loire estuary—its signal is visible more than 15 kilometers away.

The Saint-Louis Church, built between 1875 and 1884, will surprise you with its rare neo-Byzantine style in the region—dome, vaults, and Eastern arcading in a Loire town is unforgettable. Inside, admire the classified high altar composed of fourteen precious marbles, and the grand canvas by Alexis Douilard depicting the Death of Saint-Louis at Tunis.

The Star Garden, a permanent work from the Estuary tour created by Japanese artist Kinya Maruyama during the 2007 biennial, sits along the Loire's edge east of town. Inspired by the Great Bear constellation and the four cardinal points, this garden with viewpoints and boardwalks offers one of the best vantage points over the estuary. Ideal for closing this road trip facing the river widening toward the Atlantic.

activities.text: Follow a few kilometers of the Martinière Canal by bike or on foot from the Carnet locks. This 15-km maritime canal, built in the 19th century to link Nantes to Saint-Nazaire while bypassing the Loire's sandbanks, was a hydraulic feat for its day: 55 meters wide, over 5 meters of draft, ten years of work. At the height of the Cold War, between 1958 and 1968, the United States ran a NATO base here to store strategic equipment—an episode that appears in no tourist guide.

seo.h1_title: Loire-Atlantique Road Trip: Nantes and the Côte de Jade
seo.intro_paragraph: From Nantes and its Machines of the Island to the salt marshes of Guérande, this 7-day road trip traverses two strikingly different faces of Loire-Atlantique. Inland, Italianate Clisson and its Muscadet vineyards on granite; on the coast, fishing huts on stilts in Pornic, the medieval ramparts of Guérande, La Baule's 9-kilometer beach, and Saint-Nazaire's industrial maritime heritage make this department among the most varied in the Pays de la Loire.
seo.seo_hook: From Nantes' mechanical elephant to Guérande's salt marshes: Loire-Atlantique blends urban creativity with maritime tradition.
featured_list: Nantes: cultural and creative capital with the Machines de l'Île
Guérande: intact medieval town at the heart of the salt marshes
La Baule: 9 kilometers of beach and over 4,000 Belle Époque villas
Clisson: Breton neoclassical town with Italian influences and Muscadet on granite
Saint-Nazaire: polar submarine and giant shipyards

itineraries.title: Loiret Road Trip: Orléans and the Châteaux of the Loire
itineraries.subtitle: In the footsteps of Joan of Arc along a UNESCO-listed Loire, between medieval strongholds, Eiffel's canal bridge, and the canals of the Venice of the Gâtinais.
itineraries.climate: Best season: April to June and September to October, with temperatures ranging from 15 to 25°C — ideal for exploring châteaux. Avoid July-August when heat can be oppressive, and November to February when grey skies and frequent Loire mists dominate the landscape. Spring is particularly enchanting in the gardens.

visits.text: Begin at Sainte-Croix Cathedral, one of France's five largest Gothic cathedrals: 140 metres long, 53 metres wide, with a spire reaching 106 metres. Its construction spans from the 13th century until 1829 — King Charles X inaugurated the portal on 8 May of that year, exactly 400 years after Joan of Arc lifted the siege. Henry IV financed its reconstruction from 1601 onwards, and Louis XIV had his royal sun added to the transept's rose windows, with his motto Nec Pluribus Impar. Don't miss the stained glass of the lower nave: ten grand scenes recount Joan of Arc's life, from Domrémy to Rouen. The great bell, named Sainte Jeanne d'Arc, weighs six tonnes.

In Place du Martroi, Joan of Arc's equestrian statue was cast in 1855. Look at the bas-reliefs on the pedestal: they retrace the whole epic, from the appearance of the voices to the liberation of Orléans. The originals are kept at the Museum of Fine Arts — the bronzes you see are casts. Every 7 May in the evening, during the Johannic Festivals, the city solemnly hands over the banner from this square.

The Joan of Arc House is a 1960s reconstruction of the residence of Jacques Boucher, treasurer to the Duke of Orléans, where Joan stayed from 29 April to 9 May 1429 during the siege. The original was burned in 1940. On the ground floor, a multimedia room screens a 15-minute panoramic film on the Hundred Years' War and the Maid's epic, with interactive terminals and mapping of her route. Upstairs sits the world's largest documentary collection dedicated to Joan of Arc: 37,000 books, journals, maps, engravings and films, accessible by appointment.

The Hôtel Groslot is among Orléans's most distinctive monuments. Its façade of red bricks arranged in lozenges was built between 1549 and 1558 by Jacques Groslot, bailiff of the city, under architect Jacques Androuet du Cerceau. King Francis II — married to Mary, Queen of Scots, son of Henry II and Catherine de Medici — died there on 5 December 1560, aged 16, while presiding over the Estates-General. The room where it happened is now the wedding hall, where 450 civil unions are celebrated each year. The visit is free: salon d'honneur, Aubusson tapestries, coffered ceilings.

The Museum of Fine Arts of Orléans occupies a building facing the cathedral. Its collections span from the 15th to the 20th century: Italian primitives, French school from the 17th and 18th centuries, pastels by La Tour. The bequest of Aignan-Thomas Desfriches in the late 18th century formed its core collection. You'll also find the original bas-reliefs from the pedestal of the Joan of Arc statue and works by Girodet. Allow at least 90 minutes for a proper visit.

activities.text: Walk along the redeveloped Loire quays to the George V bridge. The tree-lined promenade offers a panorama over the royal river — UNESCO-listed in 2000 — and its sandbanks. Guinguettes set up in season between May and September. It's one of the best places to take the measure of France's longest river from the bank.

Every year from 29 April to 8 May, the Johannic Festivals commemorate the city's liberation in 1429. Period-costumed processions, medieval markets, concerts and sound-and-light shows on the cathedral: it's France's oldest national festival still celebrated. If planning a visit during this window, book accommodation well in advance.

Wander Place du Châtelet and the pedestrian streets of the centre. On Saturday mornings, the market sets up under the plane trees with local producers, flowers, and Loire Valley specialities such as cotignac, a quince paste sold in small round wooden boxes — a typically Orléans souvenir since the Middle Ages.

visits.text: Caesar's Tower is Beaugency's oldest monument: this square Romanesque keep was built by Lancelin I, lord of Beaugency, between 1015 and 1030. It stands 36 metres high and commanded both the citadel's defences and control of the bridge over the Loire. In 1567, a fire during the Wars of Religion gutted the interior — only the shell of the four walls remains. The Tower is only accessible during Heritage Days, but its silhouette dominates the town from any street. Historians compare it to the keep of Loches, from the same period.

Beaugency Château has housed a digital art centre since 2021. Originally built in the 15th century by Jean de Dunois — the Bastard of Orléans, Joan of Arc's companion-in-arms — it later belonged to the Dukes of Orléans until the Revolution. In the 19th century it served as a poorhouse, then for decades as the Orléanais Museum. Today, its medieval and Renaissance halls host immersive light and digital installations. An unexpected experience within 15th-century architecture. Buy tickets in advance during peak season.

The Notre-Dame abbey church dates from the 12th century — it's where two councils were held that changed the history of France: in 1104, Philip I was ordered to separate from Bertrade of Montfort; in 1152, Louis VII the Young had his marriage to Eleanor of Aquitaine annulled, and she wed Henry II of England a few weeks later, indirectly triggering the Hundred Years' War. Push open the door to see the 12th-century carved capitals and the still-intact Romanesque choir.

Beaugency's old bridge spans the Loire on some twenty stone arches. The first mention of a bridge at this spot dates to 1145. It's one of the rare old bridges still standing on the Loire. From the bridge, the view of the medieval town's towers — Caesar's Tower, the abbey church belfry — is the classic photo of Beaugency. Go at the end of the day for the light.

activities.text: Walk along rue du Pont and its half-timbered houses from the 15th and 16th centuries. The Renaissance town hall — listed as a Historic Monument as early as 1840 — is worth a stop: upstairs, the ceremonial hall holds eight 17th-century embroidered hangings. The climb toward the château offers open views over the Loire and the slate roofs.

Rent a bicycle and follow the Loire à Vélo path on the levees between Beaugency and Meung-sur-Loire. The track is flat, waymarked and hugs the river between vineyards and wooded islands. Plan 15 to 20 km depending on your halfway point. Bike rental is available in town.

visits.text: The Château de Meung-sur-Loire is nicknamed the château of two faces — with good reason: on the town side, the 13th-century façade shows its medieval defensive towers; on the garden side, an elegant 18th-century classical façade, bishop's blood red in colour, opens onto a 7-hectare park. The château was the residence of the bishops of Orléans from the Middle Ages until the Revolution. It welcomed Louis XI, Francis I, and Joan of Arc herself, who took it back from the English on 14 June 1429. Its darkest part: the oubliettes. The poet François Villon was imprisoned there in 1461 by Bishop Thibault Daussigny — he spent four months there in terrible conditions. These underground chambers can still be visited and the staging is worth the detour.

The Saint-Liphard Collegiate Church raises its Romanesque bell tower at the heart of the town. The crypt goes back to the 6th century and holds the tomb of Saint Liphard, the hermit who gave the town its name. The present collegiate church dates mainly from the 12th century; note the carved capitals and the Romanesque arches of the nave. It was around this sanctuary that the episcopal lordship of Meung developed.

Water mills line the channels of the Mauves that runs through the town. These medieval installations driven by the river bear witness to the milling activity that made Meung prosperous for centuries. Some buildings are still recognisable as you walk along the town-centre watercourses.

activities.text: Stroll the château's 7-hectare park. Beneath the foliage you can still make out the layout of the English-style garden created on the eve of the Revolution. Lime-tree alleys, the bed of the landscaped rivers and the ghost of a music pavilion — designed by Le Camus, architect to the Duke of Choiseul — compose a romantic tableau. Bishop Jarente de la Bruyère had invested his entire fortune to recreate a little Versailles here; the Revolution drove him out before he could enjoy it.

Wander Meung's medieval centre streets. The town has preserved its period urban fabric: narrow lanes, half-timbered houses, and a few hundred metres on, remnants of the old Loire bridge that Joan of Arc attacked on 15 June 1429 to cut English reinforcements before the Beaugency victory.

visits.text: The Château de Sully-sur-Loire is one of the finest examples of a medieval fortress on the Loire. Commissioned in 1396 by Gui VI de La Trémoille, it rises on the left bank of the river, surrounded by moats thirty metres wide, still filled with water. Its most precious treasure is invisible from outside: in the keep's roof space, a 14th-century pointed barrel timber frame in oak, in an exceptional state of preservation. Specialists date it precisely by dendrochronology — the trees were felled in the winter of 1388-1389. Voltaire was exiled here in 1716 by the regent; Louis XIV stayed as a child during the Fronde. Don't miss the ten tapestries of the Psyche hanging, Flemish work from the 17th century.

The château's park invites a leisurely wander around the moats. Centuries-old trees, the perspective onto the circular towers and the view over the Loire make for a very photogenic setting. It's also in this park that the Heures Historiques festival is held every May, the largest multi-era gathering in France: between 1,200 and 1,500 costumed reenactors parade from Prehistory to the wars of the 20th century.

The Saint-Ythier Collegiate Church blends 12th-century Romanesque with flamboyant Gothic. It holds the tombs of the lords of Sully. Just nearby, spot the House of Henry IV, a 16th-century dwelling, and the timber spire of Saint-Germain Church — one of the tallest in France.

activities.text: Every year between May and June, the Sully and Loiret Music Festival offers classical, baroque and jazz concerts in the château and other heritage sites in the département. Created in 1973, it's one of the oldest festivals of its kind in the region. Check the programme before your stay if you're coming during this period.

Follow the banks of the Loire by bike or on foot. The Loire à Vélo passes through Sully between levees and wooded islands. The path between Sully and Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire (8 km) is particularly pleasant and takes you to the Benedictine abbey of Fleury, founded in the 7th century, which holds the relics of Saint Benedict.

visits.text: Gien Château overlooks the Loire from its polychrome brick platform — an Early Renaissance façade commissioned from 1482 onwards by Anne de Beaujeu, daughter of Louis XI and regent of France. It was she who transformed the former medieval fortress into a comfortable residence. Since 1952, the château has housed the Museum of Hunting, holder of the Musée de France label: falconry, venery and shooting are illustrated through paintings by Desportes and Oudry, 17th-century tapestries, antique weapons and mounted Chambord stags. A collection of 4,000 hunt buttons and hunting horns completes the display.

The Gien pottery works were founded in 1821 by an Englishman, Thomas Hall, who had spotted the site's advantages: siliceous pebbles from the Loire for the pastes, the state forest for the kilns, and the canals for transport. For two centuries the manufactory has kept alive the famous Gien Blue. The museum retraces the firm's history through its historic collections — armorial tableware, tile panels, fine faience — and a guided tour of the works (by reservation, every Wednesday morning) lets you see the artisans at work.

The stone bridge spans the Loire opposite the château. The view from the bridge — brick château against the sky, river and wooded islands — is Gien's postcard image. To the left, looking upstream, Sainte-Jeanne-d'Arc Church raises its red and black brick tower at the top of the mound, right beside the château.

activities.text: On Saturday mornings, the market enlivens the Loire quays opposite the château. It's the chance to find Gien faience pieces at factory prices in the surrounding shops — seconds and end-of-line stock available at the manufactory shop. Several local artisans also exhibit at the town's seasonal markets.

Use the afternoon to explore the Faience Route between Gien and Briare. This circuit links workshops, museums and ceramic and faience shops within a radius of about thirty kilometres. Gien is also a stop on the Jacques-Cœur tourist route and on the Loire à Vélo.

map_keywords: Museum of Two Maritime Traditions Briare

visits.text: The Briare canal bridge is the must-see monument of eastern Loiret. Built between 1890 and 1894 by the Gustave Eiffel company for the masonry and Daydé & Pillé for the metal trough, it was inaugurated on 16 September 1896. Its 662 metres in length, its 14 piers in the Loire and its 72 lamp posts make it the largest metal canal bridge in France — for a century it was the longest in the world, overtaken only in 2003 by the Magdeburg canal bridge. Crossing it on foot, you have the canal water at your feet and the Loire 11 metres below. The effect is striking. Listed as a Historic Monument in 1976, it draws 300,000 visitors each year.

The Musée des Deux Marines retraces the history of river navigation on the Loire and the canals. Models of flat-bottomed boats, photographs of the boatmen and onboard objects reconstruct life on the water in the 19th century, when the Briare Canal — one of France's oldest canals, opened in 1642 — linked the Loire to the Seine across 54 kilometres and 38 locks.

activities.text: Operators offer electric boats for hire without a licence to navigate the canal running alongside the Loire and pass beneath the canal bridge from the water. It's the best way to understand the structure from the inside. Allow around 2 hours for a comfortable round trip.

Settle on a terrace by the marina to watch the pleasure barges pass through the locks. Briare has 7 locks and 14 bridges — its boatmen called it the town of 14 bridges. The Briare Canal still links the Loire to the Loing Canal and the Seine basin today.

visits.text: Montargis, the Venice of the Gâtinais, is worth an early start to walk its bridge circuit before the flow of visitors. The town has 132 bridges and footbridges spanning the Briare Canal, the Loing and several watercourses, cutting the old town into small islets. The Pêcherie quarter — the former fishermen's quarter that supplied Paris with live fish via the canals — is the most picturesque: half-timbered houses over the water, footbridges and cobbled lanes. Don't miss the Victor Hugo Footbridge, built in 1881 to plans by the Eiffel company, arching like a rainbow over the canal.

The Girodet Museum is set in the Durzy Garden. It pays tribute to Anne-Louis Girodet-Trioson, born in Montargis in 1767: a pupil of David and winner of the Prix de Rome in 1789, he was one of the pivotal painters between neoclassicism and romanticism. The museum, holder of the Musée de France label since 2002, displays paintings, sculptures and drawings from the 16th to the 20th century, with fine pieces by David, Géricault and James Pradier. The collection brings together more than 6,000 works.

The remains of Montargis château dominate the mound north of the town. Of the royal fortress that welcomed several kings of France, only a few sections of wall and a landscaped park remain. But the view over Montargis and its canals from the heights is worth the detour.

activities.text: Don't leave without tasting Montargis pralines. Legend attributes them to the kitchen officer of the Duke of Plessis-Praslin, who is said to have invented this confection in 1636 — almonds caramelised in cooked sugar. Several confectioners keep the recipe alive in the town centre. If you're lucky, you'll see the artisans working the boiling sugar in copper cauldrons.

From April to October, operators offer 2-hour guided cruises on the Briare Canal from Saint-Roch port. It's the most pleasant way to see Montargis from the water, with lock passages and commentary on the history of the canals. Book ahead in July-August.

On Saturday mornings, a lively market sets up in the town centre. Gâtinais producers, market gardeners and artisans bring the quays and squares to life. It's also the chance to find forest honey, poultry from the region and, naturally, pralines in every form.

seo.h1_title: Loiret Road Trip: Orléans and the Châteaux of the Loire
seo.intro_paragraph: Follow in Joan of Arc's footsteps at Orléans — Gothic cathedral begun in 1287, the Maid's House, the Hôtel Groslot where Francis II died — then trace the Loire upstream to the medieval strongholds of Beaugency, Meung-sur-Loire and Sully, whose 14th-century timber frame is a conservation masterpiece. Descend toward Gien and its faience works founded in 1821, admire the Briare canal bridge built by Eiffel in 1896, and finish in Montargis, the Venice of the Gâtinais and its 132 bridges over the canals. Four days along a UNESCO-listed Loire between royal châteaux, industrial heritage and Loire Valley gastronomy.
seo.seo_hook: Joan of Arc frees Orléans, châteaux guard the Loire, Eiffel spans the river, canals mirror façades. The Loiret: river and history.
featured_list: Orléans: 140-metre Gothic cathedral inaugurated in 1829 and city of Joan of Arc
Beaugency, Meung-sur-Loire and Sully châteaux: medieval strongholds on the Loire's edge
Briare canal bridge: 662 metres of Eiffel metalwork, inaugurated in 1896
Montargis, the Venice of the Gâtinais: 132 bridges and pralines invented in 1636

itineraries.title: Lot-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Villages
itineraries.subtitle: From bastide to bastide, between the Lot Valley and Dropt vineyards
itineraries.climate: Best time: April to June and September to October, with temperatures of 16–26°C and generous sunshine. Avoid July–August (intense heat up to 35–38°C, afternoon storms). Mild winters (8–12°C) but rainy; roads are passable year-round.

visits.text: Start with Saint-Caprais Cathedral, built in the 12th century on the foundations of a 6th-century basilica sacked by the Normans in 853. Its history is eventful: converted into a hay store for the horses of the revolutionary army in 1791, it did not officially become a cathedral until 1802, after the destruction of the former Saint-Etienne Cathedral. Listed as a historic monument in 1862 and inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as part of the Routes of Santiago de Compostela since 1998, it is worth visiting for its interior, painted from floor to ceiling. The decoration was created between 1845 and 1869 by Jean-Louis Bezard, a pupil of Ingres, who depicted the martyrs of Agen, including Saint Caprais himself. Do not miss the grand Stoltz organ with its 45 stops, said to have been donated by Empress Eugenie in 1858.

The Pont-Canal is Agen’s other source of pride and one of the most spectacular structures in south-western France. Built between 1839 and 1847 from dressed Quercy stone, it measures 539 metres, has 23 arches and carries the Canal latéral à la Garonne across the river. Its foundation stone was laid with great ceremony by the Duke of Orléans, son of Louis-Philippe, on 25 August 1839. It remained France’s longest canal bridge until the Briare Canal Bridge opened in 1896. Walk across it or follow it from the riverbanks: the view along its arches is well worth seeing, especially in the late morning.

The 13th-century Jacobins Church has housed part of the Fine Arts Museum’s collections since 2025 while the museum is closed for renovation. Housed in four 16th- and 17th-century townhouses, the museum is one of the most important in south-western France. Its collections notably include five paintings by Goya, bequeathed in 1899 by the Count of Chaudordy, French ambassador to Spain. Goya’s self-portrait, dating from around 1783, is its centrepiece, alongside the Venus of Mas-d’Agenais, a Gallo-Roman sculpture from the 1st or 2nd century discovered in 1876. Check the progress of the collections’ relocation to the Jacobins Church before your visit.

Wander along Rue des Cornieres with its medieval arcades and half-timbered houses. It is Agen's historic shopping street, where shops and cafes follow one another beneath covered galleries typical of the bastides of south-western France. A cafe terrace under the arcades is the obvious place to watch local life go by.
Head to the place des Laitiers, which marks the site of the former Saint-Étienne cathedral, destroyed during the French Revolution. Today it is a lively square where a market is held.

activities.text: Visit the Halle du Pin market or Place Durand to taste Agen prunes, a speciality linked to the introduction of the Ente plum by the monks of Clairac in the 14th century. You will also find hazelnuts, foie gras, Buzet wines and farmhouse cheeses. The covered and open-air markets operate from Tuesday to Sunday morning.

Follow the Canal de Garonne by bicycle or on foot along the towpath from the canal bridge. The greenway runs beside the water for several kilometres in a setting lined with plane trees. If you have time, continue to the village of Le Passage-d’Agen: the finest view of the canal bridge is from the opposite bank.

map_keywords: Allée des 3000 pas (3,000 Steps Walk), Nérac
Moulin des Tours (Mills of Barbaste), Barbaste

visits.text: The Henri IV Chateau-Museum is one of the rare surviving Renaissance buildings in Lot-et-Garonne. Of the original four-wing quadrangle, only the north wing remains, the sole survivor of the Revolutionary destruction. What it reveals is elegant: an exterior gallery with twisted columns and carved capitals, characteristic of the so-called Louis XII style. Built in the 15th century by Alain d'Albret the Great, great-great-grandfather of Henri IV, the chateau became a royal residence in 1484 when the Albrets came to the throne of Navarre. This is where Henri of Navarre, the future Henri IV, lived with Marguerite de Valois between 1577 and 1582. Allow an hour to walk through the rooms devoted to the Albret saga and the Renaissance court of Nerac.

Behind the château lies Parc de la Garenne, where Queen Margot had the Allée des 3,000 Pas laid out, a walk of more than 2 km beneath centuries-old oaks along the Baïse. Marguerite of Angoulême, sister of François I, turned Nérac into a literary court where she welcomed Clément Marot and Lefèvre d’Étaples and influenced Calvin. Her daughter Jeanne d’Albret converted to Protestantism here. Take the time to follow the avenue to its end: the atmosphere truly feels timeless.

Along the walk, spot the Renaissance fountains: Saint-Jean Fountain, Fleurette Grotto, and Dauphin Fountain. These ornamental elements attest to the refinement of the Albret court in the 16th century. Fleurette Grotto takes its name from a local legend connected to young Henri IV.

In Petit Nérac, on the right bank of the Baïse, meander through Rue Séderie lined with half-timbered houses. The Old Bridge offers beautiful views over the port and former wharves. This is where barges loaded with Armagnac and flour once departed for Bordeaux.

Four kilometres to the north-west, the Moulin des Tours de Barbaste is a fortified mill. Built in the 12th century and bought by the Albret family in 1308, it was a favourite stopover of Henri IV himself, who sometimes signed his letters as the 'Miller of the Tours de Barbaste'. The ten-arch Romanesque bridge beside it is one of the oldest in the region. Make the detour if you can.

activities.text: The market runs on Allées d'Albret, featuring farmhouse cheeses, Quercy melons, cèpes in season, and products from Pays d'Albret. Arrive early—the best producers sell out quickly.

Head to Nérac port to board La Gabare Le Prince Henry, a boat ascending the Baïse to Nazareth Lock. The cruise lasts roughly an hour and follows Parc de la Garenne from the water—the perspective on wooded banks and château is breathtaking. Inquire for current schedules at the Albret tourism office.

visits.text: Monflanquin is one of the best-preserved bastides in south-western France. Founded in 1256 by Alphonse of Poitiers, brother of Saint Louis, it has an oval layout that is very unusual for a hilltop bastide, with streets arranged in a grid around the central arcaded square. Its fortifications, strengthened in 1282 after the territory was ceded to the English, were dismantled in 1632 on Richelieu’s orders. The village has since been classed among France’s Most Beautiful Villages. Begin at Place des Arcades: it has been the vibrant heart of the bastide for 770 years, and the Thursday market has been held here without interruption since 1256.

On the square, look out for the Black Prince's House with its 14th-century mullioned windows with bilobed tracery. Edward of Woodstock, known as the Black Prince and son of King Edward III of England, is said to have stayed here during the Hundred Years' War, at a time when Monflanquin passed alternately into French and English hands.

Saint-André Church retains its 13th-century portal. Burned in 1559 during the Wars of Religion and subsequently left in ruins, it was rebuilt: a major restoration took place in 1715, the vaults were redone around 1860 and the current bell tower dates from 1923. The somewhat composite building clearly reflects the turbulent history of this frontier bastide.

Lose yourself in the carrerots, the medieval lanes spanned by pontets, small bridges linking the houses at upper-floor level. The grid plan has remained intact since 1256 and every passageway offers a different view of the rooftops and the surrounding countryside. It is the best way to understand the urban logic of these medieval new towns.

The Bastide Museum, housed above the tourist office, recounts the creation of the 350 bastides of south-western France between the 13th and 14th centuries, covering the Franco-English rivalry, urban layouts, charters of customs and everyday life. The displays combine models, audio recordings and period costumes. A medieval escape game is also available for families.

Climb up to the Cap del Pech, the highest point of the bastide at 181 metres. On a clear day you can make out the Chateau de Biron to the south and the rolling countryside of the Haut Agenais stretching to the horizon, a landscape that really does recall Tuscany, with its rows of plum trees and rounded hills.

activities.text: Stroll around the Place des Arcades market on Thursday morning, the very same market that has been held here since 1256. Local producers from the Haut Agenais sell fruit, vegetables, farmhouse poultry, cheeses and Bergerac wines. In summer, an evening market takes over in a festive atmosphere.

practical_info.best time: Thursday morning, evening market in summer

activities.text: Book a guided tour with Janouille la Fripouille, the theatrical jester-guide who has made the bastide his playground for years. His storytelling blends verified historical anecdotes, Gascon humour and banter with the audience. The night tours in summer are especially popular, so book ahead.

practical_info.booking: Booking advised at tourism office; night tours in summer

activities.text: In August, the Medieval Days transform the village over the weekend of 15 August, with troubadours, knights fighting on Cap del Pech, fire shows and a grand period banquet in a thoroughly festive atmosphere.

visits.text: Villeneuve-sur-Lot is the largest riverside bastide in south-western France, founded in 1264 by Alphonse de Poitiers under a paréage agreement with the Benedictine abbey of Eysses. Its originality lies in its position astride the Lot. Begin with the Pont des Cieutat, also known as the Old Bridge: its uneven arches have spanned the Lot since the 13th century and three fortified towers once guarded the crossing. The view from the bridge over the pink-brick houses along the river is one of the most photographed in the department.

At the bridge's north entrance, don't miss the Chapel of Notre-Dame-du-Bout-du-Pont in rose brick. This small pilgrimage chapel once welcomed boatmen sailing the Lot before facing the rapids downstream.

Place Lafayette is the heart of the bastide, laid out in the typical grid pattern around a central arcaded square. The market hall and covered arcades house cafés and shops. Sitting at an outdoor café to watch the town come alive is a must: Villeneuve is a living town, not a museum.

The Porte de Paris and Porte de Pujols are two square red-brick towers dating from the 14th century that once closed the northern and southern entrances to the bastide. They contained portcullises and machicolations. Still standing today, they shape the urban landscape and bear witness to the fortifications built from 1313 onwards.

Sainte-Catherine Church, in Romano-Byzantine style and consecrated in 1937, merits a look despite its relatively recent construction. Financed through the support of Georges Leygues, minister and local native son, it rose on the ruins of a 13th-century medieval church. The interior holds splendid 15th-century stained glass windows recovered from the old church, plus five gilded wooden statues that are listed. Note: restoration work began in spring 2024 and will span several years.

Walk through the streets of the old centre in search of the half-timbered houses with corbelled upper floors. Their overhang above the street made it possible to gain living space upstairs without paying more property tax, which was calculated on the ground area. A very pragmatic medieval principle.

activities.text: Visit Place Lafayette market to taste Agen prunes, Quercy melons, and farmhouse cheeses. Villeneuve's market is among the region's liveliest—arrive before 10 a.m. for the best producers.

Head to the water sports base to rent a canoe, pedalo, or electric boat to navigate the Lot. The river is navigable on this stretch and wooded banks offer a peaceful contrast to town life. Allow 2 hours for a leisurely outing.
Follow the Lot's banks on the towpath—routes where horses once towed barges upstream laden with wood, wine, or prunes. The walk is easy and shaded, ideal for late afternoon.

map_keywords: Gate of the English (Porte des Anglais), Pujols

visits.text: Pujols stands at 180 metres on a spur overlooking the Lot Valley and is classed among France's Most Beautiful Villages. Enter the village through the 15th-century Saint-Nicolas Church, which is literally part of the fortifications: its bell tower rises above the north gateway and forms a single structure with the defensive walls. This rare and original architectural solution says a great deal about the military role of the site in the Middle Ages.

Open the door of Sainte-Foy Church, on the southern edge of the village overlooking the hillside. Built in the first half of the 16th century, it has a Latin-cross plan with two additional side chapels. Inside, 16th-century frescoes depict Saint Catherine, Saint George and the Assumption of Mary. The paintings have been weathered by the centuries but remain perfectly legible. Look towards the top of the castle painted on the wall, where figures acclaim Saint George as he leaves for battle. In summer, the deconsecrated church hosts contemporary art exhibitions.

At the western end of the village, the Porte des Anglais is a far more modest fortified entrance than the main gate. Local tradition holds that English soldiers fled through this passage during the Hundred Years' War. In the 13th century the village was still one of the most important strongholds in the Agenais, until the Albigensians were driven out in 1229 and its walls demolished.

Wander the lanes of Pujols between half-timbered houses and houses of white stone. Rue de la Citadelle and the covered passageways hide finely worked doorways and unexpected hanging gardens. Art galleries and craft workshops line the main street: the village has managed to attract a creative community.

The 19th-century market hall on the main square hosts the Sunday market from May to September. Its oak beams shelter local producers and craftspeople. The atmosphere is relaxed and unfussy, very different from the tourist markets of the region.

activities.text: Head to the viewpoint for a 180-degree panorama over the Lot Valley. On clear days, you can see for up to 30 km: the pink-brick buildings of Villeneuve-sur-Lot spread out below, the River Lot winds across the plain and the hills roll away towards the horizon. The sunset from this viewpoint is particularly beautiful.

Browse the Sunday market in the market hall to taste the local specialities of Lot-et-Garonne: melons, tomatoes, prunes, preserves and Buzet wines. This producers' market runs from May to September on Sunday mornings.
If visiting in summer, inquire about concerts and exhibitions organized in Sainte-Foy Church. The building's acoustics are excellent and musical evenings in this medieval setting are often memorable.

practical_info.best time: Summer; check Villeneuve-sur-Lot tourism office schedule

activities.text: Pujols is a stop on the Vézelay route, the GR 652, towards Santiago de Compostela. Even if you are not walking all the way to Spain, follow the GR downhill from the village to Villeneuve-sur-Lot: the view of the bastide from above is completely different from the perspective below.

map_keywords: Basilica of Notre-Dame de Peyragude, Penne-d'Agenais

visits.text: Penne-d'Agenais is one of the most strikingly perched medieval strongholds in Lot-et-Garonne. From below, you can spot the gleaming zinc dome of the Basilica of Notre-Dame de Peyragude from afar. Park at the bottom and walk up through the cobbled lanes — it is the best way to discover the village layer by layer. The first stone of the Romano-Byzantine basilica was laid on 14 May 1897, but it was not completed until 1948. Inside, 47 stained-glass windows created between 1946 and 1956 by master glassmaker Jacques Leuzy depict the life of Mary. Behind the building, a grotto houses the original church where the Virgin has been venerated since the year one thousand — according to legend, a Marian apparition in 1562 called for it to be rebuilt after its destruction by the Protestants.

The basilica's summit offers a breathtaking panorama over two valleys: the Lot to the north and the Boudouyssou to the south. Sunset from the terrace ranks among the department's most spectacular. Plan to be there late afternoon.

On the way down, pass through the Porte de Richard, one of the village’s surviving fortified gateways and a remnant of the defensive network that made Penne ‘the key to the Duchy of Guyenne’, as the English called it in the Middle Ages. Richard the Lionheart, son of Eleanor of Aquitaine, built a powerful fortress here in the 12th century because of the site’s strategic position above the Lot.

On Place Aliénor d'Aquitaine and Mercadiel Square—the old medieval market square—admire restored half-timbered houses and white-stone façades characteristic of Agenais. Art galleries and artisan studios lining the steep lanes make Penne an active village, not merely a setting.

activities.text: Walk down to the Port de Penne on the banks of the Lot. The site has yielded Azilian remains, the Azilian being a Mesolithic culture dating from around 10,000 years before our era. Today, boaters moor here in complete tranquillity. The contrast between the stronghold perched above and this quiet port below is striking.

Penne-d’Agenais holds its market on Sunday mornings in a friendly atmosphere. A few local producers sell cheeses, jams, preserves and locally grown vegetables. It is small but authentic, with no mass tourism.

Penne-d'Agenais lies on the Santiago de Compostela route. Local operators offer boat trips on the Lot from the port—hour-long or half-day cruises to explore the river's meanders between cliffs and orchards.

visits.text: Notre-Dame Church in Marmande, listed as a historic monument since 1862, is a fine example of southern Gothic architecture built between the 13th and 14th centuries. In 1672, lightning struck the bell tower, where the town’s consuls had foolishly stored its gunpowder reserves. The explosion destroyed the choir and shattered the bell tower. Only the copper cockerel from the original spire survived. Inside, do not miss the Entombment, the 17th-century Baroque altarpiece in gilded wood and the 19th-century organ by Cavaillé-Coll, a world-renowned organ builder.

Adjoining the church's south flank, the Renaissance Cloister bears the date 1540 carved at its north entrance. It's among the region's finest, with elegant arcades and balanced gallery proportions. Only the south galleries and part of the east gallery remain—the Wars of Religion between 1560 and 1569 destroyed the rest. A stroll under the arcades ranks among Marmande's most pleasant moments.

The Cloister Garden, laid out as a formal topiary garden in the 1950s, has held the Remarkable Garden label since 2007. Inspired by the gardens of the Château de Langeais, it features boxwood parterres and yews clipped into cones, spheres and pyramids around a central pool. It is a cool, peaceful space in the very centre of town, perfect for a midday break.

Stroll Rue Labat and its 16th-century half-timbered houses. These dwellings with overhanging upper stories testify to Marmande's Renaissance merchant prosperity. Richard the Lionheart had granted it a charter of customs as early as 1182, conferring privileged status on the Garonne's left bank.

On Place Clemenceau, look for the Pomme d’Amour statue, named after the local nickname for the tomato. Marmande has been France’s capital of the beefsteak tomato since the 19th century, when market gardeners from the Garonne plain popularised it throughout France. The Albert Marzelles Museum, awarded the Musée de France designation in 2002, presents exhibitions throughout the year.

activities.text: Walk around Marmande market to taste the famous local tomato: growers from the Garonne plain display their harvest from June to September. Red, ribbed and perfectly sweet, the Marmande tomato bears no comparison with industrial varieties. The market is held three times a week, early in the morning.

Follow the banks of the Garonne across the Plaine de la Filhole, the green meander west of the centre. The towpath runs alongside the river through poplars and willows, a walk of 3 to 5 km depending on how you feel, flat and easy.

Walk behind the church to find the remains of the Chemin de Ronde and the Tour du Passeur, the only surviving traces of Marmande’s medieval fortifications. These ruins frame a secluded municipal garden that few visitors discover.

visits.text: Duras Castle overlooks the Dropt Valley from a rocky spur. Its origins date back to the 12th century, when a viscount of Bézaume built a fortress on this outcrop. The building belonged to Pope Clement V through his brother Gaillard de Got before passing to the Durfort family, dukes of Duras, who transformed it into a country residence in the 17th century. The first duke, Jacques Henri de Durfort, began rebuilding the main residential wings in the late 17th century according to the architectural conventions of the period. Listed as a historic monument in 1970, it now contains 35 rooms refurnished in medieval and Grand Siècle styles through a partnership with the Mobilier national launched in 2016. The view from the terraces over the Dropt vineyards is one of the finest in the region.

Inside, do not miss the recently refurnished Great Hall of the Marshals and the Kitchen of the Hundred Bundles. Two figures dominate the visit: the first Marshal of Duras and Claire de Kersaint, Duchess of Duras and friend of Chateaubriand, whose correspondence is presented in the apartments.

The Maison des Vins de Duras, in the town itself, offers an introduction to the Cotes de Duras vineyard. The appellation, granted in 1937 among the first in France, covers around 1,230 hectares across 15 communes. Francois I himself described this wine as a 'nectar'. Dry whites, sweet whites, roses and reds: the range is complete.

Look for the Clock Tower, the only listed remnant of the former fortifications of the Duras bastide. It once guarded access to the plateau from the lower town. A walking route then follows the cobbled streets of the town, where white-stone houses and winegrowing façades bear witness to 800 years of vine cultivation.

activities.text: Taste the Cotes de Duras at the Maison des Vins. Reds with aromas of blackcurrant and pepper, crisp dry whites or golden sweet wines: the winegrowers on hand introduce a terroir that is often overlooked and well worth the detour. Exports to the Netherlands took off from the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685, carried by the Protestants driven out of the region.

practical_info.best time: Monday to Saturday; check current hours

activities.text: Local operators offer visits to nearby wine cellars, with guided tastings and tours of the wineries. This is where the appellation reveals its different terroirs: Agenais molasse for the white wines and limestone-clay soils for the reds. Book ahead if you are visiting as a group or outside the high season.
The Monday morning market in the town of Duras is modest but authentic. Local producers, regional wines and a few craftspeople bring the aisles to life in a typically French village atmosphere.

visits.text: Casteljaloux is the only spa town in Lot-et-Garonne, nestled among the Landes pines on the edge of the Landes de Gascogne. The Bains de Casteljaloux are the focal point of a stay here: the thermal water is drawn from a depth of more than 1,200 metres and emerges naturally at 42°C, rich in chloride and sulphate minerals. It is recognised for its effects on joint pain, lower-back pain and neuralgia. The modern thermal centre opened in 1995, but the reputation of its waters dates back to the 19th century, when the town was known as ‘Casteljaloux-les-Bains’. Two pools, one indoor and one outdoor, along with hot tubs, a sauna and a hammam make up the thermal leisure area, ideal for a restorative stop at the end of the road trip.

The Church of Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption is listed as a historic monument. Built in the 15th century and altered in the 17th, it contains fine stained-glass windows and overlooks the old centre of the town. Casteljaloux was a Protestant stronghold under the Albret family: Jeanne d'Albret and her son Henri of Navarre stayed here regularly, making the town a bastion of Protestantism until the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685.

The 16th-century Maison du Roy now houses the tourist office. Its name comes not from Henri IV but from Louis XIII and Louis XIV, who stayed here when passing through the region. The building has kept its handsome half-timbered facade.

Walk through the lanes of old Casteljaloux to find the 15th- and 16th-century half-timbered houses with overhanging upper floors. Around ten survive, one of which is listed as a historic monument. Remnants of the 14th-century ramparts still partially surround the historic centre.

activities.text: Lake Clarens, 2 km south-west of the town, is Casteljaloux’s recreational lake. It was created between 1974 and 1976 and opened in 1977. Its 15 hectares are bordered by fine sandy beaches and pine-covered shores, with supervised swimming in summer, fishing, pedal boats and canoeing. A walking trail circles the lake; allow 45 minutes for a leisurely circuit.

In season, the Lake Clarens leisure centre offers giant inflatable structures on the water, treetop adventure courses, zip lines and an orienteering trail through the pines. Operators also offer flyboarding and paddleboarding. It is ideal for a final active day before continuing your journey.

Treat yourself to half a day at the thermal baths or book an individual session in the thermal leisure area. You do not need to be undergoing medical treatment to enjoy it. The outdoor thermal-water pool at 34°C is particularly pleasant at the end of the day. Book online or directly at reception.

Waymarked trails through the Landes de Gascogne forest start in Casteljaloux. The maritime pine forest stretches endlessly to the south. Walking or cycling for a few kilometres beneath the pines, amid the quiet scents of resin and moss, provides a striking contrast with the medieval bastides visited since the beginning of the trip.

seo.h1_title: Lot-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Villages
seo.intro_paragraph: Lot-et-Garonne reveals itself one bastide at a time: Agen and its 23-arch canal bridge, Nérac where Henri IV grew up amid hunting and walks, Monflanquin perched on its hilltop since 1256, Villeneuve-sur-Lot, the great riverside bastide, and finally the Côtes de Duras vineyards and the Landes pines of Casteljaloux. A generous, little-visited region where every arcaded square has its own story.
seo.seo_hook: Royal bastides, Agen prunes, Dropt vineyards and Landes thermal springs - Lot-et-Garonne off the beaten path.
featured_list: Agen: 539-metre canal bridge with 23 arches and a cathedral on the Santiago de Compostela route
Nérac: Former Henri IV residence and Queen Margot's riverside promenade along the Baïse
Monflanquin: Bastide founded in 1256, classed among France's Most Beautiful Villages
Duras: Ducal château and AOC Côtes de Duras vineyard since 1937

Nérac Château, primary residence of Henri IV and Queen Margot 1577–1582
