itineraries.title: 4-Day Moselle Tour: Metz, Bitche Citadel and Chagall’s Stained Glass
itineraries.subtitle: From Chagall's stained glass to Vauban's fortresses, Moselle unveils its frontier treasures
itineraries.climate: Best period: May-June and September-October, with temperatures from 15 to 24°C, ideal for visiting Metz and the citadels. Avoid January-February (grey, cold 0-5°C, minimal sunshine). Summers are hot with frequent thunderstorms in July-August.

visits.text: Metz’s Saint-Étienne Cathedral displays 6,500 m² of stained glass, an absolute French record ahead of Chartres with its 2,600 m². Nicknamed the “Good Lord’s Lantern”, it is bathed in changing light, where Marc Chagall’s mystical blues converse with Hermann de Münster’s medieval windows. Its naves rise 42 metres beneath the vaults, the third-highest elevation in France. Between 1958 and 1970, Chagall created Old Testament-inspired windows for the ambulatory and north transept, including the Sacrifice of Isaac and Jacob’s Dream in shades of supernatural blue, cosmic green and mystical red.

Centre Pompidou-Metz rises like a spaceship set down on the landscape, with an 8,500 m² hexagonal woven-timber roof inspired by a Chinese hat. Designed by Japanese architect Shigeru Ban and Jean de Gastines and inaugurated in 2010, it offers 5,000 m² of exhibition space beneath a structure comprising 18 km of glued-laminated timber beams. Its spire reaches 77 metres, a reference to the creation of the original Paris Centre Pompidou in 1977. The 15 m-wide galleries frame views of the cathedral, railway station and Parc de la Seille.

On Place Saint-Louis, the 13th-century medieval arcades form a setting of golden stone where the footsteps of Lombard money changers and merchants once echoed. The half-timbered façades and wrought-iron signs recount eight centuries of international trade. Take time for a coffee beneath the vaults, where the heart of Metz has beaten since the Middle Ages.

activities.text: Stroll through the German Imperial Quarter, an architectural laboratory built between 1902 and 1918 under Wilhelm II. Avenue Foch is lined with neo-Romanesque and Art Nouveau villas with polychrome façades, while the monumental 1908 railway station in grey sandstone evokes Rhineland castles with its 40 m central tower. This kaleidoscope of Wilhelmine styles offers a unique immersion in Belle Époque Prussian urban planning, with more than 800 listed buildings.

practical_info.note: Depart from the station (1908) toward Foch Avenue and Esplanade

activities.text: The Musée de la Cour d’Or reveals 2,000 years of Metz history in the former Petits Carmes convent. First-century Gallo-Roman baths, Roman mosaics and Romanesque sculptures stand beneath centuries-old vaults. Its Merovingian collections rank among the richest in France and include the treasure from the Metz-Sablon necropolis. Do not miss the medieval Greniers de Chèvremont incorporated into the tour.

visits.text: The Temple Neuf raises its 1904 neo-Romanesque silhouette on the Petit-Saulcy island, surrounded by the waters of the Moselle. Built during the German period for the Protestant garrison and equipped with its 1904 Walcker organ, it forms a romantic scene with the weeping willows, particularly popular with photographers at dusk, when its grey Vosges sandstone takes on pink hues.

Saint-Pierre-aux-Nonnains Church, built in the 4th century, is one of the oldest churches still standing in France. Its 3 m-thick Gallo-Roman walls have survived sixteen centuries, from a Roman civic basilica to a Benedictine abbey church founded in 972. Its carved 7th-century Merovingian capitals are among the jewels of Lorraine’s pre-Romanesque art. The building now hosts concerts and exhibitions.

The Château de la Grange unfolds its French formal gardens, an eighteenth-century aristocratic residence miraculously preserved. Allow about 28 km from the stage town, 30 minutes by road. Gilded panelling, Aubusson tapestries and Louis XV-Louis XVI furniture make up a refined interior untouched since 1731. The 25-hectare terraced gardens designed by Achille Duchêne offer a soothing view over the Moselle countryside and the Belle-Isle water tower.

activities.text: Explore the islands of Metz on foot, a string of green spaces set on the Moselle between the Temple Neuf and Jardin Boufflers. From the lake to the banks of Parc de la Seille, footbridges link these havens of urban nature where Metz residents come for fresh air. Pedal boats and rowing boats await those who enjoy leisurely boating along 3 km of landscaped riverbanks.

The Jean-Marie Pelt Gardens, a former botanical garden created in 1866, contain more than 2,500 plant species across 4.4 hectares. Tropical greenhouses covering 800 m², a rose garden with 80 varieties and a Japanese garden create a botanical journey across the continents. Collections of medicinal and aromatic plants perfume the air in fine weather. The koi pond and ecological garden complete this haven of urban biodiversity.

visits.text: The Tour aux Puces, a 14 m medieval keep perched on its mound, has housed Thionville’s museum of history and archaeology since 1905. Its collections retrace 2,000 years of this border town’s history, from its Celtic origins to the two world wars. From the top, the view encompasses the slate roofs of the old town and the meanders of the canalised Moselle. The medieval underground passages contain remains of the former 11th-century fortress.

The casemates of Thionville Castle plunge visitors into the depths of the fortress built by Vauban in the 17th century. These underground galleries, dug beneath the ramparts over 500 metres, served as a shelter for 1,500 soldiers and as an ammunition depot. The cool atmosphere, at 12°C all year round, and subdued lighting recreate the ambience of old strongholds, with their firing positions and wells.

Amnéville Zoo, about 12 km from the stage town, 12 minutes by road, ranks among the finest animal parks in France with 2,000 animals of 360 species over 18 hectares. From the gorillas of the Orangutan Jungle (6,000 m²) to the polar bears of the arctic area, from Siberian tigers to African elephants on the 3-hectare plain, each continent reveals its wildlife in vast, naturalised enclosures. The 1,000 m² tropical vivarium and the lorikeet aviary delight young and old alike. Sea lion shows and free-flying birds of prey punctuate the day.

activities.text: Stroll through the 14-hectare Parc Napoléon, Thionville’s green lung, landscaped in the English style in 1859. Its winding paths follow a 7,000 m² pond where black swans and mandarin ducks glide. A neoclassical bandstand, playgrounds, a rose garden and shaded benches make it a favourite Sunday meeting place for families. The park also contains the 1870 war memorial and several contemporary sculptures.

The 16th-century belfry and the cobbled streets of the old town tell the story of a town shaped by the Franco-German wars. Arcaded squares, Renaissance townhouses and fountains create a setting where French and Germanic influences mingle. The 15th-century Gothic Saint-Maximin Church watches over this preserved architectural heritage.

visits.text: The Jardin des Faïenciers in Sarreguemines extends the museum visit outdoors across 8,000 m². Created in 2009 by landscape architect Philippe Niez, it combines industrial heritage with contemporary planting. Dye plants used to produce glazes, including madder and woad, aquatic species along the Blies stream and katsura trees (Cercidiphyllum) with their gingerbread scent create a sensory journey through the seasons. Glass cubes house changing plant arrangements.

Walygator Grand-Est amusement park offers its thrills with 40 attractions across 45 hectares of forest. Three roller coasters, including the Anaconda with its 36-metre loop, thrill rides and family attractions are laid out on different levels in a preserved woodland setting. Thrill seekers will enjoy the Monster (35 m of free fall) and the vertiginous drops at 90 km/h. A water zone, shows and entertainment complete the offering.

activities.text: Amnéville Thermal Baths offer a relaxing break in 2,500 m² of thermal-water pools heated to 34°C. A hammam, Finnish sauna, Roman caldarium and eight outdoor hot tubs provide relaxation after sightseeing. The thermal centre also offers 60 treatments and massages by reservation, as well as approved spa programmes for rheumatic and respiratory conditions. The Vitalis relaxation area has a water slide and a counter-current river.

practical_info.note: 2,500 m², swimsuit required, spa reservations advised

activities.text: Walk along the Orne Valley, a former iron-and-steel industrial area converted into a 15 km green corridor. Hayange’s vegetation-covered slag heaps and the former wastelands around the blast furnaces bear witness to the region’s metallurgical past. Nature is reclaiming the area, with wild orchids and rare butterflies, while peaceful trails lead walkers through a landscape combining heritage and biodiversity.

visits.text: The Sarreguemines Earthenware Museum presents two centuries of ceramic expertise in the former apartments of director Paul de Geiger (1871-1914). The Winter Garden, listed as a historic monument in 1979, dazzles with walls entirely covered by 600 m² of earthenware tiles created between 1880 and 1882. Its monumental 3 m majolica fountain, Carl Schuller's allegories of Earth and Fire and its 10 m-high ceiling form an Art Nouveau masterpiece. Fine earthenware, stoneware and porcelain bear witness to 200 years of production that employed as many as 3,000 workers.

The Moulin de la Blies, a museum annex housed in a mill dating from 1725, reveals the secrets of earthenware production. Millstones and grinders prepared the 50 tonnes of clay required by the factory each day. The 11 m-high bottle kiln dating from 1865, the last surviving witness to the first Industrial Revolution, could fire 15,000 pieces per batch at 1,280°C. Throwing and glazing demonstrations bring the traditional skills of the earthenware makers back to life.

The Casino des Faïenceries, a 1906 Art Nouveau building with façades decorated with 800 m² of polychrome ceramics, bears witness to Sarreguemines’ industrial golden age. Floral designs featuring wisteria and climbing roses in glazed earthenware illustrate how the factory’s artisans applied their creativity to architecture. Unfortunately closed to the public, the building can still be admired from outside for its spectacular façades.

activities.text: Stroll along the Sarre and Blies, the two rivers whose confluence gave the town its name. The landscaped Brouazin and Lebrun quays provide 3 km of riverside walks overlooking the converted buildings of the former earthenware factories. Restored barges and sightseeing boats enliven the water in fine weather. The Franco-German garden symbolises cross-border reconciliation.

Discover the borderland heritage of Sarreguemines, a crossroads town between France and Germany, 2 km from Saarland. Its proximity to Germany is reflected in the Wilhelmine architecture, bilingual signs and local cuisine combining quiche Lorraine and fleischnacka. The weekly market, held on Wednesdays and Saturdays, has attracted visitors from both sides of the Rhine since 1297.

visits.text: Bitche Citadel crowns a pink sandstone spur at an altitude of 300 m. This military masterpiece was built to plans by Vauban between 1679 and 1697, then rebuilt by Cormontaigne between 1741 and 1754. Its 500 m of underground galleries carved into the rock contain an immersive 50-minute audiovisual tour recounting the heroic siege of 1870-1871, when 2,400 French soldiers under Commander Teyssier resisted 20,000 Prussians for 230 days, a French record ahead of Belfort’s 104 days. The 1794 relief model, listed as a historic monument, reproduces the fortress in minute detail at a scale of 1:600 across 42 m².

The rampart walk runs for 980 m around the pink sandstone fortifications, offering unrivalled views over the town of Bitche, 300 m below, and the forests of the Vosges Regional Nature Park stretching up to 15 km into the distance. Twelve information panels describe the evolution of military architecture from Vauban to the Maginot Line. Viewing points on the Saint-Sébastien, Bourbon and Sainte-Catherine bastions punctuate this free route, which is accessible to everyone.

activities.text: The Altschlossfelsen raises its 30-metre red sandstone cliffs on the Franco-German border, about 14 km from the stage town, 20 minutes by road, a popular climbing site with 80 routes and a natural viewpoint over the forests of the Palatinate. The waymarked paths of the Vosges club wind between erratic blocks with fantastic shapes carved by wind erosion over 250 million years. Ruins of the thirteenth-century medieval castle perch at the summit at 389 m.

practical_info.note: 150m elevation gain, hiking boots recommended, climbing possible

activities.text: The Pays de Bitche invites visitors to hike through the forests of the Northern Vosges Regional Nature Park, a UNESCO biosphere reserve since 1988 covering 130,000 hectares. Ponds created by Cistercian monks in the 12th century, ancient peat bogs harbouring carnivorous sundews and stands of century-old beech trees reaching 40 m form unspoilt landscapes where roe deer, wild boar and lynx roam freely. The area has 1,500 km of marked trails, including the GR53.

practical_info.note: Northern Vosges Park, UNESCO, many marked circuits

visits.text: Phalsbourg, a fortified town founded in 1570 by Count Palatine Georges-Jean de Veldenz-Lützelstein, retains its two monumental gates dating from 1680: Porte de France to the south and Porte d'Allemagne to the north, witnesses to its strategic role as the lock barring the Vosges passage. The arcaded Place d'Armes, the 1770 Lastours barracks and 18th-century townhouses evoke the period when 4,000 French garrison troops defended this passage. The history museum recounts the story of the town that inspired the Lorraine writers Erckmann-Chatrian and their Histoire d'un conscrit de 1813.

The Saint-Louis crystalworks have carried on a centuries-old glassmaking craft since 1586, becoming a royal manufactory in 1767. Allow about 25 km from the stage town, 25 minutes by road. Visit the workshops where master glassmakers blow crystal at 1,450°C with age-old gestures: gathering the parison, blowing and hand-shaping vases, glasses and art objects. The museum displays 2,000 exceptional pieces. The shops offer contemporary creations and end-of-series items at gentle prices.

activities.text: The Saint-Louis-Arzviller inclined plane, Europe’s only transverse boat lift, was inaugurated in 1969. It raises barges through a height difference of 44.55 m in 4 minutes, instead of the full day formerly required to pass through 17 locks. Board a boat for a spectacular crossing in which it glides inside a huge water-filled caisson weighing 5,000 tonnes, travelling along rails inclined at 41%. Guided tours cover the 108 m-long machinery room and the counterweight mechanism. More than 8,500 boats and 100,000 visitors discover this technical achievement designed by engineer Robert Vadot each year.

practical_info.note: Recommended boat tour, machinery tour, reservation advised in high season

activities.text: The Marne-Rhine Canal runs for 314 km through tunnels and forests between Alsace and Lorraine, with 178 locks. Its renovated towpaths offer 45 km of pleasant walks and cycle rides through the Zorn Valley, in a peaceful atmosphere where only the lapping of the water accompanies your progress. Remarkable engineering structures and chamber locks punctuate this route, inaugurated in 1853.

visits.text: The Chapelle des Cordeliers, a 13th-century Gothic choir dating from 1265, houses the largest stained-glass window ever created by Marc Chagall: La Paix, a monumental work measuring 12 m high by 7.50 m wide, weighing 900 kg and containing 13,000 pieces of glass. Produced between 1974 and 1976 in the Simon-Marq workshops in Reims by master glassmaker Charles Marq, the window illuminates the choir with celestial blues and blazing reds, depicting the Creation, the Tree of Life and biblical figures in translucent colour. Moses carrying the Tablets of the Law and the prophets seem to float in space. Side windows added in 1977 complete the ensemble.

The Musée du Pays de Sarrebourg, housed in a contemporary building dating from 2004, continues the Chagall theme with the La Paix tapestry, measuring 4.71 m by 6.36 m. Created by Yvette Cauquil-Prince in 1994, it is a textile interpretation of the design for the United Nations stained-glass window in New York. The building also houses remarkable Gallo-Roman archaeological collections: 2nd-century mosaics, polychrome capitals from Tarquimpol and earthenware from the Niderviller factory (1748-1827), whose decoration rivals the refinement of Sèvres.

activities.text: The garden of the Chapelle des Cordeliers is a contemporary 1,200 m² meditation space created in 2007, where Chagall’s recorded voice recites his poems. Glass cubes containing trees and plants with changing colours, hedges of varying heights and fragrant plantings continue the dialogue with the stained glass in a setting of greenery and transparency. Quotations from Cendrars, Aragon and Apollinaire punctuate the walk.

practical_info.note: Free access, recorded poems, planted spaces

activities.text: Explore the Gallo-Roman remains around Sarrebourg, the ancient crossroads of Pons Saravi between Metz and Strasbourg on the Roman road. The Croix-Guillaume site at Saint-Quirin, about 15 km from the stage town, 15 minutes by road, reveals a settlement of the Vosges foothills from the first to the fourth century. The baths of Tarquimpol (first to third centuries), about 25 km from the stage town, 25 minutes by road, with their exceptional polychrome capitals, testify to the importance of this territory under the Roman Empire, which numbered 15,000 inhabitants.

visits.text: The Lorraine American Cemetery in Saint-Avold, dedicated in 1960, is Europe’s largest American military cemetery from the Second World War. Across 46 hectares of immaculate lawn, 10,489 white Carrara marble crosses are arranged in nine symmetrical plots forming an ellipse. The 20.40 m-high neoclassical memorial chapel contains monumental statues and ceramic wall maps recounting the military operations of autumn 1944. A 4 m statue of Saint Nabor carved from Euville stone overlooks the site. The Tablets of the Missing bear the names of 444 missing service members. It is a deeply moving place of remembrance for those who liberated Lorraine between August 1944 and March 1945.

The Notre-Dame-de-Bon-Secours Basilica, a Baroque jewel dating from 1764, dominates Saint-Avold with its two 52 m twin towers. Gilded Rococo stucco, trompe-l’œil frescoes from 1765 and Louis XV furniture create an exceptionally rich interior with a carved pulpit and monumental high altar. The 1769 Silbermann organ, listed as a historic monument, delights music lovers during the international festival’s summer concerts.

activities.text: The 10th-century Saint-Nabor abbey church, rebuilt in the Baroque style in the 18th century, retains a 12th-century Romanesque crypt and 15th-century Gothic elements. Saint Nabor, the town’s patron saint and a Roman soldier of the Theban Legion martyred in 303, has been honoured here since 965. His relics have attracted pilgrims since the Early Middle Ages. The church also contains remarkable 18th-century Baroque furnishings, including carved choir stalls.

The mining and industrial heritage of the Saint-Avold area tells the story of coal (1856-2003) and chemicals, which brought prosperity to the Lorraine coalfield with 16,000 miners in 1958. Slag heaps turned into green spaces, headframes preserved at Freyming-Merlebach and former red-brick workers' rows bear witness to this social history. The Musée Les Mineurs Wendel at Petite-Rosselle, about 14 km from the stage town, 15 minutes by road, retraces that story.

practical_info.note: Miners Wendel Museum at Petite-Rosselle (15 km)

visits.text: The Georges de La Tour Departmental Museum honours the master of chiaroscuro, born in this salt-producing village in 1593. His candlelit paintings illuminate the darkness with mystical, theatrical light, revealing the faces of card players, penitents and meditative saints with poignant realism. The museum displays an exceptional collection of 17th-century Lorraine paintings, including works by Jacques Callot and Claude Deruet, contemporaries of La Tour. Its contemporary 2003 architecture incorporates the former 18th-century salt storehouse.

The 13th- to 15th-century Saint-Marien Collegiate Church retains 16th-century Renaissance stained glass and remarkable liturgical furnishings: 18th-century choir stalls, a 1749 Wegmann organ and Baroque paintings. Its squat 50 m bell tower rises above the village’s interlocking-tile roofs, a sandstone sentinel overlooking the former salt marshes that brought Vic prosperity from the 11th to the 17th century, when 27 salt works produced 60,000 tonnes of salt a year.

activities.text: Discover the history of salt in the Saulnois, a land of 400 salt-water springs exploited since the Gallic and then the Gallo-Roman periods. During the Middle Ages, the salt marshes of Vic, Moyenvic and Marsal produced “white gold” by solar evaporation in lead pans. This little-known heritage shaped Lorraine’s economy until the 18th century and was controlled by the bishops of Metz, who drew immense revenues from it. The flat landscape, with ponds glittering as far as the eye can see, retains its unique character.

practical_info.note: Salt history, exploited Antiquity-18th century, salt museum at Marsal (15 km)

activities.text: Stroll through the narrow streets of Vic-sur-Seille, a characterful village of 1,200 inhabitants with houses built from pink Vosges sandstone. Former salt works with their Gallic salt-production ceramics, 16th- and 17th-century Renaissance townhouses, sandstone fountains and washhouses recount the prosperity of a town that exported its “white gold” by river to Nancy, Metz and even Burgundy. Parts of the medieval walls survive.

seo.h1_title: 4-Day Moselle Tour: Metz, Bitche Citadel and Chagall’s Stained Glass
seo.intro_paragraph: Discover Moselle, a land of contrasts where the 6,500 m² of stained glass in Metz Cathedral, including works by Chagall, rival Vauban’s fortifications in Bitche. From Sarreguemines earthenware and the Saint-Avold American Cemetery with its 10,489 graves to the Saint-Louis-Arzviller inclined plane and Centre Pompidou-Metz, this 4-day itinerary reveals an unexpectedly rich borderland heritage between France and Germany.
seo.seo_hook: Metz Cathedral, Chagall’s stained glass and Bitche Citadel: explore Moselle, a borderland between France and Germany.
featured_list: Metz Cathedral: 6,500 m² of stained glass, a French record, including Chagall’s works in the north transept (1958-1970)
Bitche Citadel: heroic 230-day siege in 1870 and an audiovisual tour through 500 m of underground galleries
Sarreguemines Earthenware Museum: the 1880 Winter Garden, listed as a historic monument, and 200 years of ceramics
Chagall's Peace Window at Sarrebourg: 12 metres high, the artist's largest ever (1974-1976)
Saint-Avold American Cemetery: 10,489 graves across 46 ha, Europe’s largest US World War II cemetery
Centre Pompidou-Metz: 8,500 m² hexagonal woven-timber roof, 77 m spire and architecture by Shigeru Ban
Saint-Louis-Arzviller inclined plane: a boat lift unique in Europe, overcoming a 44.55 m height difference in 4 minutes
Amnéville Zoo: 2,000 animals of 360 species across 18 ha, among France's finest animal parks

itineraries.title: Road Trip Pyrenees-Atlantiques: Basque Country and Bearn
itineraries.subtitle: 6 days from Biarritz to Bayonne through the pilgrim roads to Santiago, Bearnese fortresses and salt thermal springs — an itinerary between the Atlantic and the Pyrenees.
itineraries.notes: The Rhune Train (Day 2, departing from Col de Saint-Ignace station) is closed outside season — check opening dates. Pau Castle (Day 9) can only be visited on guided tours. The Pau funicular is free.
itineraries.climate: Best period: May to September, temperatures 18–25°C on the coast, cooler in the mountains. Avoid October–March: abundant rainfall (up to 1500 mm/year in elevated areas), Pyrenees passes closed or snow-covered in winter. Summer remains mild thanks to Atlantic influence, perfect for combining beach and mountain.

visits.text: Start at Virgin's Rock, the iconic symbol of Biarritz. This rock, tunneled through by Napoleon III in 1864, is connected to the shore by a 76-meter metal footbridge built in 1887 by the Schryver workshops of Haumont — not by Eiffel, contrary to local legend. The statue of the Virgin Mary, installed in 1865, commemorates according to tradition the miraculous return of Biarritz whalers guided by a light during a storm. Go in late afternoon: the light on the ocean from the rock is spectacular, and in rough seas waves crash just meters below your feet.

The Biarritz Aquarium has occupied an Art Deco building facing Virgin's Rock since 1933. Its aquariums recreate the depths of the Bay of Biscay — sharks, rays, octopuses — with a dedicated seal zone that appeals to children. Plan about 1.5 hours for a complete visit.

Climb the Biarritz Lighthouse for the most complete view of the city. Built from 1830 and in service since 1 February 1834, this cylindrical tower, 47 metres tall, stands 75 metres above sea level on the Pointe Saint-Martin. Its 248 steps lead to a 360° panorama: to the north the Landes beaches, to the south the rocky Basque coast, and on clear days the Pyrenees on the horizon. Its copper dome is adorned with twelve bronze lion heads, each one different.

Stroll along the Grande Plage, set between the Casino Municipal and the Hôtel du Palais — the former imperial residence of Napoleon III and Eugénie, who made Biarritz the fashionable European resort of the Second Empire. The promenade offers a sweeping view over the bay, the lighthouse and the Belle Époque villas stepping down the cliff.

activities.text: The Côte des Basques is the birthplace of surfing in Europe: it was here, in 1957, that Peter Viertel rode the first French wave. The beach is still one of the busiest spots on the continent today. Operators offer beginner lessons for all levels, summer and winter alike. Arrive early in the morning in July and August — the beach fills up fast.

The Cité de l'Océan offers an interactive immersion in the marine world: a surf simulator, 3D animations and the Seaborg, a recent immersive installation. Ideal for families or on rainy days — Biarritz gets a few even in season.

Cross the Port-Vieux at low tide. This small sheltered cove between the cliffs is Biarritz's first harbour, used for centuries. In calm weather it is the town's most protected swimming spot — far quieter than the Grande Plage.

map_keywords: Church of Saint John the Baptist Saint-Jean-de-Luz

visits.text: The church of Saint-Jean-Baptiste is one of the most beautiful in the Basque Country — and one of the most closely tied to French history. It was here that Louis XIV married Maria Theresa of Austria on 9 June 1660, after the signing of the Treaty of the Pyrenees. The church was still a building site that day; temporary facades had been put up for the occasion. The gilded wooden baroque altarpiece, one of the largest in the Basque Country, was completed in 1669. The three tiers of carved oak galleries frame the nave on three sides — a feature of the churches of Labourd. Look for the walled-up door on the right-hand side: this is where the royal couple left, and it was sealed immediately afterwards so that no one else could use it.

The Maison Louis XIV, built in 1643 for the shipowner Joannis Lohobiague, was the king's lodging for forty days. Louis XIV called it his "Little Louvre." It is one of the few houses in France to have belonged to the same family since it was built. Its pink sandstone facades and corner towers reflect 17th-century shipowner architecture. Check the opening hours before you come — it is open only part of the year.

The House of the Infanta, built around 1640 by the shipowner Joannot de Haraneder, hosted Maria Theresa of Austria for her wedding to Louis XIV. The two newlyweds were 22 years old and doubly first cousins. Its two galleries with five Italian-style arcades overlook the port. The inscription carved above the door says it all: "I received the Infanta in the year sixteen sixty, I have been called the Infanta's castle ever since."

activities.text: The Port des Pêcheurs comes alive at dawn. Trawlers unload anchovies, tuna and hake from the bay of Saint-Jean. Stroll among the colourful boats and drying nets, then head to the covered market to buy fresh fish and gâteau basque.

The Rhune Train departs from Col de Saint-Ignace station, 7 km from Saint-Jean-de-Luz. This rack railway built in 1924 climbs in 35 minutes to 905 meters altitude at Mount Rhune's summit. At the top, pottoks — semi-wild Basque ponies — and griffon vultures roam free, and the view encompasses the ocean, beaches and the Pyrenees. Book your ticket online in season: queues can be very long in summer. The train does not operate in winter.

Watch a game of Basque pelota at the fronton by the harbour or in the trinquet. Chistera, bare hand, cesta punta — each variant has its own rules and champions. Games are held all summer long, and some are free. This is the national sport of the Basque Country, played here since the 16th century.

visits.text: The Caves of Sare descend into the mountain for nearly a kilometer and reveal 45,000 years of human presence. The sound and light tour reveals stalactites, stalagmites and traces of the first inhabitants of the Basque Country. Thirteen species of bats live there. Ideal on rainy days — and Sare sees plenty!

Detour to Ortillopitz House, 3 km from the village. Its foundations date back to 1540 and the house in its current form dates from 1660. It is a typical Labourdin etxe: a self-sufficient farming estate with vineyard, flax, old vegetable garden, stone wash house, spring and traditional livestock. The interior preserves its original furnishings. It is one of the best ways to understand what 17th-century rural Basque life was like.

The Church of Saint Martin in Sare raises its bell tower in the middle of the village. Typical of Labourdin churches with their wooden galleries on several levels, it stands above the fronton — the pelota court — which is the real heart of village social life. Sare has more than 80 carved stone door lintels recorded throughout its streets.

activities.text: Take the Galtzada from the village center. This ancient medieval flagstone path connected Bayonne to Spain over the mountains. The GR8 and GR10 hiking trails follow it in parts, offering scenic loops with views over Mount Rhune. Plan 2 to 4 hours depending on the loop chosen.

Push on to Ainhoa and Ascain at the end of the day. These two Basque villages are listed among France's Most Beautiful Villages — Ainhoa notably for the half-timbered houses lining its pelota square. Compare the architecture of the two villages: same logic, same materials, but each house tells a different story through its carved lintels.

map_keywords: Castle of the Barons d'Ezpeleta Espelette town hall

visits.text: The Castle of the Barons d'Ezpeleta has dominated the village since the year 1000 — the Barons d'Ezpeleta came from a noble family of Navarre. In 1694, their last descendant, Baroness Juliana Henriquez, gave the castle to the villagers. Now the town hall, it also houses a permanent exhibition on Espelette pepper. Listed as a Historic Monument since 1993, it was renovated in 1998. The adjoining cemetery contains the Art Deco tomb of Agnès Souret, the first Miss France, elected in 1920.

Construction of the Church of Saint Stephen began in 1593. Its fortified keep-like bell tower and its interior galleries on three levels are typical of Labourdin churches. The Baroque gilded wood retable, the entirely painted 17th-century ceilings and a painting attributed to José de Ribera deserve a careful stop. It has been listed as a Historic Monument since 1925.

Wander through the lanes of Espelette to see the white facades with red shutters of the Basque Country — a colour known as euskal gorria. From late August to November, strings of scarlet peppers hang on the facades, drying in the sun before being ground into powder. Espelette pepper obtained AOC status in 2000 — it covers ten municipalities of the Labourd and rates 4 on the Scoville scale, less hot than cayenne pepper but far more aromatic.

activities.text: The village market sets up in the morning. Ossau-Iraty sheep's cheese, veal axoa, gâteau basque and pepper in every form — powdered, on strings, as jam, in chocolate — fill the stalls. On the last Sunday in October, the Pepper Festival turns the whole village into a giant market with concerts and cooking contests.

Hike the Mondarrain, which peaks at 749 metres. Part of the Natura 2000 network, this massif is home to semi-free-roaming pottoks, griffon vultures and protohistoric remains (a cromlech) visible on the summit rocks. From the top, the view takes in the Atlantic coast, the Pyrenees and the Basque villages stretching towards Spain. Allow about 3 hours for the loop.

visits.text: The Porte Saint-Jacques marks the historic entry of pilgrims into the town and is part of the UNESCO property inscribed in 1998. At 39 rue de la Citadelle you will find the pilgrims' welcome office — this is where walkers have their credencial stamped before tackling the crossing of the Pyrenees. More than 60,000 pilgrims pass through each year on their way to Roncevaux, 8 km away.

The Citadel stands 80 metres above the town on the hill of Mendiguren. Built around 1625 on the site of the castle of the kings of Navarre, it was reworked by Vauban after his inspection in 1685 — he found almost nothing to change, so excellent was the existing work. Now a listed Historic Monument occupied by a secondary school, it can be visited in summer on guided tours that go down into the underground passages and reveal the period bread oven. The view over the Cize valley and the Pyrenees is exceptional.

Walk down the rue de la Citadelle, paved and lined with pink sandstone houses. The carved lintels bear the names of the houses, the year of construction and the initials of the first owners. The Church of Notre-Dame, 14th-century Gothic with its facade of pink Arradoy sandstone, is a listed Historic Monument. Look for the gateway that incorporates the bell tower, on the left as you enter — this arrangement is rare.

The Prison of the Bishops, at 41 rue de la Citadelle, takes its name from the presence of three bishops of Bayonne during the Western Schism, between 1383 and 1417. The building later served as a prison until the 20th century. Its vast pointed-arch vaulted hall in the basement, with chains still fixed to the walls, today houses a permanent exhibition on the Road to Santiago.

activities.text: Walk the full rampart walkway that runs along the walls of the upper town — 269 steps lead up to the terrace from the place des Casernes. The view from the watchtower above the Porte Saint-Antoine is one of the finest in the inland Basque Country: the gave, the green valley and the first Pyrenean peaks.

The Monday morning market is held on the place des Remparts. Sheep cheeses, Banca trout, Irouléguy AOP wines — one of France's smallest wine regions, a few kilometres away — and Itxassou cherry jam fill the stalls. A producers' market is added every Thursday in summer.

map_keywords: Place du Bayaà salt spring Salies-de-Bearn

visits.text: The Salies-de-Béarn thermal baths occupy a Moorish-inspired building opened in 1889 — the architect Adrien Lagarde drew inspiration from the mosque of Cordoba for the two-tone facade and the minaret tower. An earlier establishment had opened in 1857; a fire in 1893 led to a complete rebuild. The virtues of the thermal waters were recognised by the Academy of Medicine in 1891 for rheumatology, gynaecology and childhood development disorders. The spring, 200 million years old, contains 300 grams of salt per litre.

Descend into the crypt of Place du Bayaà to see the salt spring fountain. Since 1587, only the Corporation of Share-Holders — descendants of Salies' original inhabitants — has the right to exploit this source. Their ownership right was recognized by Henry III of Albret in 1588. According to founding legend, the spring was discovered by a wounded wild boar that took refuge in the marshes and emerged covered in salt crystals before dying.

The Salies salt works produce around 2,000 tonnes of salt a year, a salt used to cure PGI Bayonne ham. Extraction goes back to the Bronze Age — pottery fragments dating from 1500 BC bear witness to it. The site houses a museum space on the history of production, along with shops selling salt and cured products.

The Church of Saint Vincent blends 11th-century architecture with Gothic style. Its Baroque altar dominates a nave restored several times. The historic quarter around the church is full of Bearnese half-timbered houses on stilts from the 14th to the 17th century, some of them straddling the Saleys — the river that runs through the town and earns it the nickname of the Bearnese Venice.

activities.text: Spa operators offer baths and treatments using the salt water of Salies, heated to 32°C and rich in 26 trace elements. An experience open to everyone, including outside a medical cure. The water makes you float naturally — as in the Dead Sea. Book ahead.

Stroll along the Saleys, which runs through the historic quarter. The half-timbered houses on stilts, the stone bridges and the colourful facades make up a scene that the people of Salies compare to Venice. In September, the Salt Festival enlivens the whole town centre for several days.

visits.text: The ramparts of Navarrenx are the first examples of bastioned fortifications in France — built between 1538 and 1547 by the Italian architect Fabricio Siciliano on the orders of Henry II of Albret, king of Navarre and grandfather of Henry IV. Vauban visited the place in 1685 and found nothing to change, so far ahead of its time was the Italian design. These walls, 1.7 km long, 10 metres high and 4.50 metres thick, encircle the medieval bastide founded in 1316. Listed as Historic Monuments, they can be walked freely from the rampart walkway.

The Porte Saint-Antoine, also called the Gate of Spain, is the main entrance to the bastioned town. It is UNESCO-listed as part of the Roads to Santiago de Compostela — Navarrenx is a stage on the Via Podiensis, the Le Puy route, three days' walk from Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port. Once past the medieval bridge, 873 km still separate the pilgrim from Santiago de Compostela.

The Church of Saint Germain was built between 1550 and 1560 on the site of the old church of the bastide, demolished because it stood too close to the new walls. Jeanne d'Albret had Calvinism recognised there as the official religion; Louis XIII had the first Catholic mass celebrated there in 1620. The U-shaped Arsenal, built in 1680 on the site of the House of the Kings of Navarre, today houses an interpretation centre on the bastioned town, with models and plans.

activities.text: The gave d'Oloron flows at the foot of the ramparts. It is reputed to be one of the best salmon rivers in France and hosts a fishing championship every year. The fish ladder near the Massey dam allows you to watch salmon during their migrations. Operators offer canoeing and kayaking from April to October.

Do the full circuit of the ramparts from the rampart walkway — about 2 km of panoramic walking. From the watchtower above the Porte Saint-Antoine, the cannon pointing due west offers a surprising view of the medieval bridge and the gave. On clear days, the Pyrenees stand out on the horizon.

map_keywords: Cathedral of Saint Mary Oloron-Sainte-Marie Romanesque portal

visits.text: The Cathedral of Saint Mary is Oloron's flagship monument. Its 12th-century Romanesque portal — created by two different artists including the "Master of Oloron" — is one of the finest in the Southwest. It depicts preparations for a medieval banquet with scenes of local life: wild boar hunting, salmon fishing, bread and cheese cutting. Glass beads were inserted into the eyes of the figures to bring them to life — look closely. Listed as UNESCO World Heritage in 1998 under the Roads to Santiago, the cathedral was in service from the 12th century onward and was reworked several times. The Gothic chevet with ambulatory dates from the 14th century.

The Sainte-Croix quarter, perched on its hill, is the medieval heart of Oloron. The Tour de Grède rises above the rooftops and offers a panorama over the Pyrenean chain. The paved lanes and half-timbered houses create the atmosphere of a medieval town barely altered by the centuries.

Head to the confluence where the gave d'Aspe and the gave d'Ossau meet to form the gave d'Oloron. This meeting point offers a panorama over the first Pyrenean summits and marks the start of the two great valleys running down towards Spain. Operators offer canoeing and whitewater sports on the gave.

activities.text: The Basque-Bearnese beret is still made in Oloron. Workshops have kept this craft alive since the 19th century — one local factory has been producing berets since 1840. A workshop visit lets you see the fulling and shaping stages. Ten kilometres away, Tissages Lartigue have carried on the art of weaving Basque linen for more than four generations.

The Aspe valley opens due south from Oloron. An hour's drive brings you to the Somport pass at 1,632 metres, the French-Spanish border and a stage on the Road to Santiago — pilgrims coming via Arles crossed this pass. The road follows the gave d'Aspe between beeches and firs, with some chance of spotting vultures and, more rarely, the brown bears of the Basque Country.

visits.text: Pau Castle is the most visited monument in Bearn — around 100,000 visitors a year. Its 33-metre brick tower was built by Gaston Fébus in the 14th century. This is where Henry IV was born on 13 December 1553, a fact attested by an 18th-century inscription. At his birth, his grandfather rubbed his lips with a clove of garlic and had him breathe in Jurançon wine — a Bearnese custom. He was then placed in a giant tortoise shell, his legendary cradle, kept ever since in the king's chamber. That shell remains the national museum's most emblematic object. The visit is by guided tour only and lasts about an hour.

The boulevard des Pyrénées unrolls 1,800 metres of panoramic promenade, created gradually between 1893 and 1899. On clear days — winter and spring are the best seasons — the Pyrenean chain unfolds from the Pic du Midi d'Ossau to the Pic d'Anie, and the Spanish Pyrenees can be made out on the horizon. It is one of the most spectacular urban panoramas in France.

The Museum of Fine Arts presents a European collection from the 15th to the 20th century: El Greco, Rubens, Degas share space with regional painters. Plan 1.5 hours to tour it completely. The building itself, from the 19th century, is an example of classical museum architecture.

activities.text: Take the Pau funicular, put into service in 1908 and free from the start. In a few minutes it links the railway station to the boulevard des Pyrénées at the level of the place Royale. A century-old technical curiosity that remains the pleasantest way to get up to the town centre from the station.

Beaumont Park spreads its 11 hectares in the heart of the town. Century-old sequoias, a rose garden, a lake and a bandstand adorn this 19th-century English-style garden. The Jurançon hillsides are 10 minutes away by car: the vineyards produce two very different AOC wines — a dry wine with character and a sweet moelleux renowned ever since Henry IV was baptised with it.

map_keywords: Cathedral of Saint Mary Bayonne UNESCO

visits.text: Construction of the Cathedral of Saint Mary in Bayonne began in the 1240s under Champenois influence — the architect drew on the plans of Reims for the choir and of Soissons for the chapels. It was only more or less completed in 1451, when the French took Bayonne back from the English. Its two 85-metre spires were finished in the 19th century. Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1998 as part of the Roads to Santiago, it deserves at least an hour — look at the coloured keystones representing the different quarters of Bayonne.

The Rayonnant Gothic cloister adjoining the cathedral is one of the largest in France. Built between the 14th and 16th centuries, in the Middle Ages it was a meeting place for the guilds and the quarter assemblies. Its galleries preserve enfeus (tombs set into the walls) and funerary slabs from the 14th to the 18th century. Freely accessible, it offers a rare space of calm in the heart of the busy town.

The Basque Museum and Museum of the History of Bayonne occupies a 16th-century house on the banks of the Nive. Its collections trace Basque culture from the Neolithic to the 20th century: costume, pelota, architecture, maritime traditions. Allow an hour and a half to go round it all.

Walk the Vauban ramparts that have encircled Grand Bayonne since the late 17th century. From the Mousserolles bastion, the view takes in the confluence of the Nive and the Adour. Bayonne was long the main stronghold of the Southwest, and its fortifications are part of the network of Vauban sites.

activities.text: Petit Bayonne is packed with pintxo bars and restaurants along the Nive. Pintxos — Basque tapas on toasted bread — are ordered standing at the counter, as tradition has it. The quarter is liveliest in the evening, especially on Thursdays and Fridays. Take the chance to try veal axoa, piperade and local anchovies.

Bayonne chocolate dates back to the 17th century — in 1609, Jewish craftsmen driven out of Portugal by the Inquisition brought the secrets of cocoa making to Bayonne. The town has been known as France's chocolate capital ever since. Several artisan chocolate makers carry on a four-century-old tradition under the arcades of the rue Port-Neuf. Look for a dark chocolate with a high cocoa content, sometimes flavoured with Espelette pepper.

Visit the Halles de Bayonne to find Bayonne ham IGP — salted with salt from Salies-de-Béarn and air-dried in the Pyrenees for at least 7 months. The tradition goes back to the Middle Ages; the Bayonne ham fair has been held since 1462. Every year at Easter, the Ham Festival draws thousands of visitors to the quays of the Adour.

seo.h1_title: Road Trip Pyrenees-Atlantiques: Basque Country and Bearn
seo.intro_paragraph: From Biarritz, birthplace of European surfing in 1957, to Bayonne, chocolate capital since 1609, this 6-day road trip crosses Basque Country and Bearn through Saint-Jean-de-Luz where Louis XIV married Maria Theresa on June 9, 1660, Espelette pepper AOC since 2000, the Renaissance ramparts of Navarrenx built in 1538 — France's first — and Pau, where Henry IV was born on December 13, 1553. Between Atlantic and Pyrenees, each town brings its own character: medieval fortresses, salt thermal baths, Roads to Santiago and Basque and Bearnese gastronomy.
seo.seo_hook: Surfing in Biarritz, royal wedding in Saint-Jean-de-Luz, Espelette pepper and the Road to Santiago: Basque Country and Bearn in 6 days between the Atlantic and the Pyrenees.

Saint-Jean-de-Luz: Basque fishing port and church of Louis XIV's 1660 wedding

itineraries.title: Seine-Maritime Road Trip: The Cliffs of Étretat, Rouen & Jumièges Abbey
itineraries.subtitle: From the arches of Étretat to the ruins of Jumièges, the Alabaster Coast reveals its treasures
itineraries.notes: A nine-day journey along the Alabaster Coast and the meanders of the Seine. From chalk cliffs sculpted by the elements to the majestic ruins of Benedictine abbeys, this circuit unveils the soul of maritime Normandy, between authentic fishing ports and thousand-year-old Gothic heritage.
itineraries.climate: Best period: May–June and September, temperatures 15–22°C, ideal for cliff walks and Rouen exploration. Avoid November–March (frequent rain, strong coastal winds, slippery cliffs). The Étretat cliffs are spectacular but dangerous in windy conditions.
specialties: Sole dieppoise with cream and mussels

map_keywords: Le Secq des Tournelles Museum Rouen

visits.text: Great Clock — This fourteenth-century Gothic belfry houses one of Europe's oldest astronomical clocks, with a mechanism dating to 1389. The Renaissance arch, built between 1527 and 1529, spans the pedestrian street with its 2.5-meter gilded dial showing a sun with 24 rays against a starry blue background. A single hand marks the hour while a globe indicates the moon's phases.

Old Market Square — This is where Joan of Arc was burned on May 30, 1431. The Church of Saint-Joan of Arc, inaugurated in 1979, features an audacious architecture shaped like an inverted flame and houses Renaissance stained glass windows from the former Church of Saint-Vincent, destroyed during the war.

Saint-Ouen Abbey Church — A masterpiece of Rayonnant Gothic built between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries, this former Benedictine abbey impresses with its 137 meters of length and fourteenth-century stained glass windows among the most complete in France. Its grand Cavaillé-Coll organ from 1890 features 64 stops.

Le Secq des Tournelles Museum — Housed in the former fifteenth-century Church of Saint-Laurent, this museum, unique in the world, presents 12,000 pieces of decorative ironwork from the third to the nineteenth centuries: signs, locks, grilles, and everyday objects testifying to the craftsmanship of master ironworkers.

activities.text: Joan of Arc Historical Museum — Set in the archbishop's palace where Joan was condemned and later exonerated, this immersive scenographic journey traces the Maid's destiny through testimony, projections, and reconstructions of the 1431 trial.

Eau-de-Robec Street — This picturesque cobbled street runs alongside a canal where dyers once washed their fabrics. Its half-timbered houses from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, restored after the 1944 bombing, transport visitors into medieval Rouen.

Rouen Botanical Garden — This 8.5-hectare botanical garden, created in 1840, shelters over 5,600 plant species, tropical greenhouses, and a rose garden. A green haven in the city's heart, perfect for wandering among botanical collections and century-old trees.

map_keywords: Le Secq des Tournelles Museum Rouen

visits.text: Saint-Catherine Heights — From this 150-meter-high hill overlooking the left bank, embrace all of Rouen in one sweeping view: the cathedral painted by Monet, the spires of Gothic churches, the Seine's meanders. The viewpoint immortalized by Impressionist painters in the nineteenth century.

Jumièges Abbey — Founded in 654 by Saint Philibert, this "most beautiful ruin in France" according to Victor Hugo raises its 46-meter twin towers in the heart of a 15-hectare English-style park. Destroyed by the Vikings in 841 and later turned into a quarry after the Revolution, its Romanesque remains bear witness to Norman monastic power. About 20 km from Rouen, 20 minutes by road.

Rouen Cathedral — Immortalized by Monet in 30 paintings, this Gothic cathedral built from the twelfth to sixteenth centuries boasts the highest spire in France, reaching 151 meters. Its lace-like stone façade, the Butter Tower funded by Lenten dispensations, and the tomb of Richard the Lionheart make it a Norman heritage jewel.

activities.text: Seine Meanders — Take the free ferry route crossing the river between Jumièges and Duclair. These landscapes of meandering waters bordered by orchards, limestone cliffs, and Norman villages inspired Impressionist painters in the nineteenth century.

Fruit Route — Between Rouen and Le Havre, this scenic route winds through the apple and cherry orchards of the Pays de Caux region. In spring, blossoming trees offer an enchanting spectacle along the Seine's meanders.

Village of Villequier — This romantic village on the banks of the Seine is home to the house where Victor Hugo lost his daughter Léopoldine, drowned in 1843. The museum devoted to the writer displays manuscripts, letters and mementoes of the tragedy that inspired Les Contemplations. About 30 km from Rouen, 30 minutes by road.

visits.text: Saint-Joseph Church at Le Havre — A 107-meter lantern tower designed by Auguste Perret, this reinforced concrete masterpiece inaugurated in 1957 deploys 12,768 colored glass panes by Marguerite Huré that bathe the interior in mystical light. A symbol of the reconstruction of Le Havre, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

Le Havre Rebuilt City Center — Razed by 80% in 1944, Le Havre was reborn under Auguste Perret's direction. This reinforced concrete urban ensemble, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 2005, deploys an orthogonal grid of 133 hectares—a unique model of modernist urbanism.

MuMa — André Malraux Modern Art Museum — Facing the sea, this glass and metal building houses France's second Impressionist collection after Orsay. Boudin, Monet, Renoir, Dufy: over 200 works testify to the rise of a movement born on the Normandy coast.

activities.text: Perret Show Apartment — Furnished in 1950s style, this reconstructed apartment at 181 Rue de Paris offers insight into the model home imagined by Auguste Perret: modular rooms, herringbone parquet, and functional furniture from the reconstruction era.

Le Havre Port — France's leading port for foreign trade and container traffic, Le Havre extends over 27 km of docks. Cruises allow you to discover historic basins, modern terminals, and the Seine estuary.

Le Havre Beach — Stretching 2 km, this pebble beach bordered by colorful beach huts offers views of cargo ships entering the port and the Alabaster Coast cliffs. Sunsets over the estuary attract walkers and photographers.

visits.text: Aval Cliff and the Needle Stack — This monumental arch, compared by Maupassant to an elephant plunging its trunk into the sea, rises over 80 meters high. At its feet, the Hollow Needle, 55 meters tall, made famous by Maurice Leblanc in Arsène Lupin's adventures, has kept its secrets for centuries.

The Manneporte — The most imposing of Étretat's three arches, this "great gate" in old French unfolds an opening 50 meters high and 40 meters wide. Maupassant claimed a ship could sail through under full canvas. Accessible at low tide from Jambourg Beach.

Amont Cliff and Notre-Dame-de-la-Garde Chapel — On the east side of the beach, this cliff offers a panorama of the village and the Aval arches. The sailors' chapel, rebuilt after 1944, has watched over fishermen since the eleventh century. A memorial recalls the 1927 Atlantic crossing attempt by Nungesser and Coli.

activities.text: Étretat Gardens — Perched on the Amont cliff, these contemporary 8,000 m² gardens designed by Alexandre Grivko blend vegetal sculptures and artistic installations with a plunging view of the Needle and the Manneporte.

Arsène Lupin Estate — Maurice Leblanc's house-museum, acquired in 1919, immerses visitors in the world of the gentleman-thief. Secret passages, puzzles, and period décor recreate the atmosphere of the detective novels.

Étretat Beach — This gray pebble beach, framed by cliffs, was the heart of the fishing village before the nineteenth-century seaside boom. The "caloges," old upturned fishermen's huts, once stored gear and catches.

visits.text: Abbey Church of the Holy Trinity — 127 meters long, this Benedictine abbey founded in 658 houses the Precious Blood, a relic brought back from the Holy Land. Its Gothic lantern tower has overlooked the town since the thirteenth century.

Bénédictine Palace — A neo-Gothic and neo-Renaissance masterpiece built between 1882 and 1900 by architect Camille Albert, this "Versailles of industry" houses the Bénédictine liqueur distillery. The 27 plants in the secret recipe created in 1510 by monk Dom Bernardo Vincelli are revealed in the spice room.

Cap Fagnet — The highest point of the Alabaster Coast at 110 meters, this promontory offers a panorama over Fécamp, the cliffs, and the Channel. Remains of the Atlantic Wall and a sailors' chapel recall the site's turbulent history.

activities.text: Fisheries Museum — Housed in a former cod-drying warehouse, this museum traces the epic of Fécamp's Newfoundland fishermen who sailed to the Grand Banks from the sixteenth to twentieth centuries. Collections of scale models, tools, and testimonies of this maritime adventure.

Fécamp Port — This natural harbor wedged between two cliffs was France's leading cod-fishing port until the 1970s. Today, trawlers and pleasure boats share the quays with construction sites for the offshore wind farm visible on the horizon.

Fécamp Cliffs — The coastal trail allows you to walk along the chalk cliffs framing the town. Head north toward Senneville or south toward Yport: spectacular hikes on the GR21 with views over the Channel and layers of flint.

visits.text: Dieppe Castle-Museum — This fortress of sandstone and flint, built in the fifteenth century on the cliffs, overlooks the port and the beach. Its collections of carved ivories, a Dieppe tradition since the sixteenth century, rank among France's richest with over 2,000 pieces.

Saint-Jacques Church in Dieppe — A flamboyant Gothic masterpiece from the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, this maritime church features carved friezes depicting distant peoples, testifying to the voyages of Dieppe's navigators to Africa and Brazil.

Dieppe Waterfront and Beach — France's oldest seaside resort, visited by the Duchess of Berry as early as 1824, Dieppe stretches 1.8 km of pebbles before a lawn where the international kite festival takes place every two years.

activities.text: Varengeville-sur-Mer — This artists' village overlooking the sea is home to the seaside cemetery where Georges Braque rests, the Church of Saint-Valéry with stained glass by this same Cubist painter, and Shamrock Garden with 2,000 varieties of hydrangeas.

Saturday Market in Dieppe — One of Normandy's largest markets takes place every Saturday on the Grande Rue and the town center squares. Fresh fish from the port, local Pays de Caux produce, and antique dealers have enlivened the town since the Middle Ages.

Le Pollet District — This fishermen's quarter on the port's east bank preserves its colorful houses and working-class atmosphere. The Church of Notre-Dame-de-Bon-Secours has watched over sailors since the seventeenth century.

visits.text: Château d'Eu — King Louis-Philippe's favorite residence, where he received Queen Victoria in 1843 and 1845, this sixteenth-century castle transformed into a Romantic palace houses the Louis-Philippe museum. Its collections trace the history of the July Monarchy and royal visits.

Notre-Dame-et-Saint-Laurent Collegiate Church in Eu — Founded in 1186 by Henry II Plantagenet to atone for the murder of Thomas Becket, this Gothic collegiate church houses the effigies of the Counts of Eu and an eleventh-century Romanesque crypt. The Duke of Guise married Catherine of Clèves here in 1570.

activities.text: Eu Forest — This state-owned forest of 9,300 hectares, one of Normandy's largest, offers hiking trails through a centuries-old beech and oak woodland. The rides laid out for royal hunts converge at star-shaped junctions.

Jesuit College Chapel — Built in the seventeenth century for Jesuits settled by Catherine of Clèves, this Baroque chapel houses the tombs of the Dukes of Guise and a remarkable timber roof shaped like a ship's keel.

visits.text: Cliffs of Le Tréport — These chalk cliffs rise to 106 meters. The Calvaire des Terrasses offers a panorama over the Bay of the Somme, the slate roofs of the harbor, and the Picardy coast as far as Mers-les-Bains.

Le Tréport Funicular — This funicular inaugurated in 1908, renovated in 2006, climbs the 106 meters of elevation in 47 seconds through a tunnel carved into the cliff. Free to ride, it connects the port to the upper town and the Calvary panorama.

Le Tréport Fishing Port — Leading fishing port for scallops in the Eastern Channel, Le Tréport perpetuates centuries of maritime tradition. Trawlers unload sole, mackerel, and shellfish onto lively quays.

activities.text: Mers-les-Bains — This neighboring seaside resort on the Picardy coast lines 300 Belle Époque villas with polychrome façades listed as historical monuments. Their carved wooden balconies, bay windows, and ceramics form a unique architectural ensemble.
Le Tréport Beach — This pebble beach bordered by cliffs has welcomed Parisians since the railway arrived in 1873. Colorful beach huts and seafood restaurants perpetuate the seaside tradition.

Saint-Jacques Church at Le Tréport — This flamboyant Gothic church from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries dominates the port with its massive silhouette. Its pendant vault keys and Renaissance porch testify to the port's prosperity in the Middle Ages.

visits.text: Notre-Dame Church in Caudebec — Called "the finest chapel in the kingdom" by Henry IV, this flamboyant Gothic church from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries displays a lace-like stone façade with 333 statues. Its Renaissance organ and stained glass rank among Normandy's artistic treasures.

Templars House — This thirteenth-century half-timbered medieval house, among Normandy's oldest, houses a local history museum. Its carved beams and low rooms testify to the civil architecture of the Middle Ages.

activities.text: MuséoSeine — This modern museum opened in 2015 traces the history of the river, of navigation, and of the tidal bore that surged over Caudebec until 1963. Scale models of Viking ships, gabare sailing barges, and river barges evoke 2,000 years of river history.

Seine quayside at Caudebec-en-Caux — Along the river, the walkway follows the quays and opens onto a clear view of the meanders and of the cargo ships heading up toward Rouen. A simple moment to grasp the bond between the town and the Seine.

Boucles de la Seine Normande Regional Nature Park — This 89,000-hectare park protects the Seine's meanders, the Brotonne and Roumare forests, the marshes, and the orchards. Hiking, bird-watching, and discovery of Normandy's rural heritage.

seo.h1_title: Seine-Maritime Road Trip: The Cliffs of Étretat, Rouen & Jumièges Abbey
seo.intro_paragraph: From medieval alleys in Rouen to the dizzying arches of Étretat, this 5-day circuit unveils the treasures of Seine-Maritime. Chalk cliffs sculpted by the elements, thousand-year-old abbeys, authentic fishing ports, and Gothic heritage compose a journey between land and sea on the Alabaster Coast.
seo.seo_hook: Chalk arches at Étretat, thousand-year-old abbeys, and Norman ports: Seine-Maritime reveals its finest treasures.
featured_list: Étretat: Hollow Needle and 80m-high arches
Jumièges: finest ruin in France
Rouen: Great Clock from 1389
Fécamp: Neo-Gothic Bénédictine Palace
